Trump’s new attorney general poses a huge threat to abortion rights | Moira Donegan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:00:02 UTC
20:00:02 KST

The abortion pill is a miracle. Mifepristone, then called RU-486, was synthesized by a French lab in the 1980s; in combination with misoprostol, commonly used as ulcer medication, it cuts off the body’s supply of progesterone, halts the development of a pregnancy, and incites contractions, which empty the uterus. The drug allows pregnancies to be terminated with a shocking degree of reliability and ease. Gone are the concoctions of ergot and Spanish Fly dispensed by 19th century midwives, which only sometimes worked to induce a miscarriage; gone are the backroom procedures of the pre-Roe US, when drunk, lascivious, incompetent or cruel providers wielded bent coat hangers in dirty rooms. The abortion pill is safe, effective and cheaper than ever. And since Dobbs, it’s everywhere: even if you live in a state with an abortion ban, you can get the pills shipped to your house in the mail. Since Roe was overturned, there has not been a return to the terror of mass death that marked the pre-Roe era of septic abortion wards, where women routinely found themselves maimed, sickened or killed. There’s exactly one reason why: because illegal abortions were largely unsafe without the pill, and they are extremely safe with it.
So of course, the Trump administration and their allies on the American right are trying to get rid of it. And this month, they gained a powerful new ally when Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer and an anti-abortion zealot, was confirmed as attorney general.
The vote, in which Blanche was confirmed by a margin of one along party lines, was conducted in the wee hours of the morning on 8 August. Maybe that’s because the Republicans who confirmed him didn’t want anyone to see what they were doing. Blanche has, after all, been shockingly subservient to Donald Trump, and seems poised to complete the president’s long-brewing transformation of the country’s chief law enforcement agency into a vehicle for score settling, personal vendettas, distributing favors to the administration’s friends and suppressing dissent from its political enemies. But perhaps most incendiary is what Blanche has said, publicly and privately, about how he intends to use the justice department and its vast array of oversight powers, legal prerogatives, and investigatory purview to curtail abortion access nationwide – and to shut down the life-saving distribution of mifepristone, in particular.
In a call facilitated by the White House faith office just days before he was confirmed, Blanche reportedly told Christian conservative leaders that as attorney general, he would move more aggressively than his predecessor Pam Bondi to outlaw the mailing of mifepristone across state lines, and target the Democratic-controlled states that have protected abortion most effectively. Blanche, who was then the acting AG, told the religious group Intercessors for America that the justice department was working “so that the Dobbs decision becomes permanent in every single state.” “We don’t have complete victory yet,” Blanche said, “but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and, and, and it will be permanent.”
Exactly how Blanche intends to secure his victory over women’s freedom is unclear. But as AG, he has several paths at his disposal. His comments on the call prompted widespread speculation that Blanche could call for enforcement of the Comstock Act, a long-dormant law from 1873 that has been unenforced for years and has been partially repealed in the past. Anti-choice advocates say it could be used to legally ban the mailing of abortion pills, thus cutting off access for many women who live in states with bans. In 2022, the Biden justice department declared that medical providers could not be prosecuted under the Comstock Act for mailing abortion pills; as the attorney general, Blanche would have the power to reverse that decision. The Comstock Act’s application would be particularly significant, as it could be used to halt virtually all commercial traffic in abortion pills – not only mifepristone, but also misoprostol, the second drug, which has sometimes been used to induce abortion on its own. Such a move would reverse the miracle of the pills, pushing many desperate women towards methods that are less effective and can carry grave dangers.
Another path that Blanche could take to restrict abortion access would be to sue the states that seek to protect it. On the call, Blanche explained his reasoning: “If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that. They can’t do things like they’re doing with mailing in mail-order drugs.”
Here, Blanche appeared to be referencing shield laws, legislation passed in a number of Democratic-controlled states that prohibits state authorities from participating in other states’ abortion-related investigations and prosecutions. The laws mean that doctors operating out of states like New York or Washington can prescribe and ship abortion drugs to people living in places such as Texas or Arkansas, safe in the knowledge that their own state police will not come knocking at their door to serve another state’s warrant or extradition order. Blanche’s comments suggest that his Department of Justice might sue to have the shield laws declared illegal, thus significantly curtailing liberal states’ rights to choose their own law enforcement priorities and granting conservative states the power to enforce their own laws even beyond their borders.
Blanche also appeared to indicate that he would seek to restrict abortion access using other agencies’ powers. On his call with leaders of the Christian right, he said his department was “working hand in hand” with health agencies to make Dobbs permanent. The FDA, which expanded access to mifepristone in 2021 under the Biden administration and made the change permanent in 2023, has been under intense pressure from anti-choice allies in the Maga coalition to revise that guidance, making the drug ineligible for telehealth prescriptions and requiring patients to retrieve it from providers in person, a regulatory move that would also serve to cut off access in Republican controlled states. But the anti-abortion movement is pushing the FDA even further: it has succeeded in getting the agency to initiate a “review” of mifepristone’s safety (though the safety of the drug has been proven by nearly four decades of use worldwide and hundreds of studies), which is widely seen as a pathway for the FDA to create a pretext to remove mifepristone from the market. That’s not fast enough for some on the misogynist right: Louisiana has sued the FDA, asking it to forbid mifepristone from being prescribed via telehealth, in a case that is set to be heard by the ultraconservative fifth circuit next month. So far, the justice department has supported the drug’s online availability in court. Under Blanche, it could reverse that stance.
Trump has been gunshy about pursuing the agenda of his antiabortion allies since returning to office. He appears to have been spooked by the political reaction to Dobbs, which was credited for the Democrats’ better-than-expected showing in the 2022 midterms, as well as with a slew of pro-choice victories in special elections in the years that immediately followed the decision. The anti-choice movement has even been angry with Trump for the slow pace of his anti-abortion agenda since his return to power in 2025. Which is not to say that the Trump administration has given the movement nothing: enforcement of the Face Act, a federal law meant to stop anti-choice protestors from physically blocking clinic entrances, has been all but abandoned since Trump returned to the White House; some who were prosecuted under the law have even been pardoned and remunerated by Trump, at taxpayer expense. But until now, Trump has faced a looming threat that seems to have slowed the pace of his anti-abortion policymaking: the 2026 midterms. Soon, that obstacle will be removed. The appointment of Todd Blanche is a dark signal for women’s rights: more abortion restrictions can be expected in 2027.
- 
  Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

Mysteries of the commonplace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Static electricity is all around us. Who among us has not experienced a painful zap when touching a doorknob after crossing a carpeted room? And what child has not experienced the thrill, or mortification, of looking like a porcupine after having their head rubbed with a balloon?
Given its ubiquity, you would think that we know all there is to know about static electricity, especially since it can be a hazard for tasks as varied as assembling circuit boards, refueling airplanes or keeping the wheels on a Mars rover turning. But what actually causes electric charge to leap from one object to another remains elusive. Centuries of efforts by scientists have failed to solve its mysteries — but researchers are not admitting defeat.
In June, Science News’ senior physics writer Emily Conover ventured to a meeting of the Electrostatics Society of America, a hotbed of physicists, chemists and engineers who are fascinated by the complexities of triboelectricity. From Conover’s reporting, I learned what makes it so hard to identify the workings of static electricity: the vast number of factors that can affect it. This growing realization also makes earlier research look less than reliable. Her reporting reveals the challenges and researchers’ dogged efforts to surmount them.
For decades, Science News has invested in sending our staff writers to scientific conferences. Being there makes it possible for them to learn about early-stage research and potentially major advances that haven’t gone public, and to make connections with scientists that will pay off for years to come.
In this issue, we also explore efforts to understand a common yet elusive virus. Almost all people are infected with the Epstein-Barr virus. While many go through life unaffected, the virus can cause serious illnesses, including mononucleosis, certain cancers and multiple sclerosis. Researchers are developing vaccines that could prevent people from contracting the virus in the first place — or stop it from reactivating in people already infected. But taming MS, one of the more debilitating outcomes of infection, remains a challenge. Freelance journalist Michael Marshall reports on new research that reveals just how wily the virus is at evading the human immune system — revelations that could someday help us live with this unwelcome guest while also avoiding its worst behavior.

Set Up a Separate Work Profile on Your Android Phone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Our phones have become do-it-all gadgets. They enable us to keep in touch with one another, track how many steps we're taking each day, snap photos of everything, and access the collective knowledge of humanity. All that universal functionality extends across both our work and personal lives.
The gadget that pings you on Slack when your colleague has a question is the same one that alerts you when your friend has just outscored you at Wordle. That blurring of boundaries can be a problem.
There is actually a solution to this, at least if you're using an Android phone. Android supports the use of multiple profiles (based on Google accounts), so you can switch between two different ones as needed. The most obvious use case for this is to split up your work and personal usage.
It's essentially like having two phones on the same physical device: The profile that's active dictates the apps you can use, the notifications you see, the browsing history you can dig into, and the files you've got access to, all dictated by the Google account.
Note that while this feature has been around in Android for a long time and is available on many handsets (including Pixel phones), not every Android manufacturer has implemented it. It's not available on Galaxy phones, for example, though Samsung does offer something similar with the Secure Folder.
Get Started
To begin with, you're going to need two Google accounts, but many of us already have a Google account managed by work anyway. If not, you can set up a new Google account, free of charge, to use as the basis of the work profile on your phone: Head to the Google account portal on the web, then click Create an account.
The details you'll need to provide include a first name, your birthday, and a Gmail address you'd like to register to use with the account—this is what you'll use to sign in to this account on your phone and on the web. You get some suggestions for an available address based on your name, but you can also come up with something custom as long as no one else has taken it first.
Once you've got a second account you can use, open Settings, then choose System > Users. Tap Add user, then Next, and you're able to give a name to the second user account. With that done, select it from the Users screen, choose the Switch to... option, and you'll be taken through the process of signing in to your secondary Google account.
The setup process that follows is very similar to the one for setting up your phone in the first place. You can set a PIN code, a fingerprint scan, or a face scan (depending on the options your phone offers) to stop other people from accessing your account, and you will be asked to work through the various Android terms-and-conditions screens.
Using Your Second Profile
After you've set up a second profile, you'll be taken straight to it. It will make your phone look like a brand-new device, with the default home screen layout and wallpaper in place. Any configuration changes you've made to Android on your main account will have to be done on this secondary one too.
There are a couple of ways to switch between profiles. You can head to Settings > System > Users and pick an account from the list, or you can do a two-finger swipe down from the top of the screen to open Quick Settings and tap the user account icon underneath the widgets (it's just to the left of the settings cog icon).
You'll need to configure all of your apps again on this secondary account—which is the point of the extra profile, after all. Open up Google Photos, for example, and you'll be prompted to go through the process of choosing your backup options again. You'll also need to install the apps you need on this secondary account, which can be a different set from those on your other profile.
Some parts of the Android experience are shared between profiles, including Wi-Fi network information. However, you won't be able to see saved files or apps in your second profile from your original one (or vice versa). You might want to install a third-party cloud storage app if you need to share files between accounts regularly.
On the Settings > System > Users screen for your primary account, you'll see an Allow user switch option: You can turn this off if you want to temporarily disable user switching (it removes the icon on Quick Settings, for example), but it won't remove the second account from your phone. To do that, select it on the Users screen and pick Delete user.

Ukrainians rally in 11 cities worldwide on 22-24 August to demand Europe use Russia’s frozen billions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:58:54 UTC
19:58:54 KST

Ukrainians and their supporters are holding rallies across dozens of countries from 22 to 24 August, marking 35 years of Ukrainian independence with four demands—including that Europe use frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine.
Among the rallies listed by ICUV are:
- Saturday, 22 August: Seoul—Seoul Plaza, 17:00.
- Sunday, 23 August: Linköping—Stora torget, 16:30; Basel—Wettsteinbrücke, 15:00.
- Monday, 24 August: Sydney; Lyon—Place Bellecour, 18:00; Nantes; Leipzig—Augustusplatz, 17:30; Thessaloniki—“Epoxon” Theater, 18:00; Vilnius—Cathedral Square, 18:00; Rzeszów; Alicante.
ICUV and the Communities Army of Ukraine are supporting local Ukrainian communities in organizing the rallies. ICUV has published rally details and printable materials online.
The demand has a number behind it
About €210 billion in Russian central bank assets remain immobilized in the EU, most of them held in Belgium. When the European Council met in December 2025 to finance Ukraine through 2026 and 2027, one option was a €140 billion reparations loan based on those assets.
Belgium opposed the proposal. The EU instead approved a €90 billion support loan financed through market borrowing and backed by its budget, leaving the Russian principal immobilized.
That choice leaves European taxpayers covering the loan’s debt-servicing costs and bearing its financial risk while Russia’s assets remain untouched.
If Russia launched this war, why are European citizens paying for it?
The argument has moved before
When Ukrainian communities rally, the answer from some politicians is familiar: legally impossible, governments will never agree.
The #MakeRussiaPay campaign began nearly three years ago as a grassroots initiative and grew into a multi-level advocacy effort on one principle — Russia must pay for the war, not European taxpayers.
At a rally in Brussels co-organized by ICUV, activists unrolled a meter-long receipt itemizing Russian crimes in Ukraine against the frozen Russian central bank assets held worldwide.
In 2024, G7 leaders agreed to provide about $50 billion in loans to Ukraine, to be repaid with revenues generated by immobilized Russian sovereign assets.
In December 2025, Ukrainian communities rallied in 13 European cities on the eve of the European Council summit, and the reparations loan — dismissed as unrealistic a year earlier — was on the agenda inside the room.
It did not pass. Ukrainian advocacy did not secure direct access to the frozen assets, and Belgium’s objection held. What changed is that the question is no longer whether Russia’s money can be used, but when, and under what legal structure.
What the rallies are asking for
ICUV and the Communities Army are campaigning on four demands this year:
- Make sanctions bite. Twenty-one packages have been adopted; Russia works around them through third countries, shadow fleets, and re-exports. The problem is enforcement, not new declarations.
- Make Russia pay. Direct transfer of frozen Russian assets into a dedicated reconstruction and defense fund.
- Sky shield. Ukraine intercepts drones effectively; Russia has shifted to mass ballistic strikes. A unified air-defense system with partners, countermeasures against guided bombs, and joint production of anti-ballistic systems.
- Justice and accountability. In May 2026, 36 countries and the EU adopted an agreement establishing the Management Committee of the Special Tribunal on the Crime of Aggression. Its entry into force remains pending while some participating states complete internal procedures.
Europe’s governments now face a straightforward choice: keep asking their own taxpayers to carry the cost of a war Moscow started, or use the money of the state that started it. This weekend, Ukrainians abroad will say which one they expect.

George Russell cruises to sprint race win at F1’s Dutch Grand Prix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

George Russell cruises to sprint race win at F1’s Dutch Grand Prix
ZANDVOORT, Netherlands (AP) — George Russell started the second half of the Formula 1 season in style as he eased to a sprint race victory on Saturday ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix.
Russell started from pole position, quickly built a gap to Lando Norris in second and managed the pace from there, taking his first win since the Austrian Grand Prix in June.
“Obviously a great start to the weekend,” he said.
Charles Leclerc snatched second off Norris with a daring pass into the inside of the first corner with six laps to go, but couldn’t get close enough to try passing Russell.
Norris held off a late charge from Russell’s Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli to stay third as Antonelli pulled out of a potential overtaking move on the final lap.
“We just don’t have the pace in general, especially in the slow-speed corners,” Norris said.
Fourth-place Antonelli, starting fifth after car damage in qualifying, still managed to extend his standings lead by three more points to 53 because his closest challenger Lewis Hamilton could only manage seventh for Ferrari.
F1 still hasn’t had a wet race this year but came tantalizingly close as rain fell as the drivers were heading back to the pits, seconds after the sprint finished.
“If there was one more lap it would have been a very, potentially, different end to the race so I’m glad the rain came when it did,” Russell said.
While it stayed dry, overtaking was difficult, even in a year where the cars’ electrical power has made back-and-forth passes common. The overtakes by Leclerc and Antonelli were the only changes of position anywhere in the top 11 finishers.
That should make grid position even more important than usual when qualifying takes place later Saturday for Sunday’s Dutch Grand Prix.

Russia Deploys 8,500 North Korean Troops to Kursk, Including 400 Drone Operators
Russia has deployed approximately 8,500 North Korean troops to its Kursk region, including hundreds of trained drone operators who could be used in reconnaissance and attacks against Ukraine, CNN reported on August 21.
The deployment includes around 1,000 engineers and sappers as well as 400 unmanned aerial vehicle operators, Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) told CNN.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Skibitskyi, the North Korean drone operators are likely to be involved in both reconnaissance missions and strikes against Ukraine.
Ukrainian intelligence assesses that the North Korean troops are not expected to fight directly on Ukrainian territory. Instead, their primary role is to reinforce Russian rear positions, allowing Moscow to redeploy its own forces for assault operations.
Around 90 North Korean military personnel are also currently stationed in Voronezh, where they are assisting Russian forces with missile launches, according to Skibitskyi.
In total, approximately 25,000 North Korean troops have already rotated through the Russian military, he said.
The deployment is part of deepening military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang. Skibitskyi said North Korea had requested a Russian S-400 air defense system in exchange for providing personnel and had already received a Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery system.
The latest assessment follows Pyongyang’s denial of reports that it could send tens of thousands more troops to Russia. On August 19, North Korea dismissed claims that it could deploy as many as 50,000 additional soldiers to support Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, calling the reports baseless.
Kim Yo Jong, a senior North Korean official and sister of leader Kim Jong Un, rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s assessment that Pyongyang could deploy another 30,000 to 50,000 troops to Russia, claiming that the reports had been fabricated by the Ukrainian president.

UNITED24 Turns 4 With Nearly $4 Billion Raised for Ukraine—and a New Mission Ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

UNITED24 Turns 4 With Nearly $4 Billion Raised for Ukraine—and a New Mission Ahead
Four years after its launch, UNITED24 has grown from a wartime fundraising platform into a global support network spanning more than 140 countries and nearly $4 billion raised for Ukraine—now expanding again with new programs and partnerships.
Ukraine’s official fundraising platform UNITED24 marked its fourth anniversary with UNITED24 MODE, its third major summit in Kyiv, bringing together government officials, servicemen, medics, athletes, creators, partners, and ambassadors while unveiling new initiatives for the next stage of its work.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The August 21 event was opened by UNITED24 initiator, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who highlighted the platform’s achievements and thanked people around the world who have supported Ukraine since its launch in 2022. Eight donors were awarded Ukraine’s Order of Merit for their contributions.
“I want to thank everyone who chose Ukraine’s side in this war. I thank all of you that UNITED24, our Ukrainian government fundraising platform, has been operating for the 5th year. A tool that helps Ukraine build thousands of strong and heartfelt connections with the whole world,” he said.
“Over the entire duration of UNITED24's activity, from the founding of the platform in 2022 until today, almost $4 billion have been raised for the needs of Ukraine via this fundraising alone. Every donation, every manifestation of support for Ukraine from different parts of the world creates an extremely strong emotional connection with Ukraine—faith in Ukraine, as well as in values that inspire our people to defend in war and achieve results,” Zelenskyy added.
Over four years, UNITED24 donors, partners, ambassadors, and governments of friendly countries have raised $3.9 billion for Ukraine through five program areas.
Those funds have helped purchase hundreds of drones and ground robotic systems, ambulances and armored medical evacuation vehicles, equip hospitals with modern medical technology, rebuild dozens of schools and bridges, and provide assistance to thousands of people.
The summit also brought two major announcements.
UNITED24 and Ukrainian game developer GSC Game World launched their second joint fundraiser, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Cost of Hope, which will support humanitarian demining in the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone.
UNITED24 also unveiled its sixth program, Sports Development, created together with Ukraine’s Ministry of Youth and Sports.
The summit program covered Ukraine’s international visibility, defense technology, humanitarian demining, healthcare, public advocacy, opportunities for younger generations, sports development, and Ukraine’s Antarctic program.
Among those attending were, Serhii Kyslytsia, Andrii Sybiha, Matvii Bidnyi, Mstyslav Chernov, Daria Bilodid, and Mykhailo Kokhan.
UNITED24 ambassadors Katheryn Winnick, Liev Schreiber, José Andrés, and Oleksandr Zinchenko participated directly in panels connected to their areas of work.
Mark Hamill, Timothy Snyder, Scott Kelly, Misha Collins, and Ivanna Sakhno joined the summit remotely.
The event was sponsored by longtime UNITED24 partner Uber, which has supported Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale war of aggression and has already helped fund 62 ambulances for Ukrainian medics, as well as Ukrainian defense technology company Fire Point, which partnered with UNITED24 for today’s summit.
During the summit, another UNITED24 partner, Help Ukraine Now, contributed an additional $200,000 for new resuscitation vehicles.
The anniversary underscored how far UNITED24 has expanded since Zelenskyy launched the platform in May 2022. What began as a centralized way for people abroad to donate directly to Ukraine has grown into a global fundraising network spanning defense, healthcare, reconstruction, education, humanitarian needs, and now sports.
More than $3.9 billion has been raised from donors in over 140 countries since the platform was created.
UNITED24’s ambassador network includes Barbra Streisand, Liev Schreiber, Mark Hamill, Mark Strong, Katheryn Winnick, Ivanna Sakhno, Alyssa Milano, Hilary Swank, Misha Collins, Imagine Dragons, Demna, Michel Hazanavicius, Scott Kelly, Bear Grylls, Timothy Snyder, Richard Branson, Brad Paisley, Francis Fukuyama, José Andrés, Nobel laureates Paul Nurse, Edward Moser, and May-Britt Moser, as well as Ukrainian athletes Andriy Shevchenko, Elina Svitolina, Oleksandr Usyk, and Oleksandr Zinchenko.
Four years after its launch, UNITED24 has evolved beyond a fundraising tool into one of Ukraine’s largest international networks connecting individual donors, companies, governments, and public figures directly with projects supporting the country.

US orders major Colorado River water cuts for California, Nevada, Arizona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:51:42 UTC
19:51:42 KST

Merve Berker
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
US federal officials announced Friday that California, Nevada and Arizona will face significant reductions in Colorado River water allocations over the next two years as authorities respond to a prolonged drought affecting the basin, CBS News reported.
Under the Bureau of Reclamation's plan, the three states will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet annually, with the possibility of deeper cuts depending on future conditions.
Arizona will bear the largest reductions, while Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico will not face cuts for now. Mexico will also reduce its water intake by 250,000 acre-feet under a US-Mexico treaty.
"We've been in this 26-year prolonged drought period," Interior Department Assistant Secretary for Water and Science Andrea Travnicek said.
"We continue to see a prolonged drought in our future. So continuing to work together as a whole within the basin is going to be extremely important," she added.
The Colorado River supplies water to an estimated 35 million to 40 million people, according to the Bureau of Reclamation.
Federal officials said the current rules governing the river expire in October, while the seven basin states have yet to reach a long-term agreement on sharing its water.
Officials said the basin experienced its lowest snowpack on record last winter, increasing pressure on agriculture, industry, wildlife, hydropower production and communities dependent on the river.
Arizona Department of Water Resources Director Tom Buschatzke said the reductions "will provide substantial stability" for 2027 and 2028 while negotiations continue on a longer-term framework.
California's chief Colorado River negotiator, JB Hamby, described the agreement as "some badly needed near-term certainty at a moment of extraordinary risk," but stressed it is "a bridge, not a permanent solution."

david gianotten of OMA on why local context matters in shaping future cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:50:00 UTC
19:50:00 KST

rethinking the city through everyday life
The idea of the city is increasingly being measured not only by what it can produce, but by how it allows people to live. Across Amsterdam, Rome, Taipei, and other cities where OMA works, David Gianotten sees this shift as a changing way of working with the city. For the OMA managing partner and architect, questions of housing, mobility, public space, density, and community cannot be separated from the particular histories and conditions of each place.
That position places him somewhat at odds with the appeal of universal urban formulas. The fifteen-minute city, which has become one of the most influential planning ideas of recent years, proposes a simple ambition: organize neighborhoods so that everyday needs can be reached within a short walk or cycle, reducing dependence on cars while bringing living, working, leisure, and services closer together. But Gianotten is wary of treating the concept as a blueprint. ‘The core idea of the 15-minute city is that urban life is organized around neighborhoods where most daily needs can be reached within a short walk or cycle,’ he tells designboom in our exclusive interview. ‘While I see the 15-minute city as a valuable framework, I would be cautious about treating it as a universal planning model.’
For Gianotten, the important question is not whether every city should become a fifteen-minute city but what conditions allow a city to become more accessible in the first place. That means infrastructure, public transport, cycling, micromobility, housing, and local amenities but also the economic consequences that follow when these improvements arrive. ‘New transport connections and local amenities can reshape land values, with important implications for housing affordability, development and access,’ the architect notes.
This is where the apparently straightforward promise of the fifteen-minute city becomes more complicated. A neighborhood that offers excellent public transport, walkable streets, parks, schools, shops, and cultural facilities can become more desirable precisely because of those qualities. Without mechanisms that protect affordability and diversity, the more accessible city can also become a more expensive one. Rather than rejecting the model, Gianotten therefore reframes it as‘a guiding ambition to create places where daily life is more accessible, sustainable and connected.’
VMDA – Nutcrackers | image courtesy of Plomp
the city is not designed by following a universal formula
David Gianotten’s skepticism toward universal models comes from a practice that operates across very different urban contexts. Gianotten points to OMA’s research into the shopping mall for an exhibition at Powerhouse Parramatta, where the studio examines the relationship between the mall, the suburb, and the ideal city. Victor Gruen, often described as the father of the shopping mall, initially imagined the typology as a civic center for car-oriented suburbs. Yet the model eventually became associated with suburban expansion and the decline of traditional downtowns. Its trajectory also changed according to geography. ‘In parts of Asia where cities developed around density rather than suburban expansion, malls often became integrated with public transport networks,’ Gianotten explains. In Hong Kong, where he lived for seven years, shopping, leisure, work, and mobility are often concentrated around a single transit node.
The comparison reveals why importing a planning model from one city to another can be misleading. Urban life is shaped by accumulated infrastructure, cultural habits, land values, political systems, and existing buildings. A strategy that responds to one condition may have a very different consequence somewhere else. OMA’s Roma Continua approaches the problem from this perspective, considering Rome’s future over the next 25 years as a palimpsest. ‘The challenge was to identify what already exists and add new structures and systems that can support future forms of urban life,’ Gianotten explains. The approach suggests a different understanding of urban transformation, based on accumulation. The future city does not necessarily have to erase the structures, habits, and relationships that already give a place its identity.
Roma Continua Mobility | image © IT’S, OMA, OKRA, NET Engineering, and LGSMA
from masterplan to lived neighborhood
This becomes particularly important when architecture moves beyond individual buildings and begins to shape entire districts. Gianotten argues that architects and planners can influence the direction of urban change but cannot produce that change independently. ‘We understand urban planning and architecture not merely as physical artefacts, but as a discipline deeply intertwined with social, economic and political structures,’ he tells us. For him, the architect’s role therefore extends beyond designing a physical environment. OMA’s urban projects operate through conversations between governments, developers, institutions, investors, local communities, and designers. A masterplan can establish a framework, but its success depends on the relationships and decisions that unfold around it. ‘Urban transformation rarely happens through a single grand gesture,’ David Gianotten adds. ‘It often emerges through a combination of projects operating across different timescales, from small-scale urban acupuncture interventions to major infrastructure investments.’
That idea also changes the definition of architectural agency. Gianotten sees architecture as a way of initiating processes, building coalitions, and making alternative futures easier to imagine. ‘I would say the real influence of architecture lies in bringing people together and initiating processes of change. Its limits begin when it assumes it can act alone,’ the architect highlights.
The question of who participates in that process becomes especially important when regeneration involves an existing neighborhood. In Taipei, OMA is working on the redevelopment of 1960s housing in a project commissioned directly by residents. The existing neighborhood is relatively low-density, with interconnected buildings and abundant greenery, characteristics the project takes as evidence of what residents value. ‘Through extensive conversations with residents, we learned that these qualities are precisely what they value and want to preserve,’ Gianotten reflects. The proposal reinterprets the spatial and social qualities of the existing neighborhood while accommodating future needs, marking a small but significant shift in the logic of regeneration by asking what should remain instead of what should be built.
Roma Continua principles | image © IT’S, OMA, OKRA, NET Engineering, and LGSMA
density is also a question of daily life
Housing brings the discussion back to one of the central contradictions of contemporary urbanism. Cities need more homes, but increasing residential density can easily become an exercise in maximizing numbers. In Amsterdam, where land is limited and housing demand remains high, Gianotten argues that density needs to be considered alongside the quality of everyday life. ‘As apartments become smaller and density increases, we must consider the quality of everyday life and ensure that housing does not become socially segregated,’ he shares.
OMA’s Bajes Kwartier is one example of this approach. The former Bijlmerbajes prison is transformed into a neighborhood combining around 1,350 homes with workplaces, leisure programs, gardens, and public spaces. Thirty percent of the housing is social housing, while communal spaces and public routes are integrated throughout the development. According to Gianotten, 98 percent of the materials from the demolished prison, including concrete, steel bars, and cell doors, are reused or recycled. The development also incorporates underground heat and cold storage and photovoltaic installations. In The Martin, one of the recently completed buildings within Bajes Kwartier, interlocking volumes create a more porous relationship between apartments and the surrounding neighborhood. Generous balconies and visual connections encourage residents to engage with both neighbors and public space.
The ambition is therefore not simply to put more people into a smaller area. It is to create the social and environmental infrastructure that allows density to support rather than diminish everyday life.
Roma Continua | image © IT’S, OMA, OKRA, NET Engineering, and LGSMA
designing for change rather than predicting it
If there is a common thread running through Gianotten’s thinking, it is an emphasis on adaptability. Cities cannot be designed once and then left to operate unchanged. Social habits shift, technologies develop, climates change, and economic conditions move with them. For Gianotten, the response is not to attempt increasingly precise predictions about what the city will look like decades from now. Instead, architects should establish frameworks capable of accommodating uncertainty. ‘I think adaptability comes less from trying to predict the future than from creating frameworks that can accommodate change over time,’ he says. ‘This requires collaboration across different stakeholders and disciplines. The challenges we face are interconnected, and it is rarely productive to address them in isolation. I see urban development as a continuous dialogue rather than a series of reactions to individual changes.’
Working across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and elsewhere has not led him to a single conclusion about what the ideal city should look like but rather has reinforced the importance of distinguishing between universal needs and local responses. ‘The fundamental needs and aspirations of people do not change very much,’ he observes. ‘Safety, access to resources, a sense of community, and a high quality of life are desirable. What varies is how those needs are expressed and how cities respond to them.’ That distinction may be the most useful way to understand the idea of the hyper-local metropolis. Local does not necessarily mean isolated, and global does not necessarily mean standardized. A city can share ambitions around accessibility, sustainability, and quality of life while arriving at very different spatial solutions. The more urgent question, then, may not be whether the fifteen-minute city is the future but who gets to live in it. Gianotten’s answer is ultimately less about a particular distance, density, or urban diagram than about agency. The city has to remain open to the people who inhabit it, rather than being shaped exclusively by the institutions that develop it. ‘As architects and planners, we should also reconsider the idea that we are the sole problem-solvers,’ he suggests. ‘Our role is often to facilitate dialogue, and create meaningful ways for communities to participate in shaping their environments.’
For a planning model built around proximity, that may be the harder proximity to achieve: not simply bringing homes, work, leisure, and services closer together, but bringing the people who shape the city into closer contact with the decisions that determine who can afford to remain there.

Myanmar air strike kills 14 praying at monastery, rebel witnesses say
Public buildings, most often monasteries and schools, are frequently the sites of reported air strikes according to a UN report from last week
A Myanmar military air strike on a monastery where civilians were gathered for a meditation retreat marking Buddhist Lent killed 14 people, two rebel fighters who witnessed the aftermath said.
Myanmar has been consumed by civil war since the military staged a 2021 coup ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and detaining the Nobel Peace Prize laureate.
Over the past five years, more than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed across all sides as the military battles an array of pro-democracy and ethnic minority rebels.
The Friday air strike hit a monastery hall around 9.00am in Myaung township of central Sagaing region, killing 11 men and three women, according to Nway Oo Myaung, a pro-democracy rebel who helped clear bodies.
“Older people had entered the meditation centre for three months” to mark the period of Buddhist Lent, which roughly coincides with Myanmar’s rainy season, he said on Friday.
“Those who were killed, their ages were between 50 and 70,” Nway Oo Myaung added. “It wasn’t a mistaken target, they intentionally attacked a monastery.”

Up to 30% of internet providers in Russia may shut down due to new requirements - CPD
Kyiv • UNN
The new rules provide for three types of licenses, high capital requirements, and connection to intelligence agencies’ surveillance systems. The market may become concentrated among monopolists.
Russia’s Ministry of Digital Development is preparing a reform of the internet services market that could force up to 30% of providers in the country to cease operations. The new rules provide for only three types of licenses, significant requirements regarding companies’ own funds, and mandatory connection to the security services’ surveillance system. The Center for Countering Disinformation reports this, according to UNN.
Details
Russia is taking another step toward centralizing the internet, clearing independent operators from the market. Russia’s Ministry of Digital Development is preparing a reform that could force up to 30% of internet providers in the country to shut down. The authorities want to introduce strict requirements: only three types of licenses are предусмотрены, while companies will be required to have tens of millions of rubles in their own funds and mandatory connection to the security services’ surveillance system. A significant share of regional operators do not meet these criteria
As a result, according to the Center for Countering Disinformation, if a license is revoked or a small provider shuts down, its networks and customer base will be automatically redistributed, while small operators will be required to sign agreements granting major federal players the priority right to buy out their assets.
This “reform” will effectively concentrate the entire market in the hands of several loyal monopolists. Since a centralized internet system is easier to control, Russian security services will be able to censor content much more quickly, block “undesirable” resources, and carry out total surveillance of users
To remind you
Large-scale internet disruptions were recorded in Russia, with the largest number of complaints coming from Moscow and the Moscow region. The incident occurred amid a blackout caused by a bang at a substation.

Vatican to build $148m renewable energy plant, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:43:23 UTC
19:43:23 KST

Vatican to build $148m renewable energy plant, sources say
- The Vatican will build an agrivoltaic plant to power Vatican City and nearby properties within two years.
- The plant uses will use solar panels mounted above crops, reducing evaporation and protecting plants, and will cover nearly half of the Santa Maria di Galeria estate.
- The project, endorsed by Pope Leo XIV and prioritised by Pope Francis, aims for full energy self-sufficiency without financial incentives, with surplus power supplied to Italy.
AI generated
ROME – The Vatican will build a roughly €100 million (S$148 million) renewable energy plant that could power the Holy See within two years via a system combining solar power and agriculture, sources involved in discussions on the project have said.
The agrivoltaic plant is expected to have a capacity of 80 to 90 megawatts, making it one of Italy’s largest such installations, the sources added.
In such plants, solar panels are mounted several metres above the ground so crops can grow beneath them, with the shade helping to reduce evaporation and shielding plants from extreme weather.
A joint Italian-Vatican commission met earlier in August to launch the project at the Vatican-owned Santa Maria di Galeria estate on Rome’s north-western outskirts, after Italy ratified a 2025 bilateral agreement for development of the site in 2026.
Officials disclosed no details of the project’s cost, capacity or timeline after the meeting. The sources involved in the discussions said the plant could take 18 to 24 months to complete, including permitting and administrative procedures.
The Vatican did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Vatican City, headquarters of the global Catholic Church and home to St Peter’s Basilica, is the world’s smallest country, covering 44ha and housing fewer than 900 residents.
The roughly 450ha Santa Maria di Galeria site has hosted Vatican Radio’s transmission facilities since the 1950s.
The plant is designed to supply power to Vatican Radio’s transmission station and help make Vatican City fully energy self-sufficient.
The sources said the power could also be used by Holy See-linked properties, including Rome’s Bambino Gesu hospital.
The Vatican will not benefit from the financial incentives available to Italian households and businesses that install solar power. Any surplus electricity would be made available to Italy.
Tracking solar panels would cover about 200ha, nearly half the Santa Maria di Galeria site, one of the two sources said.
The project was a priority for the late Pope Francis, the first pontiff to accept the scientific consensus on climate change, and has been endorsed by Pope Leo XIV.
The bilateral agreement between Italy and Vatican City has extended to the agrivoltaic project the special status already granted to Vatican Radio facilities, including exemptions from Italian taxes and public charges.
Italy’s ratification law states that the implementation of the agreement must not result in any new or additional burden on public finances.
Contracts for the work will be put out to tender in the coming weeks.
In 2008, under German-born Pope Benedict XVI, German companies SolarWorld and SMA Solar Technology donated the 2,400 photovoltaic panels and equipment installed on top of the Nervi Hall, which hosts papal audiences and concerts. REUTERS

Türkiye's Communications Directorate hosts STRATCOM events in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:43:18 UTC
19:43:18 KST

The STRATCOM Roundtable and STRATCOM Public Forum, organized by Türkiye's Communications Directorate in cooperation with the Embassy of the Republic of Türkiye in Tokyo, were held in Japan's capital, Tokyo on Saturday.
According to a statement by the Communications Directorate, the STRATCOM Roundtable, held under the theme Changing Global Order in the Age of Emerging Technologies, and the STRATCOM Public Forum, titled Managing Economic Security in the Age of Geopolitical Competition, were organized in Tokyo as part of the International Strategic Communication Summit (STRATCOM Summit).
The forum addressed the multidimensional effects of emerging technologies -- particularly artificial intelligence -- on global order, strategic communication and economic security.
At the STRATCOM Roundtable, held under the theme Changing Global Order in the Age of Emerging Technologies, the effects of emerging technologies on global governance, strategic communication, digital sovereignty, information security and international cooperation were evaluated from a policy perspective.
Participants exchanged views on the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI) and emerging technologies on international power balances, technological competition, combating disinformation, the use of new technologies in strategic communication, the transformation of public diplomacy and technological applications in crisis management.
Economic security
As part of the program, the panel titled Managing Economic Security in the Age of Geopolitical Competition, held during the STRATCOM Public Forum, discussed the effects of intensifying geopolitical competition on economic security policies, critical technologies, trusted supply chains, data security and the transformation of the digital economy from different perspectives.
Communications Director Burhanettin Duran also addressed the program in a video message.
Duran said the world is going through a period of profound geopolitical, technological and social transformation, adding that alongside economic power, military capacity and diplomatic influence, the ability to build narratives, shape perceptions, communicate with global audiences and build trust is becoming an increasingly important dimension of national and international power.
Pointing out that digital technologies expand access to information and communication opportunities while also creating new vulnerabilities such as manipulation, polarization and uncertainty, Duran said: "Today, we are facing a situation that can be described as both a crisis of truth and a crisis of communication.”
“These crises operate through perceptions, emotions, fears and expectations,” he said, adding: “They can affect societies before governments have the opportunity to fully understand what is happening.”
“That is why a comprehensive and multidimensional approach is needed. No country, institution or organization can achieve this alone,” Duran stated.
“We need greater international cooperation, the sharing of experience and the development of common principles," he stressed.
Stronger cooperation between Türkiye and Japan
Türkiye's Ambassador to Tokyo Oguzhan Ertugrul and Deputy Communications Director Ferhat Pirincci also delivered speeches during the panel.
Ertugrul drew attention to the uncertainties and multiple crises increasing pressure on the international order.
Emphasizing that global challenges require stronger cooperation based on justice, diplomacy and multilateralism, he pointed to the importance of regional ownership and the reform of global institutions.
Stating that Türkiye and Japan are two countries located at the western and eastern ends of Asia with complementary strategic capacities, Ertugrul said the two countries can play a constructive and proactive role in supporting global peace, stability and prosperity.
He also stressed that the event provided an important platform for raising awareness of the need for stronger cooperation and coordination between Türkiye and Japan in the face of ongoing geopolitical transformations.
Fight against disinformation
Pirincci further said emerging technologies, particularly AI, are transforming not only the economic and technological fields but also a wide range of areas from international relations to public diplomacy and strategic communication.
Emphasizing that information security and a trusted information ecosystem are among the fundamental elements of economic resilience, he noted that disinformation can have direct effects on economic stability, the investment environment and public confidence.
He said strategic communication is of critical importance for protecting accurate and reliable information, combating disinformation and strengthening societal resilience, adding that international cooperation and the development of common policies in this field are becoming increasingly important.
Pirincci also noted that Ankara and Tokyo possess significant and complementary expertise in technology, innovation, strategic communication and crisis management, adding that joint initiatives between the two countries will contribute to regional and global stability.
AK Party Deputy Chair and Head of Information and Communication Technologies Omer Ileri also spoke at the panel.
Ileri pointed out that simultaneous transformations are taking place in the geopolitical and technopolitical spheres.
He said protectionism and an emphasis on domestic production are gaining strength in geopolitical dynamics, while developments such as AI, the growing importance of data and market concentration are reshaping the technology field.
He also underlined the potential of Türkiye and Japan to contribute to the development of more consistent and human-centered approaches to these transformations.
Information manipulation
Akira Igata, project associate professor at the Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology at the University of Tokyo and director of the Economic Security Intelligence Laboratory, focused on the growing relationship between economic security and information manipulation.
Giving examples of disinformation and influence operations targeting companies operating in critical mineral supply chains and data center infrastructure, Igata emphasized the importance of public-private cooperation, information sharing and education in strengthening societal resilience.
Kazuto Suzuki, professor at the Graduate School of Public Policy at the University of Tokyo, discussed the role of critical technologies, rare earth elements and strategic minerals in geo-economic competition.
Noting that interdependencies among major powers, particularly the US and China, continue to shape economic security policies, Suzuki said diversifying critical supply chains and reducing strategic vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly important.
Kunihiko Miyake, director and special adviser at the Canon Institute for Global Studies, stressed that effective strategic communication requires a clear strategy and a strong narrative.
Pointing out that technological tools alone cannot guarantee successful communication, Miyake highlighted the importance of developing messages aligned with strategic objectives and tailored to target audiences.
Participants also exchanged views on protecting a trusted information ecosystem, ensuring the flow of accurate information during periods of economic crisis, the impact of digital platforms on the global economy and models of public-private cooperation.
Türkiye-Japan strategic communication dialogue
The events contributed to strengthening institutional dialogue between Türkiye and Japan in the fields of strategic communication and crisis communication, evaluating common approaches to communication risks and opportunities emerging in the age of AI, and increasing the sharing of international information and experience.
Held annually with international participation, STRATCOM continues to serve as a global consultation platform where current issues in strategic communication are discussed from different perspectives, bringing together public institutions, international organizations, academia, the media and the technology sector.

Sallaum Lines and Sallaum Logistics launch dedicated European automotive logistics company
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:42:04 UTC
19:42:04 KST

Sallaum Lines today announced the launch of Sallaum Logistics Ltd, a dedicated European automotive logistics company that extends Sallaum’s ocean vehicle-transport network onto the road- giving manufacturers and dealers a single accountable partner from port to dealership across Europe.
Backed by Sallaum Lines’ experience, relationships and global network in maritime vehicle transportation, Sallaum Logistics will operate as an independent road logistics company focused on the movement of finished vehicles. The company is built for automotive manufacturers, OEMs, dealership groups, fleet operators, shipping companies and logistics partners that need dependable inland transport with visibility and professional execution.
The launch connects Sallaum’s ocean and inland operations into a single vehicle-transport chain, extending its expertise from sea to road. While Sallaum Lines continues to focus on global Ro-Ro Ocean transportation, Sallaum Logistics will support the next stage of the journey: moving vehicles from ports, compounds and distribution hubs to dealerships and final destinations across Europe.
“For years, customers have trusted Sallaum Lines to move vehicles across oceans with reliability, discipline and care. Sallaum Logistics carries that commitment further inland, giving automotive partners a road logistics company built on the same principles of safety, transparency and customer commitment. This is a natural continuation of the vehicle logistics journey from sea to road.” — Sami Sallaum, Chairman, Sallaum Lines.
A Focused Road Logistics Platform for Europe’s Automotive Industry
Sallaum Logistics has been created around a clear market need: automotive customers require an inland vehicle logistics partner that can deliver the same quality, accountability and communication standards expected in maritime transport.
Rather than competing as another general road carrier, Sallaum Logistics is being built as a focused automotive logistics platform- one that combines fleet-based execution, professional vehicle handling, cross-border capability and digital visibility.
The company’s services will encompass comprehensive Finished Vehicle Logistics solutions, covering vehicle transportation from European factories and inland terminals to ports for global shipment, cross-border transport, fleet distribution services, port-to-dealer and port-to-distribution center deliveries & vice versa. Sallaum Logistics will also offer vehicle processing, pre-delivery inspection and storage at selected sites, building on existing operations at the Port of Antwerp.
Built to Reduce Complexity After the Port
In automotive logistics, the inland handover after port arrival is often where pressure increases. Customers need to coordinate transport capacity, timing, vehicle condition, route planning, delivery visibility and final-mile communication.
Sallaum Logistics is designed to take responsibility for that stage of the journey. Its role is to help customers reduce fragmented coordination, improve delivery visibility and maintain consistent standards as vehicles move across European corridors.
Scalable Fleet, Operational Discipline and Long-Term Growth
Sallaum Logistics will launch with an initial fleet of 50 truck-and-trailer units, with a plan to expand toward 300 owned trucks by 2029. The fleet will use modern multi-car transporter configurations capable of carrying up to 10 vehicles, depending on vehicle type, route and each country’s road regulations.
The company will operate a mixed fleet model combining owned and strategically leased vehicles, allowing it to scale with customer demand while maintaining professional service standards and operational control.
Fleet reliability will be supported by strict European compliance, preventive maintenance, regular inspections, driver safety policies and manufacturer service standards.
Technology Designed for Visibility and Confidence
Sallaum Logistics will use integrated fleet management systems, transport monitoring tools and logistics software to support routing, fleet optimization and operational reporting. GPS tracking, telematics, route optimization and driver monitoring will give customers improved visibility over vehicle movement and delivery coordination.
As the company grows, Sallaum Logistics plans to continue investing in digital customer visibility and reporting platforms, supporting a more transparent and responsive finished vehicle logistics experience.
European Network and Growth Vision
Headquartered in Lithuania, Sallaum Logistics will begin operations across key European automotive markets including Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Spain, France, the Czech Republic and Poland, with further expansion into key port-connected European markets.
The network will be designed around major port-to-dealer and port-to-distribution center corridors across Western and Central Europe, connecting automotive gateways such as Antwerp, Bremerhaven, Rotterdam, Marseille and inland distribution hubs.
Over time, Sallaum Logistics plans to expand across major European automotive trade corridors, supported by operational depots for vehicle handling, staging and regional fleet distribution.
Responsible Growth and Sustainability
Sallaum Logistics is being developed with a responsible growth mindset. The company aims to reduce operational emissions while improving fleet efficiency, route planning and transport reliability.
Its sustainability priorities include Euro-compliant fleet standards, route optimization, fuel efficiency programs and future electrification for suitable shorter routes.
“Sallaum Logistics was created to make inland vehicle movement simpler, more visible and more dependable. We are building a road logistics company with professional drivers, clear communication, real-time visibility and a fleet plan designed for long-term scale. Our ambition is to give customers confidence in every stage of the inland journey.” — Edvinas Rybelis, CEO, Sallaum Logistics

Why trauma changes how our memory engages with our conscious experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:41:30 UTC
19:41:30 KST

When survivors of trauma recount their experiences, they are often questioned because of how they relay their stories. They may have problems remembering what happened, or their memories may be jumbled or even contradictory. People hearing those stories—attorneys, reporters, healthcare workers or friends—may expect a clearer, linear narrative.
Those unaffected by trauma may also be surprised to hear how the person acted in the moment. It’s easy to assume that someone experiencing a traumatic event would have a “fight or flight” response, instinctively fighting off a perpetrator or fleeing the scene—but that might not be the case.
Understanding the science of how trauma affects memory and behavior reveals why these responses can actually be expected and are not contradictory.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In both my academic and clinical work as a psychologist, I have witnessed the impact trauma has on people’s memories and behaviors, especially when an event in their present life triggers something from their past.
Research shows that taking a trauma-informed approach, which prioritizes understanding and curiosity about someone’s experience as opposed to judgment or critical evaluation, increases empathy for survivors’ thoughts, feelings and behaviors.
How trauma affects the brain
According to the World Health Organization, approximately 70 percent of people worldwide report experiencing a traumatic event in their lifetime. The majority of these people do not develop PTSD, a clinical diagnosis of symptoms, such as having nightmares and flashbacks about the event, avoiding places that are reminders of it, and increased arousal that can make concentration and sleep difficult. Many survivors don’t meet criteria for PTSD but struggle with feeling distressed, depressed or anxious.
In traumatic situations, people often respond in unexpected ways, and they may second-guess themselves. This may happen particularly when someone experiences a repeated trauma, which is more likely than not due to how many people experience traumatic events.
Trauma also distorts how memories are stored and retrieved.
Research indicates that people experience traumatic memories differently than memories of other significant events, such as sad or positive experiences. Two of the main brain structures scientists believe are involved in storing traumatic memories are the hippocampus—responsible for memory storage—and the amygdala, which is responsible for processing emotions.
During trauma, the amygdala becomes highly active, processing emotions such as fear, and the hippocampus becomes overwhelmed by stress, leading to problems with memory storage.
Traumatic memories do not follow a neat, linear story. Instead, people may experience the memory as disconnected fragments of sensations, emotions, smells or images. Such memories cause the body to reexperience the past threat as if it is happening in the moment. This may cause a person to feel like running away or fighting back—flight or fight. Or they may freeze.
In other words, people don’t have the distant perspective they often feel with other memories from the past. Rather, they may feel they are reliving the original experience.
Misinterpreting victims’ behaviors
With this understanding, consider someone who experiences a trauma at the hands of a professional during an appointment. They may appear outwardly calm while it happens and then leave the session as they typically would—checking out, providing payment and possibly even scheduling the next appointment. While their response to act normally may seem odd, such behavior makes sense for someone trying to escape a threat.
Fight, flight or freeze responses have become widely known in popular culture. In a freeze response, a person’s mind goes blank and they may be unable to speak, leading to a “deer in the headlights” behavior.
On the other hand, a person may act paradoxically—perhaps by going on about their day as if nothing happened. They may not report the event or may question whether the incident even occurred. This represents another survival response—the lesser-known fawn response. This way of handling stress occurs when someone acts calm, appeases the threatening person and retreats to de-escalate the situation. Instead of literally backing away, in this example, the person metaphorically backs away by completing the session and exiting as expected without further conflict.
Outsiders may misconstrue these behaviors as evidence that a trauma did not actually happen or that a survivor lacks credibility. But that logic reflects common misconceptions about how people “should” remember or respond to trauma.
If this was the person’s first experience with a traumatic situation, afterward they are likely to feel afraid, disoriented or hyperalert. However, if they had previous similar experiences, this scenario may trigger past memories in the moment. This can muddy the experience even further, making it difficult to recall the incident later, especially under stressful circumstances.
When a survivor reports an incident and ultimately testifies against someone who harmed them, memory recall might be uniquely affected. Most people in this situation would be highly stressed, especially if the perpetrator were in the room.
To make matters worse, the feeling that the recalled memory is actually happening in the moment and not in the past may cause a survivor to convey a more fragmented story. They may also have either a more intense or detached emotional experience, depending on their own trauma responses.
Legal and other professionals unaware of the range of natural responses to trauma can easily misinterpret these behaviors as signs of lying or malingering.
In reality, the percentage of people who falsely report sexual assault, for example, is low—between 2 percent and 10 percent.
Providing better support
Research shows that people who better understand nuances of trauma and mental health in turn are more empathetic toward survivors. Some healthcare settings have adopted a trauma-informed approach to prevent retraumatization and build safety. Studies show that even being attentive to word choice can help ensure effective care for patients that avoids victim blaming.
A trauma-informed approach can also improve legal and justice systems so victims are better supported. This includes understanding why accounts aren’t linear and not equating memory inconsistencies with lying.
Research also shows that trauma-informed responses are equally important in everyday relationships. In friendships and close relationships, or in the workplace, patience and empathy convey a sense of respect, safety and trustworthiness. These offer a strong foundation for positive social and working relationships, which can lower a survivor’s distress and support their healing.
When people have a greater understanding of how trauma affects the brain, they gain insight into how survivors think, act and process their memories. What initially looks confusing or inconsistent is actually behavior that flows logically from a traumatized brain.
Having a trauma-informed perspective helps people to be better friends, co-workers and professionals. By extension, responding from this awareness may even help survivors understand their own reactions and experiences, which may ultimately aid their healing and ability to lead fulfilling lives.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Death Toll Mounts After Russian 'Barbaric Double-Tap' Strike On Ukrainian Shopping Mall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:37:30 UTC
19:37:30 KST

A Russian drone attack on a shopping mall in the south-central Ukrainian city of Kryviy Rih on August 21 killed at least 16 people and left more than 130 others injured, including 23 children, some of them in critical condition.
A day later, nine people were still unaccounted for. The fire engulfed over 9,000 square meters and took hours to extinguish.
Two Russian jet-powered drones struck the largest shopping mall in the city early afternoon on August 21. The attack came as many residents were out shopping at the end of the work week.
"There was smoke. Everyone was shouting," Yuliana, a mall employee, told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service.
She said the attack caused parts of the ceiling to collapse in a parking garage where some shoppers and staff had sought shelter during an air-raid alert, and that a car was blocking the entrance, forcing people to climb over metal barriers.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Russia deliberately struck the site twice, and that the second wave of drones came after emergency responders arrived at the scene.
"Such barbaric double-tap strikes are intended to maximize civilian casualties. They prove Russia's status as a terrorist state," he wrote calling for “criminals responsible for such atrocities” to be brought to account.
Air defense failed to detect the drones because they flew at an "exceptionally low altitude," according to Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the city's defense council.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a native of Kryviy Rih, reiterated his call for air defense support -- new supplies of ballistic and other missile interceptors -- from international partners.
"Every day that Ukraine lacks air defense is a sacrifice that could have been avoided," he wrote on August 22.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc's defense and foreign ministers would discuss Ukraine's air defenses during their first meeting after the summer break in September.
The attack "shows the absolute and utter depravity of Moscow's war," Kallas wrote on X. "This is terror by design. Russia wants to make Ukrainian cities unliveable."
She also vowed to unveil "the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war" to further increase pressure on Russia to end the war.
The attack comes after a series of other Russian air strikes on Ukrainian cities this week.
On August 20, Russia launched a large barrage of ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones at Kyiv, killing at least 17 people in and around the capital.
On the night of August 21-22, Russia struck a railway infrastructure facility in the capital, Kyiv. One person died in the attack.
Zelenskyy said the Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Donetsk, Sumy, Kherson, Chernihiv, and Mykolayiv regions also came under attack overnight, with damage reported to residential buildings, energy and railway infrastructure facilities, and civilian enterprises.
Moscow has gained little ground at the front line in Ukraine since the beginning of the year, and has intensified its strikes against the country, often hitting civilian infrastructure and causing civilian casualties.
Ukraine has sought to bolster its air defense capabilities with help from the United States and its European partners but is struggling with a lack of US-made Patriot missiles. Washington has sent mixed signals about a potential agreement to grant Kyiv a license to produce Patriots.
Meanwhile, Kyiv continued targeting oil and military infrastructure inside Russia, with the country now facing its worst fuel crisis in years.
Early on August 22, Ukrainian drones hit an oil refinery in Novokuybyshevsk in Russia's Samara region, 900 kilometers away. One person was killed, the local governor said.
The day before, the Ukrainian military targeted a Russian oil facility in Perm, more than 1,600 kilometers from Russia's border with Ukraine, and a military air base in the Volgograd region.
Kyiv's forces also hit a warehouse of major e-commerce retailer Ozon on August 22, expanding its attacks on the sector after weeks of strikes on facilities belonging to Russian online giant Wildberries.
Ozon confirmed the strike, saying 500 employees were evacuated "within minutes," but added that some had sustained injuries.
"We continue, through our long-range sanctions, to bring the consequences of the war back to where it came from," Zelenskyy said on August 21, referring to the campaign.

'Judges are not gods, won't get every judgment right': Outgoing SC Judge Sanjay Karol in farewell speech
