'Judges are not gods, won't get every judgment right': Outgoing SC Judge Sanjay Karol in farewell speech
Edited by: Kanchan Yadav / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 22, 2026, 16:10 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
NEW DELHI: Retiring Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Karol in his farewell address on Saturday, said judges "are not gods and they will not get every judgment right." He also urged other judges to look beyond the facts of a case and see the person behind every litigant.The Supreme Court bid farewell to Justice Karol on his last working day, with Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and senior members of the Bar, including Solicitor General Tushar Mehta and Supreme Court Bar Association president Pradeep Rai paying tribute to the outgoing judge.“We, as judges, are not gods. We will not get every judgment right. What was always in our hands was simple: to see the person, not just the petitioner. A petition can only tell you the facts of a case, but it cannot tell you what the person has already lost or what he is hoping to seek from the courts. And perhaps that is why I have always said that judging requires a certain level of humility,” Justice Karol said.“The Constitution does not ask us merely to apply the law correctly. It asks us to apply it justly. That is perhaps why the responsibility of judging has always seemed larger to me than simply deciding who is legally correct,” he added.
Justice Karol, who was elevated to the Supreme Court on February 6, 2023, reflected on his nearly four-decade journey in the legal profession. He said the courtroom had never been merely a workplace for him, but a vehicle for something “greater and more important” than himself.“I will not pretend that this journey has been mine alone. This courtroom has not left me; it has supported me,” he said.Karol spent 40 years in courtrooms, initially as an advocate and later, for 19 years, as a judge. He said judges must learn to listen not only to arguments but also to the “eloquent silences” in courtrooms.“In the silence of the Bar, there is a way of listening,” he said, stressing that the judicial process was also about understanding what people were seeking “in the spaces between the words”.Recalling his first visit to Courtroom No. 1 of the Supreme Court in 1996, Justice Karol said the Bench appeared to him to be almost six feet above the ground.“Judging from there has taught me something about this courtroom's symbolism. From below, the height of the bench can appear to signify authority. From the comfort zone, it signifies something quite different, and that is responsibility with dignity and honesty,” he said.Justice Karol said the Supreme Court's true significance lay in the faith of ordinary citizens who approach it believing that someone would listen.“But we must also remember those who never reach those doors because justice is too distant, too expensive, too intimidating,” he said.Reflecting on constitutionalism and justice, Karol said concepts such as law, due process and constitutional legality could be understood through the idea of “dharma”, which he described not as ritual but as duty.“The duty of a judge is to respect justice and see that the person standing before the court, however small, however wretched, is seen and heard,” he said.Addressing the Bar, he said the principles of judging extended beyond courtrooms and judicial robes, with every individual responsible for judging their own choices, conduct and use of power.“There may be no courtrooms, no robes, no technical grounds, but in these small choices, each of us dispenses the measure of justice that we take,” he said.“A judge is a judge before he dons and after he takes off the robes,” he added.Referring to a point made by CJI Surya Kant a day earlier, Justice Karol said India had not only a living Constitution but also had to “live the Constitution”.“The greatness of our Constitution is tested not only in great cases. It is tested in ordinary conduct,” he said. Concluding his farewell address, Justice Karol said he was returning to “the most distinguished constitutional office," that of the ordinary citizen.
Born on August 23, 1961, Karol studied in Shimla and obtained his law degree from Himachal Pradesh University. He became advocate general of Himachal Pradesh in 1998 and served until 2003, and was designated a senior advocate in 1999.He was appointed a judge of the Himachal Pradesh high court in March 2007 and became chief justice of the Tripura high court in November 2018. He was later transferred as chief justice of the Patna high court in November 2019 before being elevated to the Supreme Court in February 2023.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

Syria requests to join anti-chemical weapons partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:34:16 UTC
19:34:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria requests to join anti-chemical weapons partnership
Syria on Friday said it had requested to join the International Partnership Against Impunity for the Use of Chemical Weapons on the anniversary of a 2013 chemical attack on a suburb of the capital Damascus.
In a joint statement with France commemorating the attack during former leader Bashar al-Assad's rule on rebel-held areas, Syria announced its bid to join the partnership of dozens of countries, launched by Paris in January 2018.
France welcomed the step as "a clear demonstration of Syria's commitment to strengthening accountability and justice and combating impunity" following its more than decade-long civil war.
Damascus and Paris also said they "commemorate the victims, extend their deepest sympathies and solidarity to their families, and reaffirm their joint commitment to supporting efforts to uncover the truth, ensure justice, and hold those responsible for these crimes accountable".
In August 2013, the Syrian army under Assad was accused of using chemical weapons to target areas then under rebel control.
According to US intelligence and rights groups, more than 1,400 men, women and children died as a result.
With Syria at the height of its civil war, the Assad government denied responsibility, but agreed to hand over its chemical arsenal in order to avert US strikes.
Assad went on to remain in power for more than a decade, only to be ousted in 2024 by Islamist-led rebels, headed by now President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Survivors of the attacks, including medics, at the time risked their lives by posting dozens of videos online, and spoke to journalists about the horror they had witnessed.
The footage showed dozens of corpses, many of them children, outstretched on the ground.
Other images showed unconscious children, people foaming at the mouth and doctors trying to help them breathe.
The scenes provoked revulsion and condemnation around the globe.
'Painful chapter'
A United Nations report later said there was clear evidence sarin gas had been used.
Syria agreed to join the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) and disclose and hand over its toxic stockpile under Russian and US pressure, averting the threat of strikes by Washington and its allies.
But that was not the last of the chemical attacks: the OPCW went on to blame Assad's forces for others later in the civil war.
Marking 13 years since the attack, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani called it "one of the most painful chapters in Syria's history".
"Tomorrow, the Syrian Arab Republic begins a new phase in dealing with the legacy of these weapons. We have initiated the necessary technical and logistical procedures for their disposal, in cooperation with our international partners," he added, also vowing to pursue those involved in the attack.
Several Syrian officers linked to the attack have been arrested since Assad's fall.
Syria's civil war began in 2011, with a brutal crackdown on dissent that yielded an armed rebellion. More than half a million people ended up being killed, with millions more forced into exile.
The OPCW reinstated Syria last month, five years after taking the unprecedented step of stripping it of its voting rights.

It Is Not Putin’s War. It’s Russia’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:31:00 UTC
19:31:00 KST

In a recent issue of The Economist, one of Russia’s richest men set out why the West should worry less about Ukraine and more about Russia. In an opinion piece and nearly 60 hours of interviews, the sanctioned oligarch Andrey Melnichenko argues that “broken Russia” would be bad for the world.
In his account, the war did not begin because Russia chose to invade; it began when trust between great powers broke down, at which point “politics does not direct events; it is led by them.” Ukraine appears mostly as scenery. That is a sophisticated version of long-established trickery allowing Russia to escape accountability for its crimes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Western media have developed a weird habit. Russia invades Ukraine, but headlines often say “Putin” did. Russian missiles kill civilians, but are then called “Putin’s missiles.” And the pattern continues. This is a factual error, a moral dishonesty, and a strategic mistake.
Putin ordered the invasion. But he is not personally flying fighter-bombers, developing lethal drones, and celebrating murderous missile strikes on TV. Russians do that: Russian officers, Russian engineers, and Russian journalists.
This is Russia’s war. Meekly calling it “Putin’s war” is preposterous and negligent.
Putin does not wage war alone
“Putin’s war” may sound fitting because Russia is a dictatorship. It is inaccurate because, for all the tawdry uniform posturing by Putin, wars are not fought by dictators. Russia’s war is fought by its army, and depends on millions of Russian men and women who keep the war machine running. Moreover, a seemingly victorious initial onslaught drew undeniable public support, with only cracks in the triumphant narratives causing visible discontent (more on that later).
Russian Strikes Damage Infrastructure and Utilities in Odesa Region, Injuring 1
This does not mean that every Russian bears the same guilt as a war criminal in Bucha. Criminal guilt is individual, but political and historical responsibility is broader. Nations can be responsible for wars even when individuals differ in their degree of culpability.
We say Nazi Germany invaded Poland. We do not reduce that war to Hitler. Nor did responsibility end with him. Germany paid reparations, lost territory, was occupied and partitioned, and saw hundreds of thousands investigated and tried. Yet for Russia, Western discourse grants a conspicuous exemption.
The euphemism gives Russia an indulgence – at home and abroad
At home, a criminal war does not require every citizen to be a fanatic. It requires enough willing participants and supporters, and enough people who choose comfort over conscience. For the latter, “Putin’s war” provides an easy moral escape route. It tells them: this is not really about you. It is one man’s responsibility.
Abroad, the myth of an inculpable and almost holy Russia is preserved: a Russia of ballet, literature, and the mysterious Russian soul. Meanwhile, Russian troops level Ukrainian cities. This is how the “good Russians” narrative works: they oppose the war in words while defending Russia as an entity that must remain intact.
Of course, there are Russians who genuinely oppose the war. But they are exceptions to a national pattern, not proof that the pattern does not exist. And if Russia as a nation is not responsible for a war fought by its own state, army, and citizens, the concept of responsibility in international relations becomes void.
The bet on ‘ordinary Russians’ has failed
Apparently, one reason for the “Putin, not Russia” formula is tactical. The idea was to avoid alienating ordinary Russians in the hope that they might eventually turn against the war. After more than four years of mass slaughter, that hope looks naïve and oblivious. Bucha, Mariupol, the stolen children, and missile strikes on Ukrainian apartment blocks did not produce national unrest. The endless funerals of Russian soldiers did not produce one either.
Russia’s polling environment is obviously distorted. Still, Levada published a defense of the center’s methodology, arguing that response rates have not meaningfully changed since before the war. The available data do not support the notion of a hidden anti-war majority. Russia Matters, summarizing Levada’s February 2026 data, reported that 72.2% of respondents supported the actions of the Russian army, with opposition at only 16.7%. That same survey, ostensibly, found 67.2% wanting negotiations to begin. However, most of that 67% want the war ended only on Russia’s terms. Other research using Gallup and Levada data found evidence of strong public support for the war.
What has produced tangible irritation in Russia is not the murder of Ukrainians, but inconvenience at home: fuel shortages, Internet outages, and other consequences of the growing reach of Ukrainian drones.
Months of Ukrainian strikes on targets inside Russia have done something four years of war never managed: produced visible public anger, caught on camera and in social media posts. They have even translated into a marginal dip in Putin’s approval rating.
“It is not just the fuel shortages and internet outages that make people angry, but the widening gap between reality and the Kremlin’s rhetoric,” writes The Economist. In other words, as long as they were comfortable and realities aligned with the government’s narratives, the people largely accepted the war.
This contrast is revealing. Four years of Ukrainian suffering did not shake Russian society. Disruption to Russian comfort did.
The case of Melnichenko as elite whitewash
The Economist’s package around Melnichenko is a fine specimen of Russian elite demagoguery. Russia starts a war, commits atrocities, threatens Europe. Yet somehow the warning offered is not about a broken Ukraine and the menace Russia poses, but about the danger of a broken Russia.
The essay’s word choices are revealing. Melnichenko writes that Russia concluded diplomacy had run its course and then “acted” – not invaded. He calls the 2014 popular revolution in Kyiv a “political upheaval.” He traces the war’s origins to a familiar claim: that Moscow’s security concerns went unheeded.
Melnichenko writes that it is “in Russian eyes, a war against the West as a whole.” He does grant Ukraine a paragraph – with a passing acknowledgement that it is more than a battlefield, but a “society and a political will” that has paid a heavy price – yet that sentence organizes nothing else in the essay. Moreover, that paragraph ends with a sweeping claim about a negative relationship between Ukrainian security and “Russia’s sovereign agency.”
The argument from start to finish concerns Russia’s relationship with the West. What Ukraine’s security actually requires is left out. The victim becomes secondary. The aggressor becomes a system whose integrity must be handled with utmost care.
Worth noting, too, is what is absent. In an essay of over 3,000 words, countless war crimes go unmentioned. There is just a line about a “terrible price.” Everything else is written in the register of an engineer: sovereignty, fertilizer flows, nuclear risk. He presents himself as a neutral system-thinker rather than a political actor. A sanctioned oligarch – that essentially means a part of the Russian exhaustive state system – presenting a political and moral crisis as disinterested physics is yet another round of profoundly dishonest and dangerous manipulative rhetoric.
This is why the West must stop using language that narrows responsibility to Putin. The “it’s Putin” formula is not merely an innocent journalistic blunder. It helps Russia’s elites whitewash Russia, evade national responsibility, and persuade Western audiences that the supreme post-war priority is keeping the Russian imperial polity intact.
But why should the West be fixated on preserving the very entity that has brought war and nuclear blackmail back to Europe? A stable peace cannot be built on comforting the aggressor. It must be built on guaranteed security for the victims and assertive prevention of future aggression.
Damage to deterrence and accountability
If the war is understood as Putin’s personal project, then the lesson for Russia’s institutions is simple: wait him out. One day Putin will leave or die, and everyone else can claim they were merely trapped inside his system. That destroys deterrence. For deterrence to work, Russian elites must understand that aggression carries consequences.
It also complicates post-war accountability. It becomes harder if the West accepts the ludicrous fiction that the war is somehow detached from Russia itself. Who is responsible? If the answer is “Putin,” then Russia escapes yet again. And if Russia escapes, it will learn nothing except that it can repeat it all under another ruler.
Say what happened
Saying that every Russian is guilty of every Russian crime would be false and unjust. But saying “Putin” instead of Russia distorts reality, comforts the passive, assists Russian soft power, weakens deterrence, and enables future evasion of responsibility. Putin gave the order. But Russia is waging the war. When discussing the war, the better term is Russia’s war against Ukraine. Because that is what it is.
A country that destroys another country cannot be allowed to hide behind the name of one man. History should not record this as Putin’s aggression. It should record the truth: Russia invaded Ukraine, Russia devastated Ukrainian cities, Russia murdered Ukrainians, and Russia must be held responsible.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

The SNP MSP for Inverclyde has questioned why management at Ferguson Marine failed to secure additional work, describing the announcement of job losses at the Port Glasgow yard as a wake-up call for the company’s leadership.
Stuart McMillan, whose constituency covers the yard, posted his response on Tuesday after Ferguson Marine opened a voluntary redundancy programme expected to see up to 70 employees leave.
He said: “There have been many well documented challenges at Ferguson Marine and the yard needs to become competitive.
“Today’s announcement must be a wake-up call for management. The order book remains empty until the Scottish Government finalise the direct award.
“Why have management taken their eye off the ball and not secured additional work?
“I have concerns about the loss of skills and knowledge as many of the older workforce have been with Fergusons for many years. Their experience is important for training apprentices.”
The framing puts him at odds with others who have commented on the announcement, who have directed their criticism at ministers rather than at the yard.
Paul Sweeney, the Labour MSP for Glasgow and a former shipyard worker, told the UK Defence Journal that the award of phase one of the Small Vessel Replacement Programme to Remontowa in Gdansk rather than to Ferguson Marine had directly caused the job losses.
He said: “They can’t secure additional work because Scotland doesn’t provide shipbuilding project finance through its state investment bank. Every other shipbuilding nation does this. That leaves Ferguson dependent on government contracts, but they have been awarded to foreign shipyards.”
Mr Sweeney said the Scottish Government has placed £550 million of orders with foreign shipyards since 2022 with none going to Scottish or UK yards, and that Caledonian Maritime Assets had recently drawn up tendering requirements for a ferry contract in terms that excluded British yards from bidding.
GMB Scotland, the largest union at the yard, called the losses a betrayal of a blameless workforce and blamed ministers for failing to deliver new contracts while sending work overseas. Louise Gilmour, the union’s Scotland secretary, said: “Shipbuilders needs ships to build so where are those promised to Ferguson Marine? If they ever come, who will build them?”
Ferguson Marine’s own account attributes the reduction to the completion of Glen Rosa rather than to any failure to win work. Graeme Thomson, the chief executive, said the yard faces “an inevitable gap in workload while we work with the Scottish Government to make the relevant preparations to enable us to proceed with contract negotiations.”
Mr McMillan’s point about the order book is not disputed by any of the parties. The Scottish Government announced in March 2026 that it intended to make a strategic direct award covering four vessels, two ferries for Caledonian Maritime Assets under the Small Vessel Replacement Programme along with a marine protection vessel and a marine research vessel, and due diligence on that award remains under way.
Where the accounts diverge is on whether the yard could realistically have won commercial work in the meantime. Ferguson Marine has held subcontract work from BAE Systems on the Type 26 frigate programme, fabricating structural units for assembly at Govan, and Mr Sweeney said that subcontract has now come to a conclusion.
Stephen Flynn, the Economy Secretary, said the redundancies would put the yard on a more competitive footing and were necessary to help secure a viable future, adding that he had been assured they would not affect Glen Rosa.

Your Expired Visa Card Could Be ‘Zombified’ to Make Contactless Payments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

As the controversial vehicle surveillance giant Flock Safety continues to expand, WIRED got the code for the company’s new AI policing tool and reconstructed the software to show that its capabilities go far beyond reading license plates and tracking vehicles. We also published the story this week of a Rhode Island police officer who was subjected to five internal affairs investigations in less than two years after he publicly questioned his department’s use of Flock cameras.
Following incidents of high-profile rogue activity by some of its AI agents, OpenAI said this week that it is halting model training runs and overhauling internal safety protocols. The company said that its upcoming Astra model may represent a turning point of “critical” cyber capabilities.
A reverse-lookup identification service exposed millions of photos of people’s faces in a database accessible through the open internet. Meanwhile, Meta ran advertisements for an app that promised to nudify female politicians, including one ad featuring a pornographic video that included a deepfake resembling a well-known US politician. Apple removed the app from the App Store after WIRED’s inquiry.
And WIRED spoke with Andy Yen, CEO of the privacy-focused digital services company Proton, about the privacy implications of AI and how access to encryption can continue to expand in this new technological era.
But wait, there’s more! Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. And stay safe out there.
Fraudsters Could Use “Zombified” Expired Visa Cards to Make Contactless Payments
Many people know that any active credit card represents a fraud risk the minute a card is lost, stolen, or otherwise gets out of their hands. Less expected is that an expired Visa card, too, could serve as an errant key into their bank account if it’s left unattended or discarded intact, discovered by a fraudster, and “zombified” using a new technique researchers recently revealed.
At the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference last week, researchers at the University of Massachusetts Amherst warned that fraudsters could make contactless payments using expired credit cards issued by Visa by proxying them through a man-in-the-middle app that relays the credit card’s data through a pair of phones. Due to issues in the authentication chain of contactless payments, the researchers found that whether an expired card’s transaction would be disallowed was left to cryptography implemented differently by various card issuers. Visa’s had a particular flaw allowing out-of-date cards to pass its check. (Visa didn’t respond to requests for comment from tech news outlet the Register, which reported on the research this week.)
In fact, as the researchers describe it, Visa’s essentially passed on the task of authenticating these transactions to the cardholder’s bank—and while some banks prevented the use of the zombified cards, others didn’t. The result is that fraudsters could in some cases dumpster dive for an expired card and use it to make payments from the unwitting owner’s account—particularly at point-of-sale terminals where no human is present to look askance at their phone-based proxy setup.
The lesson: When that Visa card expires, a pair of scissors can ensure it doesn’t reanimate in someone else’s hands.
Apple Sent Out an “Unprecedented” Number of Hacked-Device Warnings
Apple has long sent out notification to the owners of iPhones and other devices it’s detected may be the target of what it calls “mercenary spyware”—sophisticated, stealthy malware installed by a government or state-sponsored hacker-for-hire. Last weekend, the number of those alerts sent to potential victims spiked to an “unprecedented” number, according to TechCrunch, which spoke to security analysts who investigate potential spyware intrusions. The alerts, which were sent out to potential hacking targets in 110 countries, reached numbers of users more than 30 percent higher than previous rounds of these alerts, by the estimate of Mohammed Al-Maskati, who leads a team of security investigators at Access Now, a digital rights group that Apple refers victims to in its spyware alerts. At least one target, TechCrunch noted, was a Ukrainian soldier, who said that others in the Ukrainian military had also received the alert. Sophisticated iPhone hacking campaigns may well be on the rise: Just this year, researchers at iVerify and Google uncovered two iOS mass-hacking tools known as DarkSword and Coruna.
Ukraine Says It Hit Russian Ecommerce Giant With a Cyberattack—and Drones
In Russia’s decade-plus cyberwar against Ukraine, it has at times experimented with combined physical and digital attacks, such as triggering a hacker-induced blackout in a Ukrainian city in the midst of an air raid. Now, as Ukraine increasingly strikes back against Russia in an effort to impose cost on its invaders, it appears to have tried a similar tactic. The Ukrainian military this week claimed to have carried out a disruptive cyberattack against Russian ecommerce giant Wildberries—by some measures, the Russian equivalent of Amazon—in the midst of drone attacks that have also destroyed parts of the company’s warehouse infrastructure, according to cybersecurity news outlet The Record. While Wildberries is largely a consumer retail business, The Ukrainian Main Intelligence Directorate also claimed that it is part of Russia’s sells military logistics and played a role in financing the war in the Ukraine. The Record couldn’t confirm the exact effects of the cyberattack on Wildberries, but it notes that Russian media has reported that the company has lost nearly 13 million square feet of warehouse space to drone attacks.
US Agencies Warn of AI-Aided Hacking Targeting American Infrastructure Systems
Hackers’ exploitation software, like all software, is now rarely written one keystroke at a time. So perhaps it’s little surprise that hackers targeting US infrastructure equipment are among those using AI to automate their work. A group of US agencies including the NSA, the FBI, the Department of Energy, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency warned in an advisory this week that AI-assisted exploitation software was targeting Siemens programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, devices used to digitally control physical systems. Among the industries that use the targeted devices, the advisory warns, are manufacturing, chemical, energy, water, food, and agriculture facilities. “Using AI to generate exploitation scripts represents an evolution in threat actor capabilities, dramatically reducing the technical expertise and time required to develop working ICS exploitation scripts and malicious tools,” the advisory reads, using the term ICS to mean “industrial control systems.” This inevitable adoption of AI-coded hacking tools comes in the midst of an unprecedented campaign of likely-Iranian hacker disruptions targeting US water and wastewater facilities in dozens of utilities across seven US states.

DiMino also formally announced Kuwait’s acceptance into the US State Partnership Program and its pairing with the Maryland National Guard, according to the statement.

KATHMANDU, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Nepal's foreign trade recorded significant year-on-year growth in the first month of the current 2026-27 fiscal year amid a surge in both imports and exports, according to the Department of Customs.
A monthly report released on Friday by the department shows that Nepal's international trade rose 35.44 percent year on year to about 226.14 billion Nepali rupees (about 1.47 billion U.S. dollars) during mid-July to mid-August, compared with 166.97 billion rupees during the same period of the previous fiscal year.
Exports surged more than 61 percent to 38.70 billion rupees, while imports increased over 31 percent to 187.44 billion rupees.
Despite the strong growth in exports, Nepal's trade deficit widened 24.88 percent year on year to 148.73 billion rupees during the first month of the fiscal year. ■

2026-08-22

by Xinhua Writer Lu Junyu
RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- An "offline AI box" for classrooms without internet access and a smart platform optimizing waste-cooking-oil collection routes to tackle river pollution were among practical solutions presented by young innovators at the Brazilian finals of the 2026 China-Latin America Challenge to Alleviate Poverty.
Launched in 2024 by Tsinghua University alongside leading Latin American institutions, this year's competition brought together 666 participants across 88 universities and organizations from China, Brazil, Chile and Peru. Of 119 cross-border teams, 12 gathered in Brazil and Chile, bringing fresh perspectives to local poverty reduction.
Joining the initiative reshaped the perspective of Leonardo Vaz, a computer engineering student at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ). When Tsinghua team leader Zhang Henan got in touch, Vaz saw a hands-on way to tackle educational challenges in underserved regions of his own country.
As part of Team "Lighthouse," they collaborated to engineer an "offline AI box" designed for remote rural schools lacking electricity and internet connectivity. Educators load digitized course materials onto the portable device in connected areas, and students in isolated communities can then access resources and interact via a local hotspot on their mobile phones.
"This week, we did a field visit to an educational program in a favela, interviewed a math teacher to present our project, and tried to gather information and ideas to improve," Vaz recalled.
Navigating an 11-hour time difference between Brazil and China was no easy feat. "Our calls had to be scheduled at dawn in Brazil or late at night in China, but we overcame it. Collaborating with my Chinese teammates to tackle real-world challenges has been an absolute honor," he said.
Deploying technology across borders demands not just technical capability, but deep empathy and local knowledge.
"Poverty is complex, and solutions can not simply be copy-pasted from one nation to another," said Chen Taotao, director of Tsinghua University Latin America Center. "The core of China-LatAm cooperation lies in mutual learning. Chinese technology faces realistic localization challenges when adapted to Latin America's unique infrastructure and social landscape. Only through field testing and joint on-the-ground teamwork can these barriers be bridged," Chen said.
Ana Celia Castro, director of the UFRJ Institute for Advanced Studies, emphasized the need to move from concepts to action. "Innovative ideas only gain transformative power when they truly land on the ground," Castro said, highlighting the importance of building long-term mechanisms that engage businesses and civil society.
Addressing real-world issues was central to this year's items, which featured 26 practical prompts submitted by the participating organizations.
To tackle river pollution in Rio's Pavuna-Meriti basin, one team developed an AI-powered app connecting waste pickers with local businesses to collect used cooking oil -- drawing inspiration from China's mature supply chain for converting waste fats into biofuel.
"We realized that existing recycling programs in Brazil rarely reach informal waste pickers or low-income neighborhoods," said Wu Zongqin, a master's student at Tsinghua University. "We wanted our project to tackle deep-seated challenges like fatbergs, rather than just scratch the surface."
As global challenges grow increasingly interconnected, international collaboration among the next generation offers a beacon of hope.
"Young people from China and the Latin American region are learning how to listen to each other, understand different realities, and work together to solve real problems, from education and healthcare to agriculture and sustainable energy. This is what makes this challenge truly special," said Lv Xingcan from Envision Group, a key corporate supporter of the project.
Reflecting on the evolution of the program, Chen sees a promising road ahead.
Looking ahead, Chen envisions a collaborative ecosystem uniting academics, enterprises, and governments. But for students like Vaz and Zhang, the impact is already real -- measured by call by call across an 11-hour time zone. ■

Mexico resumes livestock sales to US under tight controls over screwworm risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:23:01 UTC
19:23:01 KST

Mexico resumes livestock sales to US under tight controls over screwworm risk
HERMOSILLO, Mexico (AP) — At daybreak, rancher Martín Alfonso Ibarra takes advantage of the cooler hours in northern Mexico’s desert to oversee the milking of his cows and tend to 16 prized calves. Soon, he hopes, they will be headed north to the United States as a yearlong ban on Mexican cattle imports comes to an end.
The ban, imposed over concerns about a flesh-eating parasite known as the New World screwworm fly, dealt a blow to cattle and beef industries on both sides of the border, exacerbating a livestock shortage in the U.S. and hurting a Mexican ranching sector already weakened by drought and a cattle export business that generated $1.2 billion for Mexico last year.
Now, the U.S. is set to resume livestock imports from Mexico beginning Aug. 24 at the Douglas, Arizona, border crossing, which borders Agua Prieta in Mexico’s Sonora state. If the reopening goes smoothly, the U.S. Department of Agriculture could allow imports through additional ports, though shipments will initially be subject to restrictions aimed at preventing the spread of the parasite — which has already crossed the border, with authorities battling cases in Texas and New Mexico.
The screwworm gets its name from the maggots’ habit of burrowing — or screwing — into a wound, according to the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service. Any warm-blooded animal, including wildlife, pets and occasionally even humans, can be infested.
In Mexico, the screwworm outbreak was detected in November 2024 and has spread to 30 of the 32 states — most recently in Sonora, where the first case was reported Wednesday in the community of Munihuasa, near the borders with Chihuahua and Sinaloa, states where infections have also proliferated.
To date, Mexico has 1,969 active screwworm cases, which represent less than half of the infections reported a year ago, a decline that authorities say shows progress in containing the outbreak. Still, they acknowledge eradication will take time.
New US controls are expected to slow shipments
Against that backdrop, Ibarra and thousands of other ranchers in the northern state of Sonora are preparing to resume live cattle exports. But optimism is tempered by new U.S. controls expected to slow shipments across the border.
“This is not over yet,” said the 58-year-old rancher, adding that the export halt cut his income by 40% last year.
According to the protocol defined by U.S. authorities, in the first week of reopening, only 700 cattle per day will be allowed through; this will rise to 900 in the second week and will gradually increase until reaching 1,300 cattle per day, veterinarian Arturo Ruiz, responsible for animal health for the state of Sonora, told The Associated Press.
The new rules also require cattle to be fitted with radio-frequency identification tags in their ears and screened by electronic readers and trained dogs. Officials from the U.S. Department of Agriculture will conduct the inspections before allowing the Mexican cattle to cross into Arizona, Ruiz explained.
Mexico accepted the U.S. protocols, but the restrictions have frustrated some local ranchers.
“We are at a complicated moment when we need authorities to think less politically and more technically and reasonably,” said Juan Carlos Ochoa, president of the Regional Livestock Union of Sonora, referring to tensions between the Mexican and U.S. governments when the ban was first imposed in May 2025.
Ochoa said the new U.S. restrictions would limit shipments and argued that a greater flow of cattle across the border is needed to address supply shortages in both countries.
A cautious optimism as imports resume
Although both countries felt the effects of Washington’s decision, the impact was greater in the U.S., particularly for consumers facing record-high beef prices that led some to cut back on meat.
Juan Carlos Anaya, general director of agricultural consulting firm Grupo Consultor de Mercados Agrícolas, said U.S. ranchers were unable to make up the supply shortfall, contributing to closures at some meat-processing plants and hurting feedlot operations.
Before the border closure, Mexico exported about 1.2 million head of cattle to the United States each year, mainly from its northern states. When exports were suspended, Mexican ranchers turned to the domestic market, where they sold their cattle for nearly 40% less than they had received in the U.S. — a loss of income that forced many to sell some of their cattle or cut spending and investment.
Back in Sonora, in the stifling August heat of the capital, Hermosillo, Ibarra was cautiously optimistic about finally sending his 16 calves to the U.S. But he said he would temper his expectations until October, when the cattle have gained enough weight and the sale could be finalized.
“There’s no need to get too excited,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Beyond the history books: Inside the hidden world of modern slavery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:19:48 UTC
19:19:48 KST

- i24NEWS
- International
- Beyond the history books: Inside the hidden world of modern slavery
Beyond the history books: Inside the hidden world of modern slavery
From forced labor and child marriage to the exploitation of migrant workers, tens of millions of people remain trapped in forms of slavery that have adapted to the modern economy
For most of us, "slavery" belongs to the distant past, an archaic term associated with the 19th century or even Biblical times. But the reality on the ground is that slavery, in most of its forms, still exists. It has simply changed shape and embedded itself in the modern labor market.
What is modern slavery?
"Modern slavery" is an umbrella term for situations in which a person is forced to work or live under another person's complete control, deprived of personal freedom and unable to leave because of threats, violence, coercion, deception or the exploitation of extreme power imbalances. Human rights organizations also classify forced marriage, including child marriage, as a form of slavery, and the figures are staggering: around 50 million people are trapped in modern slavery today.
That figure includes roughly 28 million people in forced labor and another 22 million in forced marriages. Because much of the phenomenon is hidden within the informal economy, there is no precise real-time count, but the Global Slavery Index provides the most comprehensive picture available.
Isn't it an exaggeration to call harsh working conditions slavery?
Words matter. Terms such as "genocide" and "Holocaust" still carry enormous weight and touch a raw nerve. The current climate of antisemitism is a reminder that without a place of refuge, the security of Jews around the world could once again be called into question. Some survivors of the 20th century's horrors are also still with us, making this, for many, living history rather than some distant past that can safely be forgotten.
"Slave," by contrast, has become almost casual vocabulary, precisely because we feel so far removed from its original meaning. No Jew today walks around worried that the Egyptians might enslave him again, or that he could suddenly be thrown into a minivan and wake up in the desert on his way to build "Burj Khalifa 2."
Some may jokingly describe sitting in front of a computer in an office as slavery. The thousands of migrant workers from Southeast Asia who died from heat and exhaustion while building Qatar's World Cup stadiums would probably disagree.
Where is modern slavery worst?
As with almost every question involving modern slavery, the answer to which country is the world's worst offender depends on how you measure it. Is importing exploited labor from abroad worse than enslaving your own citizens? At what point do appalling working conditions become slavery even in the absence of whips and chains?
More than half of all people living in slavery worldwide are concentrated in just five countries, reflecting both their enormous populations and systematic labor exploitation: India, with some 11.05 million people; China, 5.77 million; North Korea, 2.7 million; Pakistan, 2.35 million; and Russia, 1.9 million.
Measured as a share of the population, however, the highest rates are found primarily in dictatorships and countries plagued by prolonged conflict.
North Korea: 104 people per 1,000. The regime holds hundreds of thousands of people in kwanliso prison camps, where political prisoners are subjected to forced labor.
Eritrea: 90 people per 1,000. National service is compulsory and can continue indefinitely, effectively functioning as state-imposed forced labor.
Mauritania: 32 people per 1,000. Traditional chattel slavery, inherited from mother to child, continues to exist.
Saudi Arabia: 21 people per 1,000. The kafala, or employer-sponsorship, system can leave foreign workers with little legal protection and heavily dependent on their employers.
In China, between one and two million Uyghurs, a persecuted Muslim minority, have been held in detention facilities in Xinjiang and forced into labor connected to the cotton and electronics industries.
In Mauritania, exploitation is deeply rooted socially and culturally, while human rights activists attempting to free enslaved people have themselves been arrested by the authorities.
The conditions that allow exploitation to thrive
Modern slavery feeds on a legal and economic environment that magnifies the imbalance of power between employer and employee. In vulnerable sectors such as agriculture, caregiving and construction, workers may be effectively tied to a single employer, geographically isolated, burdened with debts incurred through recruitment fees and constantly afraid that losing their job will also mean losing their legal status and being deported.
Even in developed countries, exploitation often exists in the gray zone between the legal and the illegal. In the United States, the 13th Amendment abolished slavery but retained an exception allowing compulsory labor as punishment for a crime. Around 800,000 prisoners perform prison labor, often for negligible wages.
In the Western private sector, criminal networks exploit legal loopholes and vulnerable migrants to keep workers in subhuman conditions. Cases uncovered in Australian agriculture, for example, have involved workers being forced to labor under threats of death and for virtually no pay.
Israel: Failure to identify victims, little enforcement
Although slavery and forced labor have been explicitly prohibited under Israel's Penal Law since 2006, the criminal ban has not translated into effective enforcement. A 2020 report by TraffLab, a research group at Tel Aviv University's Faculty of Law, found deep structural failures in the state's handling of the problem.
The first major obstacle is identification. Israeli authorities rarely identify victims of labor trafficking on their own, with the overwhelming majority instead coming to light through civil society organizations. Between 2015 and 2017, for example, not a single man was identified in Israel as a victim of trafficking for labor exploitation.
The result is that exploited migrant workers can end up being treated primarily as immigration offenders, detained or deported before the abuse they suffered is ever properly investigated.
Criminal enforcement is extremely limited. The number of investigations is negligible, and indictments are almost never filed. Although labor trafficking accounts for nearly half of officially recognized trafficking victims in Israel, only around 6% of police investigations deal with this form of exploitation. Israel's most recent conviction for holding migrant workers in conditions of slavery dates back to 2012.
Is there a way out?
Eradicating modern slavery requires moving beyond isolated interventions in the most extreme and violent cases and addressing the structural conditions that make exploitation possible in the first place.
In Israel, experts have recommended re-establishing a dedicated police unit, bringing welfare and legal professionals into the victim-identification process and creating a complete separation between agencies responsible for protecting workers and those responsible for immigration enforcement and deportation.
Ultimately, there is also a moral and social responsibility that falls on all of us as citizens of developed countries. People who travel thousands of miles to do the exhausting and difficult jobs many of us no longer want to do, in agriculture, construction and caregiving, are entitled to humane treatment, full pay and the time off guaranteed to them by law.
Economic development is measured not only by the height of a country's skyscrapers, but by its ability to protect the most vulnerable people who helped build them.

US President Donald Trump says the project is being funded by private donors and companies.
US President Donald Trump announced that a new White House ballroom will cost nearly $400 million, funded entirely by private donors and corporations.
"We're spending hundreds of millions of dollars on the ballroom, and it's all from people like me and great companies that are putting it up. It's going to be close to $400 million, and it's all paid for by patriots and patriotic companies, big companies. I'll name the companies probably over the next couple of weeks, but I want to ask if they mind. But and really, most of them have said you could use my name gladly. So that's all money. No, no taxpayer money for the ballroom at all," Trump said.
Meanwhile, the Supreme Court has cleared the way for construction to continue for the time being.
The temporary order was issued just hours before lower-court rulings were set to halt above-ground work on the project due to a lack of congressional approval.
Trump thanked the high court and the chief justice during his remarks later Friday during a political appearance in South Carolina.
“When they say proceed, I think that's a good thing. That's a good thing,” Trump said.
The test of the limits of presidential power
The case reaches the nation's highest court as Trump exercises unprecedented assertions of executive power, increasingly seeking to reshape the capital to reflect his own vision.
The administration contends that the president holds absolute authority to alter the White House and other federal properties at his discretion, maintaining that the ballroom construction must proceed on national security grounds.
However, when Trump initially unveiled plans for the new facility, he made no mention of national security, instead framing it as a privately funded project supported by himself and other donors.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation counters that the president lacks the unilateral authority to carry out the work, which involved razing the East Wing. Legal counsel for the organisation accused the White House of attempting to "outrun the courts" by speeding up construction.
The full Supreme Court is expected to deliberate next on whether building work can proceed as the broader legal battle plays out.
Trump expressed appreciation for Friday's development, claiming in a social media update that the project remains "under budget and ahead of schedule."

Texas seeks federal probe of airport washing facilities, Muslim group denounces move
Texas Governor Greg Abbott on Friday sought a federal probe into airport facilities for ritual washing before Islamic prayers, a move that a Muslim advocacy group called an "anti-Muslim political stunt."
In a letter to the Department of Justice, Abbott called on the department to immediately review the ablution facilities at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport and George Bush Intercontinental Airport, casting them as discriminatory.
"Because the airports receive federal funds, they are subject to numerous conditions attached to that funding - including the requirement to comply with all applicable laws prohibiting discrimination," Abbott's office said in a statement.
Many Muslims wash their faces, arms and legs before daily prayers.
"These are not 'Muslim-only' spaces any more than a nursing room or an interfaith prayer room is 'Christian-only' or 'mothers-only,'" said the Texas chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, an advocacy group.
"They are accommodations, open to any traveler, that happen to be used mostly by the Muslim community. That is not discrimination. That is what accessible public infrastructure looks like," CAIR-Texas said in a statement.
Last week, Abbott referred the airports to US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy for investigation and threatened to revoke state funding.
Following that referral, Abbott said, DFW abandoned its plans to install more ablution facilities. The airport said this week that officials had "determined the originally anticipated benefit may not be achieved" if the stations were built.
There are about 4.5 million Muslims in the US, including more than 300,000 in Texas, the World Population Review says.
US rights advocates say Islamophobia has risen since the September 11, 2001, attacks on New York and the Pentagon, and more recently because of anti-immigration policies, white supremacy and the fallout of Israel's war in Gaza.
Rights advocates have also documented a spike in anti-Muslim messaging and rhetoric in U.S. political campaigns as Muslim American politicians have risen to prominent offices and roles.
Republican governors in Florida and Texas have cast CAIR, which has opposed Republican President Donald Trump's crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests, as a terrorist group.
CAIR and other civil rights groups have denounced the claims and said Republicans have attempted to stoke fear against Muslims.

More than 16,000 doses of Ervebo vaccine arrive in Ebola-hit DR Congo
The doses are the first of 70,000 allocated for Kinshasa as experts warn of the virus’s exponential spread.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has received more than 16,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine as the country faces its deadliest-ever Ebola outbreak.
The 16,250 doses arrived in the capital, Kinshasa, late on Friday evening, comprising the first of 70,000 that the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners pledged to provide on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Ebola outbreak ‘growing faster, wider’ as DRC death toll passes 2,500: UN
- list 2 of 4DR Congo to receive 70,000 doses of Ervebo vaccine as Ebola infections surge
- list 3 of 4How Ebola became the deadliest outbreak in DR Congo’s history
- list 4 of 4DR Congo’s Ebola outbreak ‘global emergency’ as infections pass 5,000: WHO
More doses are set to arrive next week.
Although the vaccine is approved against the Zaire strain of the virus, the Bundibugyo strain currently circulating in the country has no approved vaccine or treatment.
Early data from animal trials show it may offer some protection, according to the WHO.
Samuel Roger Kamba, the DRC’s health minister, told reporters Ervebo had been used several times in the past, including “on a very large scale” during the 2018 to 2020 outbreak.
Of the 70,000 doses intended for the DRC, 20,000 will be part of a late-stage clinical trial to test its effect on the Bundibugyo strain, the WHO said. The remainder is allocated to front-line and health workers.
The outbreak has killed more than 2,500 people out of nearly 5,300 confirmed cases, with the United Nations warning this week that infections continue to spread “exponentially”.
Although the outbreak was declared in mid-May, it is believed to have started weeks beforehand. Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, meanwhile, shows that transmission has not yet peaked and could reach three times its known rate.
Efforts to contain the virus have been stymied by ongoing armed conflict, delays in identifying cases and a lack of infrastructure in eastern DRC, experts say.

Hit by Trump tariffs, Quebec loses appetite for quick separation from Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:13:18 UTC
19:13:18 KST

Hit by Trump tariffs, Quebec loses appetite for quick separation from Canada
MONTREAL, Aug 22 - When U.S. President Donald Trump levied 50% tariffs on Canadian steel in June last year, a steel factory in Canada's mostly French-speaking province of Quebec lost about a third of its orders for bolts and fasteners in less than a week.
The factory owner - The Heico Companies - froze hiring, closed a plant in the region and laid off several dozen people, said David Jeannotte, an operations director, whose own brother lost his job. The cuts were part of 140 layoffs by the company, mainly in Quebec.
The factory's troubles reflect broader anxiety over the fallout from Trump's trade war in Quebec, which is due to hold a provincial election by October 5. But while some previous economic slowdowns in the province prompted an increase in separatist sentiment, polls show that this time around, support for an independent Quebec is at its lowest level in decades, at about 30%.
“As long as Trump will be in his chair, I don’t feel that we even need to talk about that,” Jeannotte said.
Others in the region are echoing Jeannotte’s concerns, saying the threat Trump poses to Canada means the best way to preserve Quebec's unique French culture is to stay within Canada -- at least for now.
Trump's threats to make Canada the 51st state and the whiplash from his tariff policy have spurred an outpouring of Canadian patriotism in Quebec, a province that regularly threatens to break away and has had two previous referendums on the issue.
As the country's only majority French-speaking province, Quebec has a long-established separatist movement that argues independence from Canada is the best way to protect its distinct culture and language. Quebec has never formally signed the Canadian Constitution and separatists argue French Canadians are often overlooked by the English-dominated majority.
CAMPAIGN OF FEAR
The separatist Parti Quebecois currently holds a slim lead in provincial election polls and a win would mark the party’s return to power after a dozen years. But analysts say a vote for the party would be more about disappointment with the ruling party than an endorsement of the PQ’s independence platform.
While the PQ is committed to a third independence referendum if it wins, leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon vowed that won't happen while Trump is president, a tacit recognition of falling support for independence. Quebec narrowly voted to stay in Canada in a 1995 referendum, spurring a national reckoning that resulted in the federal government asking the Supreme Court to clarify the legal procedure for separation.
On Tuesday, Plamondon said in a post on X that deciding Quebec’s political fate “must not be hijacked by the upheaval of American politics, the outbursts of an unpredictable president or by a campaign of fear.”
The explicit acknowledgment of the risk Trump poses to Quebec's independence movement aligns with a broader pattern in which the U.S. president's policies and rhetoric, including his stance on Greenland, have undermined separatist causes elsewhere.
In both Scotland and Catalonia, efforts to break away from the United Kingdom and Spain have been complicated by uncertainty stemming from Trump's tariff threats and criticism of NATO.
A delayed Quebec sovereignty vote would be one less headache for Liberal Prime Minister Mark Carney, who himself upended polls favoring the Conservatives to win a national election last year after promising to be a tough negotiator with Trump.
Carney faces another separatist movement in oil-rich Alberta, which has its own referendum scheduled for mid-October. While conservative Alberta’s burgeoning independence movement aligns with Trump’s brand of conservatism, Quebecers have largely supported the rest of Canada in pressing back against the U.S. president’s tariffs and threats of annexation.
“Postponing a referendum is unfortunately a choice we have to accept,” said Stéphane Bédard, a former interim leader of the PQ. “Quebec is stronger than it’s ever been, but the external factor of Trump has created a lot of insecurity, so we have to be realistic.”
Trump is more disliked in Quebec, arguably the country's most progressive province, than anywhere else in Canada.
According to August data from the pollster Angus Reid, only 10% of Quebecers have a favourable view of the president, and even a deal to lower tariffs is unlikely to reverse public opinion.
“Trump represents everything that Quebec has fought against for the last 60 years in terms of creating a modern, progressive society,” said Jonathan Kalles, former Quebec adviser to ex-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. Trump's conservative policies as well as his administration's comments that the province's French language requirements are a "trade irritant" are both unpopular.
The financial impact from his policies is also strongly felt in Quebec and economists note the province is among the worst hit by Trump's tariffs, given its concentration of industries like steel and aluminum.
A March report from the Bank of Montreal estimated Quebec's economy would grow about 1% this year, compared to more than 2% for Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Jeannotte, of factory near Montreal, said that before Trump levied tariffs on Canadian steel, about 90% of its products were destined for the U.S., with its bolts used in New York’s Empire State Building. Jeannotte said some staffers work without pay on some days and others have voluntarily reduced their hours.
AT THE NEGOTIATING TABLE
Still, some Quebec separatists say independence remains critical, even now.
Marie-Anne Alepin, president of the separatist Société Saint-Jean-Baptiste de Montréal, said Carney's decision to eliminate a tax that helps finance Canadian programming would cut funding for Quebec's French-language productions, highlighting that as an example of why the province should become independent. Ottawa has pledged to replace the tax with government funding.
“Canada is not capable of defending Quebec's interests,” Alepin said. “(Quebec) has to be at the negotiating table and to do that, we have to be a country.”
Vincent Rainville, a fourth-generation Quebec dairy farmer who owns more than 250 cows, disagreed, saying Trump's policies have complicated efforts to strengthen Quebec's economy and that a national response is required. Nearly half of Canada’s dairy farms are in Quebec.
"It's not just Quebec, it's all of Canada and all our industries that have been affected," he said. “If I supported an independent Quebec, I would not want to talk about that policy now." REUTERS

After running onto the grounds of a school on Stepan Bandera Street, he pulled out a knife and deliberately stabbed a 55-year-old junior sergeant of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center three times: twice in the neck and once in the forearm. After that, the attacker began threatening a police officer with the knife. The law enforcement officer used his service firearm
According to law enforcement officers, the attacker, who sustained wounds to his leg and abdomen, was hospitalized and is currently in the hospital. Meanwhile, the serviceman died from his injuries despite resuscitation efforts.
The deceased had been mobilized at the end of June this year and was deemed fit for service in support units based on his health, in connection with which he was assigned to the notification group of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center
At the scene, law enforcement officers seized a knife. Under the procedural guidance of the Halych District Prosecutor's Office of Lviv, the attacker was notified of suspicion of murdering a person in connection with the performance of that person's official duties and threatening to murder an employee of a law enforcement agency in connection with the performance of that employee's official duties (Clause 8, Part 2, Article 115; Part 1, Article 345 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
Investigative actions are currently ongoing, and all circumstances of the incident are being established.

Swiss grape harvest begins earlier than usual
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:07:51 UTC
19:07:51 KST

Swiss grape harvest begins earlier than usual
In many regions, the grape harvest is set to begin as early as August this year. The yield is likely to be lower than in other years, but the quality of the 2026 vintage is "promising".
Several winegrowers, such as the Obrecht family in the Jenins wine-growing region of the Bündner Herrschaft, have already started harvesting grapes this week. This means that the “Läset” is taking place around three weeks earlier than usual in most of Switzerland’s wine-growing regions.
In the cantons of Schaffhausen and Thurgau, wine-growing commissioner Hansueli Pfenninger is expecting “a very early start to the harvest” – from the end of August. This situation has already occurred in 2003 and 2018. And just as in those two exceptional years, Pfenninger is also expecting an outstanding vintage in 2026.
Small grapes
In Graubünden, too, the drought will affect the grape harvest, predicts his colleague Walter Fromm. However, the lack of moisture does not affect all regions to the same extent. West of Maienfeld and east of Fläsch, the vineyards with light soils and low water-retention capacity are most at risk. It is also striking in many places that the grapes have turned out very small due to the lack of water.
+ Swiss winegrowers begin harvest in mid-August for first time
In some cantons of French-speaking Switzerland, there has never before been such an early grape harvest in August. Rémy Alain Reymond, head of the Neuchâtel Office for Viticulture and Agroecology, speaks of a “historically early ripening”. “We had expected a very early vintage, and yet many winegrowers are still surprised by it,” he added.
In Valais, the grape harvest is expected to begin in the week of August 24 for certain well-exposed vineyards and to extend to the entire region from August 31 onwards, which is particularly early. “According to ripeness checks, we are currently between six and twelve days ahead of 2022, which was a hot year,” the Valais Office for Viticulture and Wine told the Keystone-SDA news agency in response to an enquiry.
In the canton of Geneva, the harvest timing is classified as “rather normal for a year with a heatwave”, explained Dorian Pajic, head of the Viticulture and Oenology Programme at the Cantonal Office for Agriculture and Nature.
Heat determines quality
Finally, in the canton of Vaud, the grape harvest will begin in early September, around two days later than in 2003. It holds the record for the earliest harvest, as François Montet, president of the Vaud Winegrowers’ Association, emphasised. He noted, however, that the heatwave had no influence on the timing of the harvest.
This is determined by the timing of the vines’ flowering, which in turn is influenced by the spring warmth. The summer heatwave, on the other hand, determines the quality, he said, predicting that the 2026 vintage would be of very high quality.
Nevertheless, there are some concerns. According to oenologists, extreme heat and very strong sunlight can cause the grapes to scorch and suffer sunburn, which may lead to crop losses. Water shortages are also detrimental to the harvest yield. That is why many winegrowers are hoping for a few rain showers before they begin the harvest.

H1N1 on rise in Delhi
NEW DELHI: The ministry of health and family welfare (MoHFW) on Saturday has urged people to recognise the H1N1 symptoms early and seek medical advice if they persist.In a post on X on Saturday, the ministry said swine flu can show up through symptoms including fever, cough, sore throat, headache, runny nose, body aches and fatigue. It advised people not to ignore persistent symptoms and to seek medical advice at the nearest healthcare centre.The health ministry’s advisory also lists lethargy and loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting, joint and muscle pain, diarrhoea and headache among the common symptoms associated with swine flu.
Explaining the symptoms and transmission of H1N1, Dr (Major) Rajesh Bhardwaj, founder, ENT and Sleep Expert, MedFirst ENT Centre, said, “H1N1 infection, or swine flu, can be somewhat more dangerous and serious, which is why we are more concerned about it.”He said the infection spreads through respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and can also spread through close contact with an infected person.
“The symptoms include high fever, body aches, weakness, lethargy, cough, sore throat, difficulty breathing, and sometimes loss of the sense of smell. There can also be throat irritation and cough,” Bhardwaj said.
Staying home while sick reduces exposure to others. Covering coughs and sneezes, washing hands regularly and improving ventilation can also limit spread.
A mask can be particularly useful when someone has respiratory symptoms and must enter a crowded indoor setting.The Delhi government, in a post on X, shared precautionary steps. "Vigilance and timely treatment are extremely crucial for protection against H1N1," it wrote.It advised people to cover their nose and mouth while coughing or sneezing, wash their hands regularly, consult a doctor if symptoms appear and avoid taking medicines without medical advice.
On Friday, Union health minister JP Nadda reviewed Delhi’s preparedness for influenza and vector-borne diseases as Delhi has reported 2,392 influenza A cases this year, including 1,777 H1N1 infections.

Poland Maintains Long‑Term Legal, Financial Protections for 1.7 Million Ukrainian Refugees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:04:00 UTC
19:04:00 KST

Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Poland has provided legal and financial protection to 1.7 million Ukrainian citizens who were forced to leave their country due to the war, the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported.
The ministry noted that the assistance provided to Ukrainians represents one of the largest displays of public support in the country following the onset of Russian aggression.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Polish MFA, approximately 77% of Poles have actively participated in helping Ukrainian refugees in various ways. Furthermore, 7% of Polish citizens opened their own homes to host Ukrainians fleeing the conflict.
The total volume of funds spent by Polish society to support Ukrainians has exceeded 10 billion zlotys.
The Polish foreign policy department emphasized that these figures demonstrate the enormous scale of assistance Poland has provided to Ukrainians since the start of the full-scale war.
Changing public sentiment
The release of the refugee data follows recent polling indicating growing reservations among the Polish public regarding their country’s future role in supporting Ukraine.
An Opinia24 poll published in late July found that a majority of Poles oppose their country supporting Ukraine’s efforts to join the EU. The survey indicated that 52% of respondents opposed Poland supporting Ukraine’s EU membership efforts, compared with 33% who favored such support.
Ukraine Appoints 16 New Judges to High Anti-Corruption Court
Opposition was notably stronger regarding the potential deployment of Polish troops to Ukraine following the war. Sixty-five percent of respondents rejected the idea of sending Polish forces to supervise a ceasefire or peace agreement, while only 18% supported the proposal.
When asked whether their attitudes toward Ukrainians had changed since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, 54% of respondents said their views remained unchanged. However, 36% stated their attitudes had worsened, while only 3% reported an improvement.
Historical disputes and military aid
Views on continued military support remain closely divided, particularly when framed around historical disputes. When asked about assistance in the context of Ukraine’s commemoration of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), 44% of respondents said Poland should suspend military assistance, while 41% said Warsaw should continue supporting Ukraine.
A separate IBRiS poll published earlier in July found that 52.2% of respondents supported continued Polish military assistance overall, while 45.2% opposed it.
The Opinia24 survey also demonstrated approval for Polish President Karol Nawrocki’s recent decision to strip President Volodymyr Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state decoration. Fifty-five percent of respondents supported the decision, while 27% opposed it.
Poland has served as a major transit hub for international military and humanitarian assistance and has provided substantial weapons supplies to Ukraine since February 2022.
However, disputes connected to the UPA and the wartime massacres of Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia have remained a persistent source of tension between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The force said on Saturday the men, aged 31 and 44, were arrested last Thursday on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud.

He added that the suspects had rented a hotel room as an operations centre, where officers found a modem pool – a device that allows users to control multiple SIM cards simultaneously – nine mobile phones and 110 SIM cards.

Global data shows a sharp rise in adult ADHD diagnoses and medication prescriptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:00:45 UTC
19:00:45 KST

Diagnoses for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have increased in many countries across all age groups, our latest review has found. We have also shown that prescriptions for ADHD treatments have seen similar increases across all age groups.
Our latest review, published in the Journal of Psychopharmacology, drew together the recently published research on ADHD diagnoses and prescriptions across the world.
We found that in the UK, increases in recorded ADHD diagnoses and treatment prescriptions occurred across all age groups between 2000 and 2018.
The greatest rise in ADHD diagnoses across this period was among children. However, there was also a distinct increase in adults. For example, among men aged 18-29 there was an approximately 20-fold increase in diagnoses and an almost 50-fold increase in prescriptions.
The sex ratio of ADHD diagnoses in childhood and adolescence was approximately 4:1 male to female. However, the ratio of diagnoses in adulthood is nearly 1:1. This shift may partly reflect increased recognition of how ADHD presents in girls and adults – groups that have historically been underdiagnosed.
Alongside these increases in ADHD diagnoses, there has also been an increase in prescriptions for ADHD treatments.
In England, prescriptions of central nervous system stimulants (the main prescription treatments for ADHD) increased by 32% in adults over 18 in 2021-22. In children under 17, prescriptions increased by 12% from 2022-23. This was also the first time that more adults were prescribed these drugs than children since records started in 2015.
A retrospective study of over 154 million people from 13 countries, including in North America, Europe and Asia, demonstrated that use of ADHD medication prescriptions had increased in these regions as well.
Why diagnoses and prescriptions are increasing
A few key factors can largely explain the increase in both ADHD diagnoses and prescriptions that we’ve seen. This includes increased public awareness of the condition, better understanding by doctors of the way symptoms present and the availability of new and improved medications.
Additionally, there is better awareness of how ADHD manifests in groups who may have previously been missed because their symptoms did not match with those typically exhibited in boys and adolescents. This includes women and girls and people with predominantly inattentive symptoms.
However, these factors may only tell part of the story. Our review also revealed other drivers may deserve careful consideration.
For instance, there has been much debate over whether there is an issue of overdiagnosis and over-prescribing. Legitimate questions about whether some attention difficulties might be over-medicalised have also been raised. On the other hand, some authors have argued that there is no evidence to suggest overdiagnosis is occurring in the UK.
Understanding the full picture requires looking beyond the obvious explanations to examine cultural, economic, social and technological pressures in a globally competitive environment that may be influencing both diagnosis rates and treatment choices.
Looking forward
The rising rates of ADHD diagnoses and treatment represent a complex picture. There have been genuine improvements in recognising a real disorder that was historically overlooked (particularly in adult men and women), better clinical awareness and perhaps also some degree of over-identification in certain environments.
What seems clear is that ADHD, long thought of as a children’s disorder, is now being treated as what it truly is: a lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder affecting millions of people across the globe.
As awareness continues to grow, the challenge ahead lies in preserving limited NHS resources, while ensuring those who genuinely need these resources have improved access.
The wait time for an ADHD diagnosis in England currently ranges from two to 15 years. With increasing rates of diagnoses and prescriptions to manage ADHD, there are concerns that demand will soon outstrip NHS capacity entirely.
What could be a solution is the discovery of ADHD biomarkers – an objectively measurable indicator of a biological state or condition that can be detected in signatures in the brain. Currently, ADHD is diagnosed by a doctor who often has to rely on self-reported symptoms. Having biomarkers could improve the accuracy of diagnoses, ensuring those who have the condition get the support they need earlier on.
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
