Facing exile and persecution, an Iranian dissident crossed from devout Muslim to student of Judaism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:51:45 UTC
18:51:45 KST

Behnam Vali Heydarian, or “Ben Vali,” has lived what he feels like have been several lifetimes across four countries.
Raised as a Muslim in Kuwait, he became a devout follower of Islam before converting to Christianity in Iran, becoming a Christian pastor in Georgia, and eventually, an unrecognized refugee in Switzerland, where his spiritual journey has led him toward Judaism.
Heydarian spoke extensively with The Jerusalem Post, detailing Iran’s campaign of transnational repression, multiple attempts on his life, and the devastating consequences he could face if deported from Switzerland to Georgia and, ultimately, back to Iran.
He also discussed his pro-Israel activism. In this regard, Heydarian said he has been ostracized by the humanitarian community to which he once dedicated his life, solely because he supported the Jewish state and its people.
Heydarian was born in Kuwait in 1981 to two Iranian parents who were forced to return to Iran when the Gulf War broke out, finding himself in a country suffocated by radical Islam.
His early years in Kuwait left him fluent in Arabic, a skill that ultimately led to his selection at just 14 to compete in a Quran recitation competition. He questioned nothing and was content in Tehran.
It was not until he was 17 that he began to understand the regime’s brutality, when the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps raided the University of Tehran in response to protests over the closure of a reformist newspaper. While the regime acknowledged the deaths of only two people, rights groups estimated that as many as 17 were killed and dozens disappeared.
Like many, Heydarian participated in demonstrations against the brutality. But he did not truly divorce himself from the illusion of safety until he was 19, when men believed to be members of Iran’s security forces abducted his father.
“A lot in my life changed. It was a tornado,” he said, describing how men in an unmarked car took his father, who was never seen again.
With his father gone, Heydarian had to become his family’s provider. The time he had to dedicate to work left him with little capacity to pray, though he remained a devout Muslim.
“I was busier, so I practiced less. That kind of dragged me away from being a radical jihadi,” he noted.
A hunger for God
His business pulled him away from practicing Islam; it also took a significant toll on his health. At 29, Heydarian suffered a heart attack. His neighbor, with whom he had developed a close bond, had a dream that Heydarian’s home was on fire and entered the house just in time to find him collapsed on the floor.
Paramedics were filling out the forms to have the morgue collect his body when Heydarian came to. While technically dead, Heydarian shared with the Post that he had a vision of himself being dragged into a dark pit.
“I was dragged into it, and I was going down. It was really scary. I was dragged into something dark, a pit, and then suddenly everything stopped,” he recounted. “I was somewhere, nowhere, which was totally dark. And then my life started to appear, like 35-millimeter film frames.
“I was living there again, but everything was different. I lived all 29 years of my life over. Everybody I had met in this world, I saw again over there, and I begged almost everybody, ‘Please help me go from that world to this world.’ Nobody was able to do it,” Heydarian said.
“Finally, I met my mom. We talked a lot. Suddenly, I felt fire, flames of fire, on my body. I opened my eyes, and there was my neighbor and two ambulance technicians who had come to give me CPR.”
Heydarian believed at the time that he was in Barzakh, an Islamic concept describing an intermediate realm where souls wait after death for a final day of judgment.
When he became a Christian, he interpreted the experience as Hell, but now he thinks it may have been the Bosom of Abraham, a biblical phrase describing a place of comfort with the patriarch Abraham for righteous souls.
The brush with death profoundly changed Heydarian. He renewed his devotion to God and searched for his mission in life. Describing an intense “hunger” to know God, he explained how he returned to the religious texts he had once won competitions reciting, only to find that they pointed in the “opposite direction” from what he was seeking.
Praying to God for guidance, he stumbled upon two New Testament verses online: “A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another” (John 13:34).
Deeply impacted by these verses, Heydarian said he decided to read the whole New Testament. “When I finished, I said, ‘That’s it. That’s exactly the character of this God. He is exactly the God I have been thirsting for.’ So I started believing in Him, and I would say I gave my heart to the Lord at that time.”
When Heydarian approached his friends about his newfound beliefs, he discovered that they had all already converted but were scared of speaking to him given how devoutly he had followed Islam.
Relieved to have found acceptance, he spent years attending secret home churches and distributing copies of the New Testament across Iran, an offense for which Iranian authorities have imprisoned Christian converts and, in some cases, imposed severe sentences.
Barring a few close encounters with the regime’s security forces, Heydarian practiced his new faith in relative peace for two years, until he learned that a friend, Hamid, had been shot and killed by police while driving to meet him.
“Seven bullets were fired into his car. Three hit his body, and four hit the car. Later, we tried to find out what had happened ... There was a camera nearby, and when they reviewed the footage, they saw that the police had shot him,” Heydarian said. “They made sure he was dead and then left. His family tried to file a complaint and find out what had happened, but the process was blocked. That’s what usually happens in Iran.”
A year later, in 2017, another of Heydarian’s friends was arrested. Heydarian feared that his friend would not remain silent under torture, so he decided to flee. Heading to the Turkish border, Heydarian initially planned to make his way to Ecuador. But he later abandoned that plan, took the first bus out of the area, and eventually found himself in Georgia.
Within days of arriving in Georgia, the generosity of a young Polish volunteer who spoke English helped Heydarian find both a place to live and work at a hostel.
He applied for asylum, but his application was promptly rejected, setting off a years-long legal battle. It was not until his sixth hearing in 2021 that the courts finally conceded he needed to remain in the country.
Though technically safe, Heydarian soon discovered that his activism came with a cost. When he began volunteering to help Iranians and speaking out against the violence accompanying the suppression of the 2019 protests, he learned that Iranian oppression did not stop at the Turkish border.
“After the uprisings in Iran, I couldn’t ignore the reality, the truth, and the voiceless people who were suffering there,” he said.
Reaching out to other politically active friends, they decided they should be doing more. Through his connections with major international aid organizations, including UNHCR – the UN Refugee Agency, World Vision International, and several European groups, Heydarian thereby became increasingly politically active.
Eventually, he wrote to multiple ambassadors in Georgia, urging them to take action on behalf of the Iranian people.
The letter, he said, “backfired.”
A Moroccan acquaintance subsequently tried to stab him. Authorities characterized the attack as stemming from a nonexistent love triangle, Heydarian said, rather than recognizing what he believed was political motivation.
In the years that followed, Heydarian said, he was repeatedly followed, assaulted, and his car vandalized. Each time, he said, authorities promised to investigate but never followed through. On several occasions, documents were stolen while valuables were left untouched.
People told Heydarian that the Iranian embassy had been asking questions about him. His church received suspicious visitors, and on one occasion, armed men attempted to enter his apartment.
In another incident, he said, he was returning from a swim when four men blocked his path to the bus station.
“They were talking on the phone. One of them was confirming my identity. I heard them speaking in Russian. One of them said, ‘Oh, it’s him, it’s him,’ and the guy on the phone asked, ‘Is it him?’ The person on the other end said, ‘Yeah, it’s him, it’s him.’ Then they came toward me and started beating me,” Heydarian said.
He described faking unconsciousness in order to escape, ultimately losing several teeth in the attack. Heydarian said he then ran to a police station, where officers turned him away and told him to return to the scene and call for help.
The Georgian Interior Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
Allies turn enemies after October 7
After October 7, Heydarian said, another part of his life began to unravel.
He received harsh and sometimes abusive messages from fellow humanitarian workers angered by his support for Israel after the Hamas massacre. People he had once considered allies, he said, quickly turned their backs on him.
“I was kind of banned or kicked out from the whole environment of human rights in Europe,” he said.
Heydarian showed the Post an admonishing letter he received from one organization he worked for because he had posted a clip from the Israeli comedy show Eretz Nehederet.
Outside the deliberate hostility, the UN had also allowed Iran to deliver food packages to refugees in Georgia, including Iranian asylum seekers fleeing from the regime.
Showing the Post a letter penned by the Islamic Republic’s embassy, Heydarian said the comments about being stuck in a foreign land with no family were designed to torment him. He has not been able to see or speak to his mother for years.
The Hamas attack reminded Heydarian of the violence he had witnessed in Iran. Alongside his longstanding search for God, he said that recognition drew him toward the Jewish community.
Mikheil Grishashvili, a Jewish community leader and representative of the Peace Synagogue in Georgia, confirmed to the Post that Heydarian has been an active member of the community since 2023.
“He was an active, hardworking, kind, and responsible person, and he very quickly became part of our community,” Grishashvili said, adding that Heydarian became increasingly involved in Judaism.
But as his relationship with the Jewish community deepened, Heydarian said pressure from the Georgian authorities also intensified.
He said his bank accounts were repeatedly frozen and that his refugee status was threatened after he failed to register as a foreign agent in connection with his humanitarian work and a company he had established. He also claimed that, despite the EU and US continuing to fund organizations for which he worked, he personally faced increasing financial and legal pressure.
Ibrahim Alvac, the representative of a Swiss lawyers’ bureau representing Heydarian, told the Post, “Heydarian’s public position towards Israel and his engagement with Judaism are relevant elements of his personal and political profile.”
Referencing Heydarian’s current immigration process to Switzerland, Alvac went on to say that “these activities predate the current stage of his Swiss immigration proceedings and are [well] documented.”
“These circumstances are relevant to his overall profile because they are publicly documented and could therefore potentially become known to Iranian authorities. Whether and to what extent they increase the risk he would face in the event of a return to Iran is ultimately a matter requiring an individual assessment,” the Swiss lawyer added.
The pressure on Heydarian intensified when an individual whom he believes was connected to the Georgian security services confronted him.
According to Heydarian, the man warned him to stop his political activism or risk losing his temporary refugee status.
“He was very friendly at first, as they usually are, but there were very meaningful words and sentences: ‘Do this, don’t do this. Be aware of this. Be aware of that.’ In other words, he was framing the situation. He was essentially dictating what I should,” Heydarian said.
“In 2023, I was intimidated by the same guy. He told me that if I didn’t do certain things, my status would be revoked, which is what’s happening. He wanted me to stop every type of demonstration, not have demonstrations in front of the Iranian embassy or in front of the parliament.”
Rather than wait to see whether the threat would materialize, Heydarian traveled to Switzerland for a convention. While there, he applied for asylum, but he said his application was rejected.
“I came here on a business visa, but they wrote that I had arrived in Switzerland illegally. Then they said Georgia was a safe country, regardless of the documents I provided,” he detailed.
He went on to describe what he called the severe emotional toll the constant threats and fear have taken on him.
Without legal status and fearing for his life, Heydarian is now living in hiding while appealing Switzerland’s decision to reject his asylum application.
He said people have written directly to Switzerland’s Interior Ministry offering him employment and housing, but he never received a response. He has also written to the UN Committee against Torture, but says he was told that his case was not relevant because he was not currently being tortured.
After years of escaping persecution, Heydarian now finds himself in a different kind of limbo: unable to return to Georgia, terrified of being sent back to Iran, and without a country willing to offer him a permanent place of refuge.
Despite spending years defending the rights of others, he fears there may be no one left to defend him until it is already too late. Yet, as he continues his journey toward Judaism, Heydarian says he has faith that he will be shown the way to wherever he is destined to fulfill his purpose.

'Will not step down': Manan Mishra reiterates stance as plea in SC seeks his removal as BCI chief

'Will not step down': Manan Mishra reiterates stance as plea in SC seeks his removal as BCI chief
Edited by: Rajeev Singh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 22, 2026, 15:20 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Manan Mishra also addressed the recent controversy involving students of NALSAR University of Law.
NEW DELHI: Bar Council of India (BCI) chairman and Rajya Sabha member Manan Kumar Mishra rejected demands for his resignation, saying he holds the position through an election and represents around 25 lakh lawyers across the country.Mishra made the remarks a day after a group of lawyers from different Bar Associations in Delhi staged a protest outside the BCI office in New Delhi.
The protesters raised several concerns, including Mishra's long tenure, the lack of welfare measures for advocates and the proposed increase in the enrolment fee for lawyers."I have served as the chairman of the Bar Council of India for 12 to 14 years because I was elected. Manan Mishra represents 25 lakh lawyers; he will not step down simply," Mishra said, responding to the protest.He further said: "I am an elected representative. I was neither selected nor nominated to the Bar Council of India. It is a statutory body established under the Advocates Act."The lawyers demanding his resignation also sought the implementation of an Advocate Protection Act and questioned the proposed increase in registration fees at State Bar Councils.
Supreme Court petition challenges Mishra's tenure
Amid the controversy, a petition has also been filed in the Supreme Court challenging Mishra's continuation as BCI chairman. Filed by advocate Yogamaya MG through advocate Deepak Prakash, the plea alleges that his uninterrupted tenure for more than a decade is contrary to the rules governing the BCI.The petitioner has relied on Rule 12(2) of the BCI Rules, which provides for a two-year tenure for the chairman and vice-chairman, or until they cease to be members, whichever is earlier.The plea has also challenged an April 21, 2025 Gazette notification that allegedly extended Mishra's tenure until 2030. It has asked the Supreme Court to quash the notification and direct the BCI to withdraw or rescind it.According to the petition, Mishra first became BCI chairman in 2012. Although he briefly left the post in 2014, he returned as chairman in November that year and has remained in the position since then. The petitioner has claimed that his re-election in March 2025 was his seventh consecutive term.The plea has argued that the absence of a cumulative limit on repeated re-election allows the office to remain concentrated in one individual for an extended period."Although Rule 12(2) prescribes a two-year tenure, no meaningful restriction exists upon repeated re-election. Consequently, the office has remained with the same individual for nearly twelve years. Such prolonged concentration is prima facie inconsistent with the representative scheme embodied in Section 4(1)(c), under which every State Bar Council contributes to the composition of the Bar Council of India. A national institution representing the entire legal profession should not permit its highest office to remain concentrated indefinitely in one individual or a narrow regional grouping," the petition stated.The petitioner has sought Mishra's removal and fresh elections within a time-bound period under independent supervision. It has also asked for a cumulative cap on the number of years a person can serve as BCI chairman, along with a rotation system and cooling-off period to allow representatives from different states and regions to head the council.The plea has further sought an independent committee headed by a former Supreme Court judge or former chief justice of a high court. The proposed committee would be assisted by an auditor nominated by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), along with financial and technical experts.The petition has also sought an independent inquiry into the functioning and finances of the BCI Trust, "PEARL-FIRST", and the financial affairs of the All India Bar Examination.It has called for a time-bound audit of statutory funds, All India Bar Examination receipts, institutional receipts, trust finances, vendor contracts and related party transactions.As an interim measure, the petitioner has proposed an independent administrative committee to oversee the BCI if the Supreme Court orders Mishra's removal.The plea has also referred to Mishra's political role. It noted that he became a Rajya Sabha member after being nominated by the BJP in 2024.The petitioner has clarified that it is not claiming that Mishra's political affiliation alone makes him ineligible to remain BCI chairman. Instead, it has raised concerns about the combination of political office and leadership of the statutory body responsible for regulating the legal profession."Petitioner does not seek the removal of any individual merely because of political affiliation or personal disagreement with any office bearer. Nor does the petitioner invite this Court to substitute its own opinion for that of the statutory authority. The challenge is directed against structural illegality, alleged concentration of institutional control, prolonged concentration of statutory power, violation of mandatory statutory provisions governing tenure and elections, arbitrary exercise of regulatory authority, absence of transparency and accountability, and failure to preserve the representative democratic character contemplated under the Advocates Act, 1961," added the PIL.
Mishra defends action over NALSAR student controversy
Mishra also addressed the recent controversy involving students of NALSAR University of Law in Hyderabad and the Chief Justice of India (CJI), who is also the university's chancellor."Lately, there has been a lot of irresponsible and absurd commentary circulating on social media. Students from NALSAR University, Hyderabad, decided to boycott the Chief Justice of India - who is also their Chancellor - and refused to attend the convocation ceremony where he was to preside," Mishra said."As the Chairman of the Bar Council of India, I found this deeply objectionable," he added.According to Mishra, the BCI initially issued an order stating that the enrolment of the students involved would not be processed. He said the decision was withdrawn within 15 minutes after their grievances were addressed."Within 15 minutes, that order was revoked, and the students' grievances were addressed," he said.Mishra alleged that the episode was later used by members of the Aam Aadmi Party and a group he described as the "CJP group" to demand his resignation."I have served as the Chairman of the Bar Council of India for 12 to 14 years because I was elected," he reiterated.He also said around 15 students had gathered outside the BCI office on Thursday night to demand that he step down."Yesterday, about 15 students came here at night demanding a resignation," Mishra said.Meanwhile, another group of lawyers gathered in support of Mishra and defended his position as an elected representative of the legal profession.Advocate Satyam Singh said protests alone could not remove the BCI chairman because he had been elected by members of the legal community."The BCI Chairman is an elected official who has been consistently voted into office. He hasn't been appointed through a selection process or an exam where you can simply show up and demand his resignation," Singh said."He represents 2.5 million lawyers across the country, representing them successfully for years on end," he added.On the NALSAR controversy, Singh said the issue should be viewed in the context of respect for legal institutions."The CJI is the head of the Constitution--in a sense, its guardian--while NALSAR students are future lawyers and judges who will become part of this profession, whether on the Bar or the Bench. If they do not respect or trust that institution, where does that leave us?" he said.Singh also defended Mishra's decision to issue the initial order, while acknowledging that it was subsequently withdrawn."He withdrew it and admitted it was issued in haste. However, it was necessary to send a message that one must trust and respect the institution; that was the intent behind the move," Singh said.
Lawyers raise welfare and fee concerns
The protest, however, was not limited to the demand for Mishra's resignation. Lawyers also raised broader concerns about welfare measures and working conditions within the profession.
Advocate Raman Sharma alleged that there had been no significant nationwide welfare scheme for lawyers despite Mishra's long tenure as BCI chairman.Advocate Umesh Kumar raised the issue of a national insurance scheme for lawyers and objected to the proposed increase in enrolment fees to Rs 22,500.Other protesters, including advocate Perdeep Nagar, called for greater scrutiny of lawyers' credentials and urged the BCI to give greater attention to the welfare of members of the legal profession.

He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

Germany is allocating an additional EUR 50 million in humanitarian aid to Ukraine and EUR 10 million to NATO’s CAP (Comprehensive Assistance Package) fund, Federal Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Germany Johann Wadephul said.

Russia’s gold reserves fell to their lowest level since January 2020 - Bloomberg
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:38:36 EEST
18:38:36 KST

Russia’s gold reserves fell to their lowest level since January 2020 - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
The Russian central bank’s gold reserves fell to 73.2 million ounces. Over seven months, their value decreased by $33.7 billion.
Russia's gold reserves have fallen to their lowest level since January 2020. As of August 1, the Central Bank of Russia held 73.2 million ounces of gold, 1.6 million ounces less than at the beginning of the year. Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to data published by the central bank on Thursday, Russia's bullion reserves had fallen by 1.6 million ounces since the beginning of the year, to 73.2 million ounces as of August 1. This is the lowest figure since January 2020
As a result, according to the available data, the value of the bank's gold reserves decreased by $33.7 billion over seven months.
The Bank of Russia was once the world's largest sovereign gold buyer, purchasing a significant share of the country's production before suspending acquisitions in early 2020. Two years later, its pledge to resume purchases helped absorb some of the supplies that the country was trying to export amid sanctions imposed over its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but the bank never resumed large-scale purchases
According to the publication, the central bank began reducing its gold reserves last year as the Ministry of Finance "sold precious metals and foreign currency from the National Wealth Fund to help cover the budget deficit caused by declining energy revenues."
Under the so-called mirror mechanism, the central bank conducts matching operations in the domestic market to offset the impact of these government transactions on the ruble and the financial system
To remind you
The Central Bank of Russia sold 21.8 tonnes of gold to cover the budget deficit. Reserves are declining due to falling oil revenues and high military spending.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The attack followed an air raid alert issued in the city earlier in the day due to the threat of incoming drones.
Additionally, the Supernova+ Telegram channel reported preliminary information suggesting that a vessel caught fire following the strike on the port.
Official Russian authorities have not yet commented on the incident or provided details on potential damage or casualties.
Refinery and logistics strikes in Samara
The attack on Yeysk coincided with drone strikes targeting infrastructure in Russia’s Samara region early Saturday morning.
A drone strike caused a fire at the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery, a Rosneft facility with a design capacity of approximately 8.8 million tons of oil per year.
Simultaneously, reports emerged on social media regarding an attack on a major fulfillment center belonging to the e-commerce company Ozon in Samara. Video footage purportedly showed the moment of impact, with subsequent reports indicating an ongoing fire at the 75,000-square-meter facility, which is one of the largest in Ozon’s federal network.
Russia’s Shopping Mall Strike on Zelensky’s Hometown Kills 15, Injures 130 as Rescue Continues
Ozon is one of Russia’s two largest online marketplaces, alongside Wildberries. Together, they controlled 77% of all marketplace orders in the country in 2024.
Campaign against Russian e-commerce
The reported strike on the Ozon facility follows a sustained, month-long campaign targeting the logistics infrastructure of its main competitor, Wildberries.
Ukraine began targeting Wildberries infrastructure on July 18. Over the subsequent month, at least 22 of the marketplace’s warehouses were hit, representing the loss of about 2.395 million square meters of warehouse space, or 43% of the company’s total capacity.
The most significant recent strike occurred on Aug. 16, which completely destroyed the company’s 230,000-square-meter complex in Koledino (Podolsk), reportedly Wildberries’ largest hub. Analysts estimated that goods worth 78 billion rubles ($918 million) were destroyed in that single fire.
As of mid-August, analysts from Data Insight and the Association of Suppliers of Goods for Trading on Electronic Platforms estimated the total value of goods destroyed across all affected Wildberries warehouses to be between $5.2 billion and $8.2 billion.
Recent operations had disabled seven of Wildberries’ 10 largest logistics centers, asserting that the marketplace is a legitimate military target because dual-use items have been available for purchase on the platform.

Albanese: Canberra to join Australia’s gun buy-back programme after Bondi attack
Australia’ capital territory, home of the capital Canberra, has agreed to a scheme which will tighten checks for gun licences and crack down on hate
Australia’s capital will join a gun buy-back as part of a response to a shooting spree that killed 15 at a Jewish festival in Sydney, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Saturday.
Albanese’s centre-left government enacted laws in January for the gun buy-back, tighter checks for gun licences and a crackdown on hate in the wake of the December 14 gun attack at a Bondi Beach Hanukkah celebration in Sydney, the capital of New South Wales.
The state, Australia’s most populous, became the first to commit to the plan, which will launch on November 2.
The Australian Capital Territory, home of the national capital Canberra, has agreed to a similar scheme in an effort to make sure “an antisemitic terrorist attack like we saw at Bondi can’t happen again”, Albanese said.
“I thank the ACT Government for their collaboration as we work to take guns off our streets in order to better protect Australians,” he said in a statement.
The ACT has 23,000 guns and more than 7,000 firearms licence holders, the statement said. It did not say when the ACT buy-back would begin. Albanese’s office did not immediately respond to a request for details.

Storms and gales hit Poland: homes flooded, trees down and thousands of emergency callouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:36:38 UTC
18:36:38 KST

Night storms hit residents in many parts of Poland. Firefighters responded over 4,000 times; 12 scout camps were evacuated as a precaution amid floods and power cuts.
Across the country, firefighters are battling to deal with the weather front moving across Poland. Since midnight they have already responded to more than 4,000 call-outs to remove fallen trees, secure damaged roofs and pump water from flooded streets and buildings, the State Fire Service reported at 10:00 on Saturday.
Due to the forecast weather conditions, 12 scout camps have also been evacuated as a precaution. "Participants and staff have been taken to permanent buildings" - Brigadier Karol Kroć from the State Fire Service told the Polish Press Agency. He stressed that so far there have been no reports of injuries.
By midnight, eight camps had been evacuated: one each in Lower Silesia and Małopolska, two in Mazovia, two in Wielkopolska and two in Warmia and Masuria. After midnight a further four camps had to be evacuated in Łódź Voivodeship.
Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that, in view of the strong gales and the meteorological situation, the Territorial Defence Forces remain on heightened alert to support public administration and emergency services in dealing with the effects of dangerous weather phenomena.
Most flooding in Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship
According to the duty officer at the Provincial Fire Service Command in Toruń, in the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship firefighters were most often called out to pump water from basements, properties and streets. There were far fewer interventions involving fallen trees and branches.
In Łódź Voivodeship firefighters mainly dealt with the effects of strong winds - fallen trees and broken branches. There were also several instances of water being pumped out, but no roofs were torn off. "It wasn't tragic, but reports are still coming in" - said the duty officer at the Provincial Crisis Management Centre in Łódź.
The situation is also difficult because of power cuts. Around 19,400 households are without electricity. The largest numbers of customers without supply are in the Tomaszów Mazowiecki area - around 5,500, Zgierz - 4,400, and Piotrków Trybunalski - 3,200.
Storms and strong winds in Wielkopolska
In Wielkopolska, overnight storms and heavy rainfall mainly caused trees to be toppled and local flooding of properties and basements.
In Warmia and Masuria firefighters recorded more than 90 call-outs related to heavy rain and strong winds. Most interventions involved pumping water from flooded roads, properties and basements.
Łyna exceeds warning level
The overnight rainfall, which locally reached as much as 90 mm, also affected water levels. The Regional Water Management Authority (RZGW) in Białystok reported that at the Olsztyn-Kortowo gauge the level of the Łyna river exceeded the warning level of 160 cm by 5 cm.
In the Bartąg area, water overtopped the embankments and then spread over wasteland and into the so-called encircling ditch. Allotment gardens in Olsztyn were also flooded. According to the RZGW, the situation on the Łyna is now beginning to stabilise and the water level is gradually falling. Services continue to monitor the state of the river.
In Mazovia the highest number of interventions were recorded by firefighters in Warsaw and the districts of Piaseczno, Grójec, Pruszków and Wołomin. "Reports are still coming in" - said Brigadier Łukasz Darmofalski of the Mazovian fire service.
Call for caution
Because of the strong wind, Kampinos National Park has appealed to residents and tourists to exercise particular caution. "Avoid open spaces and places exposed to the wind. During strong gusts, do not stop under trees" - the statement reminded. Before setting off on the trails, people were also advised to check the latest forecasts and weather warnings.
Due to the weather, the gardens of the Wilanów Palace Museum and the Royal Łazienki Park in Warsaw, as well as Warsaw Zoo, have been closed until further notice.
On Saturday the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management issued warnings for storms in the southwest of the country and strong winds in the Podlaskie, Mazovian, Łódź and Warmian-Masurian Voivodeships. Strong gusts of wind are also still occurring in the Warmian-Masurian, Pomeranian, Świętokrzyskie and Lublin Voivodeships.

"Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walkbacks of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement on X.

U.S., Canada fail to reach trade deal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:32:09 CST
18:32:09 KST

WASHINGTON/OTTAWA, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- The United States and Canada failed to reach a trade deal on Friday, and the White House said that it would impose 50-percent tariffs on certain imports from Canada on Saturday.
Meanwhile, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada would retaliate on the new tariffs.
Carney said Canada has suspended trade negotiations with the United States and recalled its negotiators to Ottawa, following new tariff threats from Washington.
The decision was made after last-minute changes proposed by the U.S. side were deemed "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," he said in a statement.
The United States imposed a 50-percent tariff on 20 billion U.S. dollars' worth of Canadian goods on Saturday that came into effect just after midnight (0400 GMT).
In response to the U.S. measure, Carney said Canada will match those tariffs "dollar for dollar" to protect its workers and businesses.
In the coming days, the government will introduce additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses, building on the nearly 25 billion dollars in support provided over the past 18 months, he said.
"Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walkbacks of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement on X.
"In addition, Canada is continuing to maintain its prolonged retaliation against the United States, including, among other things, flat-out prohibitions on certain American goods and services," he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed three proclamations on July 20 to impose additional 50-percent tariffs on certain goods from Canada in response to Canada's "discriminatory treatment of American products."
The collapse in negotiations marked a sharp reversal from three days earlier. Trump said late Tuesday that the tariffs scheduled to take effect Wednesday were paused for three days, and that the United States and Canada had reached a deal pending the finalization of formal documents.
Carney later said in a statement that substantial progress has been made, "although there is important work still to be done."
The rift comes as the United States, Mexico and Canada are trying to renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), a trade agreement that Trump negotiated in his first term and once praised as a triumph.
The United States has begun formal talks with Mexico to revamp the agreement, but talks with Canada have not yet begun.
The USMCA is a trilateral trade pact that replaced NAFTA when it took effect on July 1, 2020. On July 1, 2026, the United States officially declined to renew the agreement for another 16-year term, triggering an annual review process until the pact expires in 2036. ■

Mainland Chinese research ship spotted near Taiwan’s largest naval base
The Tong Ji, operated by a Shanghai university, has a range of advanced equipment and can collect data that may have military uses
A mainland Chinese research ship has sailed close to a key Taiwanese naval base, marking its third appearance near the island since May.
The Tong Ji is a 2,000-tonne scientific research vessel operated by Tongji University in Shanghai. It was spotted 28 nautical miles (52km) southwest of Liuqiu, an island also known as Lamay, on Friday morning, according to the Taiwanese authorities.
Liuqiu sits off the southwest coast of Taiwan’s main island, close to the city of Kaohsiung – home to Taiwan’s naval academy and largest naval base.
The Taiwanese coastguard said they sent ships to monitor the Tong Ji’s movements and broadcast warnings ordering it to leave. They said the vessel had sailed away to the southeast.
On Thursday night, it had been spotted about 25 nautical miles northwest of Hua islet in the central Taiwan Strait. A coastguard vessel sent to shadow the mainland ship tried to force it to change course.
Commissioned in 2025, the Tong Ji is an advanced research ship designed for a wide range of scientific and engineering operations, including surveys, environmental monitoring and offshore engineering work, according to its operators.
In particular, the vessel can deploy remotely operated underwater and surface vessels and is equipped with a range of acoustic equipment, including a variety of sonar systems.

Pollard sets out plan for UK to win NATO manufacturing work
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:30:10 BST
18:30:10 KST

The Ministry of Defence is working through a series of NATO mechanisms to secure British industrial benefit from the alliance’s push to expand collective manufacturing capacity, Luke Pollard has told Parliament in a written answer.
The Minister of State for Defence was responding to James Cartlidge, the Conservative MP for South Suffolk, who asked what steps the department is taking to ensure UK defence manufacturers benefit from the new NATO commitment.
Mr Pollard said the department is “leveraging NATO mechanisms, including the Defence Production Action Plan, the NATO Defence Industrial Production Board, and the Innovation Scale-Up Package, to boost an aggregated demand, improve interoperability, strengthen supply chain resilience, and provide clearer long-term demand signals to industry.”
He said the Defence Industrial Strategy and the Defence Investment Plan reinforce that approach by supporting collaborative programmes with allies, listing deep precision strike, air defence, autonomous systems, munitions production, future combat air and anti-submarine warfare.
Those programmes, he said, help British firms “access new export and multinational procurement opportunities and take advantage of the shift to ‘always on production’.”
The phrase points at what has become the central problem of European rearmament, defence manufacturing has historically worked to intermittent orders, with production lines opened for a batch and then closed, an arrangement that keeps peacetime costs down but leaves no capacity to surge when demand rises. The war in Ukraine demonstrated how long it takes to reverse that, particularly in artillery ammunition, where output could not be raised quickly because plants had closed, tooling had been scrapped and specialist suppliers had left the sector.
Aggregated demand is the mechanism NATO is using to address it. If several allies commit to buying the same equipment on a predictable schedule, a manufacturer can justify investing in capacity that no single national order would support, and smaller states gain access to production they could not sustain alone.
The commercial question for British firms is whether they end up as prime contractors on those programmes or as suppliers into consortia led from elsewhere. European Union funding instruments for defence production have generally restricted or discounted participation by non-member states, and Britain’s access to them has been the subject of negotiation since 2024, which is part of why the answer emphasises NATO mechanisms rather than EU ones.
Mr Cartlidge served as Minister for Defence Procurement in the previous government and now shadows the defence brief.

Government still weighing decision on restricting proxy voters, Hong Kong official says
Proposed changes to law on buildings management meant to combat bid-rigging but limits to proxy votes could be too strict, home affairs director says
Hong Kong authorities have yet to decide whether to restrict proxy voters at homeowners’ meetings to relatives or other flat owners of the same estate under proposed law amendments meant to combat bid-rigging, the home affairs director has said, arguing such a move could be overly strict.
Director of Home Affairs Priscilla To Kit-lai said on Saturday the proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance were aimed at enhancing the legitimacy of proxy votes amid concerns that voting results could be manipulated by a minority.
But she said the government had yet to decide whether proxy holders should be limited to the owners’ relatives or other owners in the same estate.
“For example, an elderly person living alone might have a familiar friend in a different housing estate who helps the person – that’s acceptable now,” she said on a television programme.
“But it might not be possible if we add proposed restrictions. We need to see if society feels this is too strict.”
Issues of building management and owner governance came under intense scrutiny during an independent committee hearing looking into the cause of the devastating fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po that killed 168 people last November, with testimonies alleging bid-rigging and proxy vote collection.
In a consultation document released earlier this month, authorities laid out five major directions for proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance, which regulates incorporated ownership in buildings.

Number of electric cars in Belarus up by 15,000 in January-July 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:27:00 UTC
18:27:00 KST

MINSK, 22 August (BelTA) – How the Belarusian nuclear power plant contributes to the development of electric transport was described to journalists by Belarusian Energy Minister Denis Moroz during the electric vehicle rally BelNPP – Clean Energy of Peaceful Atom, BelTA has learned.
The Belarusian nuclear power plant satisfies about 40% of the country’s total demand for electricity. So far it has generated more than 65.5 billion kWh of electricity. This result allows replacing the consumption of natural gas and thereby reducing the foreign currency burden on the Belarusian economy.
The construction of the nuclear power plant became one of the factors that gave momentum to the development of electric transport in the country. “The emergence of a reliable and stable source of electricity allowed working out approaches that stimulate the development of electric transport. Today more than 65,000 electric vehicles drive on the roads of Belarus. Compared to the same period of last year the indicator has almost doubled,” the energy minister said.
At the beginning of 2026 there were about 50,000 electric vehicles in the country. In more than six months their number grew by approximately 15,000.
The energy minister added: “The development of electric transport provides not only additional driving comfort, reduces noise and environmental burden, but also allows increasing the total economic effect: fuel consumption is reduced, which means the foreign currency burden on the economy decreases.”
In his words, Belarus is one of the leaders in the post-Soviet space in terms of the number of electric vehicles per capita. The country is also supposed to increase the fleet of electric vehicles to 300,000 by 2030 or to about 10% of the total number of automobiles.
Charging infrastructure is developing at the same time. “Just a few years ago Belarus had about 1,000 electric vehicle charging stations with a fleet of approximately 10,000-12,000 electric vehicles. Today there are already more than 65,000 electric vehicles, and the number of charging stations exceeds 2,700,” the minister said.
Since the beginning of 2026 the network has increased by approximately 500 stations. By 2030 the total number of electric vehicle charging stations is supposed to rise to 15,000.
“To ensure genuine comfort of traveling by electric vehicles, it is necessary to develop charging infrastructure not only within population centers, but also along motorways. Today charging stations are installed at almost all Belorusneft gas stations. Their number is not sufficient yet. Their workload is particularly high on weekends. However, there are state programs for the development of charging infrastructure, which include attracting additional operators. They will develop charging infrastructure on highways and install fast and super-fast charging stations,” Denis Moroz concluded.
The BelNPP – Clean Energy of the Peaceful Atom event is aimed at promoting Belarus’ achievements in nuclear power engineering, the role of the Belarusian nuclear power plant in developing eco-friendly segments of the economy, including electric vehicles. The event was organized by the Energy Ministry in partnership with the Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom with support from the Minsk City Executive Committee and the Ostrovets District Executive Committee.

U.S. Navy awards second CHAOS contract for cheap missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:26:24 UTC
18:26:24 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Zone 5 Technologies a $65 million contract to build a maritime strike variant of its Rusty Dagger cruise missile under the CHAOS program.
- The award follows a $70 million CHAOS contract the Navy gave CoAspire in July for its RAACM-ER maritime missile.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Zone 5 Technologies a $65 million contract to build a maritime strike variant of its AGM-188 Rusty Dagger cruise missile under a new program aimed at fielding low-cost precision weapons for the U.S. and its allies.
The award is an Other Transaction Agreement, a contracting mechanism the Pentagon uses to move faster than traditional acquisition rules allow. CMG Networks brokered the deal on behalf of the Naval Aviation Systems Consortium. Under the agreement, Zone 5 will design, build, test, and deliver a CHAOS-specific version of the Rusty Dagger for the Navy’s Coalition Heterogeneous Affordable Offensive Strike program, which is intended to field affordable, scalable precision strike weapons against land targets and moving maritime targets.
“Zone 5 is proud to partner with the Navy on CHAOS and deliver industry-best scalable maritime strike capabilities to the U.S. and our allies,” said Thomas Akers, CEO of Zone 5 Technologies.
Zone 5 is working on the effort with PAE Munitions and its Precision Strike Weapons program office, PMX-201, the company said. Zone 5 said it will draw on its experience fielding precision strike weapons across multiple service branches and international partners to provide a strike capability it described as credible, affordable, and scalable.
The award is the second CHAOS contract the Navy has issued for a low-cost maritime strike missile. In July, the Navy selected CoAspire for a $70 million agreement to develop a ground-launched maritime variant of its Rapidly Adaptable Affordable Cruise Missile-Extended Range, known as RAACM-ER, which has a claimed range of about 1,800 km (1,120 miles).
The Rusty Dagger, designated AGM-188A by the U.S. Air Force, originated as a low-cost cruise missile developed for the Air Force’s Extended Range Attack Munition program, which began in 2024 to address long-range strike requirements tied to Ukraine. The missile falls in the 200 kg (450 pound) weight class, including a roughly 45 kg (100 pound) warhead, and is powered by a single PBS Aerospace TJ80 turbojet engine. Its air-launched range is reported to exceed 930 km (500 nautical miles) at high subsonic speed. The missile is built within the size and weight envelope of a Mk 82 general-purpose bomb, allowing it to be carried by aircraft already equipped to drop that weapon.
The Rusty Dagger has already seen combat use. Zone 5 has said the missile is in production for Ukraine’s Air Force, and reporting on Russian territory has documented missile debris linked to Zone 5 through a recovered guidance antenna. The Air Force has separately selected Rusty Dagger for its Family of Affordable Mass Munitions program, which called for producing more than 1,000 units in its first year of production, according to Zone 5. The Air Force’s proposed fiscal 2027 budget outlined plans to buy nearly 28,000 Family of Affordable Mass Munitions rounds over five years. The Air Force Research Laboratory separately awarded Zone 5 a $12 million contract in June 2026 to develop manufacturing technology intended to scale Rusty Dagger production, with work centered in Miamisburg, Ohio.
Zone 5 Technologies, based in San Luis Obispo, California, was acquired by Norway’s Kongsberg and now operates as a Kongsberg company. The company describes itself as an aerospace engineering and production firm focused on modular, open-architecture counter-UAS interceptors and affordable ground- and air-launched effects. Founded in 2011, Zone 5 employs more than 500 engineers, technicians, and support staff, with manufacturing operations in California, Texas, and Ohio.

US, Iran trade threats as Washington prepares new sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:17:00 UTC
18:17:00 KST

The United States and Iran traded defiant messages ahead of Monday’s expected announcement of new U.S. economic sanctions targeting Iran and potentially key trading partners such as China.
Nearly six months into the war, the two sides were no longer exchanging fire but had made little progress toward peace talks. Meanwhile, oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have virtually halted as Tehran seeks to preserve its leverage by threatening to strike unauthorized tankers attempting to pass through the strategic waterway.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scheduled to hold a news conference at 2:00 p.m. EDT (6:00 p.m. GMT) Monday, when he is expected to unveil what Washington has described as “the toughest sanctions in history” against Iran and urge China to cooperate with the United States.
China buys more than 80% of Iran’s seaborne oil exports, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. Beijing has called for diplomacy and a negotiated resolution.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Saturday that the expected U.S. sanctions announcement amounted to an “assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations.”
“Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law,” he said in a post on X.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who has warned of economic consequences for any country that provides “any type of lifeline to Iran,” said Friday that Washington was watching “what happens” in the conflict.
“They would love to make a deal, but they’re not ready to make the right deal, in my opinion,” Trump said of Iran.
While the U.S. has effectively blockaded Iranian vessels in their ports, the Strait of Hormuz remained bottled up, with thousands of seafarers stranded on hundreds of vessels. Only four commodity ships sailed through the strait Thursday, none of them large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers, according to ship-tracking data.
However, Iran has granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported Saturday.
IRNA said obtaining special permission for Iraqi tankers was one of Baghdad’s main requests during Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf’s visit to Iraq.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the U.S. military helped move a seven-day average of 8 million barrels of oil a day through the strait. That is down from more than 20 million barrels a day before the war, or about one of every five barrels consumed worldwide.
U.S. attacks have severely damaged Iran’s economy and devastated its navy and air force, but Tehran maintains enough missile and drone capabilities to impede oil tanker traffic and attack regional rivals.
Trump, meanwhile, has yet to achieve objectives he set at the start of the war, such as dismantling Iran’s nuclear program. The status of the program remains uncertain because U.N. inspectors have been shut out since 2025. Trump has also sought to create conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.
Thousands have been killed, including 168 Iranian schoolchildren on the first day of the war. The U.S. has reported more than 750 military personnel wounded and 18 killed.
The chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, promised Friday that Iran would respond to enemy threats militarily with “crushing, punishing and devastating responses.”
Still, President Masoud Pezeshkian called for a diplomatic solution.
“It would be better to end the war today, when we are powerful and have dignity, and the whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America, contrary to all regulations, attacked our schools, hospitals and infrastructure and is hated in the world,” Pezeshkian said, according to the ISNA news agency.
Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, the country’s main negotiator in mediated talks with the U.S., acknowledged the strain on Iran’s economy in comments to Iranian and Iraqi businesspeople late Thursday.
“No matter how much military power we have, we won’t survive if people are hungry and we don’t have financial turnover, economic growth and national production,” Qalibaf said, according to the official IRNA news agency.

DRC gets 16,520 Ebola vaccine doses amid deadly outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:16:00 UTC
18:16:00 KST

The Democratic Republic of Congo has received its first shipment of more than 16,000 doses of an Ebola vaccine as authorities race to contain an outbreak that has killed more than 2,500 people and is spreading rapidly across six provinces.
A batch of 16,520 doses of the Ervebo vaccine arrived in Kinshasa late Friday, Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said, with more than 50,000 additional doses expected by Monday.
“These doses would strengthen the government’s response to Ebola and contribute to the protection of populations, with the support of our partners,” Kamba told reporters at Kinshasa airport.
The World Health Organization said Thursday that 70,000 doses of Ervebo would be supplied to Congo from the global Ebola vaccine stockpile. Of those, 20,000 doses will be used in a Phase 3 clinical trial examining whether the vaccine can protect against the strain responsible for the current outbreak, while 50,000 will be administered to frontline and health workers.
The vaccine, developed by Merck and manufactured in Germany, is licensed and recommended for outbreaks caused by the Zaire strain of Ebola. The current outbreak, however, is being driven by the Bundibugyo strain, for which no vaccine or specific treatment has yet been approved.
Scientists do not yet know whether Ervebo provides protection against Bundibugyo. Early evidence, including animal studies, suggests it could offer some cross-protection, prompting WHO experts this month to recommend a large-scale human trial.
Kamba said Ervebo has been used extensively in previous Ebola outbreaks, including during the major epidemic that struck Congo and neighboring countries between 2018 and 2020.
“This vaccine has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak,” he said.
The latest outbreak, Congo’s 17th, was officially declared May 15 but is believed to have been spreading for weeks before that. It has reached 56 health zones across Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo provinces, many of which face severe health care shortages, limited government presence and persistent insecurity involving armed groups.
The Health Ministry’s latest situation update puts the number of confirmed infections at 5,290, including more than 2,500 deaths.
The outbreak is showing no signs of slowing. Julien Harneis, the United Nations’ senior Ebola coordinator, warned Friday that the epidemic is “growing exponentially.”
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, also warned that communities affected by the outbreak are not receiving enough support to contain the virus.
The group said training for health workers and community leaders must be urgently expanded, particularly on detecting suspected cases, referring patients and preventing and controlling infections within communities.
The uncertainty surrounding the Bundibugyo strain has increased the urgency of developing targeted vaccines. Two candidates are already in clinical trials, one developed by U.S.-based Moderna using mRNA technology and another by the University of Oxford in Britain.
A separate vaccine known as rVSV Bundibugyo is also being developed by Singapore-based Hilleman Laboratories and has been described by WHO as the most promising candidate specifically targeting the strain.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids and can cause severe fever and other life-threatening symptoms. The disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past five decades.

Canada vows 'dollar for dollar' response as US imposes 50% tariffs
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:14:46 EEST
18:14:46 KST

Canada has suspended trade negotiations with the United States and promised matching retaliation after Washington imposed 50% tariffs on about $20bn of Canadian goods following the collapse of talks between the two countries.
Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the decision shortly before the US tariff deadline expired on Friday night.
The new duties took effect at 12.01am Eastern Time on Saturday and cover goods that do not receive preferential treatment under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The affected trade represents about 5% of Canadian exports to the United States.
Carney said Canada would respond “dollar for dollar” and ordered Canadian negotiators to return to Ottawa.
“Last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal,” Carney said in a statement.
He said negotiators had made progress but had failed to secure terms that met Canada’s objectives. Ottawa plans further measures to support workers and businesses affected by the tariffs.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer blamed Canada for the breakdown.
“Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week,” Greer said in a statement.
He accused Canada of introducing new demands and reversing earlier commitments. Greer described the failure to reach an agreement as a “missed opportunity”.
A senior Trump administration official said that Canada had sought further concessions on steel, aluminium, vehicles and softwood lumber. The official said no further negotiations were scheduled.
The two governments had spent three days in talks in Washington after US President Donald Trump extended an earlier tariff deadline.
According to Reuters, negotiators had discussed reductions in existing US duties on Canadian steel, aluminium and vehicles. The BBC reported that talks included proposals to cut steel and aluminium tariffs from 50% to 25% and vehicle tariffs from 25% to 15%.
Canada had also faced US demands concerning dairy access, retaliatory vehicle tariffs and restrictions imposed by Canadian provinces on sales of American alcohol.
The latest tariffs cover a range of Canadian products, including dairy products, clothing, cement, industrial machinery and hockey equipment among those affected.
Existing US tariffs already apply to Canadian steel, aluminium, vehicles and lumber.
The United States and Canada exchanged about $880bn in goods and services last year.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford backed Carney’s decision and called for a matching response to the US measures.
“The prime minister has my full support for a strong response – tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar,” Ford wrote on X.
Business groups on both sides of the border have warned that higher duties will raise costs and affect supply chains.
The US Chamber of Commerce said this week that higher tariffs would increase costs for US households and put jobs linked to North American trade at risk.

Terrorists kill, kidnap worshippers during Friday prayers in Nigeria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:13:00 UTC
18:13:00 KST

Terrorists attacked two villages in central Nigeria’s Niger State during Friday prayers, killing and kidnapping an unknown number of people before a rival militant group intervened and triggered a clash that allowed some residents to escape, survivors and a lawmaker told AFP on Saturday.
The attack took place Friday in Dikera village and nearby Binzi in Borgu Local Government Area, an area in western Niger state near Nigeria’s borders with Kebbi and Kwara states and neighboring Benin. The region has faced growing attacks by armed groups operating across the porous borders of Nigeria’s northwestern states and the Sahel.
Jibril Ahmad, a survivor of the attack in Dikera, said hundreds of fighters belonging to the Lakurawa militant group stormed the village shortly after worshippers finished Friday prayers.
“Soon after finishing the normal Friday prayer, the armed group of Lakuwara, in their hundreds, wielding guns, knives and machetes, began to attack us,” Ahmad told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
He said the attackers killed some residents while accusing them of failing to follow what the militants described as the “true teachings.”
Federal lawmaker Jafaru Mohammed, who represents the area, confirmed that Binzi was also attacked. He said numerous people were killed and many others were abducted and taken into surrounding forests, including areas toward Kainji Lake.
The victims reportedly included young men and heads of households. Local accounts also said a chief imam and a village head who had recently been released from captivity were among those abducted.
The exact death toll and number of people taken remained unclear Saturday. Ahmad and Mohammed could not provide a precise figure, while Niger state police said they were aware that worshippers had been kidnapped but had not received reports of deaths at the time of their initial statement.
Police also said difficult terrain and poor roads were complicating efforts to reach the affected communities and mount rescue operations.
The violence took an unexpected turn when fighters from another militant faction, known as Mahmuda or Mamudawa, confronted the Lakurawa attackers.
Ahmad said many residents managed to flee while Lakurawa fighters were occupied fighting their rivals.
Mohammed said Mahmuda members intervened after learning about the assault and clashed with Lakurawa because of differences between the two groups. The confrontation gave some villagers an opportunity to escape, although many others were already being led into nearby forests.
Lakurawa, also spelled Lakuwara or Lukarawa, is a relatively shadowy Terrorist organization that has operated in northwestern Nigeria and across parts of the Sahel. Researchers have linked the group to Daesh Sahel Province, which operates in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
The group first emerged in communities along Nigeria’s northwestern border around 2017 and initially presented itself in some areas as a force against banditry. It has since developed into a militant organization accused of imposing strict religious rules, carrying out attacks, seizing livestock and abducting civilians.
Nigerian authorities designated Lakurawa a terrorist organization in late 2024. Its activities have added another layer to a security crisis already involving Terrorists, criminal gangs and armed groups operating in remote forests.
Mahmuda is another militant faction that has operated in the region. Nigerian authorities claimed in 2025 that they had dismantled Mahmuda and the related Ansaru group following arrests of senior members. Reports of Mahmuda fighters taking part in Friday’s clash, however, suggest that elements of the group remain active or that its networks have survived earlier operations.
The attack highlights the increasingly fragmented nature of Nigeria’s long-running insurgency.
Nigeria has battled Terrorist violence for roughly 17 years, with the conflict initially concentrated in the northeast, where Boko Haram and Daesh West Africa Province have carried out attacks, mass kidnappings and other abuses.
Mass abductions became one of the conflict’s defining tactics, most notoriously in 2014, when Boko Haram kidnapped hundreds of schoolgirls from the northeastern town of Chibok.
The violence has since spread beyond the northeast as Terrorist factions, criminal gangs and Sahel-based militants have exploited weak security, porous borders and vast forested areas where government forces have limited reach.
Niger state and neighboring areas have become increasingly vulnerable as armed groups move through border communities and use remote forests as hideouts. The security situation has also been complicated by instability in the wider Sahel, including the 2023 military coup in neighboring Niger, which disrupted established regional security arrangements.

Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:10:17 UTC

Breadcrumb
Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack
Somali pirates hijacked an oil products tanker off Yemen, a Somali maritime security official said, the latest in a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.
Six armed pirates hijacked the Eritrean-flagged M.T. Sibu 1 on Thursday about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometers) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen, and took it toward Somalia’s Puntland coast, the official, who has knowledge of the incident, told The Associated Press on Friday.
He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not allowed to discuss the matter publicly.
The Sibu 1, managed by the UAE-based Qatrat Alnada Almasi Ship Management, was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department last year for allegedly belonging to an Iranian “shadow fleet” used to transport petroleum products seeking to evade U.S. sanctions.
The tanker had 20 crew members aboard: 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese, and one Iraqi. The nationality of one crew member was not immediately known. The vessel’s previous port of departure and intended destination remained unclear.
The hijacking came three days after pirates seized the Lutuf, a Cameroon-flagged general cargo vessel, off Somalia’s coast. The vessel had 10 crew aboard, including six Indians, a Turkish national, a Georgian national and two Serbian security guards, according to maritime tracking reports.
The Sibu 1 is the sixth commercial vessel hijacked by Somali pirates since April 21, when the Palau-flagged tanker Honor 25 was seized off Somalia. Pirates later seized the Sward on April 26, the Eureka on May 2, the Asana on July 17 and the Lutuf on Aug. 17.
The attacks have occurred increasingly far from Somalia’s coastline, including the hijacking of the Eureka while anchored off Yemen and the Asana about 65 nautical miles (120 kilometers) southwest of al-Mukalla.
The International Maritime Bureau recorded 38 piracy and armed robbery incidents worldwide during the first half of 2026, including five hijackings. Somali pirates accounted for 94% of crew members taken hostage during that period, the bureau said.
Puntland’s Security Ministry said Friday that its investigations indicated that forces beyond Puntland’s control were behind the renewed piracy, but did not identify any group or country. The claim could not be independently verified.
Puntland said it had deployed security forces along its coast and condemned airstrikes that it said struck fishing vessels and property near coastal communities where hijacked ships were being held. It called on the countries involved to explain strikes near Garacad on Aug. 18 and Aug. 20.
The ministry did not identify who carried out the strikes, and the allegations could not be independently confirmed.

Former EU Commissioner Siim Kallas dies at 77
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:09:46 UTC
18:09:46 KST

BRUSSELS — Former Estonian Prime Minister and European Commissioner Siim Kallas has died at the age of 77.
“It is with sadness that I must announce that my dear father, Siim Kallas, passed away last night,” posted EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas on Instagram.
The Estonian politician was the country’s first ever European commissioner, starting from 2004. He took up the economic and monetary affairs post under then-European Commission President José Manuel Barroso, and later served as vice-president and transport commissioner from 2010 to 2014.
Advertisement
An economist by training, Kallas started his career as president of the Bank of Estonia in 1991, where he was one of the principal architects of the country’s monetary reform. In 1994, he founded the liberal-democratic Reform Party and was elected to the Estonian parliament the following year, when he became foreign affairs minister.
Kallas was also an important figure in the Baltic country’s European trajectory: After his appointment as foreign minister, he oversaw Estonia’s bid to join the EU. He was prime minister in 2002, when the country concluded negotiations to become a member and was invited to join NATO.
“I think of courage required to rebuild a state and introduce its own currency in the early 1990s, as well as the quiet conviction he brought with him to Brussels,” wrote European Parliament Roberta Metsola on social media in response to the news. “Estonia and Europe are better because of his life’s work.”
“Through his public career, [Kallas] helped shape Estonia’s EU path and key European policies,” stated the Commission.
His daughter, Kaja Kallas, was Estonia’s youngest-ever serving prime minister, holding office from 2021 to 2024. She is now the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs for Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s second term.

Rhodope narrow-gauge railway: 100 years of magic on the rails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:05:26 UTC
18:05:26 KST

Saturday 22 August 2026 11:25
Saturday, 22 August 2026, 11:25
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Some trains carry passengers. Others carry stories, emotions and memories. The Rhodope narrow-gauge railway is one of them. For a century now, it has been running between Septemvri and Dobrinishte, crossing the Rila, Rhodope and Pirin mountains and turning every journey into an encounter with a different Bulgaria — beautiful, peaceful and seemingly untouched by time.
August 1 marked 100 years since the first train set off on the Septemvri–Velingrad section — the beginning of a journey that today is not merely a railway line, but a true legend. To mark the anniversary, Bulgarian State Railways (BDZ) is preparing to restore a narrow-gauge steam locomotive, which will once again pull special trains along the iconic route.
- St. George’s Day in Yakoruda – a romantic journey on the narrow-gauge railway
- Narrow-gauge train in the Rhodopes tops The Guardian’s 10 best scenic rail journeys in Europe
We spoke about the magic of the narrow-gauge railway, its history, and its future with Kristian Vaklinov, chairman of the Association “For the Narrow-Gauge Railway” — a man who has made the preservation of this unique railway his personal cause.
PHOTO Kristian Vaklinov
According to him, the reasons why the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway is so beloved go far beyond its stunning scenery.
“It is unique not only because it is the only remaining narrow-gauge railway in Bulgaria. It is unique because it connects people, lives and mountains. The beautiful scenery, tunnels, bridges and the railway itself turn the journey into an experience unlike any other in Bulgaria”, Kristian Vaklinov says
PHOTO bdz.bg
An engineering feat built by hand
The history of the narrow-gauge railway is a story of hard work, perseverance, and engineering daring. Construction began in 1921, and just five years later, the first 39 kilometres between Septemvri and Velingrad had been completed.
What remains remarkable to this day is that much of the route was built by hand, carved through the rocks of the Chepino Gorge, long before modern machinery made such projects easier.
“This is a true tribute to the people who built the railway. Some even devoted their lives to it without ever imagining that, a hundred years later, their work would continue to inspire so many people. The railway has 35 tunnels and over 1,000 metres of elevation gain, climbing to the highest railway station in the Balkans — Avramovo. The twists and turns of the route are another part of what attracts people from around the world, who come to admire what has been achieved. They come to see it with their own eyes, having read online that Bulgaria has this little train that has been winding its way through the mountains for 100 years”, the association’s chairman notes.
PHOTO bdz.bg
When slow speed becomes an advantage
In a world where we are all constantly rushing, the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway seems to offer the opposite — a chance to slow down.
Today, the train travels at an average speed of around 38 kilometres per hour — something that was once seen as a drawback but has now become one of its greatest attractions.
Instead of rushing toward your destination, you have time to look out the window, follow the winding rivers, count the tunnels, and admire the centuries-old forests and steep mountain slopes.
PHOTO bdz.bg
Tourists from around the world
In recent years, interest in the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway has been steadily growing. More and more tourists are choosing it as a unique way to explore the mountains.
What is particularly interesting is that an increasing number of passengers now come from different countries and continents specifically to experience the legendary little train.
According to Kristian Vaklinov, this is the clearest evidence that the narrow-gauge railway has long since evolved beyond its role as a simple means of transport and is gradually becoming one of Bulgaria’s most recognizable tourist attractions.
PHOTO bdz.bg
The steam locomotive – a long-awaited return
One of the most exciting developments surrounding the railway’s centenary is the upcoming restoration of the steam locomotive.
For many years, it was the hallmark of the special anniversary trains, and for many people, travelling behind it remains one of their most unforgettable experiences.
“A steam locomotive brings a different kind of emotion. For children, it is a true wonder, while for older people, it is a journey back to cherished memories. We are all eagerly looking forward to seeing it run on the rails again”, Vaklinov says.
PHOTO BGNES
The big dream
As the narrow-gauge railway celebrates its 100th anniversary, it is also looking to the future.
Kristian Vaklinov believes its enormous tourism potential is yet to be fully developed. His vision include more heritage trains, panoramic carriages, and themed tourist routes that would make the journey an even more memorable experience.
He is convinced that the railway deserves to be developed not merely as a means of transport, but as a national treasure and a symbol of Bulgaria’s natural beauty and engineering heritage.
PHOTO bdz.bg
A journey that stays in your heart
At the end of the conversation, Kristian Vaklinov extended an invitation to everyone who has yet to experience the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway:
“Get on this little train. It will not simply take you from one station to another; it will show you a different Bulgaria — one that we rarely get to see through a car window.”
And perhaps that is the great secret of the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway.
It does not impress with speed, luxurious carriages, or modern technology.
It impresses with soul.
For 100 years, this little train has tirelessly crossed the mountains, bringing people and generations together and proving that the most beautiful journeys are not always the fastest.
Sometimes, they are the journeys that make us slow down, look out the window, and remember that the beauty lies in the journey itself.
PHOTO bdz.bg
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov
