IndyCar drivers amazed at downtown DC course: ‘It’s stuff that you dream of’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:53:02 UTC
14:53:02 KST

IndyCar drivers amazed at downtown DC course: ‘It’s stuff that you dream of’
WASHINGTON (AP) — Even for well-traveled IndyCar drivers, a track with the U.S. Capitol in the background is a little awe inspiring.
“We get to race at a lot of cool cities, but this one is by far the best that we’ve ever had, and I can say that very truthfully,” Kyle Kirkwood said Friday. “Going by the Capitol building, the views here, all the architecture of all the buildings around here, all the museums, it’s stuff that you dream of.
“It’s a serious honor and privilege.”
This weekend’s Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the second big sporting event staged by President Donald Trump in Washington as part of the nation’s 250th birthday celebration. The first was a UFC fight card on the White House’s South Lawn in June.
IndyCar racing — an open-wheel counterpart to NASCAR — doesn’t have quite the same association with the right-wing “manosphere” or the MAGA movement, but series owner Roger Penske received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Trump in 2019 and led the effort to put together this race in the District of Columbia.
For the drivers, it’s a welcome moment in the spotlight.
“What’s been the coolest part of this week? Honestly, the media covering us,” Kirkwood said. “It’s cool to see IndyCar in this light. We don’t get these opportunities very often outside of the Indy 500, and to have an event that is sought after as much as the 500 is something that’s special.”
Washington has little history with high-level motorsports. In 2002, the parking lot at RFK Stadium on the city’s east side was transformed into a course for an American Le Mans Series event.
The Freedom 250 is downtown in one of D.C.'s prime tourist areas. If you’re not in a race car, it’s not the greatest weekend to be driving around the area given all the road closures, but if the weather holds up, the setting has the potential to be spectacular.
“As a boy from the Netherlands that just got his green card, it is really cool,” said Rinus VeeKay, who has six top-10 finishes this season. “We didn’t get too much U.S. history in school ... but learning so much about it here, seeing all the monuments and museums and just how every building kind of has a special purpose here around the city, is very cool. Getting to see the White House, this is stuff you see in movies.”
The White House is not part of the D.C. course, although after Turn 1, the track does include a lengthy straightaway along Pennsylvania Avenue, heading northwest away from the Capitol. Then there’s a sharp left turn between the National Archives and the main Justice Department building, followed by a couple quick 90-degree turns as the track navigates the city’s grid system.
After a straightaway takes drivers across the National Mall, they turn left onto Independence Avenue, passing the Smithsonian’s National Air & Space Museum. and the Eisenhower Memorial before heading north on 3rd Street to the finish line, which is just west of the Capitol.
“I think it’s more exciting when you actually get on the grounds and see what you’re about to do. I mean, when is this ever going to happen again?” said Josef Newgarden, a driver for Team Penske. “I hope it’s great visibility. That’s probably the biggest thing that it could bring to us — is visibility to people that aren’t maybe as familiar with IndyCar racing.”
IndyCar practice and qualifying are scheduled for Saturday, along with an IROC race. The IndyCar race is Sunday and set for 250 miles (147 laps) — the second-longest street circuit race in IndyCar history.
The 1.7-mile track includes seven turns in all. The Air & Space Museum and National Gallery of Art are both inside the course’s perimeter, with a fan zone between them. The track is shorter and has fewer turns than several others on the IndyCar schedule, but it’s not much different from the 1.6-mile, nine-turn circuit used in downtown Detroit.
“It’s short and snappy, but you know what? We don’t know. We haven’t driven on it yet,” driver Marcus Armstrong said. “We’ll find out tomorrow. It might even be wet tomorrow. There’s a lot of crosswalks, a lot of paint on the track, so that could be super slippery.”

Former Estonian Prime Minister, European Commission Vice-President Siim Kallas dead at 77
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:50:00 UTC
14:50:00 KST

Former Estonian Prime Minister, European Commission Vice-President Siim Kallas dead at 77
Estonian politician Siim Kallas, a former prime minister, foreign minister and vice president of the European Commission who also held several other senior positions, died overnight Friday into Saturday.
"It is with sadness that I must announce that my dear father, Siim Kallas, died last night," his daughter Kaja Kallas wrote on social media Saturday morning.
Kallas served as prime minister of Estonia from 2002 to 2003 and as European Commissioner from 2004 to 2014.
During the Soviet period, Kallas was a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. He was one of the authors of the IME plan for self-managing Estonia with Tiit Made, Edgar Savisaar and Mikk Titma. The plan proposed to make Estonia economically independent from the Soviet Union — adopting a market economy and establishing Estonia's own currency and tax system.
After Estonia restored its independence in 1991, Kallas was appointed the president of the Bank of Estonia, which at the time had only 11 employees.
Kallas entered politics in 1994 as one of the founders of liberal Estonian Reform Party, which was successful in the 1995 parliamentary elections. Kallas served as the minister of foreign affairs from 1995 to 1996. He later served as the minister of finance from 1999 to 2002.
He served as the European commissioner for transport between 2010 and 2014. Before that he was the European commissioner for administrative affairs, audit and anti-fraud between 2004 and 2009. In both Barroso Commissions he was also a vice-president.
After leaving the European Commission, Kallas ran in the Estonian presidential election in 2016, but was not elected. In October 2017, he started as the mayor of Viimsi Municipality. In 2019, he was elected member of the Riigikogu, a post he was also elected to in 2023. He resigned as MP and from politics in September 2024.
His daughter, Kaja Kallas, was the prime minister of Estonia from 2021 to 2024.
Politicians on Kallas
President Alar Karis expressed his condolences to Siim Kallas' family and loved ones, saying Kallas was a statesman who played an important role in shaping Estonia into the country it is today through bold, forward-looking goals and actions.
"The era of the Singing Revolution, the restoration of independence and the building of a free Estonia into a modern, European country needed precisely this kind of independent thinking and courage to act. Economic reforms, Estonia's accession to the European Union and NATO, the defense of freedoms — in all of this, we can see Siim Kallas' important role. He helped our country grow more confident, stronger and more European," he added.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) also expressed his condolences to the loved ones of Siim Kallas and said Kallas had been a role model for many.
"Siim Kallas was a role model for many people in the Reform Party. After all, he founded the party and his influence extended far beyond it," Michal told ERR on Saturday, describing Kallas as cheerful, well-read and someone who could offer advice on almost any subject. Michal, who joined the Reform Party as a young man and became its secretary-general while Kallas was chairman, said Kallas had been a major role model for his generation as well as a longtime personal friend, ally and mentor.

Of funds from 19 common donors in 2024, BJP got nearly four times as much as Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:46:02 UTC
14:46:02 KST

The 2024 Lok Sabha election results came as a surprise to many politicians and seasoned poll watchers alike. BJP, which had won clear majorities in 2014 and 2019, finished with 240 seats, 32 short of the halfway mark. Narendra Modi needed the support of NDA partners to form a government for a third term.When it came to political donations, however, BJP was the clear leader. India’s national parties declared ₹6,648.56 crore from 11,343 contributions above ₹20,000 in FY2024-25, according to an analysis by the Association for Democratic Reforms, or ADR. That was an increase of ₹4,104.29 crore, or 161%, over the previous financial year.BJP declared ₹6,074.02 crore from 5,522 contributions, up 171% from ₹2,243.95 crore a year earlier. Congress reported ₹517.39 crore from 2,501 contributions, an increase of 84% from ₹281.48 crore. AAP declared ₹38.11 crore, CPI(M) ₹16.96 crore and the National People’s Party ₹2.09 crore. BSP said it had received no donations above ₹20,000.Together, BJP and Congress accounted for 99.14% of the money declared by the six national parties covered by ADR. But buried inside that torrent of money was a curious crossover episode.
A TOI examination of the signed FY2024-25 contribution reports submitted by BJP and Congress to the Election Commission has identified at least 19 direct donors whose Permanent Account Numbers, or PANs, appear in both filings.Together, these donors gave at least ₹258.73 crore to the two parties.The money was not divided evenly. BJP received ₹206.64 crore, or 79.87%, while Congress received ₹52.09 crore, or 20.13%. In simpler terms, of every ₹5 contributed by these common donors, roughly ₹4 went to BJP. However, the 19 donors accounted for only about 3.4% of BJP’s total declared contributions, while the corresponding figure for Congress was 10.1%.
Business money dominates
ADR classified ₹6,128.79 crore, or 92.18% of the contributions received by national parties, as coming from corporate or business sectors. Such contributions formed 94.13% of BJP’s declared total and 74.19% of Congress’s.The classification is broader than incorporated companies. It covers the corporate and business categories created by ADR from descriptions in the party filings. The biggest channel for political money was electoral trusts.ADR found that four trusts, Prudent, Progressive, AB General and New Democratic, gave national parties a combined ₹4,024.43 crore, equivalent to 60.53% of the contributions covered by its report. Prudent Electoral Trust alone gave ₹2,180.71 crore to BJP, ₹216.34 crore to Congress and ₹16.42 crore to AAP.These trust flows have been excluded from TOI’s common-donor calculation. An electoral trust pools contributions before distributing money to parties. Unless the records explicitly establish the link, a company contributing to a multi-donor trust cannot be described as having directly funded a particular party.This analysis therefore deals only with donors appearing directly in party contribution reports.
How the number was tallied
TOI counted a donor as common primarily when the same PAN appeared in both filings, with the name and address used as additional checks. Where the name and PAN did not line up clearly, the amount was left out. Similar company names, group relationships or common addresses were not considered sufficient.ADR found 205 contributions worth ₹3.47 crore without declared PAN details across national parties, besides 33 contributions worth ₹38.8 lakh carrying missing or incorrect PAN information.ADR also found that BJP and Congress had not declared payment dates for their contributions. The filings establish that the money was received during FY2024-25, but do not allow every contribution to be placed precisely on the election calendar.
Five donors did the heavy lifting
The five largest common donors gave ₹208.5 crore, accounting for 80.59% of the ₹258.73-crore pool. The biggest was Derive Investments, a Mumbai-based investment firm. Its PAN appears against four BJP contributions adding up to ₹53 crore. Congress received another ₹5 crore from the same PAN.Next came ITC Infotech India Ltd, ITC’s wholly owned technology and digital-services subsidiary. It gave ₹33.5 crore to BJP and ₹11.5 crore to Congress, or ₹45 crore in all.ITC Ltd, the diversified conglomerate with businesses spanning FMCG, cigarettes, paperboards, packaging and agribusiness, gave another ₹39 crore to BJP and ₹4 crore to Congress. Its two-party total was ₹43 crore. ITC Ltd and ITC Infotech have been counted separately because they are separate legal entities carrying separate PANs.The fourth-largest common donor was an individual.Suresh Amritlal Kotak, a veteran cotton trader and industry figure often described by his peers as the “Cotton Man of India”, gave ₹30 crore to BJP and ₹7.5 crore to Congress, or ₹37.5 crore in all.Then came Hindustan Zinc Ltd, a Vedanta Group company and integrated producer of zinc, lead and silver. It gave ₹15 crore to BJP and ₹10 crore to Congress.
How commons donors contributed to two major parties
Two companies, a perfect 50:50 split
Most large common donors leaned heavily towards BJP. Two companies followed a strikingly different script.Century Plyboards (India) Ltd, the Kolkata-headquartered maker of plywood, laminates and other wood products, gave ₹5 crore to BJP and ₹5 crore to Congress. Star Cement Ltd, a cement manufacturer with plants in Meghalaya, Assam and West Bengal, gave ₹3 crore to each.Micro Labs Ltd, the Bengaluru-based pharmaceutical company best known for the Dolo brand, came close to an even split, giving ₹2 crore to BJP and ₹2.05 crore to Congress.Others leaned sharply towards one party.Finolex Industries, a manufacturer of PVC pipes, fittings and resin, gave ₹5 crore to BJP and ₹1 crore to Congress. Mysore Projects gave ₹3.26 crore to BJP and ₹25 lakh to Congress.Malabar Gold Ltd, the jewellery company subsequently renamed Malabar Gold and Diamonds Ltd, gave at least ₹10.0525 crore to BJP and ₹25 lakh to Congress.Christy Friedgram Industry gave ₹1.90 crore to BJP and ₹1 crore to Congress. The other verified common donors were Russell Credit, Peoples Education Society, Sri City, Muthoot Finance, T V Mohandas Pai, Josco Fashion Jewellers and H S Purewal.
Not just BJP and Congress
Tiger Associates, a West Bengal partnership that describes itself as an area distributor for Nagaland, Sikkim and Punjab state lotteries, gave ₹60 crore to AIADMK, ₹50 crore to DMK and ₹50 crore to Trinamool Congress using the same PAN.That is ₹160 crore across three parties. Of this, ₹110 crore went to the two principal Tamil Nadu rivals, AIADMK and DMK.NATCO Pharma Ltd, a Hyderabad-headquartered pharmaceutical company focused on complex generic medicines and niche molecules, appears across five party filings.Its identified contributions total ₹35.55 crore: ₹16.5 crore to BJP, ₹10 crore to YSR Congress, ₹7 crore to TDP, ₹1.5 crore to Janasena and ₹55 lakh to CPI(M).
How donors contributed to multiple parties
Century Plyboards also gave ₹1 crore to YSR Congress and ₹50 lakh to TDP, taking its identified contribution across four parties to ₹11.5 crore.Vedanta Ltd, a diversified natural-resources company with operations spanning zinc, aluminium, iron ore, oil and gas, steel and power, identified political contributions of ₹67 crore to BJP, ₹25 crore to BJD and ₹20 crore to JMM in its audited standalone FY2024-25 financial statements. That was ₹112 crore across the three parties. Its broader standalone donation-expense line was ₹116 crore.Not every multi-party combination represents political rivals. BJP, TDP and Janasena contested the 2024 elections in Andhra Pradesh as NDA allies. TDP and YSR Congress, however, fought on opposite sides.
Likewise, DMK and AIADMK were direct rivals in Tamil Nadu. BJP and BJD contested against each other in Odisha, while BJP and the JMM-led alliance were the principal opposing camps in Jharkhand.Deng Xiaoping famously said it did not matter whether a cat was black or white, so long as it caught mice. India’s donation filings offer their own lesson in pragmatism. For at least 19 donors, choosing between saffron and Congress blue was apparently not an either-or proposition.

Rs 5 crore to suppress rape case? NHRC directs Punjab to probe allegations against CM Mann’s wife

NHRC takes cognisance of complaint against Bhagwant Mann's wife
NEW DELHI: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) on Saturday took cognisance of allegations that Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann’s wife Gurpreet Kaur sought Rs 5 crore to "suppress" a rape case.The NHRC has directed the Punjab chief secretary and director general of police (DGP) to inquire into the allegations and submit an Action Taken Report (ATR) within two weeks.Commission member Priyank Kanoongo noted the complainant in the matter is a former judge of the Punjab and Haryana high court.“We have received a complaint from former Punjab and Haryana High Court Justice Ranjit Singh alleging that the wife of Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann attempted to hush up a rape case in exchange for a bribe of Rs 5 crore. ,” Kanoongo told ANI.
Kanoongo further stated that the NHRC had also apprised the ministry of home affairs (MHA) of the allegations.“We will be able to proceed with further investigation only after receiving the report from the Punjab chief secretary and DGP. Officials should exercise the powers granted to them by the Constitution for the welfare of the people. If they act under any kind of political pressure, action can be taken against them,” he added.
This comes days after the NHRC, on August 19, took cognisance of a complaint concerning the alleged non-observance of Independence Day in government schools across Punjab and sought a detailed report from the Mann-led state government.
The complaint raised specific concerns about government schools in rural, remote and border areas, where Independence Day celebrations were allegedly not held. This, the complaint argued, may have deprived students of an opportunity to participate in national celebrations.In this matter, the Punjab chief secretary has been directed to submit a detailed Action Taken/Compliance Report within four weeks. The commission has also sought relevant information from the Ministry of Education and apprised the Union home ministry for appropriate action.The NHRC is seeking to determine whether children in border areas were denied equal opportunities to participate in the observance of the national festival solely because of the geographical location of their schools.

China’s new moon mission could unlock secret of lunar ice: Why that matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:36:39 UTC
14:36:39 KST

China’s new moon mission could unlock secret of lunar ice: Why that matters
The Chang’e-7 seeks to find out more about the water trapped within the moon’s shadowed craters.
China is set to launch its Chang’e-7 unmanned, robotic space mission, possibly as early as Monday morning, to look for ice water in the permanently shadowed craters of the moon’s south pole.
This marks China’s seventh and most ambitious moon mission so far. Here is what we know about it.
What do we know about Chang’e-7?
The Chang’e‑7 launch window runs from Monday, August 24 to Monday, August 31, according to launch observers. That means the mission could lift off on any day in that period.
The Chang’e-7 comprises an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a hopper.
- The orbiter is the main spacecraft which will remain in the moon’s orbit, mapping the surface and taking images while the mission is under way. It will also relay data and communications between the other Chang’e‑7 components and Earth.
- The lander is the vessel that will touch down on the lunar surface, loaded with the necessary scientific instruments for lunar exploration, near the edge of the Shackleton Crater, a 21km-wide (13-mile-wide) pit close to the moon’s south pole. Lunar missions before this have never come this close to the pole.
- The rover is a small robotic vehicle which can drive around the landing site and which carries equipment to analyse the local environment, including rocks and soil.
- The hopper is a small robotic craft powered by solar energy, designed to “hop” – or fly – short distances from the surface of the moon and land again. It will be used to explore the Shackleton Crater.
How do we know there is water on the moon?
Over the past two decades, several space missions have established that there is water on the moon.
Since the 1960s, even before the first Apollo landing in 1969, scientists speculated that water could exist on the moon. However, when Apollo crews returned samples for testing in the late 1960s and early 1970s, they appeared to be dry.
Finally, in 2009, NASA deliberately crashed a rocket segment and its probe into a shadowed lunar crater to analyse the dust plume it kicked up. This provided one of the clearest direct confirmations that significant ice water does exist on the moon, building on earlier detections of water and hydrogen by probes.
In October 2020, NASA scientists announced that water on the moon is more widespread than previously known. They said water molecules had been found to be encapsulated within mineral grains on the lunar surface and speculated that more water is hidden in ice patches which are in permanent shadows.
NASA describes these permanent shadows as dark areas inside deep craters near the north and south poles of the moon where sunlight has not reached for millions or even billions of years. In 2018, prior to confirming it in 2020, NASA had detected water ice in shadowed parts of the moon through mapping.
Why is it important to find out more about the water on the moon?
Expanding knowledge about water on the moon is vital because ancient polar ice may have preserved a record of lunar volcanic activity and of water delivered by comets and asteroids to the Earth-moon system, offering clues to how our own oceans originally formed.
Additionally, if there is enough water on the moon that is realistically accessible, it could serve as a source of drinking water for crewed lunar missions, and could also help to keep equipment cool.
Hydrogen could also be extracted from moon water to provide fuel, while oxygen could be extracted to breathe, supporting onward missions to Mars or lunar mining.
Could anyone ‘own’ the water on the moon?
The 1967 United Nations Outer Space Treaty bans any nation from claiming sovereignty over the moon or owning it as territory. It does not explicitly prohibit commercial operations, but it requires private activities in space to be authorised and supervised by states and leaves key questions about resource ownership unresolved.
Which recent space missions have searched for frozen water on the moon?
In 2023, Russia’s lunar spacecraft, Luna-25, was launched to look for frozen water in the moon’s south pole. However, the Luna-25 spun out of control and crashed. The crash prevented any scientific data collection or water discovery.
Racing against the Luna-25 mission was India’s Chandrayaan-3, which also aimed to expand knowledge of lunar water ice. Chandrayaan-3 successfully landed in August 2023 and found critical new evidence of water on the surface of the moon’s south pole through soil temperature readings.
Why is exploring the moon’s south pole a challenge?
Attempted landings at the moon’s south pole have failed before because of its challenging terrain, which is full of craters and deep trenches.
The south pole is far from the equatorial region targeted by previous missions, including the crewed Apollo landings.
What is different about the Chang’e-7 mission?
The upcoming Chang’e-7 is aiming to expand knowledge about where, exactly, water is located in the craters of the moon, how deep it is, what form it is in and whether it is indeed possible to access it.
The Chang’e-7’s six-legged hopper has been designed to jump into and out of the deep, shadowed craters near the south pole that are hard for traditional rovers to reach, to look for water ice and other resources.
No previous space mission has used a dedicated hopper to jump in and out of lunar craters in this way.

‘It was a tsunami’: Floods leave death trail in India’s Assam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:35:50 UTC
14:35:50 KST

‘It was a tsunami’: Floods leave death trail in India’s Assam
From a father searching for his daughter’s body to a man who drowned trying to save a friend, floods take devastating toll.
Assam, India – Debiram Panika, a 37-year-old daily wage labourer from northeastern India’s Assam state, would speak to his wife and two daughters on video calls every day from Dimapur, a town in neighbouring Nagaland state where he worked.
But when his phone rang at about 11am on July 19, there was panic in the voice of his 30-year-old wife, Dipika.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3India’s severe monsoon season causes more than 100 deaths since July
- list 2 of 3On huge river island in India’s Assam, annual floods threaten local arts
- list 3 of 3‘Nowhere else to go’: In India’s Assam, frequent floods hit river islanders
“I could only see my wife telling me on the video call, ‘This is it for us. We are going to die,’ before the call was disconnected,” Panika recalled, speaking to Al Jazeera.
It was the last time they spoke. Moments later, rising waters from the nearby Dikhow River, which snakes past their village in Assam’s Sivasagar district, surged into their bamboo-and-mud home with a ferocious current and swept away Dipika and four-year-old daughter Radhika.
“The water came flooding like sea waves, and they were gone in a flash,” Panika said, as he stood in front of the ruined home he has since returned to.
Sivasagar is part of the eastern Assam region, also referred to as Upper Assam. Incessant rains between July 18 and July 20 submerged the region and the neighbouring Naga Hills of Nagaland.
Monsoon floods usually impact northern and western Assam, and parts of central Assam, the worst. But several Nagaland districts bordering Upper Assam received heavy rainfall on those three days, leading to dozens of landslides. This intense run-off swelled Naga Hills-origin rivers and caused devastation downstream.
The resultant floods killed more than 100 people, destroyed 2,700 villages, and displaced 700,000 people across the state. The state government says 1.2 million people were impacted in all, their lives disrupted.
Most waters have since receded, but Radhika’s body is yet to be found.
“I look for Radhika every day in the bushes, tirelessly,” Panika said, holding back his tears. “Her last words, calling me ‘Papa’, are still reverberating in my ears.”
Panika’s other daughter, Ridhika, 10, was at a relative’s place a few metres away when her mother and sister were swept away by the flood. Ridhika held onto a bamboo bush and was later rescued by locals.
‘Apocalyptic event’
Several riverine villages in Sivasagar have been wrecked by debris carried down by the waters of the Dikhow from the surrounding Naga Hills.
Tens of thousands of tree trunks lie piled up in places that used to be homes, as lush rice fields, the main source of livelihood, have been washed away.
Kukil Das, a 30-year-old Facebook vlogger in Debiram’s village of Nepali Khuti, told Al Jazeera that “the torrent of the flood was like an apocalyptic event seen in the movies.
“Trees as tall as 30 to 40 metres (100-130ft) came down from the hills, flooding the river, and wiped out everything as they crashed against our homes,” he said. “There is no home left. It was a tsunami.”
Das and his friend Shravan Prasad, from the neighbouring Bihubor village, said they saved at least 1,000 lives by using boats the two villages had at that time.
“We put together a group of friends with the seven boats and started rescuing people turn by turn for two days and nights without food and water,” Prasad said.
Das said the floods forced residents to take shelter on the roofs of concrete homes they could find, as cries for help and the sounds of the river washing away homes echoed in the neighbourhood.
Laxmi Sharma, who owned one such concrete house, said she provided shelter to at least 60 people on her terrace after the river water gushed into Nepali Khuti.
“People ran towards the roof of my building. We thought we were going to die,” Sharma, 46, told Al Jazeera. “But it is a miracle that we are still alive even though my house was barely out of water.”
Not everyone could escape the flood’s wrath, though.
In Sivasagar’s Simaluguri village, two friends – Reihana Ahmed, a Muslim, and Ratul Swarna, a Hindu, both in their 30s – were swept away in the torrent.
When Ahmed, a mother of two, was drowning as the deluge entered her village, Swarna, who did not know how to swim, jumped to save her without thinking about his life.
The two friends were later found dead in the paddy fields. “It was humanity that won in a disaster like this,” Ahmed’s husband Aminul Haque said with a sorrowful smile.
‘Human-made flood’
Besides the eroding banks of the Dikhow River in Prajabasti, another flood-affected village, 75-year-old Asor Ali sat in disbelief next to his wife, Jamila Khatun.
“Even the generations preceding me have not seen a flood like this,” he said, staring at the flowing river. “Even the 1950s earthquake that triggered the floods here did not do so much damage.”
A magnitude 8.6 earthquake hit Assam and Tibet across the border in 1950, altering the region’s riverine system. Nearly 5,000 people died. Since then, Assam has witnessed frequent floods, which intensify during the monsoons, says Mirza Zulfiqur Rahman, a researcher on the basin of the Brahmaputra, the region’s major river: The Naga Hills rivers that flooded Upper Assam are its tributaries.
But residents say this year’s deadly deluge is not just a natural phenomenon.
Biren Gogoi, 43, says rampant stone and sand mining in regional rivers, coupled with aggressive deforestation and coal extraction in Nagaland’s Mon district, triggered the devastation.
Global Nature Watch, an open-source online platform that provides real-time data on deforestation across the world, showed that Nagaland lost 14 percent of its tree cover between 2002 and 2025, with Mon district bordering Assam’s Sivasagar being the most affected.
According to the latest report published in 2023 by the Forest Survey of India, Nagaland has lost about 794.88 square kilometres (306.9 square miles) of forest cover between 2013 and 2023.
Al Jazeera travelled along the Assam-Nagaland border and saw signs of deforestation on the hills and mining activities in both the states. Satellite images also confirmed rampant coal mining in Nagaland’s Mon district, and stone mining crushers on Assam’s side, especially in Bihubor, one of the epicentres of the Assam flood.
While Mon’s Deputy Commissioner Wennyei Konyak acknowledged the possibility of illegal mining in the district, he added that the land was protected under Indian laws to uphold the rights of Indigenous tribes, and therefore government interference in the area was limited.
“I would not blame mining activities for the flood. It was just the wrath of nature,” he told Al Jazeera.
But experts and political leaders in Assam say mining played a direct role in the floods.
Debabrata Saikia of the opposition Congress party, who is a former legislator from Sivasagar constituency, accused Assam’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of allowing illegal excavations for stone and sand on the Dikhow riverbank, resulting in a cratered wasteland that worsened the floods.
“This unchecked plundering of riverbeds and hills under the ruling government has engineered this into a man-made disaster,” Saikia told Al Jazeera.
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, however, rejected the allegation on August 4, blaming excessive rainfall in Nagaland for triggering the Upper Assam deluge. On August 14, Ranoj Pegu, a cabinet minister in the state’s BJP government, blamed erratic rainfall due to climate change for the deluge.
Rahman, the Brahmaputra river basin researcher, believes that while the climate crisis played a role, the flood was “purely human-made”, caused by the fracturing of the landscape.
“The unrestrained stone extraction from the Dikhow riverbed has damaged the river’s natural cushion,” Rahman said. “That means the river loses the capacity to resist high flows of torrents that break embankments and cause floods.”
An official document from 2022, seen by Al Jazeera, also highlights mining as a factor in possible large-scale floods downstream on the Assam side.
Al Jazeera reached out to senior district officials in Sivasagar as well as state government officials for their comments on allegations of unchecked coal mining but did not get any response.
Back in Prajabasti village, Ali, the septuagenarian, is mentally preparing himself for future floods.
“It will happen again, so long as there is greed for land and coal in humans,” he said. “Nature pays them back.”

President Volodymyr Zelensky has enacted a National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) decision imposing sanctions on five enterprises of the Russian aluminum company Rusal and nine associated Russian citizens.
The sanctions target Russia’s largest aluminum production sites, including the Bratsk, Sayanogorsk, and Krasnoyarsk plants. According to a report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine (ESCU) titled “Salt of the Earth,” these facilities are the primary importers of alumina into Russia.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Between April 2024 and March 2025, these three plants imported over $2.5 billion worth of raw materials for aluminum production. In total, Rusal-affiliated structures control 93% of all Russian alumina imports.
ESCU analysts stated that the aluminum produced by these facilities is supplied directly to companies operating within the Russian military-industrial complex. The material and its alloys are critical for manufacturing military aviation, missiles, armored vehicles, cable systems, and components for rocket fuel and explosives.
Olena Yurchenko, ESCU director of analytics and investigations, stated that the Russian defense sector relies heavily on raw material supply chains rather than just final assembly plants.
“Therefore, strategic minerals should become a separate direction of sanctions policy: restrictions must cover importers, processing enterprises, traders, logistics companies, and other key links,” Yurchenko said, adding that this approach allows for targeting the entire military-industrial complex.

Recent sanctions on stolen grain exports
The newly announced measures follow an Aug. 14 decree in which Zelensky enacted sanctions against 13 cargo vessels, 11 Russian nationals, and 28 companies involved in the illegal export of looted Ukrainian grain from occupied territories. Eight of the sanctioned ships were sailing under the Russian flag.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner for sanctions policy, stated that Ukraine intends to share information with international partners to synchronize the restrictions across jurisdictions and prevent the grain from entering foreign markets.
Zelensky framed the grain sanctions as part of a broader strategy to limit Russia’s capacity to sustain its war effort, which includes ongoing strikes on military logistics and oil refineries in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov regions.
The president had previously noted that Kyiv was preparing new sanctions against Russia’s military industry and financial intermediaries. The move aligns with the EU’s 21st sanctions package adopted on July 23, which included 218 listings targeting individuals and entities involved in the war effort.

14 yrs on, NMC still trying to update national register of docs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:30:04 UTC
14:30:04 KST

The National Medical Commission is putting forth a new proposal for mandatory re-registration of doctors across the nation.
Fourteen years after the first attempt to update the national registry for doctors, the National Medical Commission has again proposed to make it mandatory for an estimated 11 lakh doctors in India to re-register through its web portal. This has been done through proposed amendments to the regulations governing registration and licensing. The last such attempt in August 2024 saw barely 32,000 doctors (3%) applying till December last year and just 1,800 (0.2%) being approved for registration.The Registration of Medical Practitioners and Licence to Practice Medicine Regulations 2023 notified in May 2023 stated that all doctors enrolled in the Indian Medical Register or any state medical register “shall update in the web portal of the Ethics & Medical Registration Board within a period of three months of publishing of these Regulation” and obtain the registration number, and a licence to practice which would be valid for five months. A year later, it was clear that it had failed spectacularly. In August last year, in response to a question in Parliament, the health ministry claimed that “application for issuance of National Medical Register (NMR) Identification (ID) is voluntary” though the regulation had clearly mandated it. The proposed amendments have removed the three-month clause and said the period would be stipulated later.Over 13.8 lakh doctors were registered in India at the end of 2025 and it is assumed that 80% of this number (over 11 lakh) would be available as many would have moved out of India, died or stopped practising.
“To weed out a fraction of those in the medical register, who might not be actively practising anymore, the NMC is asking all 11 lakh doctors to re-register. Instead, the commission could just take the updated state medical council registers, run a deduplication software and reach out only to those about whom there is any confusion. For the rest, they could issue a unique identification number. They are just repeating an experiment that has already failed,” said Dr KV Babu, an ophthalmologist, one of the 32,000 who had applied through the portal.Section 30 (7) of the NMC Act 2019 states: The Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) shall ensure electronic synchronisation of the National Register and the State Register in such a manner that any change in one register is automatically reflected in the other register. Six years after the NMC was constituted in September 2020, the latest draft amendments to the 2023 regulation states that the synchronization will be done indicating that it has not been done till now.
None of the fresh or updated entries in state medical registers in the past years were being automatically updated in the national medical registry.Timeline:Jul 2012- MCI Board of Governors initiate process for updating Indian Medical Register with unique numeric or alpha-numeric numberMar 2017- MCI announces proposal for all doctors to have Unique Permanent Registration Number (UPRN)May 2023- NMC’s new regulation mandating re-registration and mandating a Unique Identification (UID) Number to be generated centrally by EMRB of NMCAug 2026- Amendments to 2023 regulation- proposes making registration in national registry and new UID number valid for practice across India without having to re-register in each state

Finance Ministry denies plans to cut Estonia's farm subsidies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:28:00 UTC
14:28:00 KST

Finance Ministry denies plans to cut Estonia's farm subsidies
The Finance Ministry says farmers' fears of losing more than €100 million in EU agricultural funding are unfounded, with €2 billion planned for the sector for 2028–34.
Triin Tomingas, head of foreign financing at the ministry's State Budget Department, said Friday that under the European Commission's current proposal for the 2028–34 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), or EU budget, Estonia would receive about €6.5 billion, including roughly €2 billion for agriculture and food production.
"A total of €2 billion has been proposed for agriculture, and that's where the sector and the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture need to continue their dialogue on how to set priorities within that amount," Tomingas said on Vikerraadio.
That money, she added, will be divided between food security, innovation, competitiveness and supply chain resilience.
The latest MFF proposal would also give member states more flexibility in how they use the funds, which will be allocated in two stages — with 75 percent distributed initially and decisions on the remaining funds to follow in 2031 and 2034.
A separate €546 million allocation for Estonia is intended to help close income and competitiveness gaps in agriculture, Tomingas noted, and while some spending targets for climate, social programs and agriculture would remain, Brussels will no longer not dictate how support money allocated to a specific country is spent.
"With the rest, including that €546 million, the government is free to decide which sore spots it wants to address with the funding, and which areas to support and with how much," the ministry official said.
Of the €546 million, three quarters, or €393 million, must be allocated now, after administrative costs are deducted from the initial amount; the rest can be allocated later, she added.
Officials pledge full amount
Asked whether the Finance Ministry had earmarked any of the money for other purposes, as claimed by the Estonian Chamber of Agriculture and Commerce (EPKK), Tomingas said it had not.
"We have not redirected it elsewhere," she said. The government's preliminary proposal, she explained, sets aside €2.12 billion for the Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture, including €2 billion for agriculture, food production, rural areas and fisheries.
The EPKK threatened Tuesday to bring farmers and tractors to Tallinn over claims that the Ministry of Finance had proposed allocating €295 million to agriculture and food production instead of the €546 million in the EU proposal.
The protest has reportedly been postponed, as farmer representatives are due to meet with Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) next week.
On August 18, Michal confirmed to TV3 news that the full €546 million would go to agriculture and food production, not anywhere else.

Can Australia rebuild social cohesion? Inquiry hears calls for change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:27:40 UTC
14:27:40 KST

in brief
- Over four days, commissioner Virginia Bell heard concerns about social cohesion and antisemitism.
- The commission is in its 9th and final block of hearings.
Experts, advocates and community leaders are calling for stronger social cohesion and action on antisemitism, telling an inquiry "we need to break the cycle".
Over four days of hearings this week, commissioner Virginia Bell heard concerns about declining satisfaction with democracy, social media polarisation, racism, self-censorship and the breakdown of relationships between religious and cultural communities.
The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion also heard proposals for stronger education about Jewish Australians, better recognition of migrants’ qualifications and more effective approaches to tackling prejudice.
But the hearings also exposed difficult questions about what social cohesion should mean, including how Australia can combat discrimination without silencing debate.
The royal commission, launched in response to the December 2025 Bondi terror attack, is in its ninth and final block of hearings, with its final report due in December.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Here are the key takeaways from the week.
Questions about democracy
Professors Nicholas Biddle and Matthew Gray, both from the Australian National University, fronted the royal commission on Monday, speaking to reporters about democratic attitudes in Australia and responses about declining satisfaction with democracy.
Their June report found that satisfaction with democracy fell to its lowest level since January 2023, while principled support for democracy increased. Professor Gray said multiple factors could be at play, including social media undermining support for democracy.
"We conclude that efforts to counter antisemitism will be limited unless they also address the platforms through which distrust, polarisation and extremist narratives circulate," Gray told the commission.
He argued targeted interventions, particularly for young Australians with low educational attainment and low levels of principled democratic support, would be more effective than universal attempts to counter antisemitism.
"Because trust in core institutions is closely associated with democratic commitment, consideration should be given to how government agencies, education systems and public communications practices could be made more transparent, accountable and credible, particularly in communities experiencing disadvantage," Gray said.
Ahmed Hegazi, a strategic adviser, and his friend Joel Lazar, the chief executive of the Jewish Climate Network, also expressed concern about polarisation and emphasised the importance of cross-cultural communication.
"Humans who know their neighbours don't feel they are threats and they don't fear them, they feel connected to them," Hegazi said. "We need to break the cycle."
"There's basically no alternative to trying new things even if they're hard … as fathers of young children, we know important things are always hard," Lazar said.
Skills recognition proposed to ease tensions
Australian businessman, David Gonski told the inquiry his 24-member Antisemitism Education Taskforce was considering a proposal to improve recognition of migrants' skills and address community tensions.
Many skilled migrants were underemployed because their previous qualifications were not recognised.
"This, (a member) put to us, creates some tension and concern both within them and the people that they live with, and so on," he said on Tuesday.
"He felt that we could find a twofold solution: a solution that allowed us to have more skilled workers, and ... that would take away some of the aggravation that comes for these people."
Gonski said "there was merit" in considering the proposal but the task force had not reached a final decision. He stressed he was not suggesting further migration, but broader permissions for migrants to practice in their fields.
Gonski was appointed to lead the antisemitism education task force in December 2025 and previously filed the Gonski report on Australian education funding.
He also recommended broader education about Jewish contributions to Australia.
"We are hopeful that (the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority) will now look more broadly at not just Holocaust studies, but also more generally the contribution of the Jews and indeed the Jewish faith," he said.
"There's a lot of contribution by Jews to Australia, to the history of Australia."
Orthodox Rabbi Zalman Kastel suggested educators address specific prejudices in youth's education.
"Telling people a general message of don't be racist, doesn't cut it," he said.
Monash University lecturers Farid Zaid and Daniel Heller said students and staff had become afraid to address difficult topics, with many students struggling to hear different views.
"We both saw conversations in the classroom play out along really rigid lines," Zaid said.
"I was deeply surprised by my students' inability to distinguish discomfort in the classroom ... and distressed."
Most students and academics adopted self-censorship for fear of social media censure or official complaints. Others were inclined to, in Said and Heller's terms, "perform certainty"; project a sense of virtue over others.
"We know what's virtuous, what's moral, what's right; and anyone who disagrees is, in one way or another, morally reprehensible," Heller said.
The pair run Brave Conversations Project workshops teaching students and teachers how to stay in the room when discussions become difficult.
Terror attacks deepen Jewish-Muslim division
Faith Communities Council of Victoria's Sandy Kouroupidis said interaction between Jewish and Muslim communities had stopped altogether following the Bondi massacre on 14 December 2025, and the attack on Israel by Hamas militants on 7 October 2023.
The October 7 attacks by Hamas killed 1,200 people and resulted in 250 people being taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies. Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 70,000 people and been labeled a genocide by a United Nations commission, which the Israeli government disputes.
"We have two vice chairs; one of them is the chair of the Islamic Council of Victoria and the other one is the chair of the Jewish Community Council of Victoria," he said.
"It has been very, very challenging to get those two communities in the same room."
Jewish people had stopped attending interfaith events, while schools stopped visiting Muslim and Christian institutes.
"A lot of the Jewish schools simply don't feel safe," he said.
Social cohesion must not hide racism
Race Discrimination Commissioner Giridharan Sivaraman warned that social cohesion can camouflage racial discrimination.
"Stop talking about racism because you're disrupting the social cohesion," Sivaraman said he was told by a senior government official.
He said social cohesion policies could resemble those used to justify racial assimilation and cause distrust.
"If it's obscuring, then it's not actually solving the systemic or structural problem that you need to fix," he told the inquiry.
"If your experience of policies or laws or programs under the term social cohesion are ones where you're excluded ... or you have to assimilate ... you won't trust the institutions you're engaging with."
Sivaraman also said reports of antisemitism, particularly in workplaces, had risen sharply since the October 7 attacks on Israel.
"Workplaces ended up being a really consistent theme that came up as an area where people felt disadvantaged," Sivaraman said.
"(They felt) they couldn't express their identity, felt they were in danger of losing their job, felt the inquiry also heard conflicting views over where legitimate criticism of Zionism ends and antisemitism begins."
Separately, Rita Jabri Markwell, principal policy adviser to the Australian Muslim Advocacy Network, argued Zionism should be treated as a political ideology rather than a protected characteristic.
"It's not a race or religion," she said.
Jewish witnesses had described Zionism as inseparable from their religious and cultural identity. Markwell argued courts had increasingly taken her view and warned that treating Zionism as protected risked excluding Jewish Australians who rejected the ideology.
"The mere fact that there is a portion of Jewish people who do not accept that it is central to their identity indicates that it is an ideology," she said.

German Government Considers Closing ‘Russian House’ in Berlin – Media

German Government Considers Closing ‘Russian House’ in Berlin – Media
Germany is considering closing the “Russian House” in Berlin amid Russia’s hybrid attacks, including a drone incident at Leipzig Airport that occurred in early August.
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by DW, citing Der Spiegel.
In response to an inquiry from Der Spiegel, Germany’s Federal Foreign Office said that “in view of Russia’s actions against German cultural intermediaries and organizations, as well as against the backdrop of Russia’s growing hybrid activities,” the German government is comprehensively reviewing the legal and contractual framework governing the “Russian House.”
“This also applies to the agreements referred to in the inquiry,” the ministry said.
According to DW, German authorities are examining the possibility of terminating a bilateral agreement concluded in 2011 governing the activities of cultural and information centers. The agreement can be terminated once every five years, with the next possible date being June 7, 2027. To do so, the relevant notification must be submitted by December 6, 2026.
Another agreement, dated May 5, 2013, provides for the use of a parcel of land on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin for a 99-year term.
The publication notes that while German authorities had previously refrained from taking any action against Russian cultural centers, fearing reciprocal measures against Goethe-Institut branches in Russia, Der Spiegel reports that the “Russian House” is no longer considered untouchable, and discussions of sanctions against it are no longer taboo among German government officials.
The “Russian House” in Berlin is run by Rossotrudnichestvo, a Russian government agency. In July 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the European Union added Rossotrudnichestvo to its sanctions list and froze its assets. At the same time, organizations subject to EU sanctions may continue to maintain buildings they own and spend funds on them.
Earlier this month, German public broadcaster WDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung published a report stating that the French Interior Ministry considers the “Russian House” on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin to be a site that “Russian intelligence services use as cover.”
As Ukrinform reported, on July 4, the Russian state cultural center “Russian House” in Moldova’s capital announced that it would cease operations.

Trump heads into midterms short on foreign policy wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:07:45 UTC
14:07:45 KST

Trump heads into midterms short on foreign policy wins
WASHINGTON, Aug 22 - With the Iran war now at a costly standoff and crises from Ukraine to Gaza still unresolved, President Donald Trump's ambitious foreign policy agenda appears stuck as he heads into November's midterm elections.
The setbacks are striking for a president who returned to office last year promising to be a "peacemaker" and made resolving international conflicts a centerpiece of his second-term agenda.
Trump has grown impatient with reporters' questions and even U.S. allies. This week, he lashed out at reporters pressing him on foreign policy issues and renewed his threat to bomb Oman, a U.S. ally negotiating with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Labor Day, on September 7 this year, is traditionally when election campaigns kick into high gear, and Republicans face the prospect that unresolved conflicts abroad and their economic fallout at home could cost the party its hold on Congress.
IRAN STALEMATE TAKES POLITICAL TOLL
Trump has called off talks with Tehran after pushing for weeks for a diplomatic solution and announced on Wednesday a new campaign of "economic warfare" against the Islamic Republic in an apparent acknowledgment that months of military attacks have not forced the concessions the U.S. wants to see.
As inflation persists and the Iran war drives up gasoline prices, Trump's approval rating has fallen to another low point with just 33% of Americans in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll approving of his performance.
Other efforts to broker peace have also stalled.
On Monday, Trump's negotiator and son-in-law Jared Kushner left empty-handed from talks to advance a Gaza peace deal. And an expected visit to Kyiv by Kushner and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff to revive long-stalled negotiations to end Russia's war in Ukraine has yet to happen.
After a string of early foreign policy achievements, including a Gaza ceasefire and the capture of Venezuela's leader, Trump's record has become increasingly defined by his stalled diplomatic efforts.
"Trump has successfully challenged and disrupted the comfortable foreign policy consensus in Washington, but has not translated that disruption into a strategy with deliverables for Americans," said Asli Aydintasbas, a fellow at the Brookings Institution think tank in Washington.
IRAN WAR TESTS TRUMP AT HOME
The conflict with Iran has weighed "intensely" on the president and there is no consensus inside the White House on how to resolve it, one Trump ally said on condition of anonymity.
The pressure could increase if investors conclude the war will drag on, driving up U.S. borrowing costs and further constraining Trump's domestic agenda. Trump has said the economic costs are worth it in order to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon despite Iran's denials it seeks one.
“President Trump has successfully made America respected again, and the results speak for themselves – nine wars have ended, hostages have been freed from Gaza, trade deals are fairer, and now, Iran will be prevented from ever possessing a nuclear weapon," said White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly.
A senior Trump administration official said U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade had crippled Iran's economy and left it "completely broke," adding, "There are many levers the president can crank harder in the weeks ahead."
AN UNORTHODOX STYLE WITH MIXED RESULTS
Some experts give Trump credit for a willingness to grapple with issues they believe other presidents have been unable or unwilling to solve.
"The president wants a more stable world and that means attempting to resolve disputes, whether hot like Ukraine or cold like trade and overcapacity," said Nick Snyder, a senior fellow at Hudson Institute, adding that Trump also worked to settle conflicts between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo and Thailand and Cambodia.
Trump has upended traditional diplomatic norms of peacemaking, relying on leveraging America's economic and military might including with U.S. allies, but that unorthodox style has yielded mixed results.
He brought parties to the table with the aim of ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine, but the longest war in Europe since World War Two is nowhere near ending, with the latest Russian airstrikes killing 16 people in the Ukrainian capital on Thursday.
In Gaza, mediators fear that intensifying Israeli strikes on the enclave undermine efforts to end the conflict as both Israel and Hamas balk at conditions needed to advance a peace plan Trump forged in October last year. In Lebanon, Israeli airstrikes killed 11 people on Sunday even as a U.S.-mediated peace framework between the two countries remains in effect.
One notable success came in Venezuela, where the U.S. military captured President Nicolas Maduro without U.S. casualties. Analysts say the operation helped convince Trump that joining Israel in attacking Iran would also proceed smoothly.
But they also say that proved a miscalculation. They argue Trump has relied too heavily on applying coercive pressure even though Iran's leaders have little incentive to back down and reopen the Strait of Hormuz despite the country's weakening economy.
"He is obsessed with applying coercion, and sometimes flattery, to bend others to his will, but oblivious to their strategic goals and domestic politics. As a result, he keeps flailing and failing," said Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Meanwhile, the political clock is ticking, with Trump's Republican Party facing elections that could cost it control of one or both chambers of Congress and sharply curtail his ability to advance his agenda during his final two years in office.
Analysts say Trump's reliance on coercive pressure can bring adversaries to the table but often fails to produce lasting settlements, a dynamic that may encourage rivals to wait him out.
"U.S. adversaries understand that his political clock is shorter than theirs, and that while the United States can apply enormous coercive pressure, it may eventually lose patience," Aydintasbas said.
"Putin, Xi and Iran may therefore want to wait out Washington. After November, the incentive to wait out Trump will become even more pronounced." REUTERS

Ukraine is buying jam-proof fiber-optic drones for first time to single standard, so any maker can compete
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:07:00 UTC
14:07:00 KST

Ukraine is buying the strike drones that Russian jamming cannot touch, and for the first time, to a common standard. The Defense Procurement Agency (DOT) has announced its first purchase of fiber-optic FPV kamikaze drones built to specifications defined by the Defense Ministry, the ministry announced.
By defining the specifications a fiber-optic FPV must meet, the Defense Ministry lets any maker compete by hitting that standard rather than having each model approved individually.
That is what makes it possible to split the purchase into competing lots among many suppliers, both large and mid-sized, and to buy the jam-proof drones at scale without relying on any single producer.
Why fiber-optic drones matter
The Ukrainian Defense Ministry is looking for a specific type of drone. They use a fiber-optic cable to connect to the operator, and unlike ordinary FPV drones that need a radio signal for control and video, these fiber-optic drones do not depend on the radio channel, so they work far better in the presence of active electronic warfare.
Fiber-optic drones let an operator keep control where radio-controlled drones lose their signal, and Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said the drones give Ukraine's forces added ability to disrupt Russian assaults and conduct their own operations, striking enemy manpower.
The standard opens the field to any maker
The buy is not tailored to one producer. It is not conducted for a specific manufacturer or model, and producers can offer their own drones if they meet the defined characteristics, with the drones sorted into classes by parameters such as range (the length of the fiber-optic cable) and camera type.
The lot structure spreads the orders
Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik said the tender is structured so that various suppliers can participate. Each tender is divided into lots, with four lots per class of fiber-optic FPVs, and no participant may win more than 50% of a class's total volume.
That structure guards supply while also driving competition.
"This creates an environment for healthy competition among manufacturers, and at the same time minimizes the risks of supply disruptions," Banik added.

Sofia travel guide: How to spend 48 hours in Bulgaria’s capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:03:41 UTC
14:03:41 KST

Once known as Serdica, Bulgaria’s capital was once among the most important cities in the Byzantine Empire.
While the Balkans are growing in popularity, the distribution of tourists isn’t exactly even, with coastal destinations in countries like Croatia and Montenegro seeing the bulk of visitors.
But with Bulgaria in the spotlight following their Eurovision win, that might be about to change.
The competition itself will be hosted by Burgas on the Black Sea, but there are plenty of other cities worth visiting, like Plovdiv, Europe’s oldest continuously inhabited city, or Varna, the hometown of Eurovision winner Dara.
The most obvious starting point for a trip around the country is, of course, the capital Sofia.
Once known as Serdica, the city was conquered by the Romans around 29 BC, becoming the most important city in the region – Constantine the Great even considered making it the Byzantine Empire’s capital over Constantinople.
That history is fully on display alongside its postwar architecture and more modern history.
If a winter visit is on the cards, Sofia is well-known for its skiing, while those looking to relax can head to one of the public baths which use mineral-rich spring waters.
Things to see and do in Sofia
Wander around Ancient Serdica
Sofia is a city where old meets new quite literally. At Serdica Metro Station, you can step off the train and within moments be wandering around ancient Roman ruins.
Aside from the metro station, there are various archeological sites scattered through the centre of the city, including the remains of the eastern gate near the National Assembly and the remnants of an amphitheatre in the basement of the Arena di Serdica hotel.
Step inside the Saint George Rotunda
One of these archeological sites is home to the Saint George Rotunda, which dates back to the 4th century.
Inside, you’ll find Byzantine and Bulgarian medieval frescoes painted throughout the centuries, and while the church was converted into a mosque during the Ottoman rule in the 16th century, since the 19th century it has been returned to its original function as a church.
Visit the houses of worship in the Square of Tolerance
Outside Saint Sofia Church you’ll find a copy of the Edict of Serdica, the first to legalise Christianity in the Eastern Roman Empire in 311.
It’s fitting, then, that this is just a few minutes’ walk away from the so-called Square of Tolerance, where you’ll find St. Alexander Nevsky Cathedral (Bulgarian Orthodox), Banya Bashi Mosque (Sunni Islam), Cathedral of St Joseph (Roman Catholic) and the Sofia Synagogue (Orthodox Judaism).
As with any house of worship, make sure you dress appropriately if you want to go inside any of the buildings.
Explore Sofia’s only UNESCO World Heritage Site
On the topic of churches, Boyana Church on the outskirts of the city is a must-visit, having been added to UNESCO’s World Heritage Sites list in 1979.
Praised as being “one of the most complete and perfectly preserved monuments of east European medieval art”, the complex includes a 10th-century church, a 13th-century church and a third built in the 19th century.
The frescoes inside the second church are the highlight as “one of the most important collections of medieval paintings”.
Hike Vitosha Mountain
From Boyana Church, you won’t be too far away from the hiking trails of Vitosha Mountain.
The Visit Sofia website has details of some of the routes, including one that takes you from Boyana Church up to Boyana Waterfall, but there are longer options, too.
Go on a street art tour
Sofia’s streets are covered in murals, and if you head to one of the city’s tourist information offices you’ll be able to grab a map with details of where you can find them all.
There’s quite a few in a car park near Serdica metro station, but my favourite has to be the St. George and the dragon mural near the Arte Sofia Hotel.
Or explore the city’s post-war architecture
While much of the city’s top attractions date back to antiquity, you can also discover its communist era on a walking tour of its post-war architecture.
There’s a free map available to download on the Visit Sofia website which takes you off-the-beaten-path to hotels, housing blocks and other buildings built during this time.
Love it or hate it, brutalism had a huge impact on the city’s skyline in those years.
Browse the goods at the Women’s Market
First established in 1878, the Women’s Market, or Zhenski Pazar, is the oldest open-air market in the city.
Here, you’ll be able to grab fresh produce, spices, local sweets and clothing.
There’s a board explaining the history of the market which features photos through the decades, but I couldn’t see any explanation as to why it’s called the Women’s Market. According to the Bulgarian News Agency, the name dates back to the Ottoman era, when women were only allowed to visit the local village market or ones intended purely for women’s needs.
Explore Sofia’s craft beer scene
Bulgaria’s craft beer scene is booming, and there’s no better place to explore it than Sofia.
On my visit, I went on a crawl around the city’s top bars: You can find out where I went, and follow along yourself, here.
Where to eat and drink in Sofia
Bulgarian food hasn’t quite hit the mainstream yet, so a visit to Sofia may well be your first encounter with it.
Manastirska Magernitsa Restaurant is an excellent place to dip your toe in the waters. Found within a historic house belonging to literary critic Professor Krastyo Krastev, the menu features dishes from monasteries all over the country.
I loved the nettle porridge with cheese (trust us on this one), but the restaurant staff are super helpful and will happily make recommendations.
While Vitosha Boulevard is Sofia’s most famous street, you should head to Tsar Shishman Street for less “touristy” eateries and bars.
Next time I’ll return for…
The UNESCO-listed Rila Monastery is around two hours from Sofia, but this time around there just wasn’t enough time to fit it into my itinerary.
I’d always quite like to go hiking around the Rila Lakes, but this is dependent on the weather – even when I visited in mid-May, the lakes were still covered in snow.
How to get to Sofia
Sofia’s international airport is served by dozens of airlines, including easyJet, Lufthansa, Ryanair and Wizz Air, with the latter two having bases here.
The airport connects to the city centre by metro in around 20 minutes.

'It's a nightmare': What life is like under Mount Etna's cloud of ash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
05:02:08 UTC
14:02:08 KST

Locals living in Etna’s shadow face volcanic ash clean-up and hidden health costs. Is Sicily finally seeking solutions?
When in March 2021 Emilia Privitera started coughing relentlessly, she initially worried she might have caught COVID-19 again. Then when the test came in negative, she thought it could be just a seasonal allergy.
“But the cough persisted for weeks, and my lungs would make a strange hiss sound when taking a breath between one cough and the other,” she tells Euronews Earth. “So I went to a specialist, and he found something I’d never expected: some almost imperceptible ash particles stuck in my lungs.”
Privitera lives in Nicolosi, a town near Sicily’s second largest city, Catania. It is perched on the slopes of Mount Etna, Europe’s highest and most active volcano. At every eruption – which can take place multiple times a year – her symptoms come back, and it’s the same for hundreds of other residents in the area.
In recent weeks, an intense series of eruptions has brought Mount Etna back to international headlines for its fiery show, as well as for grounding hundreds of flights for a week.
But while millions of people marvel at these natural phenomena, less attention is paid to the people living with the consequences of steady volcanic ash release. In periods of intense volcanic activity, ashfall can reach thousands of tonnes a day, blanketing towns across the region.
The hidden health impacts of volcanic ash
Volcanic ash consists of very fine particles of rock, minerals and volcanic glass, and can easily get stuck on roofs and hard-to-reach corners of buildings and streets for years.
This ash can act as a mineral-rich fertiliser that improves soil drainage and water retention on surrounding land. But the particles also pose a hidden health risk – particularly when they are inhaled after being stirred up by wind or vehicles on ash-covered roads.
A 2013 paper on Etna's 2002 eruptions – among the most intense in recent times – found a significant increase in emergency department visits for acute respiratory illnesses, cardiovascular conditions, and eye irritation during the eruption compared with the same period the previous year.
Daniele Lombardo, co-author of the study, explains that the fine fraction of volcanic ash is capable of penetrating deep into the lungs, where it may trigger inflammation, oxidative stress and respiratory irritation, especially among children, older adults, and people with chronic respiratory disease.
The University of Palermo has also previously conducted studies investigating elevated rates of thyroid cancer in populations living in the Etna volcanic area, alongside evidence of increased exposure to trace elements associated with volcanic emissions.
Patients in Catania face a ‘worsening’ of respiratory conditions
Nunzio Crimi, a pulmonologist and allergist based in Catania, cut his summer vacation short this year after receiving a number of emergency calls from his regular patients who already suffer from respiratory disorders.
“Patients with already fragile immune systems or pre-existing breathing medical conditions, like allergic asthma and chronic bronchopneumonia, are more prone to get sick from the ashfall and can experience quite serious worsening of their conditions,” he tells Euronews Earth. “Especially those whose respiratory systems have been weakened by past experiences of pneumonia or COVID tend to suffer the most.”
During the early August Etna eruptions, the Sicilian Department of Civil Protection, which handles disaster prediction, prevention and emergency management, reported an increase in patients rushing to hospital emergency rooms in the province of Catania.
They shared similar symptoms: eye irritation or conjunctivitis, coughing, a runny or irritated nose, and sneezing. Crimi says he saw an eight per cent increase in medical appointments compared with normal.
Italy isn’t the only European country grappling with the issue. In Iceland, the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption had lasting health effects. Researcher Gunnar Guðmundsson found that respiratory symptoms and psychological distress persisted for several years among the residents most heavily exposed to ash particles, particularly those repeatedly exposed to ash resuspension by wind after the eruption.
Animals can also be severely affected by volcanic ashfall.
"If ashes are not quickly removed from the fields, the cattle can risk dying of fluoride poisoning if they breathe or eat too much contaminated grass,” Berglind Hilmarsdottir, a farmer in Dyrafjord, in the Westfiords, tells Euronews Earth.
Fluoride present in volcanic ash can form acids in animals’ digestive systems, damaging the intestinal lining and potentially causing internal bleeding. It can also interfere with calcium in the bloodstream, and prolonged, heavy exposure over several days may weaken the bones and, in severe cases, cause teeth to deteriorate.
Inefficient removal of ash puts residents at risk
For years, Catania residents have urged stronger public health preparedness for volcanic eruptions – but weaknesses still remain.
Delayed ash collection and inadequate disposal infrastructure have been prolonging residents’ secondary exposure to Etna’s fine particulate ash, exacerbating respiratory and cardiovascular health risks, according to Riccardo Castro, a local politician and medical executive at the main hospital in Acireale, a town about 20km from the Etna volcano.
“These ashes contain metals, so breathing them is not healthy,” he explains. While Castro says that short-term exposure is not considered especially dangerous, he explains that “those who are exposed to these particles several times a year since they were born, especially in towns closer to the top of the volcano, can develop serious longer-term health effects. Rapid removal significantly reduces secondary exposure.”
Castro warns, however, that some clean-up methods are actually exacerbating the situation. Using air blowers to clear streets and roofs reintroduces ash back into the air rather than permanently removing it.
‘We are left to deal with it on our own’
Privitera says it’s not just during eruptive phases that she gets sick; her cough and respiratory symptoms stick around for weeks even after the end of an eruption.
Her fellow Nicolosi citizen, Delia Zappalà, who co-owns a factory that uses lava stones to produce artistic objects, says that for as long as she can remember, her family and neighbours have had to collect bags of volcanic ashes themselves. These were often kept for months in a corner of their garden, as the municipality didn’t provide proper collective removal or guidelines on how to dispose of it. “It’s a nightmare every time, and we are left to deal with it on our own,” she tells Euronews Earth.
The Sicily Region and its civil protection department did not respond to a request for comment.
Crimi suggests that, for now, the best way for citizens to protect themselves is to wear a mask when there’s intense volcanic activity.
Privitera, who now doesn’t leave the house without a mask during periods of intense ashfall, adds: “It’s just a palliative, but until we take this more seriously, that’s the best we can do to stop coughing.”
Could volcanic ash be transformed into a useful resource?
For years, Sicilian researchers have tried to cooperate with authorities to advance solutions that minimise the health impacts of ash.
“We have drawn inspiration from Japan, where around active volcanoes such as Sakurajima, authorities integrate rapid ash removal systems. But we lag behind in terms of technology and planning, where a huge gap still remains,” says Paolo Roccaro, an environmental engineering professor at the University of Catania.
Roccaro says that, despite decades of frequent eruptions at Etna, as well as volcanoes on Sicily’s Aeolian islands, the issue keeps being treated as an emergency rather than a persistent problem that requires planning and mitigation.
He hopes a decree passed by the region of Sicily in March could encourage better coordination of ash removal – with benefits for people, business and the environment.
It aims to transform volcanic ash into a valuable natural resource by officially reclassifying it from hazardous waste to a reusable raw material. This opens opportunities for mineral-rich ash to be utilised in industries such as construction, where it can become a partial cement replacement, among other uses.
Roccaro thinks this could significantly help tackle its health effects. “More ash employed in productive activities means less flying around or piling up as waste that can potentially be tossed around again, even after a long time,” he tells Euronews Earth.
