‘We go where we are welcome’: BISR analyst on Belarus’ cooperation with ‘far arc’ countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:12:00 UTC
04:12:00 KST

File photo
                    
                    MINSK, 21 August (BelTA) – By strengthening relations with countries of the far arc, Myanmar in particular, Belarus is betting on the future. Analyst of the Belarusian Institute for Strategic Research (BISR) Sergei Tomashov made the statement on the air of the ONT TV channel.
As the expert noted, Southeast Asia is a region with a population of about 700 million. “These are countries with young populations: about 30% of the population of ASEAN member states are young people. This means a workforce and an opportunity to develop production in their own countries. This is what drives economic growth. And the world’s attention to this region has increased. Indonesia and Vietnam are two examples. These countries are in the spotlight now, with capital flowing there and new opportunities for investment and production emerging. Belarus should not miss out on such opportunities,” Sergei Tomashov said.
Speaking about Myanmar, the expert stressed that by strengthening ties with this country, Belarus is betting on the future. “Relations with every country are always built within a certain system that includes political, economic and legal factors. We have a very positive political background in our relations with Myanmar. This is leader-to-leader diplomacy that is prompting the entire state machinery to move at an unprecedented pace. And, of course, there is the legal framework, which is nearing completion. There is also the process of building trade and economic ties – establishing logistics and financial mechanisms, where progress is being made. It will take some more time for all this to become fully operational,” the expert said.
“We go where we are welcome. Where there is a need for agricultural mechanization technologies, higher yields and education. Myanmar students are already studying at our universities, and these flows will grow over time, as the value of our education remains high. In healthcare, we can offer our technologies and medicines. These supplies are already under way,” Sergei Tomashov said.
He also noted that Belarus is developing instruments to support cooperation. In particular, a pilot project has been launched to compensate manufacturers for the costs of supplying products (Myanmar also included in the list of eligible countries). This will give exporters greater confidence, he said. There are also developments regarding export credits.

Australia, UK and Canada slam Israel ending probe into aid worker killings
In short:
Australia, the UK and Canada have issued a joint statement condemning Israel for ending an investigation into the death of seven aid workers in Gaza.
Australian Zomi Frankcom, three Britons, a dual US-Canadian national, a Pole and a Palestinian were killed by a drone strike in 2024.
The three nations called the Israel Defense Forces' decision not to pursue a criminal probe "shameful".
Australia, the UK and Canada have condemned as "shameful" Israel's decision to close an investigation into the death of seven aid workers killed in Gaza in 2024.
The World Central Kitchen employees — Australian Zomi Frankcom, three Britons, a dual US-Canadian national, a Pole and a Palestinian — died in a drone strike on their vehicle convoy after overseeing the unloading of a food aid shipment.
Israel's military called the incident a "tragic mistake".
"In the more than two years since, we have been pressing for Israel to swiftly and thoroughly consider the case and hold those responsible to account," the three nations said in a joint statement.
"The announcement by the IDF [Israel Defense Forces] on 19 August 2026 that it would not pursue criminal investigations into this strike, without further explanation, is shameful," it said.
The incident in April 2024 sparked global outrage and renewed calls to ensure the safety of aid workers in Gaza.
"Announcing this decision on World Humanitarian Day, while the world honoured the courage and sacrifice of humanitarians, was particularly egregious,"
The Israeli military acknowledged a series of errors at various levels of command, but a preliminary investigation concluded on Wednesday that there was no "reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct".
"Israel extends its condolences to the families of the seven World Central Kitchen aid workers … who tragically lost their lives under deeply regrettable circumstances," Israel's foreign ministry posted on X on Friday.
'Deeply offensive'
Israel's foreign ministry said the decision not to launch a criminal probe "was made by Israel's independent military prosecution authorities on the basis of strict professional and legal considerations".
"We remain committed to the safety of humanitarian personnel, compliance with international humanitarian law and preventing such tragedies from recurring," it added.
The US-based World Central Kitchen condemned the decision not to launch a criminal investigation, calling it "inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive".
It demanded an independent commission to investigate the air strikes "because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct".
On Thursday, Australia expressed outrage at the closure of the investigation and summoned Israel's ambassador to the country.
Ambassador Hillel Newman, who has defiantly defended the IDF probe, declined to apologise to Ms Frankcom's family but expressed sorrow for the family and suggested reparations could be available.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday that further investigation of the killings was "one of the options" that should be considered, but would not reveal the Australian government's next moves.
Mr Newman said Israel was open to possible legal avenues for further investigation.

Minot, Andersen Facilities Deteriorating as Military Building Repairs Lag, GAO Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:00:55 UTC
04:00:55 KST

Vital infrastructure at Minot Air Force Base, N.D., and Andersen Air Force Base, Guam, is suffering due to years of deferred maintenance and climate-related stressors, government auditors said in a new report—two prominent examples of larger issues affecting bases worldwide.
A Government Accountability Office report released Aug. 21 states that of the Pentagon’s 736,000-plus facilities around the globe, about one-third are more than 50 years old.
Faced with many other priorities in its budget, the Pentagon aims to fund 90 percent of its maintenance needs annually. But GAO found that the military actually only hits 80 percent funding. That deferred maintenance has in many cases led to damage, corrosion and mold at facilities that house troops, dining halls, runways and maintenance depots.
As a result, the military’s maintenance backlog has grown considerably. In fiscal 2020, GAO said, the department had a backlog of $137 billion in deferred maintenance costs. Five years later, that had more than doubled to an estimated $285 billion, which GAO called “a significant and growing risk to the department’s ability to support its missions.”
The Air Force needed $5.6 billion in funding under the Pentagon’s facilities sustainment model in 2025, GAO said, but only got $4.3 billion, or 77 percent of the needed amount.
At Minot and Andersen, the situation was even worse. Andersen needed $122 million in facilities sustainment funding in 2025, but received $34.7 million, or 28 percent of the needed amount. When fiscal 2023 through 2025 were averaged together, Andersen’s funding levels equated to 37 percent of the needed amount.
Minot averaged 40 percent funding for sustainment between fiscal 2021 and 2025, GAO said. In 2025, the report said that Minot needed $75 million, but received $23.5 million, or 31 percent.
GAO said the Air Force, as well as the Marine Corps, had not measured unfunded military construction and facility repair needs. But service officials told GAO they had “substantial unfunded needs” as of May 2025. Army officials identified about $140 billion in construction and repair projects that hadn’t been funded, and the Navy identified $70 billion in construction requirements and another $37 billion in needed repairs, also unfunded.
These deferred repairs negatively affect both service members’ quality of life as well as installations’ ability to accomplish their missions, GAO said, highlighting problems with some Air Force infrastructure.
Minot officials told GAO the base’s B-52 parking area is now more than 30 years past its expected lifespan, and a project to replace its old pavement is overdue. Air Force leaders told Minot officials to repair the parking area in phases, the report said, and the base put together a plan to do so.
However, the B-52 parking repair project has had to compete with other maintenance needs, GAO said, and as of September 2024 Minot had only replaced about one-third of the parking area. The base has had to conduct multiple smaller repairs to maintain the old pavement, GAO said, which officials said is less cost-efficient than doing the complete overhaul and cost about $3.5 million.
Pictures included in GAO’s report show the Minot B-52 parking area visibly cracked and crumbling, with large patches completely bare of asphalt. The pictures were taken in 2018, 2022 and 2024, showing this issue has persisted for years.
At Andersen, construction of a hangar for repainting low-observable coating is years behind schedule, GAO said. This forces the base to maintain older hangars to house those aircraft and routinely fly them to other locations for repainting, which increases operations costs and reduces their mission availability.
Many Pentagon facilities are rapidly aging and have been in use well beyond their intended lifespan, GAO said. Auditors reported visiting a 1960s-era building at Minot where lights and elevators were out of service, and the structure was showing visible age-related decay. A photograph in the report showed water that had leaked into the building’s foundation, which led to structural concerns.
The Air Force plans to demolish that Minot building because of those problems, the report said, and scaled back its maintenance in preparation for the demolition. But the building provides necessary services to Airmen and veterans and has needed workspace, which keeps the building in high demand, GAO said.
Extreme weather and climate can worsen some bases’ repair needs, GAO said. Severe cold and freezing temperatures—for which Minot is infamously known—and heat can strain HVAC systems.
Minot officials told GAO that broken furnaces lead to pipes freezing and then bursting, and that snow melting on leaking roofs often leads to water damage. Freezing temperatures can also exacerbate cracks in pavement, such as on the B-52 parking areas.
And at coastal and island bases such as Andersen, the salt air rapidly corrodes building systems, pipes, and other equipment like HVAC units, base officials told GAO. The heat and humidity can also lead to mold and mildew that is difficult to root out. GAO included a photograph of an HVAC condenser unit with visible rust.
Extreme weather such as coastal storms can also worsen bases’ infrastructure repair needs. Officials from Andersen and Naval Base Guam told GAO that Typhoon Mawar in 2023 extensively damaged their facilities, some of which has not yet been repaired.
GAO made multiple recommendations to the Pentagon, including to fully determine the risks to missions and quality of life from underfunding facility sustainment and repair backlogs, set a strategy to fix maintenance workforce shortages, and reevaluate standards and processes for facility maintenance at installations.
The Pentagon said its existing sustainment plans already help determine risks from underfunding and lagging repairs, and planned software improvements will improve those assessments. GAO said those efforts need to be paired with department-level studies of the effect of sustainment backlogs.
But the Pentagon disagreed with a GAO recommendation to strengthen oversight of installation maintenance programs, saying that it already provides maintenance standards, and that it does not have the workforce to handle this additional work. Without a department-level policy to oversee installation maintenance performance, GAO said, there is limited understanding of how well maintenance is performed across installations.
The Pentagon’s Inspector General earlier in August also released its own report raising alarms about mold, corrosion and other poor conditions at military bases in the Pacific region, including Air Force bases such as Kadena and Yokota in Japan.

Trump Says Controversial US Attorney Ed Martin to Leave Role
Unknown

How much does it cost to fight Pauline Hanson? Labor has options
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
One Nation's fickleness goes unpunished but Labor is figuring out how to fight it
If you have a spare $5, $10 or even $42, the Labor Party has a proposition for you: help stop Pauline Hanson.
The varying price tags are attached to a stream of digital fundraising pitches that offer a window into how Labor is approaching the electoral threat posed by One Nation.
But look beyond the requests for loose change and a more sophisticated strategy is emerging.
Labor is increasingly trying not to simply attack One Nation, but to bind Hanson and the Coalition together in voters' minds as partners in a shared agenda.
"One Nation and the Coalition are on a unity ticket to undermine universal super," begins one ad featured on Instagram asking for a $10 donation this week.
For the more spendthrift Labor supporter, a sponsored post claims One Nation is "rising" and the "hard truth" is the Liberals can "only form government with Pauline Hanson".
"If everyone seeing this ad donated just $5 today, we'd have the resources to take on One Nation and the Coalition," it says.
A different post addressed to "everyone who wants to stop One Nation" asks for a $30 donation to Labor to help train party volunteers.
Labor's digital marketing strategy is clear.
First, highlight Hanson's record on issues of workers' rights, pay and conditions.
Then, warn the Coalition does not have the numbers to govern without One Nation.
Increasingly, Labor is trying to argue its two opponents have a shared policy agenda.
A shifting political agenda
This all played out in a fundraising text message sent to ALP supporters ostensibly addressed from Treasurer Jim Chalmers asking for a $42 donation because Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg "wants to scrap your super" and Hanson is "backing him".
This missive caught the attention of Hanson, who replied on X with the rebuttal Chalmers was "full of shit" as One Nation was not looking to end super.
When this column asked Chalmers for a response, he said he was "genuinely worried" about the future of super "in the hands of the Liberals, the Nationals and One Nation".
"They do not support universal superannuation and preservation at its core," he said.
Bragg's appearance at the National Press Club last week provided the impetus for this latest example of the time-tested practice of a political party seizing on a news story to animate their supporters and raise funds.
Hanson's suggestion people be allowed to dip into their super when struggling with cost of living only galvanised Labor's argument that its opponents wanted to raid Australians' retirement savings.
This month Labor's digital ads were framed around superannuation; last month it was Hanson's uncomplimentary comments about paid parental leave.
But as politically potent as those issues may be, One Nation hasn't taken these attacks lying down.
After Labor asked supporters for a $27 donation to help fight Hanson in June, One Nation launched its "Fire the Liar" campaign in response and raised more than $4 million in just five days.
The amount of "earned media" — i.e. free publicity — Hanson's fundraising campaign attracted was quite unprecedented by Australian political standards.
Despite this, Hanson has either plateaued or slipped a little in the polls following scrutiny on some of her policy positions.
But as Labor moves against one populist idea, another rises in its place.
Yesterday it was superannuation, today it is slashing the tobacco excise under the highly contested notion it would quash the illicit cigarette market.
A test around the corner
While many are looking to the Victorian state election in November as the first real-world contest between Labor and a historically popular One Nation, there is another test coming sooner.
Next Saturday, residents in the WA state seat of Secret Harbour will vote in a by-election triggered by the retirement of the local Labor member.
The outer-suburban string of coastal towns south of Perth form exactly the sort of electorate where a mix of mortgage pressure, rapid population growth and voters willing to look beyond the major parties could prove a winning combination for One Nation.
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie, whose own federal seat of Canning overlaps with parts of Secret Harbour, certainly thinks so, criticising what he has felt was a lack of effort from his state colleagues.
"We should always strive to win, and we should signal that ambition to our voters," he told the Australian Financial Review this week.
Hanson's key advantage
Labor is at an incredibly high water mark in WA and increasingly sounds far from confident about retaining Secret Harbour themselves.
The not-so-subtle pivot from Labor sources in recent weeks has been to talk up the by-election as the source of an important "lesson" for how preferences might flow in future contests with the Liberals and One Nation.
Though not totally ruling out their chances, the shifting view inside Labor that the seat could fall to One Nation also raises the stakes for Hanson.
One Labor source told this column Secret Harbour was "exactly the type of seat" One Nation could win.
"Where if not there?" they said.
Perhaps that pressure was a factor in Hanson's recent staunch defence of WA's GST deal, which has been quite the change in tune to her critical remarks of the past.
Hanson's GST conversion is a reminder of a key advantage she holds compared with — arguably — most other politicians.
She is often able to jettison a previous position no longer deemed politically useful without any blowback from voters.
Labor is clearly getting more deliberate about how it fights One Nation, from the issues it chooses to prosecute to the way it increasingly links Hanson to the Coalition.
But Hanson is adapting too and historically has had considerable freedom to tailor her pitch to the political moment.

Israel's impunity has been virtually unaffected by collective concern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Israel's increasing settler violence highlights the futility of concerned statements
Records of the village of Qusra, just south of Nablus in the Occupied West Bank, go back to Ottoman tax registers of 1596. There has been documentation of its existence and that of its inhabitants ever since.
Documenting a place, and a community, and the events that occur there, is always important.
But documenting Qusra has made it one of the stand-outs in the wider story of Israeli actions against Palestinian people which, amid the noise of Donald Trump's chaotic war against Iran, have only escalated in 2026.
Earlier this month, Israeli settlers besieged three houses in Qusra telling the families that lived there they had to leave because the settlers were going to take their land.
The settlers cut off the water and electricity to the houses. They blocked the roads.
Such actions are not unusual in the West Bank. Nor are they by any means the worst that happen there.
Coverage of Qusra easier than of Gaza
Last month, settlers set fire to the village's newly constructed mosque after an earlier clash in another village in which four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers died, after a group of settlers entered an area of the West Bank for an "unauthorised hike", according to the Israeli military.
But the besieging of the three houses and their 15 inhabitants — which has continued with the UN allowed to deliver supplies — struck a chord in the international community, and particularly in the United States.
That was possibly because one of the houses that has now come under siege belongs to a Palestinian-American, Loai Ridi.
But it is mostly because the international media have been able to document what has been going on in real time, in real pictures.
The contrast with Gaza could not be more stark.
In Gaza, where the international media has not been allowed to independently enter since October 7, 2023, the killing of more than 70,000 people according to the Gaza Health Ministry, the wounding of many more, and the continuing appalling living conditions of around two million people on a small strip of land where the majority of buildings have been flattened, occupies a strange space in history where what we see and what are told bear little resemblance to each other.
The lack of international media access leaves it in a situation in which almost every event is contested, but the Israeli ban prevents the media from testing and filtering out false claims and information.
Israeli statements in response to questions about individual incidents reduce horrific events to the language of bureaucratic failure. Whether incidents are investigated at all, or go on to be a criminal investigation, they rarely result in any real accountability even if fault is admitted.
Israel clears soldiers over Australian aid worker
This week Australia expressed outrage at the findings of an internal IDF report which found "serious failures" in the process that led to the killings of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and six colleagues in April 2024.
The IDF said: "The decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."
The humanitarian aid group for which Frankcom worked, World Central Kitchen, said that "at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody".
"It had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple air strikes. It knew our team's movements, identities and activities in advance," it said.
"The military investigation conflates different timelines and events, muddies the story and shifts the blame for the IDF's illegal conduct."
Israeli Ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman said there was no intention to kill innocent civilians and that while he could "express deep sorrow and grief" for the families, he would not apologise over the deaths as that would have "legal ramifications".
"There are a lot of haters of Israel in Australia," he added. "We have seen this time and time again."
Overnight on Friday, Canada, the UK and Australia released a further statement on the matter, saying:
"The announcement by the IDF on August 19, 2026, that it would not pursue criminal investigations into this strike, without further explanation, is shameful. Announcing this decision on World Humanitarian Day, while the world honoured the courage and sacrifice of humanitarians, was particularly egregious. This decision is both too little and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf."
But notably, the three countries went further and said: "The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability."
They said Israel "must comply with its obligations under international humanitarian law and must do more to ensure that humanitarian staff can carry out their work safely. Lessons must be learned from this tragedy."
The Israeli foreign ministry responded by saying the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation "was made by Israel's independent military prosecution authorities on the basis of strict professional and legal considerations".
"It is based on the legal threshold required for initiating a criminal investigation, which is when there is reasonable suspicion for criminal misconduct."
The credibility of the IDF account was not helped by a reminder of two other notorious incidents at the time the findings were released.
The IDF announced it would be launching criminal investigations into the now globally famous incident in which a five year old girl, Hind Rajab, was left talking to emergency services in January 2024 from a car where she was surrounded by the bodies of her six dead relatives, after an IDF strike, only to eventually die, along with two paramedics killed by Israeli forces in an ambulance that was supposed to be on a negotiated path to rescue her.
The IDF said it would also launch a criminal investigation into the killing of 15 Palestinian paramedics in March 2025 in Rafah.
Post-mortems of the dead paramedics, whose bodies had been retrieved from a mass grave that had also buried their vehicles, revealed they had been killed at close-range with "specific and intentional" bullet wounds in heads and hearts.
But given the IDF's record of failure to bring people to account, and the time that has already passed since these events took place, there is already deep scepticism about the likely outcome.
For example, The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) — set up in the little girl's name to pursue legal action against those responsible for violence against Palestinians — said in a statement that has "no confidence in the Israeli military's reported decision to open criminal investigations into the murder of Hind Rajab, six members of her family, and the two Palestinian Red Crescent paramedics" or into the targeted killing of the 15 Palestinian paramedics.
"These reported investigations, even if they do occur, should not be mistaken for a genuine step toward justice," the foundation said.
"As numerous Palestinian and international legal and human rights organisations have documented for years, Israel's internal investigations into the criminal conduct of its own soldiers are fundamentally flawed and cannot be regarded as credible mechanisms of accountability."
US criticises Israel over West Bank
Back in the West Bank this week, the IDF has played what would be politely called an ineffective role in ending the siege in Qusra.
The events seem to have been one of those lightning rod moments to galvanise public criticism of Israel and its actions in the West Bank.
That most notably came from the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee.
The evangelist is a longstanding supporter of Israeli settlements in the West Bank and follows the Israeli practice of calling the area by the biblical names of "Judea and Samaria" — to assert the traditional Hebrew ownership of the lands.
Yet Huckabee this week condemned the besieging settlers at Qusra as "Israeli terrorists" and said the siege was inexcusable.
But as the siege was occurring in front of the world's media, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his cabinet ministers attended ceremonies in the West Bank to promote massive new settlements across the illegally occupied territory.
Australia was one of 21 countries, along with Britain, France, Italy, Canada and Germany, to sign a joint statement calling Israel's particular approval of a major settlement project which will effectively cut the West Bank in half — and further separate it from east Jerusalem "unacceptable and a violation of international law".
A group that monitors and maps conflicts and protests, ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data), says it has recorded more than 80 incidents involving settlers in Qusra since the beginning of 2026, "making it one of the three locations most affected by settler violence in the West Bank".
"These incidents included property theft and destruction, razing lands, physical clashes with Palestinians, and shootings at Palestinians — one of these shootings killed a Palestinian on 14 March," the group said in a statement.
Across the West Bank, it says it has recorded "300 incidents of land seizures between 1 January and 14 August, which is already higher than the 267 incidents recorded throughout 2025".
"In such incidents, settlers established outposts, built roads, placed tents and mobile rooms on Palestinian land, or seized homes, leading to more daily friction and violence between settlers and Palestinians."
The United Nations recorded more than 2,200 Palestinians displaced by settler violence and access restrictions in the first half of 2026 alone.
All these actions by Israel, a country whose ambassador to Australia told the National Press Club in March this year "will always be a beacon of hope".
Israel's enemies, Newman said, "seek its destruction for what it represents; a modern democracy, Western civilisation, and a national home for the Jewish people. There is no other country in the Middle East that upholds the same democratic ideals of Australia as Israel does."
Netanyahu goes from Trump whisperer to Trump ignorer
Are any of Israel's actions likely to change?
The answer to this has usually been that it is really only the United States that can apply any external pressure to Israel to change its actions.
But there is an election coming in Israel.
Donald Trump also now shows little interest in the fate of the Palestinians, particularly with his Board of Peace plan blown up by the Israelis.
Netanyahu long boasted to his country that he was the Trump Whisperer. Now he is just the Trump Ignorer.
There are still actions taken by the US which are clearly read as sops to Israel.
The US, for example, this week sanctioned the president of the International Criminal Court and a prosecutor tasked with investigating crimes committed by Israel during its war on Gaza.
But it was the language used by the US secretary of state Marco Rubio in unveiling the new sanctions that was the most troubling.
In another time, it would have sounded positively unhinged for a senior American official to describe an international court as a "corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate".
But not in these times.
Loading
Israel's ongoing impunity
Israel's actions in Gaza and the West Bank reflect a sense of impunity which only continues to grow.
It is equally reflected in its actions in the region.
This week Israel launched air strikes on a Syrian air base just 70 kilometres from the Turkish border.
The Syrian foreign ministry condemned the attacks and described them as an "unjustified act of aggression, a flagrant violation of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a dangerous escalation that threatens security and stability in the region".
But, beyond the 'buffer zones' and incursions in Syrian territory that Israel has been making for some time (along with those which have effectively claimed about 20 per cent of Lebanon), the target of the strike on the air base was actually Türkiye, which Israel claims has breached an agreed status quo by taking steps to establish a military presence in Syria by letting Turkish troops deploy near the air base.
On Wednesday, Netanyahu said in a political podcast that Israel will "not tolerate a Turkish military presence, which moves to the south, because it threatens us".
Like actions in the West Bank, the US has condemned the Israeli air strikes on the base as an "unnecessary escalation" and insisted the new Syrian government is not the threat the Netanyahu government argues it is.
Once again it is being ignored.
Once again that raises the question of what other countries, like Australia, really need to collectively do — rather than just speak firmly to ambassadors.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

Space Command to Relocate 200 Personnel to Alabama This Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:58:39 UTC
03:58:39 KST

U.S. Space Command officials say they’re on track to relocate 200 personnel from Colorado Springs, Colo., to Huntsville, Ala., by the end of this year as part of a multiyear transition of the command’s headquarters.
In the year since President Donald Trump announced U.S. Space Command would stand up its permanent headquarters in Huntsville—reversing a decision by former President Joe Biden to keep the command in Colorado—SPACECOM has made fast progress on its goal to relocate its 1,800 personnel there by 2031.
During a recent tour of SPACECOM’s temporary facilities at Redstone Arsenal, officials told reporters that more than 100 personnel already have moved from the provisional headquarters at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo., many of them intelligence professionals. Other functions have also started to migrate, and by 2028, officials expect half of the command’s workforce to be based in North Alabama.
“Since the president announced on the [Sept. 2] last year that we were moving our headquarters here to Redstone, we have been moving with speed and enthusiasm to get established,” SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting said Aug. 13. “While we’re executing this move, we have been relieved of none of our day-to-day mission requirements, and I’m very proud of the command executing the mission requirements in support of the joint force and the nation.”
Whiting spoke with reporters at the site that will eventually host the command’s first-ever purpose-built operations hub, designed to house space operators and international partners in a single location. The Pentagon’s fiscal 2026 budget includes $951 million to support design and early military construction for the building; SPACECOM expects to break ground at the 64-acre site next year and be ready to move in by 2032.
Building a facility designed specifically for SPACECOM’s operational needs will be a welcome change, Whiting said. Since being reestablished in 2018, SPACECOM has operated from a number of buildings scattered miles apart that make up its provisional headquarters. In the command’s first instantiation, from 1985 to 2002, it also lacked a purpose-built headquarters.
“To get this facility is going to be an incredible accelerant to our mission,” Whiting said. “It’s going to take a lot of work and effort to get it right.”
Purpose-Built Headquarters
While Redstone already houses a number of military and government organizations—including the Missile Defense Agency, the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, and the FBI—SPACECOM is the first combatant command to reside on the installation. Other organizations may have more of a bent toward weapons development or research and engineering, but Space Command is operations-focused, bringing together partner agencies across the Defense Department and the intelligence community, as well as allied militaries. That brings unique communications and security requirements.
Col. Raymond Ruscoe, deputy director of SPACECOM’s “Redstone Transition Team,” said building the facility—and executing the move—will be no small feat.
“There’s absolutely nothing easy about any of this,” Ruscoe told reporters. “We’re trying to shoehorn our operation into a base that was not built for what we are looking to do, and then we’re trying to build probably one of the most complex and expensive military construction projects that has happened in a really long time.”
Yet plans are progressing on schedule so far and the command has been granted special authorities to go fast.
“We’re not just running with scissors in our hands—we’re running fast with scissors in both of our hands, and nobody has told us to stop yet,” Ruscoe said. “Nobody has said the expectations that we are pushing the envelope in either personnel or facilities is outside the realm of the possible.”
Another challenge of the transition is managing headquarters operations across two installations and seven facilities. The command has grown accustomed to functioning in temporary workspaces over the past several years, as Congress, DOD, and three successive presidential administrations waffled on where it would be headquartered. Still, maintaining continuity is a hurdle.
Whiting said SPACECOM is equipping its temporary workspaces with the collaboration tools needed for geographically dispersed operations.
As commander, he is traveling to Huntsville at least every six weeks and expects that to increase moving forward, noting that his home base needs to be wherever the command’s Joint Operations Center is located. That center is SPACECOM’s main command-and-control node and will not relocate to Huntsville until the permanent facility is complete in 2031. So up to that point, the commander will remain based in Colorado.
Relocating Personnel
While it’s still too early to tell how many personnel will opt to move across the country to Alabama, SPACECOM and local community officials say they’ve been encouraged by the number of personnel who have already committed to relocate.
Space Command has encouraged civilian personnel to commit to the move, offering relocation and retention bonuses to those who volunteer.
“We are trying to do everything we can to incentivize our workforce,” Whiting said in February at AFA’s Warfare Symposium. “I’ve said to our civilian workforce, I want to make this decision as difficult as it can be for them because we’re putting our money where our mouth is that we need their expertise to sustain our mission.”
Michael Ward, senior vice president of government and public affairs at the Huntsville/Madison Chamber of Commerce, said he and his team have traveled to Colorado Springs to meet with Space Command personnel who he said show enthusiasm for the move.
Ward said people are often surprised to learn about Huntsville’s quality of life and education system, built over decades of growth dating back to 1941 when Redstone Arsenal was established. Since then, the city has attracted other federal government agencies, including NASA’s Marshall Spaceflight Center, Army Materiel Command, MDA, and the FBI—which is projected to relocate another 4,000 personnel to the region over the next few years.
That means Huntsville generally has the housing, utilities, and other infrastructure in place to manage an influx of new residents, along with the cultural and recreational attractions that can draw newcomers to the region.
“This is not our first rodeo,” Ward said. “This is something that we’ve been planning for and anticipating for a long time. … I think we’re pretty well positioned.”

Southern and eastern Finland face stormy weekend
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
21:57:11 EEST
03:57:11 KST

Southern and eastern Finland face heavy rain and strong winds this weekend as a low-pressure system moves towards the country, according to forecasts from Foreca and the Finnish Meteorological Institute.
Foreca said on Friday that its forecast for the system had strengthened. The weather service now expects widespread heavy rainfall, with 40–50 millimetres forecast across parts of southern and eastern Finland during the weekend.
The Helsinki region lies within the area expected to receive heavy rain.
Most of the rain is forecast to fall between Saturday night and Sunday morning. A daily rainfall total above 20 millimetres meets Finland’s threshold for heavy rain.
The low-pressure system will develop as a weather front moves from northern Italy across Central Europe towards the Baltic region. Foreca expects the centre of the low to form near Poland before deepening as it travels north.
Rain will start spreading into southern Finland during Saturday evening before reaching wider areas of southern and central Finland overnight and on Sunday.
Foreca forecasts 40–50 millimetres of rain across a broad area in southern and eastern Finland over the weekend. That represents more than half of the average rainfall for the whole of August in some locations.
Wind speeds are forecast to increase during the night between Saturday and Sunday. Foreca said gusts in southern and eastern Finland could reach levels associated with wind damage. The strongest winds in southern Finland are expected overnight, with strong gusts continuing across central and eastern areas on Sunday and into Monday.
Winds will come from the north and north-east. Foreca said this direction increases the risk of damage because winds in Finland more often arrive from the west or south-west.
Thunderstorms are not expected to form on a broad scale, though isolated lightning is possible along the southern coast overnight.
Temperatures are expected to remain between 15 and 20 degrees Celsius in most areas during the weekend, according to the Finnish Meteorological Institute. Temperatures will fall under persistent rain and drop to around 10 degrees at night.

Batteries send power prices up in midnight charging mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:55:44 UTC
03:55:44 KST

Batteries pushed power prices sky-high in WA's midnight charging surge
In the wee hours of a cold night last month, as most West Australians slept in their beds, a strange thing happened in the state's biggest and most important electricity system.
About 1am, prices on the spot market started to soar.
They had been hovering at an elevated level of roughly $120 per megawatt-hour (MWh) but suddenly began to climb to extreme highs of more than $350/MWh.
Driving that jump in prices was no catastrophic loss of a high-voltage power line or a major coal-fired plant.
It was a spike in demand and it was coming from an unexpected source.
The surge was coming from batteries, the very things supposedly designed to prevent just such a breakout in prices.
Why it happened — in the middle of the night when there was seemingly no obvious reason — is still unclear.
But experts say the episode highlights how the way batteries are managed will determine their impact on prices as Australia transitions away from fossil fuels.
A midnight mystery
One person who has been seeking answers is Marcus Freese, an analyst at Modo Energy.
He says a few things are known based on publicly available data.
For one, the batteries that charged between 1am and 2am on July 12 were all owned by state-owned WA power provider Synergy.
Freese says the effect was significant.
Combined, Synergy's four big batteries added more than 30 per cent to demand for power from the grid at a time when prices were already high.
"The market was not tight because of demand or renewable output," Freese wrote in a report.
"Underlying demand was unremarkable for the time of day, in line with the July average for that hour, and wind generation was close to its July average.
"The price rise instead coincided with Synergy increasing charging from 229 (megawatts) to 640MW, which added around a third to system demand at the overnight trough."
Freese says it is not the first time Synergy has materially pushed up prices in the market through the "coordinated charging" of its battery fleet.
He says it appears to make little sense as a tactic.
Not only does it push up prices that will ultimately be borne by everyone, Freese says it is not even profitable for Synergy's batteries.
In this case, on July 12, he says Synergy's battery fleet lost $383,000 across the day.
In the past 13 months, Freese says Synergy has lost more than $100/MWh on 54 days, while it has earned more than $100/MWh on just 31 days.
By contrast, the company that owns WA's other two mega batteries, French firm Neoen, has made money much more often than not.
"We've now observed this dynamic across April, June, and July," Freese noted.
"Synergy's coordinated charging adds material load (demand) at the wrong time, lifts prices, and then buys into the spike it helped create."
Big bets on batteries
The events in WA are being watched closely by energy observers across the country.
More than anywhere else in Australia — and, by some measures, the world — the state has led the charge into big batteries as a way to balance an electricity system turning towards renewable energy.
From practically nothing three years ago, the amount of large-scale battery capacity in WA's main grid has risen to about 1400MW.
Collectively, those batteries regularly meet more than 20 per cent of demand for power at peak times and can sometimes provide more than a third.
Michael Sarich, a senior vice-president of global energy consultancy Rystad, says WA has bet big on batteries, partly because of a very real vulnerability.
Its main electricity grid is an island, cut off from the rest of the world and unable to tap imports when times get tough.
Those batteries, he says, are aimed at safeguarding that system.
Sarich says the daily flood of rooftop solar was previously pushing daytime prices — and demand for power from the grid — to ever lower levels.
But when the sun set and the solar panels stopped generating, he says prices were rising to highs that were even more extreme.
Sarich says batteries had flattened this price curve by soaking up excess renewable energy at times of surplus and discharging in times of scarcity.
"The role the batteries have done really well is meet that evening demand, which is why you're seeing the price curve is a lot flatter across the day," he explains.
"But the other thing you need to remember is batteries are not really generators. They're really just moving demand around throughout the day."
Battery behaviour compounds winter woes
The strengths and weaknesses of batteries have been brought into sharp relief in WA in recent months.
In its most recent snapshot of WA's "wholesale electricity market", or WEM, the market operator noted batteries had indeed smoothed prices in the three months to June 30.
Those prices, however, had flattened out at record high levels of almost $120/MWh.
According to the Australian Energy Market Operator, coal plant and wind farm outages partly caused the price pain.
But so too did increased battery charging during the middle of the day and overnight, AEMO noted.
Sarich says these factors ran headlong into other inconveniences.
He says demand for electricity in winter is simply higher, while output from wind and solar is almost invariably lower.
For Sarich, winter, not summer, is now the biggest test of electricity systems and the people who run them.
He says WA, like the rest of the country, is moving to a system powered by renewable energy.
As such, it needs to be able to cope with extended periods in winter where the wind does not blow and the sun does not shine.
"Our view is over the next few years that wholesale prices are going to remain elevated because fundamentally it's all about supply and demand," Sarich says.
"You need to have enough supply from whatever source you've got."
Sarich says WA's safety net at the moment is gas-fired power, a relatively pricey form of power.
But he also notes that batteries are increasingly "mirroring" the behaviour of gas plants when they offer to supply their power to the market.
And at times of scarce supply, as has been the case in WA over much of the winter, this meant the prices offered had more often than not been high.
Bizarrely, energy traders not authorised to speak to the ABC also noted gas generators had fired up at times to meet the demand created by Synergy's batteries.
One such energy trader described the events as "crazy".
"The other key thing is there's only a very small number of these batteries," Sarich says.
"So, they've got this sort of dominant position."
With Synergy's two remaining coal plants due to be retired next year and in 2029, Sarich says the need to build enough capacity to replace those units is becoming urgent.
He is optimistic it will, pointing to a slew of wind projects under construction or in the pipeline.
Synergy would not be drawn on why its batteries were all charged at times when spot prices were high. A spokeswoman said they were a relatively new technology whose capabilities would be monitored and refined.
She said "safe, reliable and lowest-cost" energy systems needed diverse sources of supply.
Batteries offered flexibility that would allow greater amounts of renewable energy "while enhancing system reliability through rapid response to changing system conditions".
Growing pains, growing tensions
WA's Energy Minister, Amber-Jade Sanderson, also declined to comment on Synergy's trading behaviour.
However, she did not back away from the state's plans to close its coal plants and make the switch to a heavy dependence on green power.
"We've always said that the most reliable and affordable energy mix for the future is renewables backed by batteries and gas," Ms Sanderson said.
The minister blamed outages — planned and unplanned — at coal plants and a wind farm undergoing expansion for the high prices in recent months.
"This demonstrates why we need more renewables to keep prices down," Ms Sanderson said.
She stressed that households and small businesses in WA would be shielded from any pain in the wholesale market because the government regulated prices for those customers.
Amid the upheaval, Marcus Freese from Modo Energy says scrutiny needs to be applied to a battery fleet that now in a powerful position.
He notes batteries are now setting the prices in WA's main grid, whether charging or discharging, more than 90 per cent of the time.
Given this power and the inadequacy of current regulations, Freese says there is a risk Synergy could use batteries to push up wholesale prices to benefit the utility's fleet of other coal, gas and wind generators.
He argues this may have been the case in recent months, saying Synergy's batteries "paid $7.3 million to charge whilst its generation earned $18.4 million" across more than 70 high-price charging days.
"A high charging offer increases the price paid by the battery, but it can also increase the price earned by generation in the same portfolio," Freese wrote.
Looking ahead, he says WA's battery fleet and the way it is managed will evolve.
Indeed, he says it has already changed dramatically in the past year.
Revenues from batteries trading energy had plunged, he notes, led by Synergy's losses.
So, too, had revenues for system strength and security services.
Nowadays, he says, WA batteries earned most of their money for simply being there through so-called capacity payments.
These are paid to generators or batteries as a type of insurance for making reliable capacity available when the system needs it.
While a capacity market exists in WA, it does not in the national electricity market, which covers Australia's eastern seaboard.
On the eastern seaboard, batteries earn the lion's share of their revenues by trading energy — or the "arbitrage" between low and high prices — in the wholesale market.
Freese says WA's experience suggests batteries could have a counterproductive effect on prices if they are not managed carefully.
"In a market with wide spreads and a clear daily arbitrage window, how you charge matters as much as when you discharge," Freese wrote.
Sarich says batteries are playing a crucial role in helping to keep the lights on by storing energy as the share of renewable generation grows.
But their role in driving down prices is a different matter.
"I don't necessarily believe they will lower prices," Sarich says.
"And the reason for that is they're not providing more generation.
"You kind of need to think of them as an enabler.
"It's sort of like the cost you need to pay to enable more wind and solar, which is adding more generation, and that will push the price down.
"Once you add these sort of batteries, they provide the role of making the whole system work better."

Oman and Iran on Friday discussed mounting challenges to navigation through the strategic Hormuz Strait, calling for "practical understandings" to ensure the free and uninterrupted flow of maritime traffic through the vital waterway.
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi and his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, spoke by phone amid ongoing disruptions to traffic through the strait and persistent tensions between Iran and the United States, the state-run Oman News Agency reported.
According to the news agency, the two top diplomats discussed "ways to create conditions conducive to resuming dialogue, with the aim of narrowing differences and reaching peaceful solutions ... while taking the interests of all parties into account.”
They also reportedly stressed the importance of reaching "practical understandings” with a view to restoring smooth navigation through the strategic waterway.
In early August, Tehran announced it had reached an understanding with Muscat on the geographic coordinates of a proposed maritime corridor for commercial vessels transiting the Hormuz Strait.
At the time, Iran’s foreign ministry said the two sides had agreed on the corridor’s geographic criteria, while a joint statement outlining main points of agreement remained to be finalized.
Traffic through the Hormuz Strait remains well below prewar levels amid continued security risks and frequent attacks on commercial vessels traversing regional waters.
On Friday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that traffic through the strait stood about 90% below prewar levels.
In mid-August, the UKMTO reported that maritime traffic had reached 17 percent of its prewar average after falling to 4 percent the previous week.
In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding calling for a cessation of hostilities and the restoration of shipping through the strait.
But the deal later fell through amid chronic disputes over the terms of its implementation and the future of navigation through the waterway.
The conflict began in late February with a surprise U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, to which Tehran has responded by striking targets in Israel and U.S. military bases across the region.

Tempers are flaring, fists are flying around the NFL during joint practices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:53:02 UTC
03:53:02 KST

Tempers are flaring, fists are flying around the NFL during joint practices
Joint practices are out of control when a guy like Jameis Winston, viewed as being easygoing on the field, is throwing punches and getting decked in the middle of a brawl.
Tempers have been flaring around the NFL as many teams are practicing against each other ahead of preseason games.
Winston was at the center of a fight between the New York Giants and Miami Dolphins on Thursday.
The Dallas Cowboys and the New Orleans Saints were fined $500,000 apiece by the NFL after a brawl-filled joint practice Tuesday.
There were several skirmishes between the San Francisco 49ers and Tennessee Titans last week that led to two players from each team being tossed out of practice.
“It’s not a game, so you don’t have the same, quite, guardrails on it,” Giants coach John Harbaugh said. “And it’s a violent game. And so, in this sort of an environment, you have these rules of engagement that aren’t really rules of the game. And then somebody perceives somebody else goes over the line, or they do go over the line, and somebody needs to protect somebody, and that’s where it goes. And I think as long as it doesn’t get out of control where we get a violent type of situation, it’s fine. We decided that anybody that threw a punch in those scrimmages would be treated like the game.”
The joint sessions have become the preferred way to give starters valuable repetitions in a competitive environment. Most coaches prefer to keep key starters or all their starters, in some cases, out of preseason games so facing opponents within a controlled setting has become a priority for most teams. Overall, 28 of 32 teams are holding joint practices this year.
Fights are not considered OK during joint practices
Coaches have warned their players about fighting, making it clear it’s disruptive and counterproductive.
“We don’t tolerate it,” Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said. “The way I explain it to the players, every time we do one of these — you have 90 teammates in camp. Now you’ve got 180 teammates. We’re just working against each other. OK, they’re in a different jersey, a different helmet. We’re not here to fight. We’re here to get better as an individual and a team, and hopefully we’ll all treat it that way.”
Philadelphia held two joint sessions with the New England Patriots this week. There was one minor scuffle, prompting Eagles star running back Saquon Barkley to say: “I hate joint practices, to be honest.”
“More times than not nothing good comes out of it,” he said. “When you have the work, it’s good, but then you get the pushing, the shoving and someone says this about you and it’s ‘I don’t know about that but you’re this.’ It’s immature when you get to that level. I have to do a better job, too, because I’m a little troublemaker sometimes, but I was good this week.”
Fights are inevitable considering players are going at each other, talking trash, grinding in the hot sun on humid days.
It takes plenty of discipline to show restraint.
“I love joint practices, being able to play in our defense, in our style against another team,” Arizona Cardinals safety Budda Baker said. “Yeah, the cons are fighting, but at the end of the day, we’re professionals. ... As long as you can play the game at a high level and respect the other team, fights won’t happen.”
Respect a key to keeping joint workouts professional
Baker said teams are supposed to maintain the same etiquette in joint practices as they do against each other.
“If the ball is in the air and you see the receiver in a compromising position, and I’m coming downhill on the ball, I’m not going to hit him,” Baker said. “I’m going to let him catch it and tap off. I might talk my little (trash) and tell him, ‘You probably wouldn’t have caught that.’ But you’re being a professional. You wouldn’t want to hurt your own teammates so you don’t want to hurt the opposing team in a practice.”
Fights occur when players breach that etiquette or hit a quarterback.
“You should never get close to the QB,” Baker said. “Quarterbacks are the most important position in football. Losing a quarterback in practice against another team — that’s something where fights will definitely happen.”
The Cleveland Browns and Buffalo Bills were quite chippy during their joint practice but avoided fights. Browns coach Todd Monken said players are told they’ll be tossed out of practice for throwing punches. In some cases, they might end up playing in the preseason game as punishment when they normally weren’t going to suit up.
“There has got to be an accountability and a discipline to what we do,” Monken said. “But I also want the guys to have a mindset and a personality while they’re out there as well. It’s a fine line.”

AP Sports Writers David Brandt, Josh Dubow, Dan Gelston, John Wawrow and Stephen Whyno contributed.

The week that blew up the Swans and called out AFL culture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:43:30 UTC
03:43:30 KST

The week that blew up the Swans and called out AFL culture
The disturbing and potentially criminal events at the Pullman Hotel last Monday morning have triggered the darkest chapter in Sydney Swans' history and spotlighted a sordid AFL underbelly.
The most serious allegation is that one of the players sexually assaulted a woman by touching her without consent.
None have been charged, and while the police investigation is ongoing, these events are creating a greater conversation about the AFL's handling of allegations of violence against women.
The woman who alleges she has been sexually assaulted has said she will fight.
"I am going to stand up for what is right," she told the Herald Sun on Thursday.
This latest incident has highlighted the lack of a clear "no-fault stand-down" policy in the AFL — one that has successfully been in place in the NRL.
Looking back at the past 16 years, there have been a number of AFL footballers charged with crimes such as sexual assault, rape and indecent assault, and the league has imposed varying penalties. Not one player has been convicted.
An AFL player had his contract ripped up in 2010 (his rape charges were later dropped).
In 2020, Collingwood superstar Jordan De Goey was charged with indecent assault of a woman. He played on.
In 2021, Victoria Police had to pay legal costs to De Goey after it dropped a historical indecent assault charge against him.
When Geelong star Tanner Bruhn was charged with rape and intentional sexual touching, the AFL stood him down from playing for the entire 2025 season.
Bruhn also sought a suppression order so his name was never public and he sat out Geelong's season with a reported "finger" injury. Those charges against Bruhn were dropped last November, when a key witness admitted to lying.
Previously, the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) has pushed back against a no-fault stand-down policy, which the NRL has used to great effect; it's a rule that means players facing serious charges involving women are automatically barred from playing footy.
After the charges were dropped, a telling moment came in November last year, when the AFLPA issued a firm statement opposing the young footballer Bruhn being stood down from playing for the entire season.
"Tanner was entitled to the presumption of innocence from the outset and throughout. It was clear to us that standing Tanner down would be premature and disproportionate," the AFLPA said in a statement in November last year.
The statement said the AFLPA would like to "resolve" a code of conduct with the AFL "including proper processes and a sanctioning framework".
"We remain committed to this work in the best interests of the players and Australian football," the AFLPA said.
Earlier this year, on the eve of Bruhn's first game in 17 months, Geelong coach Chris Scott was highly supportive of his player.
"It's just fantastic for him to get out there and be able to concentrate on footy after what is one of the most egregious injustices I can think of in the game," Scott said.
When contacted this week, an AFLPA spokesperson said the association had previously opposed a blanket no-fault stand-down policy, but was open to discussing it.
The NRL implemented its no-fault stand-down policy seven years ago and believes it has shifted culture.
That policy automatically removes players from playing if they are charged with a serious criminal offence carrying a maximum prison sentence of 11 years or more.
It was introduced in March 2019 and applies on full pay without prejudging the footballer's guilt.
Just months after the NRL put it in place, Dragons star Jack De Belin, then up on a sexual assault charge, opposed the stand-down policy in the Federal Court and lost.
Federal Court Justice Melissa Perry dismissed de Belin's legal challenge against the Australian Rugby League Commission and the NRL, ruling it a lawful measure to protect the game's reputation.
The NRL chief executive also has the discretionary power to stand down players whose charges involve women or children, regardless of the jail term.
The NRL is proud of this policy, which was driven by key commissioners, including former Queensland premier Peter Beattie, professor Megan Davis and now league chair Peter V'landys.
Insiders say it has been monumental in helping improve culture in the game.
While in AFL there has been the rise of the AFLW competition and more women are commentating the game, and in influential positions in footy clubs than ever before, this week, one prominent woman in the industry called out a festering "horrific misogyny".
Commentator and former player Kate McCarthy said the AFL needed to look deeply at its culture and inclusion of women.
She told the Herald Sun earlier in the week that language used by Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich in initially addressing the matter on Monday concerned her.
Pavlich spoke about the Swans players finding "themselves in this situation".
"Is there really any surprise that women within the industry experience such horrific misogyny when the role models or people in positions of power like CEOs of clubs use language saying that the 'players found themselves in this situation,'" McCarthy said.
It's also only two weeks ago AFL Hall of Famer and former Geelong footballer Sam Newman drew outrage for his comments on former AFL player manager Ralph Carr being found guilty of two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault.
"I'm just wondering what sort of evidence they had about him raping her," Newman said on his podcast. "Other than the fact she might have buyer's remorse."
Newman, at last check, maintains his AFL Hall of Fame status. This is despite the AFL stating it takes in "integrity" and "character" when it comes to holding the status.
In June this year, St Kilda great Nicky Winmar was swiftly removed from the AFL Hall of Fame after he was found guilty of three assault charges against a woman.
The sexual assault allegation against the Swans has moved those holding Australia's highest offices to make statements.
The prime minister said the "AFL certainly has to do better" and raised the NRL's leading stand-down policy on 7.30 on Thursday night.
Governor-General Sam Mostyn, a former Swans board member for six seasons, said her thoughts were with the alleged victim and that she was "shocked and troubled" by the allegations involving the team.
"At times like this, we are reminded to never take for granted the need for constant vigilance for respectful treatment of women everywhere; across clubs, the AFL, sport, and the community generally," she told ABC.
"Sadly, the lack of respect for women across the country remains an issue for us all to be concerned about, particularly in sport."
The governor-general added she believed there should be more women in positions of power and influence not only in the AFL but all sporting codes.
Whether the AFL acts on this week's events, making firm policy and broader change, remains to be seen.
In the meantime, this scandal has raised a disturbing question: has the AFL's inaction in installing a strict policy that ensures that all players are stood down automatically when they are charged with a crime against a woman created an environment where players are not wholly focused on the issue of ensuring respect for women?
Putting the most grave and serious allegation of sexual assault to the side, the reports that players felt comfortable hiring adult entertainers, allegedly doing drugs off the women's bodies and were drinking well into the early hours of Monday two weeks out from finals, have also spotlighted the fact the once-famed "Bloods culture" has run dead.
Former Swans captain Kieran Jack, who led the team to a premiership in 2012, said he felt "devastated" and "very troubled" by players' actions and that Bloods culture "feels broken".
He notably said a "lack of respect for women" cannot be tolerated.
"'Bloods culture' is often spoken about," Jack wrote on Instagram. "This was built and maintained through a core pillar of respect. Respect for each other, respect for the club, your family, the opponent, supporters and importantly, community. Right now this feels broken. A lack of respect for women cannot be tolerated."
The Bloods culture, which was created by club coach Paul Roos and players such as workhorse midfielder Brett Kirk, was founded on humility, discipline, selflessness and hard work.
More than 20 years ago, the Swans established this true team-first culture. If one player in the group broke the team rules, all would pay.
There were secret punishment sessions conducted before sunrise, and they often involved players turning up in the cold to do additional strenuous physical training like push-ups on the asphalt with their bare knuckles. These sessions were player-led and enforced.
There were no individual sponsorships with toothpaste companies. No rock-star midfielders. Players were encouraged "not to go down media street" and do unnecessary publicity.
Heading into the 2005 grand final, the Swans midfield was likened to the basic car brand "Ford Cortinas" coming up against the West Coast Eagles midfield made up of "Lamborghinis". The Swans beat the Eagles by a point and broke a 72-year premiership drought.
As Kirk said after that premiership, it was a group of men who could unequivocally trust one another. "It's hard to put a measure on it, but what you do know is that you have 100 per cent commitment and trust that the guys you're playing with that sacrifice and do anything for you, that they'll never let you down," Kirk said.
But as sources familiar with that period of time remarked this week, the Bloods culture had been betrayed, and some noted their famed unofficial "no dickheads policy" had truly been abandoned.
"We have to stop on occasions believing our own bullshit," one remarked.
John Longmire, who coached the team to the 2012 flag and was at the helm of the club until 2024, said he was saddened by the events and it would take time for the club to climb its way out of the darkness.
"The culture of the footy club has taken a big hit, and it will take time for everyone to rebuild the trust in the football club," he told Fox Footy this week.
Swans chair Andrew Pridham said he was "very proud" of the club culture. However, some believe it has been brutally exposed as having serious cultural issues when it comes to women.
But it is an issue that extends beyond the Swans, one that should trigger deep evaluation and a review. It's absolutely a review that should extend past the Swans' $70 million Moore Park clubrooms into the AFL in general.
As former AFLW player McCarthy expertly put it: "The AFL talks a lot about wanting women and girls to feel that football belongs to them.
"That can't only mean having an AFLW competition or getting more women through the gates.
"It also means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated and how the industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise."

====================================================================================================

AI's threat to future jobs considered in landmark NSW compensation decision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:43:30 UTC
03:43:30 KST

AI job disruption priced into man's compensation payout in first known case
In short:
The NSW Personal Injury Commission assessed a 34-year-old Aldi and home delivery worker suffered damages of $950,000 after a car crash on his way to work.
Commission member Phillip Carr cited uncertainties including the impact of artificial intelligence on the job market when calculating his future economic loss.
What's next?
The government says it's too soon to draw firm conclusions that AI is causing or will cause future job losses but will keep monitoring the data.
Artificial intelligence's disruptive impact on jobs was priced into an almost $1 million injury claim after a car accident left a NSW man with reduced working capacity.
It's the first known case of a legal body explicitly considering the impact of AI on the workforce when calculating a worker's future earnings.
Earlier this month, the NSW Personal Injury Commission assessed that Andrew Duong suffered damages of $950,000 after he suffered both physical and psychological injuries following a head-on collision on his way to work in 2023.
This included the 34-year-old's $400,000 of future economic loss after finding he could only continue working with restrictions, and the injuries and pain would impact his ability to find future employment if he could no longer work at his current job.
Commission member Philip Carr wrote that Mr Duong had 33 years of working life ahead of him that would be affected by his loss of capacity.
Mr Carr determined that Mr Duong should receive a "significant buffer" for the uncertainty around future loss of earnings, which included the impact of AI.
"[And] with the uncertainty of any occupation in today's workforce, especially with the advent of artificial intelligence and its workplace challenges during his working life, which requires an allowance for his future continuing loss of capacity," he wrote.
The tribunal did not find that AI had cost Mr Duong work, or predict that it would, only that AI may create more job market uncertainty that could disproportionately affect an injured worker with need for greater accommodations.
Before the crash, Mr Duong was working about 70 hours a week in warehouse roles for Aldi and Home Delivery Service.
The crash caused injuries to his right hand and wrist, shoulder, elbow and lower back, as well as a psychological injury. He had two operations on his wrist.
Mr Duong lost his Aldi job after the crash because he was not cleared to return to full-time work, but was still employed by the delivery company on reduced hours.
Mr Carr found Mr Duong could continue in that role with restrictions but said his prospects on the open labour market would be "considerably reduced" if he lost it.
Artificial intelligence was one of multiple considerations mentioned by Mr Carr when assessing Duong's capacity to earn, alongside his injuries, medication and the risk of losing his current role.
How will AI impact future jobs?
Queensland University of Technology's associate professor in economics, Dr Leonora Risse, said there was a lot of uncertainty about how AI would influence the job market.
"There's no one definitive clear result. In some ways it'll be positive, in other aspects, it will be negative," she said.
Dr Rissa said even if certain jobs or industries were not threatened by automation, there would still likely be an impact on the tasks that comprise a job and the skills required.
"Work and tasks are going to look very different," she said, adding that the job market has always been in flux as a result of technological change.
The decision comes after the federal government recently released its first ever analysis of AI's impact on the jobs market, which found no evidence of broad AI-driven disruption in Australia's labour market so far.
Modelling by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations suggested employment in a more AI-exposed occupation was about 2 per cent lower by February than under its pre-ChatGPT trend.
But the department repeatedly cautioned that this was not proof AI had caused job losses. Jobs exposed to the technology had already been growing more slowly before ChatGPT became widely available.
The government said it would continue monitoring the data as more evidence became available.
