The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has developed and submitted to the market for discussion amendments to the Rules for the Organization of Statistical Reporting Submitted to the Central Bank, the regulator said on its website.
According to the draft NBU resolution, the amendments are aimed at bringing the Rules into compliance with the requirements of Ukrainian legislation and ensuring the ability to obtain reports from respondents (statistical reporting providers) in order to monitor their compliance with these requirements.
The draft amendments to the Rules, in particular, provide for the introduction of new files containing statistical reporting indicators: RX, "Data on the number of users and user accounts to which access is provided under open banking"; N1X, "Data on accounts for which acquiring services are provided"; and N2X, "Data on the volume of transactions conducted using payment devices."
The amendments also provide for changes to the structure of 20 existing files (the list of indicators, parameters, metrics and unclassified details of indicators); the deadline (time) for submitting and/or amending nine files; the name of the respondent (statistical reporting provider) for one file; and other changes.
Comments and proposals on the draft resolution will be accepted in the prescribed form until Sept. 1, 2026.
According to the statement, the relevant resolution will take effect on January 1, 2027.

US sees 'record breaking' numbers of Muslims in US public office despite rising Islamophobia

CAIR hailed the "record breaking" figures as a demonstration that American Muslims would not be intimidated away from taking public office, despite the current climate of Islamophobia.
“Anti-Muslim extremists are attempting to tell American Muslims that we do not belong in the halls of power, these 228 public servants are proving otherwise every single day," CAIR National Executive Director Nihad Awad said in a statement to The New Arab.
"Muslim Americans are not standing on the sidelines. We are serving our neighbors, strengthening our communities, and helping shape the future of our nation. We will not allow hate, intimidation, or political attacks to silence our voices or diminish our rightful place in American civic life."
Earlier this month, the rights group slammed US President Donald Trump over statements which it said put a "target" on the backs of Muslim elected officials. A further 56 Muslim officials are serving as state representatives or senators, making up 18% of the public officials in the directory.
Other officials include 18 Muslim judges and 11 Muslim mayors. Women were also identified as representing more than 4 in 10 Muslim elected officials in the US.
“This directory represents the growing political power and civic engagement of Muslim communities across America. US op to smuggle Gulf oil unlikely to alleviate underlying risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:52:44 UTC
01:52:44 KST

Breadcrumb
US operation to smuggle oil from Gulf unlikely to alleviate ‘underlying risks’, analysts say
Despite reports that the United States is attempting to move oil out of the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to circumvent restrictions imposed during the US-Israel war with Iran, analysts have told The New Arab that any such operation is unlikely to reduce the fundamental risks facing energy shipments from the region.
Washington has reportedly been conducting a secret operation for several weeks to move up to 10 million barrels of oil per day, roughly half of pre-war export levels, out of the Gulf, according to an Axios report published on Wednesday.
Citing two US officials, the report said that between 15 and 20 tankers a day had been transiting to and from the strait through a southern channel along Oman’s coast.
However, Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme specialising in energy policy and geopolitics, said the reported operation was not a sustainable solution to the disruption in the Gulf.
"The operation itself does not surprise me, but I see it as a short-term workaround that allows Trump to claim greater control over the Strait," Quilliam told The New Arab. "The underlying risk has not changed."
He said the operation "was not sustainable and already comes with significant risk", pointing to a June incident in which a US Apache helicopter was reportedly downed by an Iranian drone while supporting earlier efforts to move oil through the Gulf.
The episode triggered a fresh round of clashes between US and Iranian forces, reflecting a pattern of recurrent escalation since the Memorandum of Understanding that ended the full-scale war in June.
"While Iran’s surveillance and coastal monitoring capabilities have been degraded by US military action, it retains the ability to launch drones and other strikes against vessels, which we have seen in recent weeks," Quilliam said.
Without US facilitation, support vessels and broader logistical backing, commercial operators would be unlikely to undertake such transits independently, Quilliam added.
"As a result, this remains a costly and high-risk enterprise that is likely to become a prime target for Iran," he said.
Difficult to verify
The report, which also said the US operation was being coordinated with Gulf states, is difficult to independently verify, according to the analysts who spoke to The New Arab.
Hamish Kinnear, principal Middle East and North Africa analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said verification was complicated by tankers switching off their transponders while moving through the strait.
"There is a delay to the satellite imagery and ship chartering data that can be used to reconcile reported volumes against actual volumes," Kinnear told The New Arab.
Quilliam similarly said the lack of vessel-tracking data made firm assessments of the scale of the operation difficult.
"Given that many of the tankers traverse the straits with their transponders off, it is very difficult to provide accurate figures for the numbers of vessels, and therefore the volumes of crude, that have exited this way," he said.
Pressure on prices
The Strait of Hormuz, through which around one-fifth of global oil consumption normally passes, has been a central point of contention in negotiations between Washington and Tehran. The near-total disruption to shipping has pushed global oil prices sharply higher, from around $60 per barrel before the war to a peak of roughly $118.
Although prices have since fluctuated, a barrel of oil was trading at around $93 on Friday, placing renewed pressure on the Trump administration, which has repeatedly pledged to bring down costs for US consumers.
Kinnear said market pricing suggested traders had already accounted for at least some successful "dark" transits through the waterway.
"For now, the industry consensus is the oil price, which is creeping up despite these new claims," he said. "The fact that benchmark prices are still below USD100 per barrel in part reflects the baked-in price impact of successful dark transits."
If US claims that traffic through the strait has increased prove accurate, Kinnear said this could strengthen Washington’s hand in negotiations with Tehran.
"That doesn’t necessarily make a deal more likely, as Tehran may seek to escalate in other ways to re-establish its negotiating position — by once again targeting energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf, for example," he added.
Quilliam said the operation should not be viewed solely as an attempt by Washington to influence oil prices. Gulf governments also had a clear interest in maintaining exports through the strait, he said.
"The US has always had an interest in ensuring oil prices sit within a reasonable range, and the price at the pump is, of course, a critical concern domestically, given the upcoming midterm elections," Quilliam said.
"However, an operation like this would obviously be coordinated with Gulf allies, who have their own important reasons to want oil to continue moving out of the strait. So, I would not characterise this as a US attempt to manipulate the market, but rather a response to pressure on oil prices, the result of which benefits both Trump domestically and Gulf allies’ budgets."

Intraday odd-lot trading to start on December 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:22 UTC
01:43:22 KST

Intraday odd-lot trading is scheduled to start in line with standard block trading from early December as part of the Taiwan Stock Exchange’s (TWSE) efforts to optimize the local intraday odd-lot trading mechanism, the exchange announced on Thursday.
Execution of intraday odd-lot trading is to begin at 9am every trading session from Dec. 7, 10 minutes earlier than the current trading time, while brokerages would start to take orders from investors for odd-lot trading at 8:30am, 30 minutes earlier than the current schedule, also in line with standard block trading, the TWSE said.
The change aims to improve convenience for investors and improve overall market efficiency, the TWSE said.
Photo: CNA
Odd-lot trading allows purchases of fewer than the standard lot of 1,000 shares and makes high-priced stocks more accessible to retail investors.
For example, 1,000 Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) shares would cost NT$2.41 million (US$75,672) based on yesterday’s closing price, but odd-lot trading allows investors to spend NT$2,410 to buy one TSMC share to have a stake in the world’s largest contract chipmaker.
To support the new arrangement, the TWSE said it would introduce pre-market information disclosure and delayed opening mechanisms for odd-lot trading to maintain transparent price discovery and orderly markets.
Opening prices and actual opening times for the same stock might differ between odd-lot trading and standard block trading, as they operate in two independent trading mechanisms, the exchange said.
The exchange would continue to review intraday odd-lot trading to further improve the trading mechanism so as to balance price discovery and stabilize market operations, and eventually promote the development of Taiwan’s capital market and enhance trading quality for investors, it said.
In early June, President William Lai (賴清德) said that the government aims to transform Taiwan’s capital market into an Asian equivalent of the tech-heavy NASDAQ market for start-ups from around the world.
Lai said that the government’s efforts include relaxing rules on odd-lot trading and day trading, which allows traders to buy and sell, or sell and buy, the same shares in a single session.

Harsher fines added to energy act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:22 UTC
01:43:22 KST

The Legislative Yuan yesterday passed a bill to authorize a repeatable fine of up to NT$750,000 for top electricity users whose renewable energy capacities do not meet regulatory requirements, although it exempts current heavy users.
The Energy Administration Act (能源管理法) amendments are now headed to President William Lai’s (賴清德) desk.
Taiwanese law mandates that industrial power users with contract capacity of at least 5 megawatts must install renewables capable of generating at least 10 percent of their contract capacity.
Photo: CNA
In May, the Cabinet proposed amendments adding further requirements for self-use power generation and energy storage equipment.
Lawmakers passed the bill without contest, in a rare show of consensus across the political divide.
The amendments stipulate that new electricity users whose contracted energy capacity meets or exceeds a certain threshold must generate renewable energy or install power storage systems for part of their own use.
While the Cabinet had sought to include current heavy energy users in the bill, the final version passed yesterday limits the scope to only newly established or expanding large energy consumers — a change that has been criticized by environmental groups such as Greenpeace.
The authority tasked with implementing the act is empowered to determine the specific legal threshold of contract capacity and the required installed capacity of renewables and energy storage to electricity use.
Regulators should warn entities that did not install renewable energy or power storage systems or had installed systems that failed to meet government standards before imposing sanctions.
Energy users who did not heed warnings would be punished with a fine of NT$150,000 to NT$750,000, and failure to comply would incur repeated penalties.
Changes to the law are to require top power consumers to appoint a qualified energy management specialist, and failure to comply would result in a NT$100,000 to NT$500,000 fine, up from NT$20,000 to NT$100,000.
Regulators would also name enterprises that endanger the public or negatively affect consumer rights with their energy consumption.
Energy suppliers would be required to publish power sales data for public and government scrutiny to facilitate energy policy, but considerations must be made to protect privacy, the amendments state.

The many tragedies of the Jason Arday case | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:22 UTC
01:43:22 KST

Hugh Muir is right to muse on the tragic nature of the Jason Arday case (A rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalism, 19 August). For it’s a tragedy in so many, many ways. It’s a tragedy that a man has died, leaving a grieving family and friends behind. And it’s a tragedy that the real and necessary objectives of diversity, equity and inclusion have been done a gross disservice by Cambridge University’s cynical tokenism.
It’s a tragedy that this lamentable affair may set back the vital pursuit of equality of opportunity. And it’s a tragedy that in place of moderate voices who understand the need for better representation but with caveats, we have bad actors who see things only through the heated lens of ideology, be that from left or right.
It’s a tragedy that the latter tendency would encourage some on the left, through anger in the wake of Arday’s death, to double down on circling the wagons for their side. And it’s a tragedy that in doing so, they risk becoming entrenched participants in a destructive culture war – and to hell with truth, integrity and decency.
And finally, it is, as Muir points out, a tragedy that in pursuit of a noble cause, some would go as far as attacking the many honourable journalists who were simply doing their job to report this story, in what is still a free press.
Colin Montgomery
Edinburgh
Hugh Muir’s article identifies what has been too peripheral in media coverage of the Jason Arday tragedy so far: that this situation has been the product of a ruthless campaign by the extreme right.
The Arday case is evidence of the extreme right’s obsession with academia as a key battleground, and the extent to which the views of a tiny number of highly marginal figures are hugely amplified by the mainstream media.
Much of the coverage of Arday’s position ignored the fact that the campaign against him had been led by Nathan Cofnas, a self-defined “race realist” with racist views who was dismissed from Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He and his like represent a minority within academia, but this summer has shown how the powerful resources of the extreme-right media machine can overpower scholarly standards.
This should be a wake-up call for all academics and universities to take seriously the power of these extreme groups and the need to hold their views to account. 
Eleanor Newbigin
Cambridge
 I agree with your editorial (17 August) concerning the role of racism in press coverage concerning Jason Arday and that journalists seeking to act responsibly should not be subjected to an onslaught of abuse any more than he was. But there is something missing from the editorial that our institutions, including our media, need to reflect on. You refer to Arday as an autistic child. That autistic child became an autistic adult, and I am not aware of the implications of this being considered in media reporting.
Carol Adams
Ballarat East, Victoria, Australia
The Guardian’s coverage of the Jason Arday story was badly misjudged. Not so much the content as the prominence given to it. For at least two days the headline piece on the website was devoted to someone I had never heard of and concerned events I had little interest in. This at a time when the world is at war and on fire.
The events leading up to the resignation of a Cambridge professor had a place in the UK news section of the website, but not as the lead story on successive days. Your self-serving editorial simply compounds this mistake. It justifies the content but makes no mention of the massive misjudgment in the prominence given to the story.
Stephen Tompsett
Winchester
 I appreciated the Guardian’s self-examination following the very sad death of Jason Arday as I have been reflecting on your coverage as well as that of other media. I would, however, urge you to expand the final sentence of your editorial, adding the words in italic here: “A society committed to equality must allow black people the same freedom as everyone else: to achieve, to excel, to teach and to lead, but also to be flawed, to make mistakes, and even to fail, without their failure becoming an indictment of their race.”
Annie Grist
Hebden Bridge, West Yorkshire
A straightforward mea culpa from Cambridge University would be more appropriate than expressions of sorrow over the tragedy of Jason Arday’s death.
The proper way to address the underrepresentation of black academics is to commit sustained time, effort and resources to the pipeline – from GCSE and A-level through undergraduate and graduate education to research fellowships and academic appointments.
Instead, Cambridge chose to make Jason Arday’s appointment into a highly public symbol of its commitment to diversity.
In doing so, the university inevitably focused exceptional attention on one individual and created circumstances in which both his record and his subsequent difficulties would receive exceptional scrutiny. Whatever the rights and wrongs of the allegations subsequently made against him, the immense pressure that followed was surely foreseeable.
Universities should address structural inequalities structurally, rather than place the burden of representing institutional progress upon individuals.
Prof John Ellis
Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge
I am deeply saddened to hear of the death of Jason Arday (Report, 14 August). I didn’t know him well enough to comment on the allegations he faced (which at the time of writing remain just that). But far from being a self-serving ladder-climber, he was a deeply thoughtful and generous colleague who cared for those he worked with and taught.
He took the decision early in his career to speak out about prejudice and reduce barriers for those who come after him, and the legacy of his work will live on. Far from Black scholars receiving preferential treatment, solid and repeated quantitative and qualitative evidence show that systematic biases are baked deep into the academic system, from postgraduate research onwards.
Yet it is so easy for us not to see racism, or not to acknowledge it. Over three decades in higher education, I have seen countless instances of plagiarism, lies on CVs and job applications, sexual misconduct and bullying by white academics; too often there has been little action taken, the academics in question have been promoted, and sometimes those raising these problems are victimised.
What can we do to honour Jason’s memory? Recognise the organised campaign of intimidation that Black and Brown students and academics are now facing in the UK, and our complicity in this tragedy; educate about the realities of prejudice; and continue Jason’s work to dismantle the barriers to higher education.
Prof Rachel Pain
Newcastle University

2026-08-21

01:43:18 KST

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) announced yesterday that it will add more NT$500 (US$15.71) prizes to its bimonthly cloud invoice lottery this year, starting with the July-August draw on Sept. 25.
Taiwan’s uniform invoice lottery is drawn on the 25th day of odd-numbered months -- January, March, May, July, September and November. Each draw covers receipts issued during the preceding two calendar months.
Lou Mei-chung (樓美鐘), director-general of the MOF’s Taxation Administration, said the ministry decided to increase the number of NT$500 cloud-invoice prizes after assessing the prize redemption rate.
Photo: Cheng Chi-fang, Taipei Times
The number of NT$500 prizes exclusively available to cloud invoice holders will be increased by 500,000 to 4.35 million per draw, up from the current 3.85 million, while the number of prizes in other tiers will remain unchanged, Lou said.
Lou said the total number of cloud invoice prizes will reach 4.466 million per draw from July through December, giving people who use electronic receipts a greater chance of winning.
Lou reminded the public that they can use the MOF’s E- Invoice Platform or its Uniform Invoice Redemption app to link various digital carriers to a mobile barcode and link a bank account to receive prize money, helping ensure they do not miss out on winnings.
Fiscal Information Agency Director-General Chang Wen- hsi (張文熙) said more than 2.85 million people have downloaded the app to date. The app was revamped on July 1 to provide a smoother and more convenient user experience.
New features include a bilingual interface and an automatic bank transfer service for prize winnings, Chang added.
Meanwhile, the agency reminded the public that the E- Invoice Platform never asks for credit card information via email or text message.
The warning came after reports of scammers impersonating companies in emails that directed recipients to fake MOF websites and asked them to enter their credit card information.

Abandoned DMZ train station: Seoul’s lonely push for peace with Pyongyang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:17 UTC
01:43:17 KST

Near the heavily fortified frontier dividing the Korean Peninsula, the abandoned Woljeong-ri Station is being recast as a symbol of South Korea’s hopes to reconcile with the North.
However, plans to reconnect South Korea’s northernmost station to the rail network come at an awkward moment, as Pyongyang ignores Seoul’s overtures while the South’s old ally Washington pursues its own talks with Pyongyang.
A turbulent few days have raised doubts about the role of South Korea in any diplomatic push, despite South Korean President Lee Jae-myung’s dovish line on the North since taking power last year.
Photo: AFP
US President Donald Trump abruptly scaled back annual military drills with Seoul this week, calling them “inappropriate and hostile” toward the North.
He also berated South Korea for not helping in his war against Iran and said he would meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un this year.
North Korea then fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles on Thursday, while Kim’s powerful sister mocked Seoul’s “master-servant” relationship with Washington.
The developments have overshadowed the Lee administration’s outreach, including the Woljeong-ri project aimed at “eventual” reconciliation.
The modest station — inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) — once sat on a line linking Seoul to Wonsan, but was destroyed during the 1950-1953 Korean War. It was reconstructed at its site in the border town of Cheorwon in 1988. It is now an attraction for visitors to the nearby DMZ separating the two countries, and the line’s former terminus — Wonsan — is in North Korea.
However, its history underscores how vulnerable such hopes are to the politics of the peninsula. Work began in 2015, but ground to a halt just a year later after North Korea’s fourth nuclear test.
The latest reboot inspires more skepticism than hope for some in Cheorwon.
“It seems like they keep trying to reconcile with North Korea [through the railway project], but from our point of view, it isn’t really practical,” resident Moon Jae-yong said.
South Korea’s reconciliation program eventually aims to restore rail links with the North.
Lee has also said he is ready for talks with Pyongyang without preconditions, including on formally ending the Korean War, which concluded with an armistice.
His minister of unification said Seoul had shifted from prioritizing denuclearization to curbing the expansion of North Korea’s nuclear program.
However, Pyongyang — emboldened by support from traditional ally China, and Russia, whose invasion of Ukraine it is backing — has been unmoved.
It has repeatedly declared itself an “irreversible” nuclear state and labeled Seoul its “most hostile” enemy.
Trump might be trying to revive diplomacy to record a foreign policy win ahead of November’s midterm elections, with many voters disenchanted by his intervention in the Middle East.
That has sidelined Seoul, with Lee voicing respect for Trump’s decision and pledging to “do his utmost” to support his peacemaking efforts.
That leaves the rail project standing as a symbol of South Korea’s lonely push for peace.
Along the disused line from Woljeong-ri toward Baengmagoji Station to the south — the section to be restored under the peace project — vegetation crowds both sides of the tracks, nearly swallowing a stone wall.
“The iron horse wants to run,” a sign reads, alongside a phrase in English: “We want to be back on track.”
Preparing infrastructure in the South now could save time if inter-Korean links are eventually restored, Kyungnam University professor Lim Eul-chul said.
“But realistically, it is virtually impossible under the current circumstances, and everyone knows that,” he said.
With few options on North Korea, Seoul has turned to projects it can “pursue unilaterally,” Lim said.
A bombed-out locomotive from the Korean War remains near Woljeong-ri Station as a reminder of the division.
It is “heartbreaking to see,” visitor Ahn Seung-hyun said.

Lee and Chow, the former chair and former vice-chair of a now-disbanded group, the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, could be sentenced to as much as 10 years in jail under a China-imposed National Security Law (NSL).
Photo: AP
It was the defendants’ repeated use of the phrase “end one-party dictatorship” rather than other political actions or beliefs that had breached the law, the judges said.
“[The defendants] intended to cause others to lose confidence in the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] by stirring up hostility and causing division, so as to achieve the objective of undermining the fundamental basic system,” the judges said. “Even though they believed and envisaged that the acts of resistance may not necessarily involve the use of violence or threat of violence, those acts would be in breach of the NSL, and carry a risk of long-term imprisonment.”
Public commemorations of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests used to be legal and tolerated in Hong Kong, but were effectively outlawed in 2020 with the enactment of the National Security Law.
Prosecutors said the primacy of the CCP was enshrined in Article 1 of the Chinese constitution.
Defense submissions that the defendants genuinely believed they were acting within the law given Hong Kong’s freedoms of speech were rejected by the judges.
“They just refused to pull back from the brink and were bent on embracing the resistance line of the Alliance to the very end,” the judges said.
Lee and Chow, who have been detained since 2021, had pleaded not guilty to the charge.
Former group chairman Albert Ho (何俊仁), who was also a former chairman of the city’s largest opposition Democratic Party, pleaded guilty to the same charge.
Mitigation hearings for Lee and Chow are to start this month.

Festival brings Greeks back to home they never forgot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:16 UTC
01:43:16 KST

It is festival day and Dino Haimandos is savoring the sight of Gokceada’s streets filled with Greek Orthodox icons for a parade led by Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I, who was born on the Turkish island.
Now 77, Haimandos returns every summer to the village where he grew up on this island off Turkey’s Aegean coastline, which he reluctantly left in 1964 following clashes between Greek and Turkish communities over Cyprus.
Every Aug. 15, hundreds return for the Feast of the Virgin Mary on Gokceada, led by the island’s most famous son, Bartholomew I, the 86-year-old spiritual head of the world’s 260 million Orthodox Christians.
Photo: AFP
Many fear the culture of the island’s Greek population risks disappearing.
Under the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, signed a year after the end of a three-year Greek-Turkish war, Athens and the nascent Turkish nation did a sweeping population exchange. However, the Greek-speaking Christian population of Istanbul, along with Imbros and Tenedos, were exempted from the swap, as well as the Turkish-speaking minority in the Thrace region.
About 1.5 million people were forced to leave lands they had called home — many after years of neighborly relations, although in some places, intercommunal tension escalated into massacres.
On Imbros and Tenedos, coexistence was never a problem, but “politics is another matter,” businessman Kristo Vogiatzis said.
Following escalating intercommunal violence over Cyprus in 1964, Ankara retaliated by closing the Greek schools on Gokceada and setting up an open prison on expropriated land by Derekoy, its biggest village.
Spooked by the move, many families packed up and left.
“Prisoners would turn up looking for alcohol and there were thefts and murders... I don’t like remembering it,” said shephard Yorgi Baki, whose cousin was murdered.
“It was so sad,” said Haimandos, who moved, but has kept strong ties to Gokceada. “I was born here and I still feel at home. I love the streets, the people. I was at school with them, we got on well.”
For everyone, Aug. 15 is when they reunite each year and the sounds of church bells and Greek greetings fill the air.
Bartholomew I comes every year to deliver a three-hour liturgy.
Singer Stelyo Berber is hoping to revive the Greek spirit and the community that once called the place home.
Every evening, he and his wife Pelin perform well-loved songs of rebetiko — the so-called Greek “blues” of exile, lost homelands and unrequited love — inside the stone tavern they run in Zeytinlikoy, the patriarch’s home village.
Berber returned to live on the island five years ago.
With the 2013 opening of a Greek school at the EU’s encouragement, “around 600 Greeks returned to live here,” boosting the numbers from less than 70 in 2005, he said.
However, it remains a modest number on an island of 7,000 residents whose population swells to 30,000 in the summer months.
Vogiatzis said his children have no interest in taking his house on the island, saying: “It’s not our history. We are Greek.”
And his Istanbul friends are all asking if and when he plans to sell.
“Prices are soaring, everyone wants a stone house,” he said.
Only Derekoy — once the richest place on the island — remains abandoned and in ruins, left to the goats of Yorgi.
Similar stories played out on Tenedos, where only 15 Greeks remain, all of them elderly. A three-hour drive from Istanbul then a 30-minute ferry ride, it is even more popular with mainland tourists.
Hakan Guruney moved to Tenedos from Istanbul in the 1980s and has spent decades trying to preserve its memories through a small private museum.
There, he showcases everyday mementos, from sweet wrappers to lacework, prayer books and postcards from French soldiers stationed there during the 1915 Dardanelles campaign.
“We drove the Greeks out and now we play their songs in our restaurants,” he said.

SEMI launches chip materials alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:16 UTC
01:43:16 KST

SEMI Taiwan launched a semiconductor materials alliance yesterday to fortify industry resilience, capitalizing on surging domestic demand fueled by advanced nodes and next-generation packaging.
Taiwan has been the world’s largest semiconductor materials consumer for 16 years in a row, the industry association said.
Taiwan purchased about US$21.7 billion of semiconductor materials last year, driven by artificial intelligence (AI)-related demand, SEMI data showed.
Photo: CNA
The spending accounted for 30 percent of global semiconductor materials consumption, totaling US$73.2 billion, the data showed.
“Demand for specialty gases, chemicals and key raw materials are rising in Taiwan, fueled by the technology advancements to 2-nanometer and advanced packaging technologies,” SEMI Taiwan president Terry Tsao (曹世綸) told a news conference in Taipei.
“Taiwan is ushering in a pivotal shift in industrial upgrades, given its advantages in industrial clusters, customer proximity and customer agility,” Tsao said.
With the expansion of Taiwan’s semiconductor materials market, establishing a localized alliance is a timely and strategic move to reinforce supply chain resilience and mitigate the risk of raw material disruptions in domestic manufacturing, he said.
Driven by skyrocketing demand for AI applications, the semiconductor supply chain is facing unprecedented capacity constraints, particularly in critical components such as substrates, ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控) vice president Hiro Huang (黃義從) told the news conference.
“For ASE, [customer] demand has outpaced supply. Overall, we can only satisfy less than half of customers’ demand,” Huang said.
The market opportunity is immense, but the industry is grappling with a staggering supply-demand gap, he said.
The massive gap is a powerful catalyst for local suppliers to enter the market, he said.
About 60 to 70 percent of raw materials used by ASE come from local supplies, he said.
ASE began sourcing T-glass from Taiwan Glass Industry Corp (台灣玻璃) two years ago, due to severe supply shortages from global suppliers, Huang said.
That has not happened in the past four decades, indicating that Taiwan-based suppliers have a chance to play a “supplementary role” to their global rivals, he said.
T-glass is a high-performance, ultra-thin specialty fiberglass cloth used as a foundational reinforcement material in advanced semiconductor IC substrates, such as ABF and BT carriers, and high-end printed circuit boards to prevent chips from warping under extreme operational heat.
“As semiconductor technologies continue to advance, the importance of materials is rising rapidly and continued innovation across the industry depends on close collaboration among partners throughout the value chain,” GlobalWafers Co (環球晶圓) chairwoman Doris Hsu (徐秀蘭) said.
Through the SEMI Taiwan Materials Alliance, GlobalWafers looks forward to deepening collaborations to improve supply resilience for critical raw materials and semiconductor materials, Hsu said.
More than 30 firms — from wafer suppliers and chip packaging service providers to suppliers of specialty chemicals and equipment — are members of the SEMI Taiwan Materials Alliance, including ASE, GlobalWafers, LCY Chemical Corp (李長榮化工) and Advanced Echem Materials Co (新應材), SEMI said.

A tiny croissant with a small, smiling face sits on a desk. Nearby, a soft strawberry with dangling legs leans against a stack of books, while a floppy-eared bunny rests quietly on a bed. These charming plush toys are part of the world of “JellyCat,” a British brand known for turning everyday objects and animals into soft, friendly characters. With their gentle colors, simple expressions, and unusually soft texture, JellyCat toys have become instantly recognizable and widely shared on social media.
Although JellyCat had been around for more than two decades, the brand’s popularity grew rapidly during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. During that time, many people were searching for small sources of comfort and nostalgia. Viral videos on social media platforms further boosted the brand’s visibility, which contributed to a sharp rise in both sales and online searches.
This growing interest in comforting objects reflects a broader consumer trend known as the “healing economy.” The term refers to a market of products and experiences designed to reduce emotional stress and support mental well-being. From meditation apps to cozy lifestyle goods, people today actively look for simple ways to relax, feel emotionally safe, or reconnect with positive memories.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片:AdobeStock
JellyCat is just one example of this trend. Many adults now collect stuffed toys from various brands, finding that these soft companions can provide emotional comfort. In a fast-changing and often demanding world, even a simple plush toy can offer a small but genuine sense of reassurance.
一個帶著小小笑臉的小可頌坐在桌上。在一旁，一顆雙腿懸掛著的軟綿草莓靠著一疊書，而一隻垂著耳朵的兔子靜靜坐在床上。這些迷人的絨毛娃娃是「JellyCat」世界的一部分，JellyCat 是英國品牌，以將日常物品和動物轉換成軟綿且友善的角色而聞名。JellyCat 的娃娃有著柔和色調、簡單的表情，以及極其柔軟的觸感，讓人一眼就能認出，且在社群媒體上被廣為分享。
雖然 JellyCat 已經存在二十多年了，但該品牌的人氣是在新冠疫情期間及結束後才迅速增長。在那段期間，許多人正在尋找撫慰和懷舊的小小來源。社群媒體平臺上爆紅的影片也進一步增加了該品牌的能見度，促進其銷量及網路搜尋急遽增加。
這種對慰藉物品日益增加的興趣，反映出一種更廣泛的消費趨勢，即所謂的「療癒經濟」。這一詞指的是一個以減輕情緒壓力並促進心理健康為目的的產品與體驗的市場。從冥想應用程式到舒適的生活風格商品，如今人們積極尋找簡單的方法來放鬆、在情緒上感到安心，或重新連結那些正面的回憶。
JellyCat 只是這股潮流中的一個例子。許多成年人如今會蒐集各種不同品牌的絨毛娃娃，他們發現這些軟綿綿的夥伴們能提供情緒上的慰藉。在步調快速且往往苛刻的世界裡，即便是簡單的絨毛娃娃也能提供小卻真實的安心感。

Words in Use
1. stack n.（整齊的）一疊
A neat stack of towels sat on the bathroom shelf.
浴室層架上放著一疊整齊的毛巾。
2. texture n. 質地，觸感；口感
The spongy texture of the cake indicates that it was baked perfectly.
這顆蛋糕鬆軟的質地顯示它烤得非常完美。
3. recognizable a. 可辨認的
The company’s logo is widely recognizable across the globe.
這家公司的標誌在全球都具有極高的辨識度。
4.pandemic n. 疫情，（大範圍、全球性）流行病
Public health measures helped slow the spread of the pandemic in urban areas.
公共衛生措施有助於減緩城市地區疫情的擴散。
5.viral a.（在網路上）廣為流傳、爆紅、病毒式的
That viral dance challenge originated from a small studio in London.
那個爆紅的舞蹈挑戰起源於倫敦的一家小工作室。
Practical Phrases
1. lean against. . . 斜靠在……之上
The heavy broom was leaning against the kitchen wall.
那把沉重的掃帚靠在廚房牆邊。
2. have been around for + 一段時間
已存在若干時間
These ancient stone circles have been around for thousands of years.
這些古代石圈已經存在數千年之久。
3. refer to. . . 指的是……
The pronoun “it” in the sentence refers to the old wooden bridge.
句子中的代名詞「it」指的是那座老舊的木橋。
4. be designed to V 被設計來……
This app is designed to track your daily water intake.
這款應用程式是設計來記錄每日的飲水量。
5. reconnect with. . . 找回與……的連結
Oscar planned a trip to the mountains to reconnect with nature.
奧斯卡計劃了一趟山區之旅，以找回與大自然的連結。

The Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute yesterday announced an action plan for conserving three endangered native plant species under the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Taiwan Ecological Network program.
The three species are the endangered Kao’s thorowax, and the critically endangered Asiatic sand sedge and Taiwan cork-tree, the institute said.
The conservation plan for the three species is grounded in scientific research, with a comprehensive assessment of their current status, ecological characteristics, population trends, reproductive biology and conservation strategies, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Agriculture
Working in collaboration with local governments, academic institutions and civic groups, the goal is to build a roadmap for native plant conservation work and prevent threatened species from disappearing, it said.
The plan for the three species is centered on the vision of protecting plant resources, sustaining ecosystem stability and ensuring sustainable survival of wildlife species in Taiwan, the institute said.
Asiatic sand sedge, or Carex kobomugi, is a perennial herb that grows exclusively on sandy beaches, it said.
This dioecious species is currently restricted to two small populations along the Yanliao (鹽寮) and Fulong (福隆) beaches in northern Taiwan, while an additional population dwells on Dongju Island (東莒島) in Lienchiang County, it said.
Asiatic sand sedge is a temperate coastal plant species distributed across the Ussuri River in Russia, Japan, South Korea and northeastern China, it said, adding that Taiwan marks the southernmost limit of its geographic range.
It has a well-developed underground rhizome system that can stabilize loose sand against coastal erosion, making it an important plant for coastal protection and sand fixation, the institute said.
Asiatic sand sedge also has genetic resources associated with heat tolerance and adaptation to climate warming, which are considered to have irreplaceable global conservation value particularly amid global warming, it said.
The Taiwan cork-tree, or Phellodendron amurense var. wilsonii, is endemic to Taiwan, the institute said.
It is a dioecious, deciduous tree distributed in northern and central Taiwan at elevations ranging from 1,800m to 2,700m, it said.
The Taiwan cork-tree has long been regarded as an important traditional Chinese medicinal resource, as its bright yellow inner bark contains high levels of berberine, the institute said.
The species is ecologically valuable as its mature fruits provide an important winter food source for wildlife including birds, squirrels and macaques, it said.
Its root system also contributes to soil and water conservation on mountain slopes, the institute said.
The cork-tree’s primary wild populations are restricted to Yilan County’s Taiping Mountain (太平山) and Nantou County’s Cueifong (翠峰) area, it said.
Kao’s thorowax, or Bupleurum kaoi, is an endemic perennial herb that is distributed mainly in low-elevation mountainous areas of northern and central Taiwan, the institute said.
The species typically grows in sunny, low-elevation hills and public cemeteries, thus known locally as “graveyard grass,” it said.
Its roots are rich in saikosaponins, making it a promising native medicinal plant resource, the institute said.
The plant is also listed as a premium medicinal herb in the ancient Chinese medical encyclopedia The Divine Farmer’s Herb-Root Classic (神農本草經), it said.
The publishing of the action plan signals that Taiwan’s conservation efforts have shifted from “prohibition and protection” to “active restoration, scientific management and sustainable utilization,” the institute said.

Douglas Hurd didn’t say ‘prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse’ | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:14 UTC
01:43:14 KST

In his letter about ever-lengthier prison sentences (18 August), Nik Wood makes two familiar mistakes in attributing the quote “prison is an expensive way of making bad people worse” to Douglas Hurd.
In fact, the line appeared in a white paper published in 1990 by Hurd’s successor, David Waddington. And there is no declaratory “is”. Instead, it warns that “prison can be an expensive way of making bad people worse” unless other rehabilitative measures are taken.
Wood suggests that Hurd was “an unlikely figure” to author such a thought. Waddington, a hardliner who supported the return of capital punishment, was far unlikelier. The true originator of the much misquoted line was probably the civil servant David Faulkner, a liberal on penal matters, whose influence on crime and punishment ended with the arrival of Michael Howard as home secretary.
Jon Silverman
Former BBC home affairs correspondent

Prosecutors expand military spies probe

Unknown Publisher

16:43:11 UTC
01:43:11 KST

Law enforcement officials have broadened a probe into a suspected network of Chinese spies, after the Kaohsiung branch of the High Court on Wednesday convicted two former military service members on espionage and corruption charges.
The court sentenced an ex-army sergeant surnamed Fang (方) to 10 years and four months in prison and an ex-air force sergeant surnamed Huang (黃) to seven years in prison.
The verdict may be appealed.
Photo courtesy of the Republic of China Military Academy
Fang and Huang were found guilty of passing military secrets to China and attempting to turn their colleagues into Chinese spies as members of Wo Long Hui (臥龍會, “Crouching Dragon Society”), an organization with links to Chinese intelligence.
Fang is also accused of filming a “surrender video” after he was recruited by the society.
The Kaohsiung District Prosecutors’ Office is investigating more than 20 persons of interest, including several serving army captains, sources with knowledge of the matter said on condition of anonymity.
The organization is believed to be targeting service members with financial problems, they said.
It lends small sums of money to cash-strapped officers until they are heavily indebted, then induces them to betray Taiwan as a way out of debt, the sources said.
Compromised military personnel must swear a loyalty oath before being offered money to steal intelligence and compromise their colleagues, they said.
The organization has a reward system based on the value of the secret provided, or the new assets members recruit, they added.
Investigators are tracing financial streams and identifying how Chinese intelligence found out which service members were susceptible to their tactics, the sources said.
It is not yet proven if the people under investigation had stolen secrets on China’s behalf, they said.
The officers have remarkably similar — if not shared — backgrounds, they said, adding that many were graduates of the Chung Cheng Armed Forces Preparatory School and the formal military academy system.
Chinese intelligence appeared to have contacted many of the officers early in their careers, when they still held lieutenancy, they said.
Alarmingly, many of the officers under suspicion were rising stars in the military, with excellent military academy grades and good service records, the sources said.

The bafflingly hard pain we feel when our children leave home for university | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

As a father who has seen both daughters fledge, I felt Zoe Williams’ pain and bafflement as her first son prepares to leave for university (My son is leaving home for university – and my severe denial has surprised me, 17 August).
No one talks about it but, from the moment of birth, parenting is continuous grieving. We mourn the loss of our one-year-old when they turn two. The fun of the early teen years are only partial compensation for never again watching our toddler invent walking. The move away from home is a big one. When it happened to us, I was grateful for all the practice I’d been gifted. But it still hit hard. Bafflingly hard.
Doug Kessler
London

World No. 3 Jessica Pegula on Thursday survived a stirring fightback from Amanda Anisimova to win 6-4, 2-6, 7-6 (7/4) and reach the Cincinnati Open semi-finals, while Iga Swiatek also advanced when Elena Rybakina retired injured.
World No. 2 Rybakina retired in the first set with an ankle problem in a setback to her preparations for the US Open Grand Slam, which is to begin on Aug. 30.
Pegula took the opening set in 34 minutes, but ninth-seeded Anisimova hit back hard to claim the second, breaking early for a 3-0 lead before Pegula took a medical timeout.
Photo: AFP
American Pegula squandered a 5-3 advantage in the decider, but prevailed in the tiebreak to set up a meeting with Swiatek, who extended her winning run to 10 matches when Rybakina retired while trailing 4-1 in the opening set.
Swiatek raced into a 3-0 lead before Rybakina got on the board, but the Kazakh was unable to halt Swiatek’s momentum and called for a medical timeout before ending the match.
The pair had also met in last week’s Toronto final, with Swiatek beating Rybakina in straight sets to claim the Canadian Open title.
Photo: Aaron Doster / Imagn Images

In the men’s draw, seventh-seeded Flavio Cobolli recovered from a sluggish start to beat home favorite Tommy Paul 2-6, 6-3, 6-4 and reach his first ATP Masters 1000 semi-final.
Cobolli, who became only the second Italian to reach the men’s last four in Cincinnati after Jannik Sinner, asked for a tub of M&M’s while leading 5-2 in the second set, later crediting the snack with giving him fresh energy.
“I felt a little bit tired and I needed some energy, some sugar, and I love M&M’s,” he said. “Chocolate with colors makes me happy.”
Cobolli broke to move 5-4 ahead in the deciding set before serving out the match in 1 hour, 57 minutes.
He faces Arthur Fils after the Frenchman swept past Argentina’s Thiago Agustin Tirante 6-3, 6-2.
Frenchman Fils broke serve to move 5-3 ahead before wrapping up the opening set and broke twice more in the second, racing to a 5-1 lead and closing out the match in 64 minutes.
In the women’s doubles at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, Taiwan’s Hsieh Su-wei and partner Jelena Ostapenko of Latvia defeated Kristina Mladenovic of France and China’s Guo Hanyu 6-3, 6-4 to advance to the semi-finals.
They were to play Alexandra Panova of Russia and Magali Kempen of Belgium after press time last night.
The Russian-Belgian pair on Thursday eliminated Taiwan’s Chan Hao-ching and Maya Joint of Australia 1-6, 6-4, 10-2 in the quarters of the US$9,415,725 tournament.

Jacob deGrom takes strikeout count past 2,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Jacob deGrom on Thursday reached 2,000 MLB career strikeouts in the second-fewest games and innings pitched in the history of the league when the Texas Rangers right-hander fanned the first two batters among his 10 K’s in a 2-0 win over the Washington Nationals.
DeGrom struck out Daylen Lile and Abimelec Ortiz, both of whom chased sliders below the zone. He received a standing ovation and acknowledged the applause by tapping his cap over his heart.
The two-time Cy Young Award winner said the achievement was “cool,” but added that he likely would not reflect on it or other personal milestones until he is done pitching.
Photo: AP
“Maybe whenever my career is over I’ll look at that kind of stuff, but even when the season’s over, I’m like: ‘I’ve got to figure out a way to get outs the following year,’” he said.
DeGrom (9-8, 3.77 ERA) allowed a second-inning single and a fifth-inning walk, both to Brady House, in six innings while throwing 94 pitches. He struck out the side in the fourth, and his 10 strikeouts matched a season best.
DeGrom was pulled from his previous start on Aug. 13 after only two innings because of triceps fatigue. Texas manager Skip Schumaker was among those who feared deGrom would go on the injured list. Instead, his start against Washington was pushed back one day.
“It was vintage deGrom,” Schumaker said.
DeGrom has 2,008 strikeouts in 1,666-1/3 innings over 272 starts since his MLB debut in 2014 with the New York Mets. He has 157 strikeouts in 126-2/3 innings this season.
Hall of Famer Randy Johnson got his 2,000th strikeout in his 262nd appearance for the fewest games. Chris Sale holds the record for fewest innings at 1,626.
The 38-year-old deGrom is the ninth active player and 95th in history to reach the milestone. He is the fourth this season, following Kevin Gausman, Sonny Gray and Aaron Nola.

Indonesian workers allege forced labor, salary cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

The Ministry of Labor yesterday pledged to launch an investigation into allegations of forced labor and wage theft made by Indonesian technicians working on renewable energy projects in Taiwan.
The ministry made the remarks hours after Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Lin Yueh-chin (林月琴), together with the Taiwan Association for Human Rights and Taiwan Climate Action Network, leveled the accusations at the Taiwan branch of the Singapore-based Sheffield Green Co at a news conference in Taipei.
Lin accused Sheffield Green, a labor agency specializing in providing workers for renewable energy projects, of recruiting Indonesian technicians with promises of high pay to work in Taiwan, but changed their contracts and slashed their pay upon their arrival.
Photo: Taipei Times
The advocacy groups had received multiple complaints from Indonesian workers about Sheffield Green’s labor practices, she said.
The company had promised a monthly salary of about NT$50,000 for skilled workers, but paid them no more than NT$100 per hour, she said.
Two of the workers told the news conference that their employers refused to pay the promised amount, saying the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) does not apply to foreign recruits working under an expedited short-term permit.
To facilitate foreign nationals working temporarily in Taiwan, the government allows entry visas or permits to be treated as work permits for those staying no more than 30 days.
For those working for up to 90 days, education and work experience requirements are relaxed to simplify administrative procedures.
Several building contractors for offshore wind farms and the state-run CPC Corp, Taiwan were among the entities that allegedly engaged in the deception, Lin said.
Article 51 of the Employment Service Act (業服務法) stipulates that foreign-based companies could supply Taiwanese companies with foreign workers possessing specialized skills on expedited work visas, Lin said.
This provision is being exploited as a loophole to abuse foreign workers, she said.
The ministry said employers have the legal responsibility to comply with their contractual obligations to foreign workers, regardless of the type of work permits.
Officials can confirm that complaints have been lodged against Sheffield Green and others for alleged failure to give workers time to recover from work-related injuries and not paying for their health and labor insurance, in addition to wage disputes, it said.
The ministry, in collaboration with the Kaohsiung and Pingtung County governments, will launch a probe into the labor practices of the companies involved, it said, adding that those found guilty of breaching labor laws would be held accountable.

CyberPower revenue, profit tipped to surpass Q2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:03 UTC
01:43:03 KST

Uninterruptible power supply (UPS) maker CyberPower Systems Inc (碩天科技) yesterday said that third-quarter revenue and profit are expected to surpass its second-quarter results and be the strongest quarter this year.
Growth would be driven by seasonal demand, including for UPS systems and data center power management products, particularly in the US market, CyberPower chairman Michael Ho (何濂洵) told an earnings conference in Taipei.
Revenue rose 13.9 percent in the second quarter to NT$3.34 billion (US$104.87 million) from the first quarter, while net profit surged 69.2 percent to NT$672.8 million, CyberPower said.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
While North America is expected to remain CyberPower’s largest revenue contributor this year, growth in Europe is accelerating, particularly in Italy, Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Finland, as the company’s expanded sales channels gradually bear fruit, Ho said.
The US, Canada and Mexico remained CyberPower’s largest market in the first half of this year, accounting for about 75 percent of its NT$6.27 billion in revenue in the first six months.
UPS systems accounted for 55 percent of CyberPower’s first-half revenue, followed by data center power management products at 37 percent, power protection and management devices at 6 percent and others at 2 percent, company data showed.
Its data center products are mainly single-phase and three-phase UPS systems, modular UPS systems, power distribution units, automatic transfer switches and battery management systems, Ho said.
The company also supplies standalone products, including single-phase and enterprise-grade UPS systems, he said.
As data center UPS products typically have higher specifications and margins, the company has stepped up investment in the segment and shifted its focus from standalone UPS products to total solutions, he said.
CyberPower sells its products mainly through distributors rather than signing large supply contracts directly with data center operators, Ho said.
Its distributors handle logistics and payments as they integrate CyberPower’s UPS products with servers, racks and other equipment to build complete solutions for end customers, he said.
Recent increases in component prices have prompted the company to raise prices in some markets, but the increases have yet to fully offset higher material costs, he said.
CyberPower has responded by securing components earlier, and seeking alternative suppliers and brands to avoid shipment disruptions, he said.
The company in January purchased a new plant and land in Cavite, the Philippines, with the new facility expected to be 2.5 to three times the size of its existing plant there, Ho said.
The new facility would provide additional capacity, with expansion plans focused there as well, he said.
About 30 to 40 percent of CyberPower’s products are made in China, with the remainder produced in the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam.
Net profit totaled NT$1.05 billion in the first half, up 142.4 percent year-on-year, or NT$11.12 per share, up from NT$4.59 a year earlier.
Gross margin rose to 58.67 percent last quarter from 53.53 percent a year earlier, supported by a NT$226 million refund of tariffs imposed by US legislation, Ho said.
Gross margin is expected to stay at about 56 percent this year, he said.

EDITORIAL: Public loses in political tug-of-war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

Amid strong economic growth fueled by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, President William Lai (賴清德) on Monday announced that the government would distribute a NT$10,000 (US$314) cash handout to all citizens next year — a move the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) characterized as the “ultimate political irony.”
Over the past year and a half, universal cash handouts have become one of Taiwan’s most politically contentious issues.
The dispute began last year, when the KMT proposed giving every citizen NT$10,000 after the Ministry of Finance reported that tax revenue for 2024 had exceeded its budget estimate by a record NT$528.3 billion, arguing that the money belonged to the public and should thus be returned to them.
At the time, the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) argued that the surplus tax revenue would better serve the public if it were invested in areas such as social welfare, national defense and economic development, rather than simply being distributed as cash.
When the government proposed a special budget in response to US tariff threats, the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party used their legislative majority to push through a version that increased the budget ceiling to include NT$235 billion for the handouts, despite government warnings that it would add NT$101.4 billion to borrowing.
The KMT’s argument was simple: Taiwan had accumulated a substantial tax surplus, and ordinary people should share in the country’s economic gains. The party packaged the handouts as a way to help families cope with rising costs and uncertainty, accusing the government of withholding money from the public and insisting that returning surplus revenue was the responsible thing to do.
However, there was an obvious blind spot in this logic: If surplus tax revenue should be “returned to the people,” why should that principle apply only to the central government?
When DPP lawmakers urged KMT-led municipalities to practice what they preach and distribute their own surplus funds, the enthusiasm faded.
The Taipei City Government insisted the issue was a matter for the central government, while Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕), who had previously called on the central government to “return the money to the public,” rejected reports that her city had a NT$12 billion surplus. She further threatened legal action against people who spread online rumors about possible tax rebates.
Now that Lai has announced a new round of payments, one might reasonably expect the KMT to celebrate. After all, this is precisely the kind of policy it has spent so long advocating for.
Instead, the party accused Lai of appropriating its idea, using the AI boom to repackage it as an “AI dividend.” It also criticized the timing of the announcement, given that local elections are approaching in November.
Then, just one day later, it changed tack again. Rather than simply welcoming or condemning the policy, it demanded that the Lai administration double the payments to NT$20,000, arguing that the government has the fiscal capacity to do so.
This behavior is anything but subtle.
If the KMT genuinely believes that cash handouts are the best way to ensure that citizens share in economic growth, then Lai’s announcement should be welcome news. After all, the ruling party is adopting a policy the KMT has repeatedly demanded.
At a time when cross-party cooperation seems increasingly difficult, this should have been an opportunity to put partisan differences aside and achieve a common goal. Instead, the KMT appears determined to oppose the government even when the government does what the party itself has demanded.
This is a troubling approach to politics. The goal of elected officials should be to serve their constituents and promote policies to improve people’s lives. If a policy is truly beneficial to the public, its merits should not depend on whether it was conceived by the ruling party or the opposition.
If the KMT views the proposed NT$10,000 as insufficient, it could make a more substantive case for a larger payment than simply arguing that the government can afford it, or propose a reasonable alternative. Better still, KMT-led local governments could demonstrate their commitment to citizens by providing additional cash payments of their own — something they have shown little inclination to do.
Citizens deserve better than a political tug-of-war over who gets the credit for which policy. They deserve lawmakers willing to set aside their differences when necessary to make meaningful progress, rather than arguing for argument’s sake.
In the end, the only group that stands to lose from these political games is the public.
For the last 15 years, China has relied on gray zone operations to advance its territorial ambitions across Asia. And for 15 years, the US has struggled to respond. But the open door on which China has been pushing may finally be closing. Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Military forces might act provocatively — even dangerously — while carefully avoiding violence, whereas law enforcement employs nonlethal violence as a first resort. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Commercial interests overriding culture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

Earlier this month, the mayor of Jian Township (吉安) in Hualien County recruited South Korean professional baseball cheerleader Ha Ji-won to serve as the spokesperson for a local indigenous harvest festival, calling her the “Amis Princess.” The move drew mixed reactions: Bringing in a South Korean celebrity as a brand ambassador and having her dress in traditional Amis clothing was questionable at best.
The harvest festival is a tradition that carries profound cultural significance for Amis. The community gathers to give thanks to heaven and earth for the past year’s blessings, and celebrate with traditional songs and dance. It is a time when community bonds are strengthened. However, political intervention has increasingly turned it into a commercial event. The cultural meaning behind the Amis harvest festival and its traditions have been reduced to secular entertainment that can be bought anytime, anywhere.
Some communities have continued to uphold the true character of the festival. One example in Hualien County is Rueisuei Township’s (瑞穗) Kiwit Village (奇美). For years, it has preserved the cultural traditions of the harvest festival and prevented outsiders from interfering, earning even greater respect and admiration for it. After all, this kind of festival, rooted in reverence for heaven and love for the people, was never meant to be a performance; it is a cultural tradition.
When commercial interests become deeply embedded, they can undermine genuine cultural traditions. If a festival’s sole purpose becomes attracting more public attention, it has essentially been sold in pursuit of capitalist interest. The harvest festival belongs to the community and is about passing on culture; it should not be commercialized for the sake of viewership.
Beyond the clothes she donned that day, how much does the mayor’s choice of spokesperson know about the culture surrounding the festival? Ha might be a popular cheerleader, but she has no connection to Amis culture, and is an unconvincing choice for ambassador.
The only reasonable explanation is that the Jian Township Office simply sought to attract more public attention at the expense of real cultural value. The question is where this attention actually goes — to Ha’s K-pop dance performance, or the harvest festival itself? The risk is that the latter’s meaning is lost altogether.
Chen Chi-nung is a former principal of Kuohsin Junior High School in Nantou County.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader

South Korea’s push for defense autonomy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:59 UTC
01:42:59 KST

The unusual convergence between Seoul and Washington toward greater South Korean defense autonomy could reshape the purpose of the US military presence on the Korean Peninsula. The implications of this convergence could strengthen or complicate US-led allied deterrence in the event of a Taiwan contingency.
For Taipei, the key question is whether Seoul and Washington agree on what US forces on the peninsula are for and whether they should be available for contingencies beyond South Korea. Even if US forces there did not directly participate in a Taiwan contingency, their role within the broader US logistical and support architecture across the Western Pacific makes it impossible to divorce the peninsula from such a conflict.
Despite the very different political outlooks of US President Donald Trump and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, last week’s decision announcement reducing the annual joint US-Republic of Korea (ROK) Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) exercise coincides with a longstanding push by some in Seoul to transfer wartime operational control (OPCON) within the US-ROK Combined Forces Command (CFC) from a US Army four-star general to an ROK Army counterpart.
For some South Koreans, especially in Lee’s progressive coalition, OPCON transfer represents more than a technical reorganization of the CFC. It raises the broader question of how Seoul and Washington should divide responsibility for defending the peninsula.
Yet, greater ROK responsibility for deterring North Korea raises an uncomfortable question that directly affects Taipei and regional allies: If Seoul assumes greater responsibility for its own defense, what purpose should the 28,500 US troops stationed on the peninsula serve? Washington’s emerging answer is greater strategic flexibility for US forces on the peninsula.
The diminished emphasis on North Korea as a direct threat to the US homeland in the recent US National Security and National Defense Strategies, alongside the growing use of US forces on the peninsula for unilateral and third-country exercises, reflects the push for greater “strategic flexibility” that CFC commander General Xavier Brunson has repeatedly emphasized.
US Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby reinforced this logic in Manila last week, arguing that stronger allies should assume greater responsibility for their own defense as Washington builds a more resilient regional deterrence architecture.
However, Seoul has its own interests. Greater South Korean defense autonomy does not necessarily imply greater willingness to allow US forces stationed on the peninsula to be employed against China in a regional contingency.
The US military presence on the peninsula remains rooted in the unfinished Korean War and the alliance’s mission of deterring North Korean aggression. Washington’s push for greater “strategic flexibility” must therefore contend with the political constraints governing how those forces can be employed beyond Korea, a reality that directly affects Taiwan’s security.
Paradoxically, the harder Washington pushes Seoul to assume greater responsibility for its defense to increase US strategic flexibility, the more it could strengthen South Korean demands for autonomy that constrain Washington’s ability to employ peninsula-based forces in regional contingencies.
OPCON transfer also carries questions of sovereignty and strategic agency alongside warfighting effectiveness. Wariness of strategic flexibility in the alliance was reflected in the 2006 joint US-ROK statement that launched the Strategic Consultation for Allied Partnership. The statement, issued at the height of the Global War on Terror, recognized the need for flexibility for peninsula-based US forces while affirming that South Korea should not be drawn into a regional conflict “against the will of the Korean people.”
OPCON transfer was also a priority for Lee’s predecessor, Moon Jae-in. Still, it remained incomplete when he left office, as COVID-era reductions in combined exercises delayed crucial capability assessments. Ironically, reducing the UFS exercise could once again complicate the capability assessments necessary to advance Lee’s push for OPCON transfer.
A Taiwan contingency could bring this paradox to a head. Washington would likely seek greater flexibility from its South Korea-based forces precisely when Seoul, fearing North Korean opportunism amid a wider regional conflict, wants more US capabilities focused on the peninsula.
Taipei therefore has an enormous stake in how Seoul’s pursuit of greater defense autonomy reshapes the US-ROK alliance. OPCON transfer could make South Korea more capable while simultaneously opening a new political argument over what South Korea-based US forces are actually for.
For Taiwan, the larger lesson extends beyond the peninsula. Assessing the US’ ability to respond to a Taiwan contingency requires more than counting US forces in the Indo-Pacific region. Taipei must also understand the alliance politics governing how those forces can be used. Developments in Seoul — and in other allied capitals — could ultimately shape what Washington is politically and militarily able to do in a crisis.
Bryce C. Barros is a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Studies. He served as a US Senate National Security Advisor from 2023 to 2024. The views expressed here do not reflect those of the US government or other affiliations.

Gray zone operations involve the assertive use of a variety of tools in ways that create conditions that can be described as neither peace nor war. Such an approach creates difficult calculations for its targets.

Exhibition showcases heat adaptation technologies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

The Ministry of Environment has set up an exhibition of heat adaptation products in front of its building to showcase the industry’s development and encourage public participation.
The ministry on Thursday held a news conference to unveil the exhibition demonstrating the cooling technologies of a “high-transparency, heat-insulating balloon canopy” and “nano-mineral diffused light net.”
Temperatures of 40°C or higher are expected to become the new normal in Taiwan within the next 10 years due to global warming and the urban heat island effect, Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Environment
The ministry has therefore been promoting interagency efforts to plant more trees to increase green shade coverage, he said.
While it is difficult to plant trees in some places and seedlings need time to grow big enough to provide shade, locally developed innovative cooling technologies can be applied to protect pedestrians against heat injuries, Peng said.
Using lightweight shading structures to provide “immediate coverage” can help reduce solar heat load, said Lin Tzu-ping (林子平), a member of the Executive Yuan’s National Urban Forest Promotion Committee.
Such measures are a key strategy for preserving people’s thermal comfort and protecting health in urban areas where planting trees might be unsuitable or where trees have yet to grow big enough, said Lin, a professor of architecture at National Cheng Kung University.
The two shading technologies demonstrated in the exhibition area are capable of blocking shortwave solar radiation by 30 to 40 percent, Lin added.
Lin Yi-chun (林怡君), who invented the nano-mineral diffused light net, said the net incorporates mica minerals produced locally in Taiwan into recycled PET polyester fibers.
It transforms harsh direct sunlight into soft, diffused light, while the nano-minerals allow the fibers to absorb moisture from the air, she said.
When the net is exposed to sunlight, the moisture evaporates and lowers temperatures, she said.
Huang Yi-xing (黃翌星), the inventor of the balloon canopy, said the balloons can lower temperatures by up to 6°C, depending on how cloudy it is.
The balloons feature a dual-layer structure and a cesium tungsten oxide nanoparticle film, making them capable of blocking 86 percent of infrared radiation and more than 99 percent of ultraviolet radiation from the sun, he said.
The exhibition, scheduled to run for 100 days, was set up to showcase how heat adaptation technoliges can be integrated into people’s lives, the ministry said.
Aided by investments from industry, more comprehensive heat adaptation strategies can be developed for outdoor workers, vulnerable groups and the general public, it said.

The UN’s most powerful body, the Security Council, met yesterday to hold another straw poll to gauge the popularity of a growing field of contenders to lead the embattled organization.
UN Conference on Trade and Development Secretary-General and former Costa Rican vice president Rebeca Grynspan was the front-runner after last month’s first informal vote, in which the council’s 15 members, including the five with veto power, pass judgement in secret on the candidates.
Argentine diplomat and International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi is also a candidate along with former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet, former Ecuadorian minister of foreign affairs Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Guyanese minister of foreign affairs Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, former Ugandan minister of foreign affairs Olara Otunnu and former Senegalese president Macky Sall.
Photo: EPA
After the first round concluded, former Ecuadorian minister of industries and productivity Ivonne A-Baki threw her hat into the race to succeed Antonio Guterres, who would complete his second five-year term on Dec. 31.
“While the first straw poll set the scene for the Secretary-General race, the second may give us some direction about where it is headed,” UN International Crisis Group head Daniel Forti said. “Diplomats expect fluctuations in the vote distribution compared to the July poll. Most will be watching to see whether the early front-runners consolidate their support or slip in the standings.”
“It is unlikely that any candidate will emerge from [yesterday’s] poll with a decisive lead,” he said.
The veto-wielding nations — the UK, China, France, Russia and the US — might wait until later to express their preferences, while new contenders could emerge, he added.
Even if a candidate earns the required nine votes from the 15 available in the Security Council, they must also avoid a veto by the five major powers, which are deeply divided. Once a candidate clears those bars, their name would go to the General Assembly of all UN members for confirmation.
The Security Council straw poll was devised in the early 1980s in an attempt to break a deadlock between two candidates shut down by vetoes.
The informal mechanism has persisted, in various forms, despite criticism from countries opposed to the opaque process.
Each member state must anonymously assign each candidate one of three labels: “encourage,” “discourage” or “no opinion.” That would give those with no support the opportunity to withdraw — although they are not obliged.
In the first rounds of the process expected to take several weeks, all ballots are the same color.
However, after an unspecified number of votes, the ballots of the five permanent members would become a different color from those of the elected members, making it possible to identify potential vetoes, without knowing which country blackballed any given candidate.
It is tradition that the UN’s top job should rotate between different regions.
Under that premise, the role should go to a candidate from Latin America this time. There are many candidates from the region, although Sall and Otunnu hail from Africa.

The Coast Guard administration (CGA) yesterday said it had warned off and shadowed a Chinese research ship sailing in sensitive waters to the nation’s west, the third time the vessel has been spotted since May.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The CGA said it would deploy its ships to respond to Chinese vessels, “firmly defending national sovereignty and ensuring the safety of our nation’s waters.”
China’s military also operates around Taiwan on an almost daily basis.

Chinese state media say the Tongji has all-weather operational capability and can carry remotely operated vehicles, laboratories and uncrewed systems.
