'His personal views': Punjab Congress distances itself from Deepender Hooda over Sajjan Kumar tribute row
Edited by: Pallavi / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 21, 2026, 18:31 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Deepender Hooda had posted a tribute on the death of ex-Congress MP Sajjan Kumar.
NEW DELHI: Punjab Congress leaders on Friday sought to distance the party's state unit from Congress MP Deepender Singh Hooda's remarks describing former party MP and 1984 anti-Sikh riots convict Sajjan Kumar as a "role model nationwide". The leaders said the party stood with those who were killed and affected by the violence and that it was Hooda's "personal views".The pushback from Punjab Congress came a day after Sajjan Singh Kumar, who was serving a life sentence in connection with the 1984 riots, died at the age of 84 at Safdarjung Hospital in Delhi.Hooda had described Kumar's death as an "irreparable loss" to the country's political landscape and said he had been a prominent figure whose connect with people was "exemplary".The remarks triggered sharp criticism from Sikh groups, opposition parties and families of riot victims, forcing Congress leaders in Punjab to clarify that Hooda's comments did not reflect their position.
'We stand with those who died'
Congress MP Gurjeet Singh Aujla said Kumar had committed "misdeeds", had been punished for them and could not be held up as a model for political leadership."Sajjan Kumar did misdeeds. He has been punished for his actions.
A leader does not lead in harming others. We stand with those who died due to him," Aujla said in Amritsar.Asked specifically about Hooda's remarks, Aujla said they should be viewed as the Haryana MP's personal opinion."It must be the personal opinion of Hooda ji but our view is that whatever happened and whoever it happened with, we stand with them, the victims," he said.Punjab Congress working president Raj Kumar Verka also sought to put the focus on the victims of the violence."Sajjan Kumar's life had been full of controversies. This is a matter related to Punjab and Punjabis have been hurt. If Sajjan Kumar is being held responsible for it, we first stand in support of those innocent people; Sajjan Kumar comes only later," Verka said."I don't know who said what. We are Punjabis and we will continue to stand with Punjabis," he added.Congress MP Manish Tewari, however, declined to comment directly on Hooda's statement, saying he had not read it."I haven't read the statement, so it won't be correct to comment on it," Tewari said
What Deepender Hooda said
Hooda's comments came after Kumar's death on Thursday.Speaking to ANI, Hooda described Kumar's death as a loss to the political landscape and praised his public connect."Today, the country's political landscape has suffered an irreparable loss... He is cited as a role model nationwide," Hooda had said.The remarks quickly became controversial given Kumar's conviction in cases related to the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, which followed the assassination of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by her Sikh bodyguards.Kumar was a three-time parliamentarian and had faced criminal proceedings over the violence for decades. His legal journey included both acquittals and convictions before higher courts.
BJP, SAD attack Congress
The BJP and Shiromani Akali Dal sharply criticised Hooda and questioned whether his remarks represented the Congress's broader position.BJP leader Ravneet Singh Bittu accused Kumar and his associates of systematically targeting Sikh families during the 1984 violence and alleged that the Congress leadership had protected him for years.Bittu called on the Punjab and Delhi Congress units to clarify their position on Hooda's comments.The Shiromani Akali Dal also demanded an apology from Hooda and the Congress.SAD leader Bikram Singh Majithia condemned the statement and said Congress should apologise."How can a person like Jagdish Tytler, HKL Bhagat...and all those who killed our innocent Sikh brothers in broad daylight and are responsible for the murder of around 3,000 people during the 1984 riots, be called role models?" Majithia said.He also questioned whether Hooda would continue to remain in the Congress after making the remarks.SAD leader Daljeet Singh Cheema said Hooda should have considered the impact of his comments on families whose homes were destroyed and relatives killed during the violence."When you glorify the life of such people in public, it causes a great deal of hurt to the Sikh community," Cheema said.The president of the 1984 Anti-Sikh Riots Victim Welfare Society, Surjit Singh, also condemned Hooda's remarks, saying victims had still not received justice.
Victims' family react to Sajjan Kumar's death
The controversy unfolded alongside emotional reactions from families affected by the 1984 violence.Ganga Kaur, a member of a riot-affected family, said members of her family had been killed during the violence."Members of our family were burned alive in front of us. Sajjan Kumar died naturally, but we would have found greater peace if he had been executed," she told ANI.Another victim-family member, who identified himself as Surjit Singh, said seven members of his family were burned alive during the riots."It is very unfortunate that Deepender Hooda is siding a criminal. He should be ashamed of praising a person who is responsible for the massacre of so many people," he said.Sajjan Kumar died at Safdarjung Hospital on Thursday at the age of 84. Hospital authorities said he had a history of high blood pressure and Parkinson's disease and had been admitted after being brought to the hospital by police with altered sensorium.Kumar had been serving a life sentence after the Delhi high court in December 2018 overturned his acquittal in the Raj Nagar case, relating to the killing of five members of a Sikh family and the burning of a gurdwara during the 1984 violence.
He surrendered and was lodged in Tihar Jail in December 2018.In February 2025, a Delhi court sentenced Kumar to another life term in the Saraswati Vihar case over the killings of Jaswant Singh and his son Tarundeep Singh during the riots. The court spared him the death penalty, citing his age, medical condition and conduct while serving his earlier sentence.In another case relating to violence in Janakpuri and Vikaspuri, a Rouse Avenue court acquitted Kumar in January 2026 of charges linked to the killing of Sohan Singh and his son-in-law Avtar Singh and the burning of Gurcharan Singh. The Delhi high court subsequently issued notice on an appeal against the acquittal.(With agency inputs)

British spy plane deploys to Norway for Arctic Stone
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
14:00:45 BST
22:00:45 KST

An RAF Rivet Joint has deployed to Ørland in Norway for a week-long exercise with the Royal Norwegian Air Force, including training intended to improve interoperability with Norwegian F-35A fighters.
An RAF Rivet Joint intelligence-gathering aircraft has deployed to Ørland in Norway for Exercise Arctic Stone, where British personnel are training alongside the Royal Norwegian Air Force and working with Norwegian F-35A fighters, the UK Defence Journal understands.
According to an RAF news update, the activity is intended to strengthen interoperability between Rivet Joint and Norway’s F-35A fleet while contributing to NATO’s situational awareness on its northern flank.
Operated by 51 Squadron, the RAF’s Rivet Joint specialises in gathering intelligence from signals across the electromagnetic spectrum. Sensors aboard the aircraft allow its crew to intercept and analyse signals while airborne, providing strategic and tactical intelligence that can contribute to a wider picture of military activity and the surrounding security environment. Ground-based specialists from No. 54 Signals Unit also process and exploit the information gathered by the aircraft.
The RAF described the aircraft’s role by stating: “The aircraft specialises in monitoring signals across the electromagnetic spectrum, giving it the ability to deliver real-time strategic and tactical intelligence in a way few other assets can match.” It added that the combination of airborne crews and ground specialists provides commanders with improved situational awareness “day and night, whatever the operational conditions.”
Exercise Arctic Stone is using that capability in two connected roles. RAF personnel are training directly with their Norwegian counterparts, including activities designed to improve cooperation between the Rivet Joint and Norway’s F-35A force, while the intelligence gathered during the deployment is intended to give commanders a clearer assessment of the operating environment.
The RAF said the exercise would allow both air forces to improve their ability to work together within NATO operations.
Norway’s location makes it particularly relevant to NATO operations in the High North, where the Alliance maintains air, maritime and surveillance activity across an area extending towards the Norwegian and Barents Seas. The RAF said the deployment reflected what it described as the region’s “growing strategic importance” and its increasing relevance to NATO’s northern defences and wider European security.
The service said: “As the security picture in the region continues to evolve, the presence of RAF assets working alongside key allies and partners in the area is becoming an ever more important part of how NATO maintains stability on its northern flank.”
Rivet Joint’s role differs from that of conventional airborne surveillance aircraft because its principal focus is the detection and analysis of electromagnetic emissions rather than visual reconnaissance alone. The RAF argues that modern intelligence operations increasingly require information from multiple sources to be combined, particularly as military communications, sensors and other systems become more digitally connected.
The deployment also provides an opportunity to test how intelligence collected by the aircraft can support other platforms operating in the same battlespace. Integration with Norwegian F-35As is intended to improve the exchange and use of information between different aircraft types, while giving personnel experience of operating within a multinational NATO environment.

Nigel Farage called us ‘nobodies’ in the Clacton byelection. He seems to treat the town in much the same way | Attieh Fard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:00:34 UTC
22:00:34 KST

In the early hours of last Friday morning, a video was posted. It showed Nigel Farage among his team of volunteers, before the votes had been counted, celebrating his victory and saying that he was not going to humiliate himself by sharing a platform at the count next to “nobodies”.
He was referring to the 33 other candidates who had taken part in what was effectively an unnecessary election, one Farage himself had instigated just a few weeks earlier to send one message: that the people of Clacton were backing him, despite parliamentary investigations into his receipt of an undeclared £5m donation. The election is over, but it’s worth thinking about Clacton and those candidates, of whom I was one.
I migrated to Britain from Iran 27 years ago, and have not been back there for 24 years because my Christian faith and my political activities put me at risk of persecution. Iran’s Islamic regime has massacred thousands of innocent people who want the democracy and freedom we have in Britain and it continues to execute protesters. Perhaps that’s why I felt so passionately about defending our democratic system in Britain from being abused.
Some in the British-Iranian community had high respect for Farage as it was not long ago that he met and embraced protesters outside the Iranian embassy in London after the Islamic regime’s massacres. Many of them were puzzled as to why I was standing against him and why I had left the Conservatives, for whom I had previously stood as a candidate in local elections, to do so. I remember Reform supporters in Surrey asking me: if Farage could not save the country, who could? My decision to stand was not a personal vendetta however. Having closely followed Reform’s campaigns on immigration, borders and security, I had seen the deep divides they created in communities.
Throughout the election, Farage did his best to keep his distance from the other candidates. He refused to engage with us, to attend hustings and ultimately to share a platform on the night of the count.
The campaign itself was revealing, as I met voters who had become disillusioned with Farage. Some were frustrated that he had never visited them or replied to their constituency emails. Others were concerned about his undeclared multimillion pound funds and connections with crypto billionaires. Some felt he had done almost nothing for Clacton, or that he had put Clacton “on the map for the wrong reasons”. Others were angry that he had triggered a byelection, wasting about £250,000 of taxpayers’ money.
Interestingly, some who had previously voted for Reform because they were concerned about immigration changed their minds when they learned more.
As an expert in immigration law, I was able to explain why the small boat crossings were happening. Leaving the EU meant that the UK was no longer part of the Dublin III regulation and could therefore no longer return asylum seekers to the first safe country in which they had arrived. When the UK left the EU, it created a legal void in relation to returning asylum seekers to EU countries.
They also learned how some of our laws do not make sense. An asylum seeker has to be physically present in the UK before making a claim, rather than being able to make a claim from overseas and have their identity and background checked before arrival.
Did they know that Farage had criticised the Rwanda scheme as a “con”? No. Did they know that he said it was “a political impossibility” to deport all illegal migrants? No.
Were they aware that he was planning to take the UK out of the Refugee Convention, which allows those being persecuted by regimes such as those in North Korea and Iran to seek protection in another country? No. Did they agree with protecting genuine asylum seekers? Yes.
Did they know that leaving the European convention on human rights without replacing it with a British bill of rights could affect British citizens and their rights relating to privacy and freedom of expression? No.
Having only two weeks to knock on doors, and a few hours each day on my feet to talk to those who were willing to listen was hard, but 126 residents backed my campaign. I have since received messages of support from some of them, telling me that if I stand again, they would help. I am honoured.
One fact became clear. People want the Clacton MP to tackle crime in his constituency, to address its infrastructure weaknesses, and to create more opportunities for its young people and families. Farage isn’t doing any of these things, so how likely is it that he can renew Britain?
Given all these issues, it was unsurprising that so much of the electorate did not support him. He won, but Nigel Farage MP has some serious work to do in Clacton.
- 
  Attieh Fard is a lawyer who was an independent candidate in the Clacton parliamentary byelection

New study shed light on how estradiol influences memory networks in middle-aged women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:00:29 UTC
22:00:29 KST

New research published in Brain Imaging and Behavior suggests that estradiol, a primary form of estrogen, influences how different areas of the brain communicate during memory tasks in middle-aged women. The findings provide evidence that higher levels of this hormone tend to allow for more efficient brain connectivity when recalling information. This research offers insights into how hormonal shifts might shape cognitive changes during the transition to menopause.
Midlife in women involves a major hormonal transition known as perimenopause, which leads up to menopause. During this period, the body experiences dropping levels of estradiol, which is the most potent and abundant form of estrogen in the human body before menopause. Because estradiol interacts directly with the nervous system, this decrease often coincides with temporary changes in mood, behavior, and memory functioning.
Scientists aim to understand why some individuals experience persistent memory difficulties as they age, whereas others maintain their cognitive performance. “Menopause is an important neuroendocrine transition and with decades of life left to live after the transition it is important to understand how the brain adapts during this time,” said Abigail Testo, a postdoctoral associate in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Vermont’s Larner College of Medicine.
Testo co-authored the study with Julie Dumas, a professor and vice chair in the same department. “We hoped with this research to add to the growing body of work being done to better understand how menopause contributes to normal or pathological aging,” Testo said.
A specific area of interest is episodic memory. This type of memory is the brain’s ability to recall specific past events or experiences, such as remembering a person’s name or recalling what happened yesterday.
To explore these individual differences, Testo and Dumas examined how estradiol levels relate to functional connectivity in the brain. Functional connectivity refers to the way distinct brain regions share signals and work together to perform specific tasks. Previous work indicates that estradiol plays a role in regulating these brain networks, but its exact influence during different stages of memory processing remains largely unexplored. The researchers aimed to see how estradiol levels affect the flow of information between brain regions when women encode new memories and when they recall them.
The researchers analyzed data from the Human Connectome Project Aging, a large database designed to track healthy brain aging. They looked specifically at 150 female participants between the ages of 40 and 55. This specific age range allowed the scientists to capture a wide spectrum of estradiol levels, as the group included women who were premenopausal, perimenopausal, and postmenopausal.
To measure hormone levels, medical technicians collected blood samples from the participants after an eight-hour fast. The average estradiol level among the participants was about 83 picograms per milliliter. On the same day, the women underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI. This imaging technique uses powerful magnetic fields to track blood flow in the brain, identifying which specific areas are active during different mental tasks.
During the brain scan, participants completed an episodic memory test called the Face-Name Encoding Task. In the first phase, called encoding, the women viewed faces paired with names and were asked to memorize them. After a brief distractor task, the recall phase began. During this stage, the same faces appeared without names, and the participants had to silently recall the correct names and press a button if they remembered them.
Following the scanning session, researchers tested the participants’ actual memory performance. They asked the women to match the correct names to ten of the faces they had just seen. Overall, the women performed quite well on this cognitive assessment. They correctly identified an average of about 7.5 out of 10 face-name pairs.
To analyze the brain imaging data, Testo and Dumas looked at the functional connections among 132 different regions of the brain. They also controlled for the age of the participants to ensure that chronological aging did not skew the hormonal data. They found five specific brain connections that were associated with estradiol levels during the recall phase of the memory task.
Specifically, higher levels of estradiol were linked to negative functional associations, meaning a decrease in synchronized activity, between certain brain areas. These decreased connections occurred between the left superior frontal gyrus and the brain stem, as well as between the right anterior middle temporal gyrus and the right posterior superior temporal gyrus. The frontal and temporal regions of the brain are well known for supporting human memory functions.
The authors suggest that the lower connectivity seen at higher estradiol levels might represent increased neural efficiency. In other words, with plenty of estradiol available, the brain might not need to work as hard or recruit as many strong connections to successfully recall the required information.
Despite the overall association between estradiol and brain connectivity, the researchers noted an unexpected detail regarding the specific menopausal stages. “We were surprised to find that these brain associations with estradiol levels were not found for women who were perimenopausal,” Testo said. “The reason this was a surprise is because perimenopause is a time with a lot of hormone variability and we thought that variability would lead to greater associations with brain functioning.”
Interestingly, the scientists found no statistically significant relationship between estradiol levels and brain connectivity during the initial encoding phase. This suggests that the hormone’s role differs depending on whether a person is actively learning new information or trying to access a stored memory. The researchers also found no statistically significant correlation between a participant’s estradiol levels and how well they actually scored on the memory test outside the scanner.
It is easy to misinterpret these brain connectivity differences as a direct indicator of everyday memory loss. Because the participants in this sample scored very high on the memory test, the data cannot establish if these specific brain connectivity patterns translate to noticeable memory deficits.
“While estradiol was associated with differences in functional association strengths, it was not similarly associated with differences in memory performance,” Testo explained. “For this reason, we can’t say if the identified functional associations are inherently good or bad for brain functioning.”
Still, the findings point to a lasting biological relationship. “Estradiol likely plays a role in brain functioning throughout the aging process, even after the reproductive period has ended,” Testo noted.
The study relies on a cross-sectional design, meaning it captures a single snapshot in time rather than tracking the same women over several years. This prevents drawing causal conclusions about an individual’s dropping estrogen levels directly causing the observed brain changes. People naturally have individual differences in their brain networks. Observing the exact same participants as they transition through menopause would provide stronger evidence of how hormonal changes alter brain function over time.
The scientists plan to address this gap in the future. “Future HCP-A releases (the dataset utilized in this study) will include longitudinal data,” Testo said. “It would be interesting to revisit this investigation as participants age and estradiol levels continue to fluctuate and decline.”
Future studies may also benefit from observing how other hormones that fluctuate during midlife interact with these brain networks. Hormones like progesterone also drop off after menopause, and observing their interaction with estradiol could offer a better biological picture.
Some participants in the current study used hormonal medications, which could influence brain connectivity differently than naturally produced hormones. Exploring the distinct effects of prescribed hormones versus natural hormones could offer a more detailed picture of cognitive aging in women.
The study, “Estradiol modulated brain connectivity in females during midlife performing an episodic memory task,” was authored by Abigail A. Testo and Julie A. Dumas.

Saab reveals concept of future unmanned fighter jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:00:05 UTC
22:00:05 KST

- Saab posted a video showing a Collaborative Combat Aircraft concept marked A3-01, featuring a delta wing and stealth shaping.
- The concept may relate to an October FMV contract for Saab to study future manned and unmanned fighter systems, with demonstrator flights planned through 2027.
Saab has released the first public look at its concept for a Collaborative Combat Aircraft, an unmanned fighter designed to fly alongside crewed jets.
The video shows an aircraft marked A3-01, featuring a delta-wing design, a single jet engine, and two intakes positioned on either side of the fuselage. The airframe shows visible attention to low-observable, or stealth, shaping. Hartpunkt reported that the overall design suggests the aircraft could be capable of supersonic flight, though Saab has not confirmed a speed capability.
Saab did not disclose a name, technical specifications, or a customer for the aircraft in its post.
“The future of air combat is not just about a single aircraft, it’s about a seamless system of systems,” Saab said in the post.
“We are proud to present our concept for a future Unmanned Fighter System. Building on Swedish aviation heritage, this platform is designed to operate in tandem with manned aircraft, ensuring maximum flexibility and safety in the most contested environments. Designed for multi-domain operations and cooperation across the air, land, maritime, space, and cyber domains.”
Hartpunkt reported that the reference to multi-domain operations suggests the aircraft is intended for more than air-to-air missions, since that phrasing typically indicates a capability to operate in at least two domains, such as air and land. The outlet said this could point to an air-to-ground strike role, an electronic warfare role, or both, though Saab’s post does not specify.
A Collaborative Combat Aircraft is an uncrewed aircraft built to operate alongside crewed fighters, typically carrying sensors, weapons, or electronic warfare payloads while taking direction from a manned aircraft or ground controller. The U.S. Air Force, Australia, and other air forces are pursuing similar concepts under their own programs.
The concept may be linked to a contract Sweden’s defense procurement agency, FMV, awarded to Saab in October. That contract covered concept studies for future fighter aircraft systems, addressing both manned and unmanned solutions from a system-of-systems perspective, along with technology development and demonstrator work. Saab said at the time that the concept and technology development phases were scheduled to conclude by the third quarter of 2026, with demonstrator work continuing through 2027, including first flights.
Hartpunkt noted that this timeline lines up with Saab’s release of the concept video this week, though neither Saab nor FMV has confirmed a direct connection between the October contract and the aircraft shown in the video.
Saab has not disclosed a program name, funding level, or development timeline specific to the A3-01 concept. The company also has not said whether the aircraft shown in the video is a design study, a planned demonstrator, or an early depiction of a program still being defined. FMV has not issued a public statement on the video.

Morocco's lower-cadmium fertiliser bound for Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:00:04 UTC
22:00:04 KST

Breadcrumb
With Hormuz disruptions, Morocco's lower-cadmium fertiliser bound for Europe
At a phosphate mine in Morocco, an excavator tears into the earth to extract a mineral that is at the centre of Europe's growing concern over cadmium in the food chain.
Morocco holds vast reserves of phosphate, a key ingredient in fertilisers.
And state-owned OCP, which has a monopoly over the country's phosphate industry, says it has developed technology to reduce the amount of cadmium in its products.
Phosphate often contains naturally occurring cadmium—a heavy metal harmful to living organisms—that can seep into farmland and eventually to food through fertilisers.
According to the French health agency ANSES, phosphate deposits in Morocco naturally contained high levels of cadmium.
In France, lawmakers overwhelmingly backed a bill in June seeking to limit people's exposure to the metal, which can damage the kidneys and has been linked to a high risk of cancer.
Two-thirds of the world's reserve
At a mine in western Morocco's Sidi Chennane, a 3,000-tonne excavator removes layers of earth to reach the phosphate below.
The rock is then washed and exported in raw form or processed into phosphoric acid at an OCP industrial complex south of Casablanca.
The acid is the main ingredient in phosphate fertilisers and is combined with ammonia or other substances, depending on the type of fertiliser being made.
Since early last year, all OCP fertilisers exported to Europe have contained less than 20 milligrammes of cadmium per kilogramme, according to the company.
That's one-third of the European Union's maximum limit of 60 milligrammes per kilogramme.
An EU official told AFP that the bloc was "not in a position to verify" whether Moroccan phosphate and fertiliser exports reduced the cadmium content, due to lack of a monitoring system.
However, the official said OCP "reported" that it had "invested in decadmiation technologies over recent years" to ensure that levels of cadmium in its exports did not exceed 20 milligrammes.
Europe accounted for 17 percent of OCP's exports last year, following Asia with 41 percent and the Americas with 31 percent.
Morocco holds more than two-thirds of the world's known reserves of phosphate with an estimated 50 billion metric tonnes, counting deposits in the disputed territory of Western Sahara, which is claimed by the pro-independence Polisario Front.
The kingdom is the world's second-largest phosphate producer after China.
OCP says it lowers cadmium levels by adding "specific additives during the treatment of phosphoric acid". The metal is captured and separated before the now-purified acid is used to make fertiliser.
The company has made significant investments in the face of "regulatory approaches that vary from one market to another", OCP Nutricrops chief executive Faris Derrij told AFP.
Derrij did not disclose the level of cadmium levels in OCP exports outside of Europe.
Pollution, geopolitics
The industry has not only faced the challenge of limiting cadmium levels.
The process of making fertiliser also generates phosphogypsum, a byproduct containing heavy metals and acidic substances also linked with several health issues.
OCP plans to build a land-based storage facility by 2027 to reduce discharges of phosphogypsum into the sea and has been researching ways to reuse the waste.
Excessive use of phosphate fertiliser on crops can itself harm the environment, said Sylvain Pellerin, a research director at France's INRAE agricultural research institute.
It can lead to water contamination and the emission of nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, Pellerin explained.
The industry is also facing the challenge of securing raw materials needed to produce fertiliser while global demand is on the rise, Pellerin added.
The US-Israeli war on Iran since late February has tightened fertiliser supplies, much of which in peacetime would have been exported from the Gulf through the disputed Strait of Hormuz.

Ebola spreading exponentially in Congo as death toll tops 2,500, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ebola spreading exponentially in Congo as death toll tops 2,500, UN says
More than 2,500 people have now died in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak, which is spreading exponentially in an area larger than France, senior United Nations Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis said on Aug 21.
Speaking on a video call from the north-eastern Congolese city of Bunia, Harneis called for more aid, saying an existing pool of funds is set to run out within weeks.
Health workers there were coming under attack by locals angered and terrified by the outbreak, and were themselves falling sick and dying from the disease, he added.
‘Fear translates into angry young men’
Congo’s 17th Ebola epidemic became the biggest in the country’s history in terms of the number of cases in late July, surpassing the previous worst outbreak in 2018 to 2020.
It is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which has no approved vaccines or treatments.
“The Ebola outbreak is growing exponentially,” Harneis said.
“The epidemic is spreading to an area that is bigger than France, and the outbreak is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response. And all of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs.”
Some 160 healthcare workers have fallen ill with Ebola, and 43 of them have died, he said.
“And then, when we do respond, apart from the threat from the virus, healthcare workers and front-line workers have been attacked by youth, ambulances have been burned and stoned, and the healthcare facilities have been attacked,” he said.
“Fear translates into angry young men who start throwing stones at their object of fear, the ambulance,” he added.
Other aid workers have said locals have believed conspiracy theories that the outbreak is a hoax, and have reacted angrily when health restrictions prevent them from personally burying loved ones.
There have been more than 260 attacks on health workers in the past six months and eight health workers have been killed, Harneis said, “which is obviously terrifying because people are already risking their lives to deal with Ebola”.
Aid cuts in recent years have reduced the capacity of humanitarian organisations, he said.
Another problem is paying the tens of thousands of people involved in tackling the outbreak, he said. Banking services were hit after the government stopped commercial flights and thereby hobbled the means by which cash is delivered to banks. REUTERS

UK-German strike programme includes hypersonic weapon
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:57:11 BST
21:57:11 KST

The UK and Germany are jointly developing deep-strike options including a stealthy cruise missile and a hypersonic glide vehicle, with both countries working towards outline entry into service during the 2030s.
The UK and Germany are working on both stealthy cruise missile and hypersonic glide vehicle solutions under their joint Deep Precision Strike programme, with outline in-service dates extending into the 2030s, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided further detail on the programme in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked what the UK’s partnership with Germany on deep precision strike weapons entails.
Pollard confirmed that a Memorandum of Understanding signed by the two countries in March 2026 has allowed British and German teams to begin aligning their military requirements and jointly examining technical solutions with industry.
He said: “The UK and Germany signed a Memorandum of Understanding in March 2026 which has enabled joint activities, including with industry, to align military requirements and invest in technical solutions under the Deep Precision Strike programme.”
The programme is examining two distinct missile approaches. Pollard confirmed: “The programme includes Stealthy Cruise and Hypersonic Glide Vehicle missile solutions.”
A stealthy cruise missile would broadly pursue survivability through reduced detectability and a powered flight profile, while a hypersonic glide vehicle represents a different technical approach, travelling at hypersonic speed following launch and manoeuvring towards its target. The parliamentary answer does not provide performance figures, ranges or details of the propulsion and launch arrangements envisaged for either solution, of course.
Pollard said the two governments had reached what he described as “positive alignment” on some of the principal requirements for the programme. He said: “There is positive alignment between the UK and Germany on key programme parameters, including operational concepts and outline target in service dates into the 2030s.”
The wording indicates that the programme remains at a relatively early technical and requirements stage, with the two countries working towards common operational concepts before later development and procurement decisions. British and German teams are currently overseeing technical work already placed with industry while preparing the next stage of contracting.
Pollard said: “Joint UK and Germany teams are now focused on delivering the currently contracted technical work with industry as well as shaping follow on contracts, underpinned in the UK by the funding outlined under the Defence Investment Plan.”
The Deep Precision Strike effort forms part of growing UK-German defence cooperation and is intended to address future requirements for weapons capable of striking targets at considerable distance. The latest answer is significant in explicitly identifying both stealthy cruise and hypersonic glide vehicle solutions as components of the work, while also placing the anticipated service timeframe in the 2030s.
The current phase is focused on technical work with industry, alignment of military requirements and the preparation of follow-on contracts as Britain and Germany determine how the programme will progress towards development and eventual fielding.

Iran quagmire: Trump’s failed strategy and its heavy cost

Trump inherited challenges. He has instead created a catastrophe—one that weakens America, strengthens Iran, and leaves the region more volatile than before. This is not leadership. It is incompetence on a grand scale.

Norway’s King Harald to remain in hospital, cancels engagements
OSLO – Norway’s 89-year-old King Harald, who has been hospitalised since Aug 17 due to complications from a blood condition, has cancelled his royal engagements in early September, the palace said on Aug 21.
Europe’s oldest reigning monarch is being treated for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue, paleness, and shortness of breath.
He was admitted to hospital on Aug 17 due to fluid retention from the cortisone treatment he is receiving, and placed on sick leave for two weeks.
“His Majesty the King will remain at Oslo University Hospital for further treatment,” the palace said on Aug 21.
It said he had cancelled his visit to the central region of Trondelag scheduled for Sept 1 and Sept 2 – after the end of the previously-announced sick leave period.
King Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991, has had multiple health problems in recent years but has repeatedly ruled out abdicating.
Several members of his family, including his son Crown Prince Haakon who is serving as regent in Harald’s absence, have visited him in hospital. AFP

The two-day conference opened on Friday with the participation of officials, political figures, diplomats and academics. It focuses on regional and international issues as well as political, security and economic challenges facing the region.

Why are Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigil organisers facing prison?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:54:44 UTC
21:54:44 KST

Why are Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigil organisers facing prison?
Amnesty International said they ‘must be released immediately and unconditionally’.
Two prominent Hong Kong activists who helped organise annual vigils commemorating China’s deadly 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown have been convicted of inciting subversion under the city’s national security law.
On Friday, Hong Kong’s High Court found former legislator Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and lawyer Chow Hang-tung, 41, guilty of what is one of the most serious offences under the sweeping security law imposed by Beijing in 2020.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pakistan’s Imran Khan back to prison after evaluation at hospital
- list 2 of 4Philippines floods fuel anger over alleged corruption
- list 3 of 4Nord Stream bombing suspect to Hollywood fixer: Who is Volodymyr Zhuravlev?
- list 4 of 4Northern Italy seeks to keep the pressure on the south as Serie A returns
The pair, who pleaded not guilty to inciting subversion, have been held in detention since they were charged in September 2021. They face up to 10 years in prison, with sentencing to take place at a later date. A third defendant, veteran activist Albert Ho, 74, pleaded guilty before the trial began.
The case is among Hong Kong’s highest-profile prosecutions under the national security law and has renewed scrutiny of the erosion of political freedoms in the territory as Beijing expands its influence there. Here is what we know.
Who are Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung?
Lee and Chow were leading members of the now-disbanded, pro-democracy action group Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, which for decades organised Hong Kong’s annual candlelight vigil commemorating those killed in the Tiananmen crackdown.
The alliance was established in May 1989 as protests calling for political reform in China gathered momentum in Beijing and other cities. Over the following three decades, it campaigned for accountability over the brutal crackdown on protests, the release of political dissidents and democratic reform in China.
Lee, a former Hong Kong politician and veteran labour activist, served as the alliance’s chairman, while Chow, a barrister, was its vice chairwoman.
Prosecutors accused the alliance and its leaders of inciting others to subvert state power. Central to the case was the organisation’s longstanding slogan calling to “end one-party” system in China.
The court ruled that the slogan sought to instigate hostility towards the Chinese Communist Party and undermine the political system established under China’s constitution. Lee and Chow maintained that their political advocacy was peaceful and protected by Hong Kong’s guarantees of freedom of expression.
Both were convicted on Friday. Ho, another former alliance leader, had already pleaded guilty to the same charge.
What happened to Hong Kong’s Tiananmen vigils?
Hong Kong was previously one of the few places under Chinese sovereignty where large public commemorations of the Tiananmen crackdown were permitted.
On June 4, 1989, Chinese troops opened fire on demonstrators after weeks of largely peaceful protests centred around Beijing’s Tiananmen Square, calling for political reform. Hundreds – possibly thousands – of people were killed, while thousands more were arrested.
Public discussion and commemoration of the crackdown have long been heavily censored in mainland China.
Hong Kong was different. Under the “one country, two systems” arrangement established when Britain handed the territory back to China in 1997, Hong Kong retained some of the freedoms unavailable on the mainland.
Every June 4, crowds gathered in the city’s Victoria Park for a candlelight vigil commemorating those killed and demanding accountability from Beijing. At their height, the commemorations drew crowds numbering in the tens of thousands.
The last major vigil organised by the alliance was held in 2019, the 30th anniversary of the crackdown. The authorities banned the gatherings in 2020 and 2021, initially citing COVID-19 restrictions. They have not resumed.
What is Hong Kong’s national security law?
The vigils ceased just as Hong Kong was undergoing a much broader political transformation following months of mass antigovernment and pro-democracy protests in 2019.
In June 2020, Beijing imposed a new national security law in Hong Kong, criminalising secession, subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign forces.
Chinese and Hong Kong authorities said the legislation was necessary to restore stability following the 2019 unrest and to ensure rights and freedoms remained protected.
Human rights groups say, however, its broad provisions have been used to dismantle much of Hong Kong’s organised political opposition and restrict some individual freedoms that once distinguished the territory from mainland China.
Since the law was introduced, leading opposition figures have been prosecuted, political organisations and civil society groups have disbanded, and independent media outlets have closed.
Why is this case so controversial?
Rights groups say the prosecution of Lee and Chow in effect criminalises peaceful political advocacy and the commemoration of one of the most difficult episodes in modern Chinese history.
Responding to Friday’s verdict, Amnesty International Hong Kong Overseas spokesperson Fernando Cheung said it showed how the national security law was being used to “punish people for peacefully remembering” the Tiananmen crackdown.
“For decades, Hong Kong was the only place on Chinese soil where large-scale public remembrance of the Tiananmen crackdown could take place,” Cheung said, describing the convictions as another step in what Amnesty says is a campaign to erase its legacy and silence demands for accountability.
Amnesty International Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks called Lee and Chow “prisoners of conscience” and said they “should never have been prosecuted in the first place”, calling for their immediate and unconditional release.

TEHRAN – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Aug 21 it is time to end the months-long Middle East war with the United States because Tehran appears to be in a stronger position than Washington.
Talks between the decades-old foes remain on hold, with both sides in the war started by the US and Israel in February locked in a stalemate.
Tehran is keeping the key Strait of Hormuz partially shut and Washington is persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.
“It is better that we bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power and dignity,” Pezeshkian said in a meeting with doctors.
“The whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasises that America has attacked our schools, hospitals and infrastructure in violation of all regulations and is hated around the world,” he said.
Pezeshkian also defended a memorandum of understanding agreed with the US in June aimed at ending the war, claiming it did not signal a defeat for Tehran.
“They cannot find even a single clause in this agreement that indicates capitulation. All the commitments concern the other side,” he said.
His remarks come weeks after Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he has approved the deal to end the war despite having “different views”.
Hardline lawmakers in Iran’s Parliament have also criticised the government over the deal, accusing it of giving concessions to the US, mostly over the re-opening of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
According to reports in US media, the American navy has been organising and protecting secret convoys of tankers through the southern sector of the strait, enabling between 5 million and 10 million barrels a day of oil to be exported.
As Tehran claimed to be in the stronger position, the US has said it would ramp up sanctions to heap pressure on Tehran.
The American plan drew condemnation from Iran’s Foreign Ministry, which accused the US of “economic terrorism” and “crimes against humanity”.
“The perpetrators and instigators of these sanctions are deserving of trial and punishment for committing such heinous crimes,” it said in a statement carried by state media.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowed on Aug 20 that Washington would “collapse” the Iranian regime with its threatened campaign nearly six months since their war began.
The comments underscored how the Trump administration is shifting to economic rather than military pressure on Tehran as the US President’s unpopular war drags on.
China also criticised Washington’s economic plan, saying that US “sanctions and pressure” would not resolve the Middle East conflict.
‘Economic D-Day’
Washington had urged other governments, including Beijing, to join efforts to isolate the Iranian economy.
Asked about US President Donald Trump’s threats, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian told reporters on Aug 21 that “sanctions and pressure will not help resolve the issue”.
“China calls on all relevant parties to take responsible measures and resolve the problem through political and diplomatic means,” he said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to visit the White House on Sept 24 when the topic of Iran is sure to come up, as it did when Trump travelled to Beijing for a summit in May.
Bessent said the plan to ramp up economic sanctions against Iran meant Washington is less likely to have to return to heavy military operations against the country.
He said he would give further details of the economic measures against Iran during a press conference on Aug 24.
Other senior Iranian officials also criticised the US sanctions plan.
“The so-called ‘Economic D-Day’ is a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X. AFP

This campaign aims to boost Black nonprofit fundraising by convincing everyday donors of their power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:53:02 UTC
21:53:02 KST

This campaign aims to boost Black nonprofit fundraising by convincing everyday donors of their power
NEW YORK (AP) — Black nonprofit fundraisers are turning to their own communities for support this month, stressing everyday donors’ power at a time when philanthropy is growing more concentrated among the affluent and some major funders have de-prioritized diversity in their grantmaking.
The BackBlack initiative has directed more than $12 million toward Black-led nonprofits over the past three years, according to founder Floyd Jones. A GivingTuesday -style campaign that runs in August, the appeal invites online donation platforms to center typically underfunded, Black-led nonprofits. Last year’s efforts drew more than 130,000 unique donors, according to Jones, with the majority of their gifts falling under $100.
This year, for the first time, organizers are also leveraging content creators to reach a new audience: Black Gen Zers. The goal is to show that philanthropy belongs to them, too — not just the historically wealthier and predominantly white charitable institutions that tend to dominate narratives about philanthropy.
“Our people have always taken care of our people,” Jones said. “I want people to feel empowered.”
The campaign could bring a boost for smaller, Black-led organizations that, according to research released earlier this year, saw no significant changes to their funding after the racial reckoning of 2020. Only a subset of larger nonprofits got temporary increases in the years that followed, according to an analysis by Candid and ABFE.
BackBlack aims to flip that narrative from one of “deficit” to one of abundance. Jones is heartened by the example of Madam C.J. Walker, a Black beauty entrepreneur widely considered America’s first female self-made millionaire. She supported Black educational efforts such as Booker T. Washington’s Tuskegee Institute and African American branches of the YMCA. She also contributed to the NAACP ‘s anti-lynching fund shortly before her death in 1919.
Jones doesn’t care if today’s donors have millions in their bank accounts, though. “It’s about doing your best,” he said.
One of BackBlack’s partnering creators pointed to the Free African Society. The nondenominational Philadelphia group, founded in 1787 by Black leaders Richard Allen and Absalom Jones, was one of the country’s first mutual aid organizations.
“We’ve always had to pool our money and resources to help each other,” said Ernest Crim III, a former schoolteacher who posts Black history videos for his 118,000 Instagram followers.
But, he added, allies must also pitch in — especially in communities that “might not have the sustainable market or income to consistently give.”
Crim is asking followers to support Black nonprofits that work on issues of youth employment. Other participating pages are focused on nonprofits providing sports access, improving health outcomes and ensuring civil rights.
Matching up to $6,000 in donations is For Good, a charitable giving platform that helps move money from more than 20,000 donor-advised funds to over a million nonprofits filtered by ZIP code. GivingTuesday manages BackBlack’s data, Jones said. Other partners include online fundraising platforms GiveButter, Every.org, Bonterra and Fundraise Up.
For Good provides back end infrastructure for consumer-based campaigns including YouTube’s fundraising pages and Patagonia’s point-of-sale donations. The creator-driven donation strategy stemmed from the platform’s success with YouTubers who launch fundraisers for the issues they discuss in their videos.
Grassroots fundraisers face competing headwinds, according to For Good interim president Tamara Mahal. The concentration of wealth has increased the share of high net worth individuals in the donor pool. But, she said, there are more ways than ever to give locally from the bottom up.
She welcomes the BackBlack campaign’s efforts to include more small-dollar givers so that nonprofits aren’t overly beholden to any one individual benefactor.
“The cause is important in and of itself. Find a nonprofit that’s doing work in your community,” she said. “And that will actually help us to diversify.”
Kaci Patterson is the founder of Social Good Solutions, a social impact consulting firm that works with funders to build support for Black-led organizations outside of “trend funding.” She finds that Black Philanthropy Month, celebrated in August, is a reminder that philanthropy is more than just “institutional” giving “held within the walls of wealth and power.”
It was fish fries and chicken dinners, she noted, that funded alternative transportation systems during the Montgomery Bus Boycott. Growing up, her own family received groceries from their community during times of hardship.
“That was philanthropy. That was someone else looking at us and investing in us and wanting us to be whole and wanting us to be well,” she said. “We’ve always had this kind of ‘we got us’ philanthropy. Let’s step into that role more confidently.”

BERLIN (AP) — A donkey on the loose in northern Germany attacked two motorists by jumping into their van on Friday, kicking and biting them along with a third woman who tried to help restrain the aggressive equine, police said.
The incident south of the coastal city of Cuxhaven came to an end as the animal’s owner intervened to secure the animal, Cuxhaven police said in a statement.
Passersby noticed the donkey, whose name is Freddy, and a horse were running loose at a roundabout in the town of Holssel. The motorists tried to secure the donkey, which “became very aggressive” and jumped into the van.

Chinese commercial space firm completes long-duration test of reusable rocket engine

21:49:58 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's commercial reusable launch vehicle sector continues to make steady progress, as a company announced on Friday that it had completed a long-duration test firing of an engine for a large recoverable carrier rocket.
Deep Blue Aerospace, a commercial space startup based in Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu Province, said it recently completed a 100-second static-fire test of its Thunder-RS engine, a 130-tonne-class liquid-oxygen kerosene engine designed for the company's large reusable rocket, Nebula-2.
The test reached 1,297.5 kilonewtons of thrust, or about 132.3 tonnes. The company said multiple short-duration test firings had been conducted previously to evaluate engine performance, with no anomalies recorded.
The recent 100‑second run was the engine's first crossing of that steady‑state duration threshold, serving as a comprehensive verification of its performance, the company said.
Rocket reusability can greatly cut launch costs and boosts launch frequency, making it key to achieving large-scale, routine access to space.
China launched the reusable rocket Zhuque-3 on Wednesday morning, achieving its first recovery of a rocket's first stage on land, marking the country's first successful land-based recovery. This mission followed the successful sea-based net recovery of the Long March-10B's first stage on July 10.
More models of Chinese reusable rockets are scheduled to conduct tests this year. ■

China's early rice output holds steady in 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:49:57 CST
21:49:57 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's early rice production remained broadly stable in 2026, with the planting area edging up slightly, official data showed Friday.
The early rice output totaled 28.29 million tonnes, staying above 28 million tonnes for the sixth consecutive year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
The planting area edged up by 22,000 mu (about 1,467 hectares) from the previous year to 71.164 million mu.
The output fell by 220,000 tonnes, or 0.8 percent year on year, while the average yield dropped 0.8 percent to 397.6 kg per mu, the data showed.
Weather conditions were generally favorable after planting, but persistent heavy rainfall and typhoons later affected production in some major growing areas in southern China, said NBS official Wei Fenghua.
China has stepped up support for grain production this year by maintaining the minimum purchase price for early indica rice and farmland fertility protection subsidies, while increasing support for crop rotation and other measures to stabilize farmers' planting expectations, Wei said.
Efforts to strengthen grain production capacity have also continued. Over 66.7 million hectares of high-standard farmland have been developed nationwide, and domestically bred crop varieties now account for more than 95 percent of the country's total planted area.
Stable early rice production, together with an increase in summer grain output, has laid a solid foundation for a bumper grain harvest this year, Wei said.
China's summer grain output totaled 150.75 million tonnes this year, up 0.7 percent year on year and exceeding 150 million tonnes for the first time, according to previously released NBS data. ■

Ukrainian Nord Stream blast suspect detained in Croatia

Ukrainian Nord Stream blast suspect detained in Croatia
SARAJEVO, Aug 20 - A Ukrainian man suspected of being involved in the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline blasts has been placed into pre-trial detention in Croatia pending a decision on his extradition to Germany, court officials said on Friday.
The suspect - described as a scuba diver by German prosecutors who have identified him only as Vladimir Z. - was arrested in the early hours on Wednesday in a hotel in the Croatian coastal city of Pula on a European arrest warrant.
German prosecutors have said Vladimir Z. was part of a group behind the blasts which followed Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine earlier that year.
The explosions - described by Russia and Western countries as sabotage - damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, a vital route for Russian gas exports to Europe, as well as the Nord Stream 2 branch, which had yet to enter service.
Another suspect in the case, former Ukrainian army officer Serhii K., was charged by prosecutors in July with orchestrating the blasts while acting on behalf of Ukrainian state entities.
That man - who was arrested in Italy in August 2025 and transferred to Germany in November - has denied any involvement in the blasts near the Danish island of Bornholm.
Court officials in Pula said the suspect arrested there this week was put in detention on Thursday following a request from the county state attorney, who has questioned him. They gave no details on whether he had entered a plea.
German courts have treated the case as falling within their jurisdiction because the damaged pipelines end in the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, and their loss affected Germany's energy security and internal safety.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said his ministry has been in contact with the Croatian authorities to facilitate the suspect's extradition but that the procedures can take time.
"We have a strong interest in clarifying the facts in this context and ... ensuring that the perpetrators are brought to Germany, where they will be dealt with appropriately,” Dobrindt added. REUTERS

Two tankers with 22 Indians on board hijacked by armed pirates off Yemen, Somalia
Edited by: Vijaya Srivastava / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 21, 2026, 18:20 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
(Representative image): The pirates, suspected of being involved in a previous hijacking, reportedly steered the vessel towards Somalia's Nugaal coast.
Two commercial vessels carrying 22 Indian crew members have been hijacked by armed pirates in separate incidents off Yemen and Somalia this week, with the sailors reported safe so far, according to a senior shipping ministry official. The Eritrea-flagged MT Sibu 1, carrying 16 Indians among 20 crew members, was seized in the Gulf of Aden on August 20, around 30 nautical miles off Yemen, while the Cameroon-flagged M/V LUTUF, with six Indians among its 10-member crew, was hijacked off Somalia's Puntland coast on August 17.
The MT Sibu 1 was taken over by six armed pirates after an unauthorised vessel approached the tanker, while eight armed pirates operating from two skiffs boarded the M/V LUTUF off Puntland. Both vessels remain under pirate control, while no injuries have been reported among the crew.
Tanker with 16 Indians hijacked off Yemen
The Eritrea-flagged oil products tanker MT Sibu 1 was hijacked in the Gulf of Aden on August 20, about 30 nautical miles off the Yemeni coast. It was carrying 20 crew members, including 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese and one Iraqi national, while the nationality of another crew member is yet to be confirmed.Maritime tracking information indicates that the tanker was approached by an unauthorised vessel before control of the ship was lost.
The shipping ministry official said, "As reported by Recruitment and Placement Service Licence (RPSL) agency - S K S Krishi Marine Services (Opc) Private Limited, six armed pirates are presently onboard the vessel (M.T. Sibhu-1) and have taken control of the vessel."The RPSL agency has been advised to submit an incident report and subsequent periodic updates through the e-Navik online marine casualty reporting system.
M/V LUTUF seized off Somalia
The Cameroon-flagged M/V LUTUF was hijacked on August 17, around 3½ nautical miles off Marraya in Somalia's Puntland region. The vessel had 10 crew members, including six Indians, one Turkish national, one Georgian national and two Serbian security guards.Eight armed pirates, reportedly carrying AK-47-type weapons and travelling in two skiffs, boarded the vessel. The crew initially took shelter in the citadel, but the pirates gained access and moved them to the bridge before taking control of the ship."The vessel is reported to have been boarded by eight pirates, armed with AK-47-type weapons and operating from two skiffs."The crew initially mustered in the citadel. However, the pirates gained access and subsequently brought them to the bridge. The vessel is currently under pirate control. No injuries have been reported thus far," he said.The hijackers, suspected of involvement in a previous hijacking, subsequently steered the vessel towards Somalia's Nugaal coast. The ship was carrying Turkish weapons, communications and satellite equipment bound for a Turkish military training facility in Mogadishu.
Indian seafarers face heightened regional risks
The twin hijackings come amid renewed security concerns for commercial shipping in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and wider Indian Ocean. Vessels in the region have faced both piracy threats and attacks linked to the conflict in Yemen.
The Forward Seamen's Union of India (FSUI) separately raised concerns over the "dangers faced by Indian seafarers amid the Iran war" and shared footage it claimed showed a vessel carrying 22 crew members, including 21 Indians, being hijacked in the Strait of Hormuz on April 22. It was unclear whether the footage related to a separate incident or the latest hijackings.India is the world's second-largest supplier of seafarers after the Philippines. The 2026 BIMCO-ICS Seafarer Workforce Report estimates that India supplies 311,936 seafarers, underscoring the scale of the country's exposure to maritime security threats worldwide.

Denmark refuses to help Germany investigate Nord Stream explosions

Unknown Publisher

Denmark refuses to help Germany investigate Nord Stream explosions
Unlike Sweden and Poland, Denmark has refused to help Germany investigate the 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
Source: European Pravda, citing Danish broadcaster DR, which reviewed the German indictment in the Nord Stream case
Quote from German prosecutors: "The Danish authorities refused to conduct an investigation on the islands of Bornholm and Christiansø because of a possible threat to national security."
Details: The document says that when German investigators wanted to question port captains and yacht owners who may have seen the yacht allegedly used by those responsible for the sabotage in mid-September 2022, the Danish authorities refused to assist Germany's Federal Police.
According to the indictment, the Copenhagen public prosecutor's office rejected the request on 14 February 2024.
Danish experts interviewed by DR agree that Denmark's refusal to assist an ally appears unusual, as legal cooperation between the two countries has so far been close.
Meanwhile, law professor Birgit Feldtmann noted that although the refusal is "unusual", Copenhagen has the legal right to reject a request for legal assistance, including from other EU countries and close allies such as Germany.
"Such a request can be rejected, in particular on the grounds that it could jeopardise Denmark's interests. That is a lawful basis," she said.
Background:
- On 19 August, Ukrainian national Volodymyr Zhuravliov, whom Germany suspects of involvement in the Nord Stream sabotage, was detained in Croatia while filming a Hollywood film about the operation.
- Another Ukrainian suspect in the case, Serhii Kuznetsov, is already in custody in Germany. He was detained while on holiday in Italy last summer.
- At the end of June, Germany's Federal Prosecutor's Office published an official statement announcing charges against him, stating that Kuznetsov and other members of the group had acted as Ukrainian military personnel.
- On 21 August, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Germany should not hold those suspected of blowing up the Nord Stream gas pipelines criminally liable.

Poland has summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) have discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból.
“Partnership requires mutual respect,” declared foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for [the] IDF’s excessive use of force[,] are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations.”
Partnership requires mutual respect. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDF’s excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations. https://t.co/9H0nhiDE4H

The incident in question took place in April 2024, when Israeli drones struck a convoy delivering humanitarian aid from World Central Kitchen (WCK), a major international food relief NGO. The attack killed seven aid workers, including Soból.
The incident caused outrage in Poland, whose government demanded that Israel fully explain the circumstances. The IDF expressed “sincere sorrow” over the deaths and pledged to carry out a “thorough and transparent” investigation.
On Wednesday this week, the IDF announced that it had closed the case after determining “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident”.
The IDF said that its troops had identified a gunman on one of the trucks in the convoy. It also claimed that WCK had hired an armed security force to protect the convoy without coordinating that with IDF authorities and that the convoy deviated from the route previously agreed with the IDF.
However, the IDF also acknowledged that it had mistakenly identified several individuals as being armed. It added that attempts to contact WCK representatives over a half-hour period while the convoy was on the move were unsuccessful.
The IDF noted that, after the incident, two military officers were removed from their positions while three others were reprimanded. But it found that there was no basis for any further action.

It also noted that Polish prosecutors are still conducting their own investigation and that the foreign ministry had informed the Israeli ambassador that they “expect the Israeli side will provide the relevant Polish authorities with all necessary explanations and materials requested”.
“The circumstances of the tragedy should be fully investigated and [we] do not accept that the perpetrators are avoiding legal and moral responsibility,” concluded the ministry, adding that “the families deserve adequate compensation”.

====================================================================================================

How an Academic Became Collateral Damage to China’s Interests in Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

On June 3, Burmese-American scholar U Min Zin disappeared in China’s southwestern province of Yunnan, where he was set to attend an academic conference. On June 12, shortly before Myanmar’s ruler, Min Aung Hlaing, arrived in China for a state visit, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian confirmed that Zin had been arrested and accused of endangering Chinese national security. No further details were provided.
On August 20, the U.S. State Department officially classified Zin as “wrongfully detained.” Assistant Secretary of State for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson pledged that the U.S. government “will continue to advocate for Mr. Zin and call for the release of all U.S. citizens who are arbitrarily detained or exit banned in China.”
Zin runs the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar, a think tank in Thailand that is critical of Myanmar’s military government and the 2021 coup that brought it to power. Initially, the arrest of Zin, a U.S. citizen, may seem like another attempt by Beijing to engage in hostage diplomacy and gain the upper hand in any potential negotiations with the United States at the September summit between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. But Beijing’s arrest of Zin actually has more to do with Myanmar itself. China wanted to remove a potentially destabilizing variable from the already unsteady foundations of Chinese investment in Myanmar, which is key to Beijing’s economic strategy in Southeast Asia.
For China, its core strategic interests in Myanmar are the stability of its shared border, the safety of its economic investments, and the closure of scam centers that ensnare and enslave Chinese nationals. To that end, Beijing supports the military junta that seized power from Myanmar’s democratically elected government. China has provided the new regime with $3 billion in economic assistance, as well as selling it military weapons.
Beijing also applies diplomatic pressure on Myanmar’s ethnic armed organizations. Beijing has not been shy about detaining leaders of these resistance groups to force ceasefires between them and the military leaders in Naypyidaw and protect China’s infrastructure projects. If a person or organization is deemed a threat to China’s interests in Myanmar, Beijing is willing and able to use its full suite of tools against them, including forced detention.
China especially wants to protect the stability of the newly elected Burmese government. Though the election was widely condemned as a sham, the nominally civilian Parliament can sign contracts and negotiate agreements that the junta cannot. The veneer of civilian administration allows for continuity in China’s projects and legal leverage should the junta’s leadership change.
Since the launch of its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), Myanmar has been a key to China’s economic strategy in Southeast Asia. Of particular importance is the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which connects China to the Indian Ocean and provides a much-needed economic infusion in China’s less-developed southwestern provinces.
As technological competition with the West intensifies, Myanmar has only grown more important. Beijing sources rare earth minerals from Myanmar’s northern Kachin State to meet its defense and clean-energy needs. Such processing involves using toxic chemicals to extract precious elements from the soil. Residents, outraged by the damage, protested the continuous harm to their environment, but by all reports, the extraction continues.
Residents of Kachin State allege that China’s rare earth mining has threatened water sources, putting their health and food supply at risk. The United Nations has reported that numerous mines have forcibly displaced civilians and received financial support from the military junta for their operations. According to the outlet Frontier Myanmar, since 2024, junta troops working with Chinese mines have routinely arrested and killed civilians at random.
The public opposition is having real consequences. In February 2022, a Chinese oil and gas pipeline was attacked by a civilian militia opposed to Chinese support of the junta. In 2024, the Burmese and Chinese governments reportedly were working together to assemble a joint security company to protect Chinese projects and personnel from attacks.
The backlash against Chinese projects endangers the vast sums of wealth that public and private enterprises have poured into Myanmar. If infrastructure investments falter, China will lose access to vast amounts of critical minerals, harming its ambitions to develop defense and other high-end technologies domestically.
China’s interests in Myanmar are not limited to critical minerals. In 2016, Chinese state-owned firms reached agreements with the Burmese government to develop a deep-water port in the town of Kyaukpyu along the Bay of Bengal. This port, in which both China and Myanmar have agreed to invest a collective $7.3 billion, would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean, allowing ships ferrying oil and other vital goods to bypass the Strait of Malacca. The Strait of Malacca accounts for over 22 percent of international maritime trade; if there were a conflict involving China, Beijing fears that its foes could close the strait to harm China’s economy and defense deployments.
The deep-sea port could also serve as a staging area for People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) vessels. While previous experts asserted that deployment of PLAN ships was unlikely due to Burmese political and legal restrictions, the financial and political leverage Beijing now holds over Naypyidaw means that if China wants it to happen, it will.
An estimated 20,000 people, mostly farmers and fishermen, will lose their land and be displaced by development of the port and its attached special economic zone. Farmers expressed frustration over a lack of consultation with the local government and a belief that the special economic zone and port will bring in Chinese workers instead of hiring locals. If backlash halts the projects or militia attacks endanger the lives of Chinese workers, the Chinese and Burmese governments would lose billions of dollars, and China would lose access to a strategic port.
Burmese activists and academics, such as Min Zin, serve as the central node informing people about Chinese investments and projects in Myanmar, including their negative impacts. In fact, Zin’s ISP-Myanmar runs a dedicated China Desk that maps and outlines China’s infrastructure investments in the region, specifically highlighting China’s influence in northern Kachin State and its development in Kyaukpyu.
While the observations and analysis of Zin’s organization were relatively benign and did not engage in fear-mongering, the simple act of shining a spotlight probably set off alarm bells in Chinese leadership circles. Burmese civilians, armed with knowledge of the negative impacts of Chinese development in their area, could make life much more difficult for Chinese investors by protesting and, more worryingly for the Chinese, encouraging civilian militias to attack the projects.
This, combined with Zin’s history of activism, likely made Zin a target. Why he decided to travel to Kunming at the invitation of a Chinese university is unknown – especially as China has previously detained scholars who are in the nation to attend academic conferences, give university lectures, or visit family members.
In 2019, a Japanese professor of modern Chinese history from Hokkaido University, Nobu Iwatani, was arrested and accused of spying for the Japanese government. Nobu had been invited to give a lecture at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Chinese authorities claimed Nobu had collected classified and illicit documents relating to the Second Sino-Japanese War, a topic especially sensitive to Beijing and central to its official narrative. Beijing released Nobu after relentless pressure from the Japanese government.
Professors Fan Yuntao, Hu Shiyun, and Yuan Keqin, Chinese nationals based in Japan, also disappeared while visiting China. While Fan and Hu returned to Japan in 2025 with little explanation, Yuan was convicted of espionage in 2024 and released in 2026.
While Zin’s ISP-Myanmar did not necessarily pose a serious risk to China’s infrastructure projects, Beijing likely found that its analysis and Zin’s connections were inconvenient to Chinese interests. China used the opportunity of Zin’s travel to Kunming to remove him from the equation.
Min Zin’s arrest signals that civilians who are inconvenient to China’s international growth and ambitions are subject to forced arrest and arbitrary detention. An active threat to the regime or its relationships is not required; even the perception of a threat is enough to result in arrest and an accusation of espionage.
While the belief that Zin’s analysis and activism may endanger Chinese investments likely motivated his detention, it also sends another message: foreigners who criticize Beijing’s policies should think twice before visiting China, lest the long arm of the state find them.
