Palestine Action ‘Barclays five’ will not be sentenced as terrorists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:42:26 UTC
21:42:26 KST

Five Palestine Action activists who vandalised a Barclays branch in Burnley will not be sentenced as terrorists, a judge has ruled.
Dubbed the Barclays five, Brendon O’Hagan, 28; Amanda Kelly, 31; Hmeera Atiqnisar, 31; Mohammed Malik, 28; and Alma Yaniv, 70, were all found guilty in June of causing damage exceeding £200,000, after breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire in August 2024.
The group targeted the site in protest at Barclays because it held shares in the Israeli weapons company Elbit Systems.
Judge Altham, the recorder of Preston, ruled on Friday that while the damage was substantial, it was not of the size of other attacks or against a sensitive property, such as an arms company, as has happened in previous Palestine Action incidents, and thus did not meet the high threshold for a terrorist sentencing.
All five will still be sentenced next month for criminal damage, but will face shorter jail terms as a result of the ruling.
After the five activists were found guilty in June, the trial judge, Philip Parry, told the prosecution and the defence he intended to consider a “terrorist connection” to the offending. It is understood this was a result of new information coming to light during the trial.
Neither the five activists nor the jury that found them guilty of criminal charges were aware that the case would be considered as terrorism until after they were found guilty.
During the hearings that took place at Preston crown court on Friday, legal representatives for the activists stated that four of them, excluding Yaniv, had admitted to being members of Palestine Action during the trial, but that this was irrelevant, because Palestine Action was not proscribed as a terrorist group until a year after the act of vandalism.
In a statement put out by the five after the ruling, the group said they were “extremely relieved that the court has seen sense” but said a terrorism sentencing “should never have been an option” and accused the state of “attempting to equate property damage to the Israeli war machine with terrorism”.
They said: “A terrorism sentence would not only aggravate our sentence significantly, it would mean we would be imprisoned as terrorists and subject to notification requirements for 15-plus years upon release. Those requirements include notifying police of any new address, bank account, phone number, email address, relationship and more. If we failed to do so, even by accident, we would face an additional five years in prison.
“The proscription of Palestine Action, the arrests of over 3,500 people under the Terrorism Act for holding signs and the sentencing of direct action activists as terrorists, are all tools being used by the state to protect the Israeli weapons industry and continue its role in the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
“The use of counter-terror powers against direct action for Palestine came after extensive lobbying by the Israeli government, Elbit Systems, pro-Israel lobby groups and politicians with vested interests.”
It was reported in October 2024 that Barclays had sold all its Elbit shares. The bank had previously said it held them only in relation to client-driven transactions, being neither an investor nor shareholder in the arms company.
Commenting on the ruling, Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said: “The fact that the defendants in today’s case were not sentenced as terrorists is welcome. No one should be treated more harshly under the law because their crimes were part of a protest against genocide or any other issue, and the misuse of terrorism powers in this way should never have even been considered.
“We now need to see the proscription against Palestine Action lifted and an end to the misuse of sweeping counter-terror powers against direct action protesters. The government should begin the process of reversing the years of attacks on our right to protest, one of the most effective tools we have to hold our leaders to account.”

Data from the European statistical office showed that fuel and lubricant prices for personal transport in the EU rose 16.9% in July year-on-year.  
The annual price growth followed year-on-year increases of 20.7% in May and 13.7% in June, Eurostat stated.
Eurostat reported that fuel and lubricant prices stood higher in 25 of the 27 EU member states in July compared to the same month of 2025.
Romania recorded the highest annual increase at 24.2%, while Germany and Lithuania followed it with 22.9% each.
Prices dropped slightly in Hungary by 0.1%, and Sweden and Ireland registered the lowest increases at 1.2% and 3.2%, respectively.
EU consumers saw diesel prices increase by 4.3% and gasoline by 4.7% in July on a monthly basis.
Diesel prices increased in 17 EU countries between June and July, with Poland leading at 13.4%, followed by Germany at 12.7% and Greece at 12.1%.
Nine EU countries experienced a drop in diesel prices, as Greek Cypriot recorded the largest decrease at 7.9%.  
Data indicated that 14 countries recorded increases and 12 countries recorded decreases in gasoline prices between June and July.
Poland saw the largest gasoline price increase at 17.2%, while Sweden recorded the most significant decrease at 11.1%.

UK awards Saab major Giraffe radar support deal
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:40:42 BST
21:40:42 KST

Defence Equipment and Support has awarded Saab UK a contract valued at £1.6 million excluding VAT to provide logistics support, supply, training and spares for the Giraffe 1X radar system.
Defence Equipment and Support has awarded Saab UK a contract valued at £1.6 million excluding VAT covering support and additional supply requirements for the Giraffe 1X radar system, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The contract was signed on 2 July 2026 and disclosed in a Find a Tender notice published on 19 August. The requirement covers Contractor Logistics Support for Giraffe 1X, including supply, training, helpdesk services and spares support. The initial contract runs until 31 March 2027, with three one-year options allowing it to be extended to 31 March 2030.
The published value is £1.6 million excluding VAT, rising to £1.8065 million including VAT.
Giraffe 1X is part of Saab’s family of mobile radar systems and is designed to provide surveillance and warning against airborne threats. The procurement notice classifies the requirement as radar equipment and places particular emphasis on sustaining the system once deployed, including the provision and return of spares and support for equipment that becomes unserviceable.
The agreement also gives the Ministry of Defence the right to make additional purchases while the contract remains in force. The options listed in the notice cover further supply as well as training, helpdesk and spares support, meaning the arrangement extends beyond maintenance of equipment already in service.
The contract was awarded directly to Saab UK rather than through a competitive procurement. Defence Equipment and Support said this was justified on technical grounds because Saab is the manufacturer and design authority for the Giraffe 1X and holds the intellectual property and proprietary information required to support the system.
The procurement notice states that Saab holds the relevant drawings and specifications and that no licences have been granted to other organisations, including the Ministry of Defence, that would allow them to obtain and use the information required to support the radars. DE&S therefore concluded that Saab was the only supplier with the specific technical knowledge necessary to deliver the requirement.
The contract includes performance measures focused on the availability and movement of spares. These cover delivery of items held within deployed spares packs, provision of equipment not contained within those packs and the return of unserviceable components from the Ministry of Defence to the contractor. Performance against the measures is due to be reported every three months.
The scale of the published contract value is notable for a logistics support arrangement. The notice does not separate the £1.6 billion figure into expected expenditure on existing support requirements and potential additional purchases over the life of the agreement, although it explicitly provides for further equipment to be bought while the contract is active.

Quota set for visitors to popular Sai Kung coastal trail in first for Hong Kong
Authorities will cap daily visitor numbers at Po Pin Chau section of High Island Geo Trail at 2,000 over several stretches in coming months
Hong Kong authorities will cap access to a popular Sai Kung trail overlooking hexagonal rock columns at 2,000 people per day during several stretches from next month and require real-name registration for visitors, marking the city’s first countryside crowd-control measures of their kind.
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department announced the arrangement on Friday for the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail, after the proposal was floated in April.
The trail is within the Unesco Global Geopark at Sai Kung East Country Park. No fees will be charged for the bookings or penalties for failing to turn up, at least for now.
“The primary reason for the arrangement is that we realise there are sudden increases in visitor numbers over holidays, and some of the capacity of certain sections is close to saturation,” department director Mickey Lai Kin-ming said.
“Through the reservation system, we hope to achieve organised crowd control and to prevent visitors from over concentrating, as well as to protect the environment and improve visitor experience.”
Lai said the move was aimed at protecting the narrow trail from “excessive wear and tear”, adding the quota would be further reviewed.

Is Pakistan’s Province Debate a Political Gimmick?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:38:00 UTC
21:38:00 KST

From time to time, the debate over creating new provinces arises in Pakistani politics. This debate receives attention in the media for a while, only to fade away after some time as if it never existed. Consequently, the airtime for proponents of new provinces disappears as well. Some view this debate as a political gimmick designed to distract the public from the real issues facing the country, while others believe that influential figures operate behind the scenes to extract concessions from those in political power by stirring up this debate. It is indeed possible for a select few to hold power while others manipulate events from the sidelines in a hybrid democracy like Pakistan, which has experienced dictatorial rule for 34 of its 79 years of existence since 1947.
The debate of dividing the existing four provinces of Pakistan and creating new provinces has resurfaced once again after a statement made by Pakistani Interior and Narcotics Control Minister Mohsin Naqvi late last month. While addressing the first Pakistan Economic Summit in Islamabad, he said:
The system we are living under has collapsed. You have been dragging this system for 70 years, and while we all want democracy, there are many forms within democracy. Problems cannot be solved through the current dispensation. If this system continues, we will still be sitting here a decade from now discussing the same issues. The only solution is to take [the matter of] administrative units, provinces or whatever you may call it, to the public.
These remarks by a minister caused an uproar across the country, with some in favor of creating new provinces and other against. The minister’s own colleagues, including Defense Minister Khawaja Asif and Prime Minister’s Advisor on Political and Public Affairs Rana Sanaullah, have not shown any particular support for the notion.
Sanaullah said the government has no plan at present regarding new provinces. He further added that different people are talking about different numbers of provinces; some suggest 12, others suggest 20, and some are even going further and suggesting 32 provinces be carved out of the current four provinces. He questioned anyone offering such suggestions without an actual plan.
Contrary to Sanaullah’s comments, Minister of State for Law and Justice Aqeel Malik confirmed the government’s intention to create new provinces. However, he said, “First, all political parties will be taken on board.”
There are political, constitutional, and legal hurdles to the creation of new provinces, which, as Dawn noted, “would have to be addressed through political consultation.” That may prove a problem for Pakistan’s current governing hybrid regime – also accused of a stolen mandate during the country’s last general elections in 2024.
As Dawn reported:
There is also speculation that the government intends to introduce constitutional amendments to bypass a provision requiring the consent of the relevant provincial assembly when a new province is carved out of an existing one.
The Constitution also requires a two-thirds majority in parliament for such an amendment.
Political experts have speculated that the government may opt for a referendum on the creation of new provinces. However, they point out that even this would require parliamentary approval.
The current hybrid coalition of six political parties was given that necessary two-thirds majority by the Election Commission of Pakistan and a Supreme Court verdict last summer. The matter of new provinces has not yet been discussed in parliament, suggesting an effort to gauge the opinion of the masses before taking any serious steps.
The debate seems to serve two major purposes for the country’s establishment: first, to divert attention from the unrest and tension in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, known in Pakistan as Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and Balochistan; second, to tweak, if not entirely roll back, the Pakistani Constitution’s 18th amendment.
In June, a wave of protests unfurled in Azad Jammu and Kashmir against the reservation of 12 seats in the region’s legislature. The crisis exposed a long-running debate about political representation, resource allocation, governance and regional autonomy. In a crackdown against the protests, according to the Jammu Kashmir Human Rights Observatory, 89 people were killed during the unrest between July 27 and August 5, which brought global attention to Azad Jammu and Kashmir. Besides this issue, Balochistan continues to simmer with tension. In July, Balochistan replaced Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as the country’s most violent province. The revived province debate may be meant to divert the public’s attention, and that of the media, from the unrest in both places.
The debate may also provide a pretext to tinker with the 18th amendment. The 18th amendment, passed in 2010, marked a pivotal transformation in the federal structure by significantly enhancing provincial autonomy. It reallocated 47 entries between federal and provincial jurisdictions and empowered provincial assemblies with greater legislative authority. It was also decided that in the National Finance Commission Award, 57.5 percent of the total proceeds would be horizontally distributed among the provinces, and the center (that is, the federal government) would keep 42.5 percent of the total divisible pool. The 18th amendment is at risk by the proposed 28th, which includes raising the voting age from 18 to 25, centralizing the creation of provinces, returning devolved subjects to the federal government, making the share of the NFC award flexible, and strengthening the local government system.
Such an expansive amendment as proposed draws both support and opposition from different parties for different reasons, but the creation of new provinces will arguably meet strong opposition from the general population. This is especially true in a province like Sindh, where the issue is more sensitive than in other provinces. Sindh was the first province that adopted the historic Lahore Resolution in favor of the creation of Pakistan. According to the provincial assembly of Sindh’s website, “On 3 March 1943, the Sindh Assembly became the first legislature in British India to pass a resolution in favor of the creation of Pakistan, aligning with the Lahore Resolution of 1940.”
Traditionally, the social and political landscape of Sindh has been characterized by isolation from the power centers. Throughout Mughal rule in India, Sindh was a peripheral region because of its geographical location. However, it was due to Sindhi clans’ resistance and rebellion against the state’s attempts to impose heavy revenue demands that the Mughal system could not be applied in its entirety. Therefore, the socio-economic and political structure that developed in Sindh was different from the northern regions of Punjab and the North West Frontier Province (NWFP), renamed as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under the 18th Amendment. Thus, Sindh was not simply an administrative territory that was created after the partition of the subcontinent. It was, rather, a historically constituted political unit that became part of the federation through a political process associated with the movement of Pakistan.
The creation of new provinces could lead to increased ethno-nationalist tensions. Any new provinces would have to be formed by dividing the existing ones, which many people find unacceptable. Pakistan’s social fabric is already significantly fractured due to various tensions, including those related to language, ethnicity, religious sects, political polarization, and economic inequality. The idea of establishing new provinces could further damage this already fragile social structure. A more viable solution to the shortcomings of the current system is to more fully implement the 18th amendment to the constitution and empower local bodies within the provinces.

Charter plane crash in Alaska kills all eight onboard near US military airstrip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:32:08 UTC
21:32:08 KST

A charter aircraft that crashed at a remote radar site in western Alaska on Thursday, killing all eight people onboard, was making its second runway approach in heavy fog when it lost contact, authorities said Friday.
The Cessna’s two pilots could not see the gravel airstrip and were flying solely by instruments when the plane crashed about midday Thursday, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, told a virtual news conference.
Regulations required that they abort their first landing attempt because of the lack of visibility, he said, and the plane crashed on its second attempt, about one-third of a mile (0.5km) from the runway. The runway is surrounded by mountainous terrain on three sides, and the Federal Aviation Administration recommends pilots use GPS and other instruments when they land there.
Onboard were the pilots, two employees of the US Army Corps of Engineers and four contractors. Two of the contractors were employees of Calista Brice, a collection of companies that perform construction, engineering, logistics and other work in remote areas.
The crash happened near Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site airport, approximately 450 miles (725km) west of Anchorage, Alaska.
“This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve,” US air force Lt Gen Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American aerospace defense command region and 11th air force, said in a statement.
The radar site is managed by the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center. It is part of a network of remote radar sites that tracks aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders, the statement from Alaskan Command said.
The statement did not provide details on the specific work the individuals were doing. It referred to the plane involved as a “civilian-contracted aircraft”.
Davis described those on board as “dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment. Our absolute priority right now is providing unwavering support to their families, friends and teammates during this devastating time. We are profoundly grateful for the swift and tireless response of our search and recovery professionals.”
The twin-engined Cessna 441 had taken off from Ted Stevens Anchorage international airport and was headed to Cape Newenham, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said. The crash happened about 12.15pm local time.
Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska posted to X on Thursday night: “I join Alaskans in condolences as we learn of the plane crash in Cape Newenham today. I’ve traveled extensively with Security Aviation throughout Alaska, and have met many of their experienced pilots.”
She expressed appreciation for the various authorities responding to the tragedy and added: “Alaska is praying for those on board, their loved ones, and the team at Security Aviation.”

US allies in Asia wary as Trump moves military assets for Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:32:03 UTC
21:32:03 KST

US allies in Asia wary as Trump moves military assets for Iran war
Allies worry about the US ability to deter China, even if the bulk of US forces remain in the region.
United States allies in Asia are watching warily as Washington scales back some military assets in the region to meet demands in the Middle East, where the US-Israel war on Iran is dragging into its sixth month.
The latest point of tension came this week as the US moved its last aircraft carrier in Asia – the USS George Washington – from Japan to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been deployed for nine months at a stretch. Multiple reports had suggested that there were food shortages on the USS Abraham Lincoln, while broken toilets and showers contributed to unsanitary conditions and poor health. Reports suggested that at least one sailor tried to jump off board.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4After GERD, can Egypt shape Ethiopia’s next Nile dams?
- list 2 of 4Pakistan’s Imran Khan back to prison after evaluation at hospital
- list 3 of 4Hong Kong Tiananmen activists found guilty of national security charges
- list 4 of 4Dozens of migrants land on Spanish coast surprising beachgoers
The news of the USS George Washington’s move away from the Asia Pacific region follows reports earlier this year that the US had moved parts of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) system from South Korea to use against Iran, as well as other reports that the US has drawn down its missile and munitions stockpiles to keep the war going.
Taken together, they dent US power projection in Asia and its ability to counter threats from China, said William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group.
“If we look at this as part of a larger trend … it certainly is creating an impact on the overall effectiveness of the US-led regional deterrence against China,” Yang said about the deployment of the USS George Washington.
While the last US aircraft carrier has left the area – for now – the Chinese fleet has increasingly ventured beyond the First Island Chain, which runs from north of Japan through Taiwan and the northern Philippines to Borneo.
The Cold War defensive line was originally designed to contain Beijing, but it has recently done little to keep China’s Liaoning and Shandong aircraft carriers from moving into the Western Pacific.
In another concerning development for US allies, Chinese coastguard activity has picked up since June in the waters east of Taiwan, which overlap with Japan’s and the Philippines’ exclusive economic zones, Yang said.
“These maritime operations are aimed at Taipei, aimed at Manila, aimed at Tokyo,” Yang told Al Jazeera. “Part of it is also testing the US reaction to these operations and the US capability to respond.”
Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist and security expert at the National University of Singapore, told Al Jazeera that US allies may worry that China will become even more emboldened as the US shifts military assets westward.
“I think US allies and partners may wonder if the move gives [China] more confidence to test and push. That could in turn put more pressure on them,” he told Al Jazeera.
Chong said the aircraft carrier’s redeployment has reduced some US operational flexibility, although US allies could still take comfort in the fact that the lion’s share of US forces remain in the region.
The Asia Pacific region hosts about 375,000 US military and civilian personnel assigned to the US Pacific Command, tens of thousands of whom are stationed in South Korea and Japan.
Chong saw the redeployment as more symbolic of shifts in the US strategy towards Asia, which under Trump sees regional allies as taking the leading role in their own defence, albeit with US support.
The US 2026 National Defense Strategy calls for increased “burden-sharing with allies and partners around the world” to counter threats from China, North Korea, Russia and Iran.
The strategy also calls for allies in Europe and Asia to raise military spending to 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and security-related spending to 1.5 percent of GDP by the 2030s.
South Korea, Taiwan, and Japan have quickly moved to ramp up their defence spending, with Taipei this week announcing it aimed to boost defence spending in 2027 by 18 percent.
Philippines Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr last month called for defence spending to rise to 4 percent of GDP to counter China, as Manila has also moved to deepen its security cooperation with Tokyo and, more quietly, with Taipei.
Chong said that going forward, he expected to see this trend deepen as Asia navigates its way forward.
“US allies and partners have already been increasing their spending and ability to work with less US support. This most recent development may further spur this trend. US allies and partners are also looking for ways to work with each other more, in addition to building their organic capabilities,” he said.
Taiwanese and Japanese security experts also told Al Jazeera they expected US interest – along with its aircraft carriers – to ultimately return to Asia.
Kei Koga, an expert in East Asian security and the US-Japan alliance at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, said deploying military assets to the Middle East was “concerning from a short-term perspective” but did not see the move as “evidence of a longer-term US strategic disengagement from the region”.
K Tristan Tang, a non-resident fellow at the National Bureau of Asian Research, took a similar view, as key assets like US Amphibious Ready Groups – which can host F-35B stealth fighters and smaller aircraft – remain in the region even as the USS George Washington has moved.
Tang also told Al Jazeera that even with the Iran war dragging on, he did not think Trump would forget about the world’s second-largest superpower.
“Deep down in President Trump’s mind, the most important thing will still be US economic interests and the economic issue with China,” he said. “China is still the most important thing.”

Israeli settlers reoccupy West Bank settlement after 21 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:30:36 UTC
21:30:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli settlers reoccupy illegal northern West Bank settlement after two decades
Dozens of Israeli settler families have moved into the illegal Kadim settlement east of Jenin, more than two decades after it was evacuated as part of Israel’s 2005 unilateral disengagement plan.
The settler-led Samaria Regional Council, which governs Israeli settlements in the northern occupied West Bank, said that around 30 "pioneer families" had returned to the site on Thursday. Footage from the area showed settlers entering under military escort and arriving in vehicle convoys carrying Israeli flags, furniture, and building materials.
The return to Kadim is the final stage in the re-establishment of four northern West Bank settlements dismantled during the 2005 plan: Homesh, Sanur, Ganim and Kadim. The plan also saw Israel withdraw its settlers and ground forces from Gaza, although it retained control over the besieged enclave’s borders, airspace and maritime access.
Israel’s parliament repealed provisions of the disengagement law barring Israelis from entering the area around the former settlements in 2023. The government later cleared the way for their formal restoration, a step Palestinian groups and rights organisations say is part of an accelerating drive to annex Palestinian land and fragment the West Bank.
Senior officials attend opening ceremony
Kadim’s opening ceremony on Thursday was attended by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, a far-right settler leader who holds extensive authority over civilian affairs in the occupied West Bank through his additional role in the defence ministry.
"Twenty-one years after the crime of expulsion from northern Samaria, today we completed the correction," Smotrich said, using the biblical term Israeli officials use for the northern West Bank. He described Kadim’s return as completing the revival of the four settlements dismantled in 2005.
Justice Minister Yariv Levin, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, minister Zeev Elkin and Samaria Regional Council head Yossi Dagan also attended the event, underscoring the level of state backing behind what was presented as a settler-led return.
Dagan said the reopening of Kadim was not the end of the movement’s ambitions. "We fixed the expulsion from northern Samaria," he said, adding that settlers would also "return to Gush Katif" — the bloc of Israeli settlements in Gaza that was evacuated under the 2005 plan.
The 30 families are expected to form the basis of a much larger settlement. Israeli media reported that plans envisage a religious community from Tel Aviv and central Israel joining the new settlement, while Dagan said Kadim would "stay and grow twentyfold".
Settlement expansion drive
The return to Kadim comes amid a dramatic acceleration of Israeli settlement expansion under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition, the most right-wing government in Israel’s history.
Israeli officials have said the government approved 104 new settlements across the occupied West Bank after taking office in late 2022, including 19 in the northern West Bank.
According to Peace Now, settlers have established 248 new outposts since the current government came to power, including 65 between January and the start of August this year. Human Rights Watch said this expansion has been accompanied by Israel-backed settler violence that is driving Palestinians from communities across the West Bank.
The reopening of Kadim also follows Israel’s military operations in Jenin, where Israeli forces have repeatedly raided the city and refugee camp, causing widespread destruction and the displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians. Israel is also constructing a military outpost near Jenin refugee camp, deepening Palestinian concerns that military operations and settlement expansion form part of a single effort to cement Israeli control over the area.
Human rights organisations have warned that the Netanyahu government is pressing ahead with settlement projects before Israel’s scheduled 27 October election, seeking to make any future reversal politically and practically difficult.
The timing has drawn particular attention because Israel this week opened tenders for 1,234 settlement units in the E1 area east of occupied East Jerusalem. Bidding is due to close on 19 October, days before the election.
E1 is a strategically significant area between occupied East Jerusalem and the illegal Maale Adumim settlement. Construction there would further sever Palestinian territorial contiguity between the northern and southern West Bank, undermining the prospect of a viable Palestinian state.
Canada, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Norway jointly urged Israel to withdraw the E1 tenders and halt settlement expansion, warning firms that participating could carry legal and reputational consequences linked to serious breaches of international law.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are illegal under international law. In its July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found Israel’s continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful and said Israel must halt all new settlement activity, evacuate settlers, and end its presence as rapidly as possible.

China is using Jiang Zemin centenary to signal political continuity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:30:06 UTC
21:30:06 KST

Xu Ying is a former Chinese diplomat who served in the US and Switzerland.
The centenary of Jiang Zemin’s birth, marked on August 17 with a memorial in Beijing attended and addressed by President Xi Jinping, was more than an occasion to commemorate a former Chinese leader. It was also an exercise in political history: a moment to locate Jiang, the era he led and the reform legacy associated with him within the broader story of the Communist Party of China’s evolution and China’s modernisation.
That is what makes the event politically significant. The question is not simply why China is commemorating Jiang so prominently. It is why the leadership has chosen this particular historical moment to reaffirm his place in the country’s political narrative and what that says about how Beijing views the road from reform and opening up to Chinese modernisation today.
Xi’s speech placed Jiang squarely within the history of the party, describing him as the core of the party’s third-generation central leadership and as a principal founder of the important notion of the “Three Represents”. It also highlighted Jiang’s contributions to reform and opening up, socialist modernisation and China’s development.
The formulation matters. It presents Jiang neither as an isolated political figure nor simply as the representative of a bygone era. Instead, it places him within a chain of political leadership and national development stretching across several decades.
For China’s leadership, historical continuity has considerable political importance. The reform era was not a single event but a succession of experiments, adjustments and institutional changes undertaken by different generations of leaders. Jiang’s years in national leadership, particularly during the 1990s and early 2000s, coincided with one of the most consequential transformations in modern Chinese history: the consolidation of the socialist market economy, the acceleration of economic globalisation, the development of Pudong, the restructuring of state-owned enterprises and China’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO).
FULL EVENT: China commemorates centenary of former leader Jiang Zemin
Those developments fundamentally altered China’s relationship with the global economy. China moved from being a relatively marginal participant in international production and trade to becoming an increasingly central manufacturing and trading power.

Turkish Airlines aims for 20% capacity boost in Asia-Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:29:58 UTC

Kenan Irtak and Emir Yildirim
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Türkiye’s flag carrier Turkish Airlines aims to increase flight frequencies in the Asia-Pacific region by up to 20% in the coming years to establish an alternative second corridor between Asia, Australia and Europe by adding second and third flights to key cities.
Murat Seker, board chair at Turkish Airlines, said in an interview with Nikkei Asia that Türkiye’s flag carrier operates an extensive network across 133 countries and 358 destinations. It has added 10 flights to reach 42 weekly services this year as part of efforts to accelerate the air carrier’s expansion in China, with existing traffic rights allowing growth to 49 flights.
Flights to Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou have been increased earlier than planned, while plans are underway to launch flights to Chengdu in November and Urumqi.
Turkish Airlines redirected wide-body capacity to high-demand markets like Japan, China, Australia, Thailand, Singapore and Vietnam in the wake of tensions in the Middle East, adding 58 weekly flights and 61 cargo flights. The move helped drive up the air carrier’s second-quarter revenue by 20.5% year-on-year to $7.2 billion, as its passenger revenue jumped 15% and cargo revenue surged 58%.
The air carrier’s total revenue rose 20.8% to $13.1 billion in the first half of the year despite increases in jet fuel prices due to tensions in the Middle East, which added $1.3 billion in costs, with total conflict-related spending reaching around $2.1 billion.
The flag carrier expanded its customer base by around 5% with new passengers while growing its market share by about one percentage point in the second quarter.
At the same time, Asian routes saw their revenue share rise by five percentage points to 32%, surpassing Europe’s 27%, while Asia’s share of total passenger traffic climbed from 10% to 12%. Passenger traffic between Africa and Asia jumped 70%, while traffic between Eastern Europe and Asia increased 40% due to shorter transit via Russian airspace.
Turkish Airlines aims to increase its current 25 weekly flights to Japan via newly acquired traffic rights in Singapore and Vietnam, while Japanese investors cover about 20% of its aircraft leasing needs, having financed over 100 aircraft worth around $9 billion in the past two decades.
The airline also plans to start nonstop flights to Sydney and Melbourne in 2028, driven by expected support from revenue generated by long-haul Premium Economy cabins, according to Nikkei Asia.
The flag carrier is also seeking global joint ventures with potential stakes of 30-50% across Asian and South American operations and cargo, as well as in aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) services.

Home Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to Albania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:25:07 UTC
21:25:07 KST

The Home Office could be blocked from deporting many young male trafficking victims to Albania after a major court ruling.
Thousands of Albanian males have been identified as potential trafficking victims in the UK in recent years. Many are sent back to their country even if they are potential or confirmed victims of trafficking, as the Home Office contends they will be safe there.
The ruling is likely to come as a significant blow to the government, which is trying to increase the number of people it removes.
Albanians have been the most common nationality forcibly removed from the UK in the last five years, with 2,247 deported in the 12 months to the end of March, accounting for a quarter of enforced returns, according to UK government figures.
Data disclosed in the court case shows that while Albanian females were previously major victims of trafficking, in their case into the UK sex industry, they have been overtaken by males – mainly boys and young men – who are trafficked into the drugs trade, either to distribute illegal drugs or to work as “gardeners” in cannabis farms.
In 2022, 4,107 Albanian males were referred to UK services over potential trafficking, in comparison with 502 women. In 2023, the figure was 3,463 males and 588 females.
The legal challenge was brought by a 21-year-old victim of trafficking from Albania who was first exploited by an Albanian gang in Belgium when he visited the country with his father at 16. He was sold to another Albanian gang, who brought him to the UK and forced him to work cultivating cannabis plants. He later escaped and was recognised as a victim of trafficking, but was denied asylum because he was told it would be safe for him to return to Albania.
A panel of three senior judges in the upper tribunal of the immigration court accepted his asylum claim and found that even though five years had passed since he was first trafficked, he remained at “real risk” from his traffickers and could not safely move back to Albania.
The judges issued new country guidance to the government, which must be considered by the Home Office before deciding whether to send male trafficking victims back to Albania.
The judgment found that while Albania has made progress on tackling corruption, it continues to be a widespread problem and that there are no dedicated shelters for adult male trafficking victims, while the risk of victims being retrafficked if returned to Albania is significant.
Islington Law Centre, which has particular expertise in representing Albanian trafficking victims, highlighted many concerning practices that gangs subject their victims to. These include deliberately videoing sexual abuse including rape of child trafficking victims and threatening to release the footage on social media; they also show videos of loved ones in Albania to young people to let them know they know who their families are; and the gangs also inflict physical injuries such as broken bones on children and young people.
Esme Madill, a solicitor at Islington Law Centre specialising in representing young Albanian trafficking victims, welcomed the judgment: “This measured judgment has been reached by a court which had the benefit of significant and detailed evidence as to the worrying issue of trafficking of boys and young men by organised Albanian criminal networks. The profiles of trafficking survivors and the risks recognised in the judgment accord strongly with what we see in our work with deeply brutalised and traumatised young survivors every week.”
Home Office sources said they were considering whether to apply for permission to appeal.

Defence forces receive first Ukrainian jet-powered interceptor
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:22:00 EEST
21:22:00 KST

Defence forces receive first Ukrainian jet-powered interceptor
The arsenal of Ukraine's defence forces has been strengthened with Alexa Spatium, the first Ukrainian jet-powered drone interceptor.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Defence
Quote: "It is a high-speed jet-powered unmanned aircraft developed by Ukrainian engineers specifically to destroy small aerial, ground and surface assets in real combat conditions."
Details: The ministry said the interceptor is primarily designed to hit Russian Geran, Geran-4, Geran-5 and Shahed-131 kamikaze UAVs. The system can also be used against reconnaissance drones, helicopters and other individual assets.
The ministry said the UAV has a number of features, including:
- a powerful turbojet engine
- a high flight ceiling
- a significant combat radius
- a wide flight range, from low to medium altitudes
- flexible combat tactics, using either pre-set coordinates or direct guidance
- a range of warhead options, including high-explosive fragmentation, shaped-charge and thermobaric warheads
- high manoeuvrability in flight
- fully remote preparation and launch
- high maximum speed and low minimum speed to conserve fuel
- effective search and targeting systems, including television and infrared systems.
Alexa Spatium is also said to have reliable control and video transmission systems.
The drone measures about 1.5 by 1.7 metres and can be launched from a mobile catapult within minutes. The interceptor is made from lightweight, durable composite material, allowing it to perform sharp manoeuvres without losing controllability.
A drone that does not complete its mission can return to the launch site and be reused.
Background: Recently, former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said that Ukraine's first jet-powered interceptor drones designed to counter jet-powered Shahed-type drones were undergoing combat testing. One of them can reach speeds of more than 600 km/h.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian’s Regular Press Conference on August 21, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
20:21:51 CST
21:21:51 KST

At the invitation of Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Kuwait Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah will pay an official visit to China from August 23 to 24.
Shenzhen TV: On August 20, in the Bangladeshi presidential election, Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir from the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party was declared the winner and became the 23rd president of Bangladesh. What’s your comment? What’s China’s expectation on China-Bangladesh relations in the years to come?
Lin Jian: China congratulates Mr. Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on his election as the president of Bangladesh. China values its relations with Bangladesh, and stands ready to work with the Bangladeshi government to deliver on the important common understandings between the leaders, promote high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, expand exchanges and cooperation in various areas, and strive for new progress in building the China-Bangladesh community with a shared future in the new era.
Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting: Donald Trump has threatened to wage a full-fledged economic war on Iran. Many say the economic threat is aimed at making up for the failure of the war, in the military domain, that the U.S. and Israel waged against Iran. What’s your take on that?
Lin Jian: Sanctions and pressure tactics are not the solution. China calls on parties to act responsibly and stick to the political and diplomatic approach.
Phoenix TV: A cross-party group of Japanese lawmakers will reportedly visit China next week, noting that the status quo of Japan-China relations is in no one’s interest. They hope to play a role in improving the bilateral ties. What’s your comment?
Lin Jian: We notice that some visionary people from both Japan’s ruling and opposition parties are deeply concerned over the current state of China-Japan relations and wish to make an effort to restore the relations to the right track. We call on those running the government of Japan to take these concerns seriously, abide by the four political documents, and create the conditions necessary for normal exchanges between China and Japan with concrete actions.
Yonhap News Agency: Yesterday the DPRK fired over ten ballistic missiles toward waters to its east. This marks its 12th launch this year and the largest-scale launch in three years. Does China have any comment?
Lin Jian: We noted the reports and do not have any new comment.
Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting: Iran has endured years of sanctions imposed by the U.S. The Islamic Republic has either managed to bypass or find alternatives. And now it is said that Trump has no tangible card to enforce what he claims as “toughest sanctions.” What’s your viewpoint?
Lin Jian: China believes that military means, sanctions and pressure tactics are not the solution. On the contrary, they will only lead to escalation that serves no one’s interests. We call for efforts to solve disputes through dialogue and negotiation.
AFP: A follow-up on Iran, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged China to join Washington in putting strong economic pressure on Iran. This was in an interview yesterday. Bessent noted that China has historically imported much of its energy from the Gulf. Does the foreign ministry have a response to these comments by Bessent?
Lin Jian: I answered a similar question yesterday. Let me reiterate, China opposes illicit unilateral sanctions that lack basis in international law and UN Security Council mandate. We call on parties to act responsibly and stick to the political and diplomatic approach.

Iran U20s beat Thailand in friendly
TEHRAN - Iran’s U20 football team continued their preparations in Thailand with a 2-0 friendly victory over the host nation on Friday.
The match was played at Chonburi Stadium, with Qasem Hadadifar’s side producing a dominant and well-organized performance to secure the win.
Mohammadmehdi Jannia opened the scoring in the 48th minute before Abolfazl Zadeattar doubled Iran’s advantage in the 71st minute.
The young Iranian side will play another friendly against Iraq on Aug. 25 as part of their ongoing training camp in Thailand.
Following the conclusion of the Thailand camp, Iran will travel to Viet Tri, Vietnam, on Aug. 27 to compete in Group C of the AFC U20 Asian Cup qualifying tournament.
Iran are drawn in Group C along with Vietnam, North Korea and Palestine.
The Persians will start the campaign on Aug. 31 against Palestine.

No clause in Islamabad MoU signals Iran's surrender

Speaking at the 31st general assembly of the Islamic Association of Iranian Medical Community, Pezeshkian defended the MoU as "honourable and valuable." He said it had been reached through unity in the Supreme National Security Council and that everyone involved had defended it firmly.
He criticised those outside the government who commented without understanding the conditions facing the state, parliament and military commanders. "They cannot find even one clause in this agreement that indicates capitulation; all the commitments belong to the other side," he said.
The president said ending the war while Iran was strong and powerful was the right course, noting that the world recognised Iran's victory and saw the United States as "detested" for attacking schools, hospitals and infrastructure in violation of all norms.
He stressed that this did not mean Iran would ever submit to aggression. "We will never bow to bullying. We will stand until our last breath and deliver a crushing response," he said.
Pezeshkian called for national unity, saying all disagreements in the country stemmed from "ego and self-interest." He said Iranians must accept different tastes and recognise that "if we are together, we are powerful, and if there is division, we will be destroyed."
The president urged the medical community to focus on treatment rather than just describing problems, and said the government needed their help to serve the people and build a model of success.

Polish police detain 23-year-old accused of plotting attacks on senior politicians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
12:20:11 UTC
21:20:11 KST

Jo Harper
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
- Prosecutors accuse suspect of activities intended to enable acts leading to genocide, crimes against peace, crimes against humanity and war crimes
Polish cybercrime police said Friday they detained a 23-year-old man accused of calling online for the killing of prominent politicians and discussing plans to organize an assassination attempt.
The Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime (CBZC) said officers identified a post on an online platform calling for the “elimination” of several people and proposing an attack on senior Polish politicians.
The message appeared in an online group devoted to firearms, according to the bureau. Authorities have not disclosed the identities of the politicians allegedly targeted.
The suspect, a resident of the eastern Lublin region, was detained following an investigation into the post and subsequently charged by prosecutors.
According to the CBZC statement, prosecutors accused him of activities intended to create conditions for acts directly leading to genocide, preparing crimes against peace, humanity and war crimes, as well as publicly inciting the commission of a crime.
Authorities have not explained why provisions relating to genocide and international crimes were included among the charges or provided details of any alleged operational plan beyond the online material.
A court ordered the man held in custody for 30 days while the investigation continues. If convicted, he could face up to 20 years in prison.
Police have not said whether investigators believe he possessed weapons or had taken concrete steps toward carrying out an attack beyond the alleged online activity.
The case comes amid heightened scrutiny in Poland of violent threats circulated online. The CBZC, a specialized national police unit responsible for combating cybercrime, has increasingly intervened in cases where social media posts have allegedly crossed from abusive language into direct incitement or preparations for violence.
Polish politicians across the political spectrum have repeatedly warned about increasingly aggressive rhetoric and threats in public debate, particularly on social media.

20 sailors kidnapped by Somali pirates near Yemen on US-sanctioned ship

Unknown Publisher

20 sailors kidnapped by Somali pirates near Yemen on US-sanctioned ship
The hijacking comes amid a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean
Somali pirates hijacked an oil products tanker off Yemen, a Somali maritime security official said, the latest in a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.
Six armed pirates hijacked the Eritrean-flagged M.T. Sibu 1 on Thursday about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometres) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen, and took it towards Somalia’s Puntland coast, the official, who has knowledge of the incident, told journalists on Friday. He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not allowed to discuss the matter publicly.
The Sibu 1, managed by the UAE-based Qatrat Alnada Almasi Ship Management, was sanctioned by the US Treasury Department last year for allegedly belonging to an Iranian “shadow fleet” used to transport petroleum products seeking to evade US sanctions.
The tanker had 20 crew members aboard – 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese, and one Iraqi. The nationality of one crew member was not immediately known. The vessel’s previous port of departure and intended destination remained unclear.
The hijacking came three days after pirates seized the Lutuf, a Cameroon-flagged general cargo vessel, off Somalia’s coast. The vessel had 10 crew aboard, including six Indians, a Turkish national, a Georgian national and two Serbian security guards, according to maritime tracking reports.
The Sibu 1 is the sixth commercial vessel hijacked by Somali pirates since April 21, when the Palau-flagged tanker Honor 25 was seized off Somalia. Pirates later seized the Sward on April 26, the Eureka on May 2, the Asana on July 17 and the Lutuf on August 17.
